News.title: Rejecting closer EU ties would be dereliction of duty, PM to say
News.content:
The prime minister is expected to tell the Commons later it would be a "dereliction of duty" to turn down a closer relationship with the European Union - if one can be negotiated with Brussels.

In a statement to MPs on Monday, Andy Burnham will argue it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain."

He first pledged to explore closer ties with the bloc at a UK-EU summit later this year at the Labour Party conference last month.

Addressing the Commons, Burnham is expected to say that a new deal with the EU could help tackle illegal immigration and boost economic growth.

He will claim that if he could secure that then "the vast majority of the public would expect us to take it".

Last month, Burnham told the BBC it was "possible" a future Labour election manifesto could promise a new in-out referendum on the EU.

A summit between the UK and the EU was due to take place in the summer but was postponed after Sir Keir Starmer announced his resignation. It has been rescheduled for next month.

The prime minister hopes to secure tweaks to the current arrangements between London and Brussels and also begin a wider conversation about the long term relationship between the UK and its nearest neighbours.

A No 10 source said: "Andy understands why some politicians don't want to face up to the reality that Brexit has not delivered what they once promised.

"But it is time for a different conversation about what our long-term relationship should be. Sticking with the status quo and not working relentlessly to secure a good deal that boosts growth would be a major dereliction of duty."

In his speech at Labour's conference, he said "immigration control" had been "weakened by Brexit" because the UK "lost collaboration with our European partners. And we are still having to work hard to bring it back".

Speaking at her party conference last week, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said it was "a terrible idea" to "reopen the Brexit debate."

"Can you imagine having to go through that again? So much time lost, arguing with ourselves with the EU. Going round in circles, businesses not knowing whether they should invest. He wants to do it all again."

The Commons sits on Monday for the first time since 15 September, having been in recess during some of the party conferences.

News.title: Russell Brand arrives at court for start of rape trial
News.content:
Russell Brand has arrived at court for the start of his rape and sexual assault trial.

The 51-year-old comedian and actor is facing several charges of rape and sexual assault against six women, which are alleged to have occurred between 1999 and 2009.

The trial at Southwark Crown Court, which could last up to 10 weeks, is expected to begin with the process of jury selection on Monday morning.

Brand pleaded not guilty to the charges during pre-trial hearings.

The comedian and actor arrived at court wearing a navy suit and sunglasses, accompanied by his wife Laura.

There was a large media presence at the court for the start of the trial, which is expected to last up to 10 weeks.

He has been charged with three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault.

News.title: Watch: CCTV shows people take cover as missile hits Riyadh airport
News.content:
Two strikes on the international airport in the Saudi capital of Riyadh have left 14 dead and more than 300 injured. There have been a series of other attacks earlier in the week.

CCTV footage from inside King Khalid International Airport shows people taking cover as one of the missiles hit the building on Saturday.

The Houthis in Yemen say they were behind the strikes and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace. The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones.

They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said. He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

News.title: Reform pledges to suspend asylum system for up to five years and deport claimants
News.content:
Reform UK has announced plans to close down the UK's asylum system for a full parliamentary term if it were elected.

The party said all new asylum applications would be rejected and existing applications voided, with all claimants marked for deportation. It said no grants of humanitarian protection or refugee status would be made, while legal refugee routes and resettlement schemes would end.

Reform said it would also scrap the asylum tribunal system and would deport 90,000 people currently with appeal cases, with home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf saying it would ensure Britain has a "functioning border".

Labour called the proposals a "clear sign of desperation and weakness".

Reform said its existing plans to make migrants who have entered the UK illegally, overstayed a visa or originated from a safe country ineligible for asylum would effectively prevent any current asylum claimant "from ever having their case heard".

The party said it would therefore "suspend the asylum system entirely for a full parliamentary term".

A parliamentary term usually lasts five years unless an early UK general election is called.

Under further proposals, Reform said it would pull the UK out of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), repeal the Human Rights Act 1998 and disapply the 1951 Refugee Convention to prevent legal challenges to its plans.

And the party said it would ban British visas for countries such as Pakistan, Somalia, Eritrea, Syria, Afghanistan and Sudan if they refuse to allow deportation flights to land in their country.

For countries without a significant legal foreign national presence in the UK, the party said it would look at tariffs on goods and services for non-compliance.

Party leader Nigel Farage said the UK is "facing a national security emergency", adding the country "cannot accept more asylum seekers while we still have no idea how many people are in the country illegally and the threat they pose."

He and Yusuf will formally announce the plans in a speech on Monday.

"We've got to prioritise the British people," Yusuf said, pointing to Britons "dying totally avoidably waiting for emergency care" and young people "being forced to stay at home with their parents well into their 30s and 40s because they can't afford to rent homes".

He added: "We will not be returning people into harm, but we have to be honest about the fact that fraud is rampant."

News.title: Burnham says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit vote
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany.

The prime minister told The Rest is Politics podcast, external that upon arriving in No 10, he had asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."

"I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas," he added.

Burnham did not provide further details about the type or extent of Moscow's activity during the Brexit referendum.

Asked about the prime minister's comments on BBC Breakfast, Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty said he wouldn't "get into specifics" of Russian interference in the 2016 vote when pushed for evidence.

"Russia clearly has attempted to interfere on a number of our democratic processes," Doughty told the BBC. "They're engaged in information warfare, they're spending Â£1.5bn this year alone on disinformation and propaganda."

Doughty also denied that Burnham was raising the issue of Russian interference in the Brexit referendum because he wants to rejoin the EU.

He said: "This is a broader point he is making about Russian attempts to destabilise and interfere in our democracy."

Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign group, said Burnham's comments were "another crude attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the decision that the British people made in 2016".

It said that foreign interference in UK elections was "obviously unacceptable" but added: "There is no good reason to believe that Russian intervention influenced the outcome of the referendum in 2016.

"It is also insulting to suggest that voters were so easily duped."

In his interview, due to be released on Monday, Burnham said he had discussed the problem of Russian interference with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during his visit to Germany earlier this week.

"There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics," he said.

He continued: "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia."

News.title: Wildlife park closed for third day after tiger attack
News.content:
Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed for a third day as investigations continue into the death of a man who was attacked by a tiger when he entered its enclosure.

The park near Doncaster was closed over the weekend after reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway on Saturday afternoon.

An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked.

A park spokesperson said: "Due to the events over the weekend, the park will remain closed today. Thank you for your understanding."

South Yorkshire Police said the man died at the scene and his family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park said the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.

Cars could be seen coming and going from the park earlier, but there were no visitors.

In a message to ticket holders on Monday morning, Yorkshire Wildlife Park said anyone with a booking would be contacted within the next five days to reschedule.

News.title: Healey faces £35bn Budget challenge to meet spending pledges, says think tank
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey faces having to find Â£35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that if the government wants to raise defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030 and lift health spending without squeezing other departments, it will need a "top-up" of billions of pounds.

Higher inflation, caused by the Iran war, could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the IFS said.

The Treasury declined to comment.

The government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.

The IFS said that Healey must set out "credible" spending plans in the Budget, which will take place on 28 October.

"A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller.

"Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course.

"Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.

Speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home.

"But Britain and our alliesâ¯can face up to these challenges together."

He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".

Miller told the BBC's Today programme that Healey had inherited spending plans for government departments where spending growth would slow in the coming years.

"[It] already looked likely that he would have to make spending cuts just to live within those," she said. "Now, along comes the Middle East war, inflation goes up and those spending plans look very tight indeed."

Added to that, the chancellor has said he wants to get defence spending up to 3% of national income. Under Keir Starmer's leadership, Healey resigned as defence secretary in June in a battle with the Treasury over military spending.

Miller said: "You put all that together, if he wanted to do all of that within current spending plans he's looking at having to cut some other services by something like Â£35bn."

She said the government would have a "tough time" if it wanted to raise taxes to stop cuts to departments and fund defence spending.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced billions of pounds in tax rises. Meanwhile, Labour pledged in its manifesto "not increase taxes on working people", ruling out rises to National Insurance, income tax or VAT. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will stick to that promise.

Miller said: "You'd really have to be scaping around and doing lots of small things to get up to big sums."

News.title: Sinn Féin ministers facing no-confidence vote after Drumcree dispute
News.content:
The DUP and Ulster Unionists share power with Sinn FÃ©in in a four-party devolved government alongside the Alliance Party.

Jim Allister has been urging the DUP to withdraw Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill as first minister.

The DUP leader Gavin Robinson told Good Morning Ulster: "When somebody breaks the law they should be punished for breaking the law."

He said that removing Little-Pengelly would "punish everybody else".

"Colleagues and I have discussed continually about options that are available to us.

"It is absurd that there will be a motion of no confidence, which we know before it starts, whether it concludes successfully, we know it can't because of the system that we have."

Robinson added that he is "not in the territory" to "destabilise".

However his party colleague, Carla Lockhart, who represents the Upper Bann constituency in Westminster, said it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont and the DUP has it "within its gift to remove" O'Neill from her position.

Robinson said that when the party comes to a "consensus, that is our position".

He added that Lockhart has "the right to stand up for her constituents".

DUP MP Gregory Campbell said his party would not be collapsing Stormont, but that he does believe that now is a time for "very stringent action".

"We have got to take some action now to ensure that the law is upheld," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.

"But we're not going to commit grievous bodily harm by walking out of Stormont."

Campbell said his party colleague Carla Lockhart is "absolutely right" when she says it cannot be business as usual at Stormont.

He said his view is that is if a minister has been "convicted in a court of law of a criminal offence, a serious criminal offence, there has to be a sanction that would prevent that person from holding office."

The DUP, he added, had the support of its members in relation to the approach it is taking.

"We've taken soundings throughout the party and people are confident in what we've been doing.

"They are looking for action, they're going to get action."

News.title: Roofing scammers con homeowners out of thousands of pounds
News.content:
Scammers pretending to be legitimate workmen are charging homeowners thousands of pounds for roofing work that is not completed, done badly or not necessary, according to Citizens Advice.

The consumer advice charity says one in 10 of all the scams it recorded over the past year were related to roofing, making it the most common type of scam brought to them.

It can leave victims like Crystal, from the Midlands, thousands of pounds out of pocket.

The 68-year-old was frightened and found it hard to sleep after a rogue builder left her roof with dislodged bricks and blocked gutters.

She said she felt pressured into agreeing to having her roof re-done and paid a total of Â£5,500, only for the original contractor to send his son instead, who left work in the eaves incomplete.

"We had heavy rain a couple of weeks after he did the job, and it ended up like a waterfall coming down the wall," she said.

Her neighbour's house was also damaged.

"They took the lead off my neighbour's side of the chimney, which caused bricks to fall into his attic and the rain to go into his house," she told the BBC.

The experience still haunts her: "I can't sleep. I don't eat properly."

In the year to August the Citizens Advice Consumer Service received 9,000 complaints about roofing work, including problems with construction, repairs and weatherproofing.

Of those 2,205, or about one in four complaints, were suspected scams, up from 2,098 the year before.

Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice, urged consumers to carry out thorough checks on traders before agreeing to hire them.

"Scammers exploit the fact that roofs are out of sight and reach, knowing most people can't easily inspect the work themselves," she said.

Victims also reported aggressive and intimidating behaviour, with three quarters of fraudsters using "doorstep" sales tactics.

Citizens Advice cited the case of Charlotte, 65, who lives alone in north eastern England.

Tradesmen she found online initially offered to fix her leaking gutter for Â£250. The two men then said there was further work that needed to be done, that would cost Â£2,500.

"An hour later they said it was sorted, but they'd found another problem," she said.

It was dark and Charlotte felt afraid. "They knew I was alone, I didn't feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid Â£3,500," she said.

But the next day she could see no sign of any work having been done, she said.

To avoid falling victim to roofing scams, Citizens Advice suggests:

Be alert: Always ask for references and for everything to be in writing. Be wary of unsolicited doorknockers and callers

Gather evidence: If a trader causes problems, be sure to take photos and gather the necessary paperwork and receipts

Know your rights: Traders must give you the information about your right to cancel in writing. If the job is not done with "reasonable care and skill," the Consumer Rights Act 2015 also entitles you to ask for the problem to be fixed or a refund

Lord Bichard, chair of National Trading Standards, said rogue traders were "criminals deliberately preying on people in their own homes".

He described roofing fraud as "particularly cruel", and said Trading Standards would pursue fraudsters through legal routes.

"Victims can lose life savings in a matter of hours and be left with damaged homes, financial hardship and a profound sense of vulnerability long after the criminals have gone," he said.

News.title: Burnham to release details of Man City meetings
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will release details of his meetings with senior figures at Manchester City.

It follows criticism of his comments in the wake of the club being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.

An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than Â£830m into their football operations.

Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanding No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

"I've been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I'm happy to do and I'm going to," Burnham told the Rest is Politics podcast., external

"I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester.

"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."

The prime minister initially told the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up following the guilty verdict before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".

However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process.

Sanctions are yet to be announced and City have lodged an appeal against the verdict.

City returned to action for the first time since the guilty verdict when they played at Liverpool on Sunday, winning 3-0.

News.title: 'Tax rises needed to plug £35bn gap' and 'Putin breaks Trump's 'ceasefire"
News.content:
Many of the front pages feature reaction to US President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. The Guardian, external and the Times, external both highlight the fact that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky appeared to be unaware of the truce before it was announced. The Daily Telegraph leads on Zelensky's claims that Russia has continued to strike energy sites, external. The headline is "Putin breaks Trump's 'ceasefire'". The paper's editorial argues that the main problem with the deal is that it "only exists in the US President's head".

According to the Financial Times, the Trump administration is threatening to cut off weapons, external supplies to Ukraine as part of efforts to stop it attacking Russian energy infrastructure. European officials have told the paper they received calls from their American counterparts discussing such plans over the weekend. The White House has declined to comment.

The Daily Mail focuses on Boris Johnson labelling Trump's agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to lift sanctions so Russia can supply diesel to US and global markets as "sickening", external. The former prime minister also says the Royal Navy should intercept any Russian fuel ships in the English Channel.

The Guardian, external reports that ministers are preparing to slash the funds available to subsidise heat pumps, as they look for savings to increase defence spending. The programme is not expected to be abolished, but sources tell the paper that hundreds of millions of pounds could be cut from the scheme's Â£2.7bn budget. A government spokesperson has said details of how investment in the country's national security will be set out this autumn.

And the world of chessboxing, external is highlighted by the Times, after one of the founders of the hybrid sport called time on his career. The paper says Matt "Crazy Arms" Read achieved the "fairytale farewell" with a final victory in the sport, which sees combatants alternate between rounds of chess and boxing. The 47-year-old is quoted as saying: "you always want to end on a high.... but to be honest Father Time has caught up with me".

News.title: Legoland Windsor evacuated over burst water main
News.content:
The Legoland Windsor attraction has closed abruptly due to a burst water main.

Customers were told to leave rides and exit the resort at lunchtime on Sunday.

Thames Water said it had to shut off the damaged main near St Leonards Reservoir to prevent flooding, which affected supplies to the theme park.

It said some local residents had reportedly suffered flooded gardens and it apologised for the disruption.

Merlin Entertainments, the operator behind Legoland, said it is continuing to work with local partners and thanked guests for their "patience and understanding".

One Legoland visitor, who came with her children from Cornwall, said the sudden evacuation felt "surreal".

The woman, who asked not to be named, said: "We were queuing for a ride and had got right to the front when, all of a sudden, everything stopped moving.

"Then they came out and said, 'Right, come on, everybody off.'

"Over the announcement system, they said there had been some sort of Thames Water disruption in the local area and they didn't have any water.

"We'd booked a night in the hotel and stayed there last night, so we're absolutely gutted because we've just had to drive home.

"It's a good five-hour drive to come up for a nice day, only to come back after half a day."

Thames Water said supplies had been restored and repairs were under way. It said it would provide an update on Monday.

A spokesperson for Merlin Entertainments said the resort was closed while Thames Water worked to restore normal service.

"We apologise for the inconvenience and thank our guests for their patience and understanding," the group said.

The BBC understands the resort will reopen on Monday under normal operating hours.

News.title: UK does not support Trump's Russia diesel deal, says Streeting
News.content:
The UK does not support Donald Trump's deal with Vladimir Putin, which would see the US purchase millions of tonnes of diesel from Russia, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House, he said the agreement had been done in the context of the US president facing elections in November and at a time when politicians across the world were under pressure to ease the cost of living.

He argued that the US and other allies should focus on increasing pressure on Russia to shorten the war "and to secure Ukraine's freedom".

Trump's diesel deal is aimed at lowering fuel prices in America, which have risen following the US and Israel's conflict with Iran.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the agreement would allow Moscow to raise funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.

In response, Trump suggested Ukraine should "get a new leader" who could reach a deal with Russia to end the long-running conflict between the two countries.

Streeting said it was a matter for Ukrainians to choose their leader but added that the country was "fortunate to have someone of his calibre, his courage and his integrity leading their war effort".

He added that responsibility for the war "lies squarely and solely with President Putin and his imperialist ambitions".

The defence secretary said it was not the first time there had been public disagreements between Washington and Kyiv, adding: "In these situations we see it as our role and our responsibility to try and bring our friends back together again."

He also sought to emphasise the US's support for Ukraine, saying there was "often an understatement" of how much help they had provided.

"We're seeing US support for Ukraine in a number of ways from the provision of weapons - and we do a lot of procurement through the Americans - through to intelligence support and through the diplomatic initiative that Washington is leading."

News.title: MPs seek to overturn ruling that stops police being sued for failings
News.content:
Backbench MPs are seeking to roll back a court ruling they say will have "devastating consequences" for victims of crime by preventing them taking legal action against the police, even when there have been grave investigative failings.

The 2025 Court of Appeal judgment, which applies to England and Wales, held that police officers are immune from civil litigation both in their role as witnesses, and for conduct or statements they make when carrying out criminal investigations.

Conservative Andrew Mitchell and Labour's Jess Phillips have submitted an amendment to a bill being debated in Parliament next week seeking to counteract the ruling.

Separately, the judgment could also be overturned at a Supreme Court appeal this month.

The MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying, including in cases where police have fabricated evidence, been dishonest or negligent, and where there has been a reckless disclosure of confidential information relating to victims.

The ruling came in a case brought by a victim of serious domestic violence who fled her abuser for a secret refuge, but Sussex Police included her new address in a file sent to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) without sufficiently flagging its confidentiality.

A CPS lawyer subsequently disclosed her address in court during a bail hearing, thereby revealing it to her abuser. As a result, she had to flee again.

The woman said the disclosure of her address had meant the place she was supposed to be safe "no longer felt safe at all" and she was still living with the impact of what happened and that loss of security.

She brought claims against both the police and CPS, arguing their failure placed her in fear for her life, compelled her to leave her home, caused her to suffer loss of earnings, and resulted in her developing a psychiatric injury. Her claims were initially rejected, reinstated on appeal, then struck out again.

The key issue was who could be held legally responsible for what happened, and who would benefit from legal immunity. Witnesses and lawyers have what is known as "core immunity" for things they say in court, so that they can speak freely there.

The Court of Appeal ruling further expanded such immunity, holding that it extends to an extremely broad range of police activity, including conduct or statements which are part of an investigation leading to a potential prosecution

Most types of legal claim are thus blocked by this immunity, including cases about serious human rights abuses and data breaches, and there are no exemptions for unjustifiable conduct.

Officers can still be prosecuted in the criminal courts and held accountable by police misconduct processes.

News.title: Swinney backs Flynn in ferry gas leak row and says 'nobody's perfect'
News.content:
First Minister John Swinney has backed Stephen Flynn in the row over whether the transport secretary had been briefed about a gas leak on a CalMac ferry.

Speaking to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme in an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Swinney said emails showed Flynn had not been briefed ahead of a Holyrood committee meeting last month.

The first minister said he had confidence in his transport secretary, who "recognised that he should have been across an issue to be in front of the transport committee and he remedied that right away".

Swinney added: "Nobody's perfect, nobody's infallible".

Flynn was appearing before the transport committee on 9 September when he said he was not aware of a BBC Scotland News story published online more than nine hours earlier.

It revealed how a faulty valve led to 700kg of flammable methane gas being vented from the side of the ferry MV Glen Sannox while it was carrying passengers from Arran to Troon in June 2025.

News.title: Man, 36, arrested six years on from double murder
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fatal shooting of two men more than six years ago.

Junior Ajose, 36, and Cheriff Tall, 21, were shot dead at a lockdown party in the Moss Side area of Manchester in the early hours of 21 June 2020.

A Greater Manchester Police (GMP) spokesperson said a 36-year-old man was detained in Turkey and transported back to England on Saturday, where he was met at Stansted Airport by GMP officers. He remains in custody.

Det Ch Insp Neil Higginson from the force's major incident team said: "This arrest demonstrates our unwavering commitment to securing justice for Junior and Cheriff and their loved ones."

"Over the last six years, myself and my officers have been carrying out multiple warrants, analysing evidence, examining devices that have been seized during the investigation and pursuing every opportunity to identify those responsible," he added.

Ajose and Tall, who did not know each other, were both shot in the head in a car park off Caythorne Street shortly before 01:00 BST and died in hospital.

GMP said it was estimated that between 300 and 400 people were present in the car park that night.

The force issued a further appeal for information on the fifth anniversary of their deaths last year.

Higginson said they were continuing to appeal for information that could help them to establish the full circumstances of what happened that night and to identify any outstanding suspects.

A Â£50,000 reward remains available for key information that leads to the conviction of the killer.

News.title: Temperatures to reach 21C as the UK set to bask in warm weather
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A warm spell of weather is set to hit the UK later this week, with temperatures due to rise to 21 degrees on Thursday.

Daytime temperatures will be above average for mid-October for many parts of the country, with Tuesday’s weather set to be “unusually mild”, the Met Office has said.

On Wednesday, the mercury will hit 19 degrees in London, with temperatures of 17 degrees also seen in Glasgow and Belfast, with overnight temperatures across England and Wales remaining at 16 degrees.

Before a band of rain arrives in the south-east of England, temperatures are likely to exceed 20 degrees in many locations on Thursday, exceeding the October average of 12-16 degrees.

A Met Office spokesperson said: “The weather is turning milder this week, with temperatures expected to rise above average for mid-October in some parts of the UK, particularly on Tuesday.

open image in gallery Rain is expected later this week as wet and windier conditions arrive on Friday ( AFP/Getty )

“These warmer conditions are being driven by a south to south-westerly airflow, bringing relatively warm air northwards from lower latitudes. Tuesday's milder weather is the result of the broader weather pattern across the North Atlantic and north-west Europe, rather than any hurricane activity.

“There is no indication that Hurricane Simon, which is currently affecting parts of the US, will have any impact on UK weather.”

Meanwhile, a government-chaired taskforce will meet this week to assess how prepared the UK is for flooding this winter.

The group aims to strengthen the UK’s resilience to flooding and drought after record temperatures and widespread drought hit the country this summer and ahead of an expected wet winter.

It comes as the Met Office has warned of a “heightened potential” for wet, windy, stormy weather and flooding this autumn – and the Environment Agency has urged households to check their flood risk, sign up to alerts and make a flood plan to prepare for any emergencies.

Here’s a look at the five-day weather forecast:

Today:

Turning increasingly cloudy through the day with outbreaks of drizzle. Some brighter spells possible to the east of high ground. Winds strengthening through the day with gales possible in the north of Scotland. Milder than of late.

Tonight:

Gales possible in north Scotland this evening. Staying cloudy with drizzly outbreaks across the south and east. A spell of heavy rain moves into the north and west. Mild.

Tuesday:

Heavy rain moves across England and Wales during the morning with blustery winds, but turning drier and brighter in the afternoon. Heavy showers move into the north later.

Outlook for Wednesday to Friday:

A band of heavy rain slowly moves south over the next few days, and rather windy in the north. Gradually turning colder and brighter from Friday with lighter winds. Mild.

News.title: France school shooting: Pupil, 14, arrested after two teachers injured by shotgun fire
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Two teaching staff have been injured by gunfire at a school in France, according to education minister Edouard Geffray.

The attacker is suspected to be a 14-year-old pupil and has been arrested, according to Le Parisien, citing police sources.

The pupil is reported to have entered the school with a 12-gauge shotgun, a hunting rifle, according to the publication.

The incident took place at the Joseph-Lakanal college in Aubagne, near Marseille.

A headteacher and a teacher were wounded in their lower bodies by the shooting and have sustained minor injuries.

It follows days of students protests and violent clashes with police. However, Le Parisien says there is “no connection to the high school protests, as this school is not affected by the blockades.”

Geffray said he would be attending the scene of the incident along with interior minister Laurent Nunez.

“Two staff members from the National Education system, a principal and a teacher, were victims this morning of gunshot wounds at Lakanal middle school in Aubagne,” Geffray wrote in a post on X on Monday.

“A student is said to be the perpetrator. I am heading to the scene immediately with @NunezLaurent and @SabrinaRoubache.

“In the face of this new attack, the National Education system will, as always, remain united and strong, around an educational community sorely tried.

“But this unacceptable act bears witness once again to the spread of unbridled violence in our society, against which we must all mobilise. In words as in deeds.”

More to follow on this breaking news story...

News.title: Yorkshire tiger latest: Woman ‘tried to pull tiger attack victim back’ before he jumped into zoo enclosure
News.content:
From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging.

At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story.

News.title: Maduro-linked fugitive with $10M bounty captured after years on the run
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A businessman sought for years by American law enforcement over allegations of bribing senior Venezuelan officials to win lucrative state contracts has been taken into U.S. custody.

A Miami federal court indicted Alvaro Pulido in 2019 and 2021 as part of a broader probe into his long-standing business associate, Alex Saab, a former ally of ousted President Nicolás Maduro.

A reward of up to $10 million had been offered by the U.S. State Department and the Drug Enforcement Administration for information leading to Pulido's arrest.

open image in gallery Colombian businessman Alex Saab attends a news conference in December 2023 ( Reuters )

His capture followed an investigation led by the DEA, the FBI, and Homeland Security Investigations, Homeland Security Task Force spokesperson Nicole Navas Oxman announced on Sunday.

Oxman provided no details on how Pulido came into U.S. hands, but noted that he is scheduled to make his initial court appearance in Miami on Tuesday.

Venezuelan officials have so far remained silent regarding the arrest, reflecting the challenge acting President Delcy Rodríguez faces in appeasing elements of the ruling coalition. Those factions want her to resist attempts by the Trump administration to round up scores of Venezuelan insiders wanted by the U.S., in some cases for years, for serious crimes ranging from corruption to drug trafficking.

The Colombian-born businessman was previously arrested in Venezuela in 2023 during a major anti-corruption drive within state oil company PDVSA. Rodríguez oversaw that initiative while serving as Maduro's vice president. She became acting president after the U.S. military ousted Maduro in January.

open image in gallery Saab pictured with Venezuela’s former president Maduro in 2024 ( AP )

According to prosecutors, Pulido and Saab created a network of offshore shell companies to route bribes to top Maduro allies in exchange for contracts to import food, medicine, and low-cost housing during a period of widespread hardship in the country.

Rodríguez deported Saab to the U.S. in May. He pleaded guilty last month in a related bribery case, agreeing to cooperate against Maduro and forfeit $195 million in criminal proceeds.

News.title: Prue Leith on one major misconception people have about getting old: ‘I get sick of hearing it’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Dame Prue Leith has criticised the stigmas surrounding old age during an appearance at the 2026 Henley Literary Festival.

The former Great British Bake Off judge, 86, was interviewed after the publication of her book Being Old...and Learning to Love It! earlier this year.

Explaining her reasons for writing the book, which explores her own relationship with ageing, Leith said: “I got sick of hearing people saying, ‘Isn’t old age terrible?’ It’s just moaning about old age, and people assuming that you’re miserable because you’re old.

“Even when I said to my publishers that I want to call the book Being Old, they said, ‘Oh, you can’t call it that. It’s far too negative.’ Well, I said, that’s why I want to write the book. What is negative about being old? I mean, don’t you remember your teenage years? I could write a book about teenagers and it would be very miserable.”

open image in gallery Dame Prue Leith at Wimbledon 2026 ( Getty Images for Pimms )

Leith went on to reflect on her own adolescence and turbulent teenage years.

“I was quarreling with my parents. I was bringing the wrong boys home,” she said. “I didn’t have a boyfriend, and desperately wanted one. I didn’t know what I wanted to do with my life. I didn’t know who I was – and that was much more stressful than being old.

“Of course there are people who are ill, and lonely, or unhappy,” said Leith. “But if there’s nothing wrong with you, for God’s sake, enjoy it. You haven’t got all that much time left. You need to grab it.”

Later in the event, Leith spoke about finding love again after the death of her first husband, property developer Rayne Kruger, in 2002, at the age of 80. The couple shared two children.

Leith subsequently started dating John Playfair, a retired clothes designer; they married in October 2016.

“It was very surprising, because I had got to really like widowhood,” she said. “You know, it was really miserable when my husband died. I had two years when I was really, really miserable. But then I got to realise that there are real advantages to being on your own.

open image in gallery Prue Leith on ‘Bake Off’ ( Channel 4 )

“You don't have anyone else to think about. You could be entirely selfish. So I had really got stuck into widowhood and liked it. And then I met John. And the most extraordinary thing is I was exactly 70 years old, and he was 64. And falling in love in old age is exactly like falling in love at 17.

“I was 70, but I had that same thing of your heart going, like a kettle drum, and anxiety about whether he'll phone or ring or something.”

“This is such a cliché to say it, but I really believe this, that you have to, if your mind stays open to new experiences and enjoyment, and just does it, there's far more likelihood of you being happy, because if you just sit at home and think, what's wrong with your life, I mean, there's lots wrong with all of our lives, but I don't think we should dwell on them.”

Henley Literary Festival ran until 11 October in the town of Henley-on-Thames. The Independent served as the festival’s official news partner for the fourth year running.

News.title: Trump under fire from his own party over deal giving Putin a ‘financial lifeline’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A bipartisan group of US senators has urged President Donald Trump to abandon a diesel supply agreement with Russia, warning that the arrangement violates federal law banning energy imports until Moscow halts its aggression against Ukraine.

"Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing (Russian President Vladimir) Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine," stated a joint release issued on Sunday by seven lawmakers, comprising four Republicans and three Democrats.

The senators also noted that the White House failed to consult Congress or provide a legally mandated explanation for its decision.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin shake hands as they meet in 2018 ( Reuters )

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," the statement added.

The cross-party pushback represents a rare rift over Trump's foreign policy just weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.

The statement was signed by Republican Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah, alongside Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, and Ron Wyden of Oregon.

Tillis warned earlier on Sunday that the diesel arrangement might be unlawful and could put American lives at risk.

open image in gallery Among the signees was Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine who is up for reelection next month ( AP )

Trump announced on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, prompting his administration to temporarily suspend US sanctions meant to deny Moscow fuel revenue for its war in Ukraine.

"I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law," Tillis, who is retiring from the Senate in January, said on NBC's "Meet the Press."

With diesel prices near record levels—impacting agriculture, home heating, and commercial transport—high fuel costs pose a political risk for Republicans in next month's congressional votes. Industry analysts noted that the agreement with Moscow is unlikely to deliver lasting price reductions.

The White House defended the initiative on Sunday. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that the administration would proceed using existing statutory authority, arguing the pact benefits the American public by reducing energy costs.

"We're going to do it with all the legal authorities we have. So, you know, anyone in Congress who says whether it's an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill (that) prohibits us from doing it is wrong," Bessent told "Fox & Friends."

open image in gallery "I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law," Tillis, who is retiring from the Senate in January, said ( AFP/Getty )

Trump last month signed a broad Russia sanctions measure into law, titled the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," named after the South Carolina Republican and long-standing defense hawk who died in July.

Other Republicans have expressed concern over the plan. Retiring Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska wrote on X on Friday that "propping up Putin's war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities."

Mike Pence, Trump's former vice president, described the decision to lift sanctions as a "betrayal" of Graham's legacy and urged the president to "rescind" it.

Amid falling approval ratings, congressional Republicans have increasingly separated themselves from the administration on various matters, ranging from policy toward Iran to trade disputes with Canada.

However, Senator John Barrasso of Wyoming, the Senate's second-ranking Republican, supported the deal during an interview on CBS' "Face the Nation," emphasizing Trump's focus on lowering consumer costs.

"The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said.

open image in gallery Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming has supported the deal ( Getty )

International figures also weighed in. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy during a Sunday phone call that the deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe," according to a statement from Carney's office.

In a social media post on Sunday, Trump claimed that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire" effective immediately, though he provided no details.

Zelenskiy said he was awaiting further information regarding the announcement.

"Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well," Zelenskiy posted on Telegram.

Moscow has not commented on the assertion, which follows weeks of American pressure on Ukraine to suspend strikes targeting Russian oil refineries.

News.title: Trump reposts Kid Rock’s rant warning of religious civil war in the US
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump has reposted a rant from MAGA rapper Kid Rock in which he said he fears his grandchildren being caught up in a future “civil war over religious ideology” with the Muslim population of Michigan, his home state.

Speaking to Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law, on her Fox News show My View Sunday, Rock weighed in on Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s midterms battle against Republican rival Mike Rogers and called the progressive “a wolf in sheep’s clothing.”

“I was born in Dearborn, Michigan,” the musician told Trump. “So was my father. Raised there. My grandfather raised him there.

“And as we know – I don’t know if people understand how it got to be one of the biggest Arab populations outside of the Middle East in the world. I call it more of a religious ideology.

“I know there are extremists and there are milder versions of it. I don’t want my grandkids to one day have to fight some civil war over religious ideology. This is scary. I think El-Sayed’s a wolf in sheep’s clothing.”

open image in gallery Kid Rock tells Lara Trump he fears a future U.S. civil war will erupt over 'religious ideology' ( Fox News )

Trump sharing the clip of his inflammatory comment on Truth Social is just the latest example of his intervening in the campaign in the hope of stoking anti-Islam sentiment against El-Sayed.

Last week, the president used his social media platform to berate the candidate as a “Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country, the Black People of Detroit, and wants to see the U.S. fail” in one post and, in another, a “RADICAL Extremist” and “Terrorist Sympathizer.”

He also repeatedly referred to him as “Mohammad” or Mohammed,” the only point on which El-Sayed retaliated. “He knows my name is Abdul,” the Democrat wrote on X. “He says it everyday. But he’s not just attacking me. He’s attacking all of us.”

The president’s repeated slights on El-Sayed as a Muslim and “Communist” – which began as soon as he beat centrist state representative Haley Stevens in his party’s primary – echo his efforts to deride Zohran Mamdani last year before the latter won the New York City mayoral race and unexpectedly found himself in Trump’s good graces.

El-Sayed has given as good as he’s gotten, however, mocking the president over his close bond with his executive assistant Natalie Harp and referring sarcastically to Vice President JD Vance’s “Ohio charisma” after the latter said his candidacy appealed only to “self-hating white liberals.”

With the Michigan Senate race looking tight, Kid Rock joined Trump at a Saturday rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, at which he invoked his history with the state to tell the crowd: “I oppose Islamist extremists whose end goal is to impose Sharia law on this nation!”

open image in gallery Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has become the subsequent of regular Islamophobic attacks from the right since winning his party’s primary in August ( Getty )

He continued: “No religious cult or ideology gets to override our Constitution. Is Islam a religion, ideology, a cult? You will never have the right to force any American citizen to live under it. I guarantee you that.”

“We will never be one nation under Muhammad because we are and we always will be one nation under God,” he concluded, offering no evidence to support the alarmism he entertained.

Clearly impressed with his performance, the president later took to the stage and said he would “like it” if the rapper ran for office.

Rock’s relationship with Trump appears to have grown closer in recent years. A spat erupted within the Department of Defense earlier this year after an Army helicopter conducted a fly-by near his home in Nashville in late March and the star revealed this summer that he likes to call the president when he has been drinking to impress his friends.

However, his allegiance to the MAGA cause has not always been fruitful: it was announced in September that the Patriots Day Freedom Fest in Kentucky, at which he was slated to appear, had been canceled due to poor VIP ticket sales.

Elsewhere in his interview with Lara Trump, Rock also claimed, “The devil lives in Hollywood,” and assured the presenter: “I’ve seen him there. That’s not a joke. People are disgusting out there.”

News.title: Cloudways and Hostinger web hosting reviewed – a tech expert’s comparison
News.content:
It can be tricky to know where to start when you’re choosing a web hosting service but, as a tech journalist, I’ve spent extensive time testing a range of options, assessing the comparing them, to bring you my recommendations.

If you’ve already started looking into different web hosting sites, you may have heard of Hostinger – I’m a big fan and consider it one of the best options around. However, if you’re looking for a more business-focused option, Cloudways is another reliable choice that’s been in operation for nearly 15 years.

With hours of testing involved across several days, I’ve been putting these two hosting services head to head, assessing their pros and cons, to see how they compare. From AI features to ease of use, here’s what you need to know about Cloudways and Hostinger before you decide which one is right for you.



How I tested

My 10-day test compared different Cloudways and Hostinger components ( Jennifer Allen / Hostinger )

I spent around 10 days using Cloudways and Hostinger. That included signing up for each web host plan and evaluating how easy it was to get started. I launched a website going through each process to see how well it worked. I also looked at additional features to determine whether the host has plenty of expansion potential. You can see my full testing criteria at the end of this article.



Cloudways Cloudways is clearly designed for more technically minded users. It provides lots of insight into your server and how well it’s running while using terms that may not be immediately obvious to novices to web hosting. Away from uploading your site, WordPress integration is also a key focus. There are multiple plug-ins and add-ons across the board. Its pricing schemes scale well so that there are inexpensive plans for beginners (albeit not quite as cheap as Hostinger) with some very high end plans for major website hosting. £7 from Cloudways.com Prices may vary

Hostinger Hostinger is the more beginner-friendly web hosting option. It only takes a few minutes to set up and there are extensive AI-powered ways to create your website. There’s no need to already know how to develop a website from scratch as Hostinger does a good job of doing all the hard work for you. Full prices can seem expensive but Hostinger seems to thrive on regular deals that provide hefty discounts. These are even better the longer you commit to a plan. £3 from Hostinger.com Prices may vary

1. Cloudways vs Hostinger: Pricing and plans

Cloudways

Pros: Three-day free trial without payment details

Cons: More expensive; small fee each month for email

Hostinger

Pros: Great deals on plans; free domain for a year

Cons: No free trial; deals can change frequently; best prices come from long-term commitments

At the time of writing, Hostinger offers some excellent deals which reduce the price of its plans. Its basic Premium package offers 20GB of SSD storage, the ability to create up to three websites and a free domain for a year, all for £143.52 for four years (which works out as £2.99 per month). The next plan up is £191.52 for four years (the equivalent of £3.99 per month) and provides 50GB of NVMe storage (which is faster than standard SSD) and the option to create unlimited websites, as well as providing support for Node.js web apps.

Hostinger offers some excellent deals that reduce the price of its plans ( Jennifer Allen / Hostinger )

The ultimate hosting plan is Cloud Startup for £383.52 for four years (working out as £7.99 per month) which increases NVMe storage to 100GB and allows for Node.js web apps and unlimited websites. There’s also VPS hosting with the KVM 1 plan offering 1 vCPU core, 4GB RAM, and 50GB NVMe disk space for £4.99 per month, KVM 2 for £6.99 per month with 2 vCPU cores, 8GB RAM, and 100GB NVMe storage, and two more advanced packages for those who need the best performance.

These VPS plans are the best thing to compare with Cloudways’s offerings, with plans only payable in US dollars rather than UK pounds. Cloudways’s most basic plan – Micro – costs $14 per month and provides you with 1GB RAM, 1 vCPU, and 25GB NVMe storage. The Small plan costs $28 per month with 2GB RAM, 1 vCPU, and 50GB NVMe, with other plans scaling accordingly. So, it’s certainly pricier. You also need to pay a small fee each month for email while Hostinger includes it as standard.

One big plus point for Cloudways is that it has a three-day free trial where you don’t even need to enter payment details. It states that you don’t get full service, but the only features you miss out on are the kind of things you only need once you’re committing to a longer plan. If you just want to see if the Cloudways interface works for you, this will be exactly what you need.

2. Cloudways vs Hostinger: Features

Cloudways

Pros: Scalable for higher traffic

Cons: May not be very beginner-friendly; time-consuming to work with

Hostinger

Pros: Quick; Great if you’re a beginner; AI-assisted support available

Cons: Harder to scale up

Both Hostinger and Cloudways offer a huge amount of different features. Each web hosting service is highly accomplished with what you prefer mostly coming down to your technical ability and what you want to look at.

Hostinger leans heavily on its beginner-friendly interface. It can get very complex if you want it to, given the company offers VPS hosting and self-hosted n8n for those who want more than just simple web hosting. It’s a similar story for Cloudways, with more jargon and more of a focus on ‘deployment’ – which is a fancier way of saying ‘launch your website’.

Hostinger breaks things down according to ability level. You can upload your own code and website or deploy a Node.js web app to do the work for you. You can also opt for the simpler solution of setting up a WordPress-based site using Hostinger’s website builder, or you can use Hostinger Horizons which is a full AI solution. The latter simply asks for some prompts from you and does the nitty gritty stuff while you wait. If you don’t know how to code a website yourself or even design it, then Horizons will soon get you all set with an online presence.

In contrast, Cloudways has you either setting up a WordPress-based site or uploading your website/code. Unusually, I never found a web file manager for Cloudways – meaning you’ll need separate software to upload your files and site. Setting up your WordPress site is pretty simple though, with some basic plugins ready installed and a nice foundation for getting things just how you want them. Expect to devote some good time to the process though as there’s little hand-holding like there is with Hostinger.

There are pros and cons to these two methods. If you’re used to designing and coding your own site, you’ll be pleased to see how easily you can see the performance of your Cloudways server while Hostinger focuses more on the content. It’ll still conveniently give you a PageSpeed Insights test from Google at any point though.

Both offer extensive security features such as free SSL certificates – although you should look out for optional extras that feel more essential such as Cloudways charging for malware protection and Hostinger Reach – its AI-powered email marketing service which comes at a small price. Spend some time truly thinking about what your website or business needs from its web hosting and price it up accordingly.

Ultimately, I found Hostinger the quicker solution. If I wanted to code my own site, that might be a different matter but as someone who wanted to save time and effort, Hostinger was hard to fault on this front. Its plain language approach certainly benefits it there, but Cloudways’ scalability is admirable for those users with lofty goals.

Cloudways also allows you to choose your cloud provider with the best options predictably costing the most. If you’re hosting a high-traffic website, Cloudways offers a ton of choices here. Each may require advanced knowledge, but it’s logical that you have that if you’re managing a significant presence online.

3. Cloudways vs Hostinger: Ease of use

Cloudways

Pros: Great for uploading a website from elsewhere

Cons: Not much help with the design; slow to set up

Hostinger

Pros: Easy to get to grips with; great if you have no experience with design or coding; clear layout

Cons: Layouts could be more aesthetically pleasing; not everyone needs (or wants) AI features

Hostinger is the more simple-to-use web hosting service of the two. Its dashboard starts you off with a to-do list that gives some guidance, as well as key security reminders like asking you to add your phone number, verify your email, and other simple (but easy to forget) tasks. From that same dashboard, you can add or create a website, manage your domain portfolio, email accounts and any VPS you may also have signed up for.

There’s a lot of information that could look confusing but Hostinger keeps it simple and easy to glance at. Adding/creating a new website is clearly laid out, avoiding using jargon to get you where you need to go.

In contrast, Cloudways is very tech focused. The dashboard helps you find usernames and passwords ready for you to upload files to your website but it’s light on assisting with design. The focus here is on setting up a WordPress-based site, but even that feels a little trickier to get around.

As someone who’s used a lot of web hosting over the years, I knew what I was doing but Hostinger is more straightforward and able to help if you lack creative skills and coding ability. On the other hand, Cloudways is a good option if you just want a place to easily upload your existing website or migrate content from elsewhere, plus there’s no sign of AI-assisted support anywhere. This is something that some people will see as a huge advantage.

There’s one small point to note when starting out. Setting up my new hosting package with Hostinger only took a couple of minutes, while with Cloudways it took seven minutes before I could actively use my new account. Once set up, both are equally speedy but it’s something to be aware of if time is short.

4. Cloudways vs Hostinger: Support

Cloudways

Pros: Live chat to ask questions; community space to discuss with other Cloudways users

Cons: No phone or AI support

Hostinger

Pros: AI assistant is genuinely helpful; video tutorials available

Cons: No phone support

Hostinger leans further into its AI features for support. Its first port of call with any query is to ask Kodee, its AI assistant which happily lingers in the corner of your browser window at all times. It’s genuinely helpful and I was pleasantly surprised by how accurately it answered my queries.

Cloudways has a live chat feature for support ( Jennifer Allen / Cloudways )

Hostinger also has an extensive knowledge base with text and video-based queries, so most problems should be solved here. If you really need to talk to someone, you can do live chat via Kodee but there’s no phone support.

Cloudways pursues a similar path. There’s no phone support and also no AI bot, but it does have a vast knowledge base. It also has a live chat that you can dive straight into without needing to humour an AI bot. Another option is to use its community centre and discuss things with other Cloudways users.

Should you get Cloudways or Hostinger?

Both Cloudways and Hostinger are high quality web hosting services. I found them to be fast, responsive and security conscious. Where things differ is how easy they are to use. If you’re new to web hosting and launching a website then Hostinger is the better option. Its AI-assisted tools provide strong guidance, but if you just want light assistance then the WordPress setup is perfect.

In comparison, Cloudways is aimed more at uploading your own website and going from there – but it means you can maintain your server more efficiently and keep on top of things. It generally requires more advanced knowledge, but I’m a fan of the Cloudways WordPress setup for quickly getting you started.

Ultimately, which is best comes down to what you need from your web hosting provider. I’d suggest Hostinger for its simplicity, while Cloudways offers a lot of great scalability options if you’re aiming to grow your online presence over time.

How Cloudways and Hostinger were tested

While spending time with Cloudways and Hostinger, I considered certain key elements. Here’s what I thought about each step of the way:

Ease of use: I wanted to see how easy Cloudways and Hostinger are to use. I was looking to see if they are beginner-friendly while also still offering everything an advanced user needs. I evaluated the amount of technical jargon involved. I also looked at how easy it is to cancel or change a plan.

Features: I looked at what features each web host offers and how that compares to the competition. I wanted to check that they were genuinely useful features but also how expansive they could be for sites that wish to grow over time. I wanted to make sure that no one is stuck with a limited plan.

Value for money: I evaluated the value for money offered by each provider. I didn’t want to focus on solely the cheapest plan but the one that represented good value for what you need from it. That also involved looking at different plans and commitment periods.

Performance: Speed and reliability is everything in a website. I checked that changes were implemented quickly and new sites were deployed rapidly. I also wanted to check that a live site was speedy to browse so that people were encouraged to look at it. Ultimately, I wanted a speedy site that rarely had any issues.

Why you can trust our reviews

Jennifer Allen is an expert in tech and websites, and writes gaming and console reviews for IndyBest. During her testing process, Jennifer evaluated everything from website building features and changing a hosting package to value for money.
