Sports.title: Jose Valenzuela Pushes WBA for Floyd Schofield Fight
Sports.content:
Jose “Rayo” Valenzuela wants the WBA to put him next in line for Floyd Schofield’s lightweight title, potentially complicating the new champion’s unification plans before his first defense is arranged.

“Let’s make it happen,” Rayo wrote on X, tagging the WBA in response to a post arguing that Schofield must first face a mandatory or leading available contender after winning the vacant belt.

Schofield defeated Lucas Bahdi in Chicago on Saturday to become champion. Oscar De La Hoya has discussed unifications, but Rayo is asking the sanctioning body to consider its own ranked contenders before moving forward with those plans.

The WBA’s September rankings listed Schofield first, Bahdi second, and Rayo third. With Schofield now champion and Bahdi coming off the defeat, Rayo has a credible case for consideration. His position does not automatically establish him as the mandatory challenger.

Rayo, 27, holds a 16-3 record with 10 knockouts and is coming off a second-round knockout win over Edwin De Los Santos on June 28. Some fans criticized the finish, believing he hit De Los Santos while he was down and arguing for a no contest or disqualification. The official result remains a knockout victory.

There is also a promotional and broadcast hurdle. Rayo fights for Zuffa Boxing on Paramount+, while Schofield is promoted by Golden Boy, whose events air on DAZN. Making the fight would require the promoters to agree on terms and a broadcast arrangement.

A WBA order could push those discussions forward, but it would not decide which platform carries the event or how the revenue is divided.

The post Rayo shared also overstated the vacant-title rule. The WBA rules version amended through April 2024 requires a non-heavyweight vacant-title winner to make his initial defense within 120 days. That provision does not itself say every voluntary defense is prohibited.

Golden Boy therefore cannot treat Rayo’s request as an official order, but neither can it assume Schofield has an unrestricted choice of opponents. Rayo has publicly asked for the opportunity. The WBA’s response will determine whether that request becomes an obligation.

Sports.title: David Benavidez May Lose His Edge at Heavyweight
Sports.content:
David Benavidez might find that moving to heavyweight strips away everything that makes him effective. Stepping through 175 and cruiserweight before chasing the big men could easily backfire on a fighter who relies on physical advantages, high volume, and quick hand speed.

Before any of that happens, he still needs to deal with Michal Cieslak, while keeping Jai Opetaia and an aging Artur Beterbiev on his radar. Jumping to heavyweight forces yet another drastic body transformation before anyone even knows if his power carries through the cruiserweight elite.

“The heavyweight division is definitely a division I’ve got my eyes on. [But] we’ve got two great fights at cruiserweight before we get up there,” Benavidez told Inside The Ring. “We’ve got Jai Opetaia, then I think Beterbiev is going to come up to cruiserweight.”

The real problem lies in what gets sacrificed when packing on bulk. Benavidez built his reputation by being the bigger man in the ring, bullying smaller opponents into the ropes, and drowning them in extended combinations. Against genuine heavyweights, that physical edge vanishes completely.

Piling on muscle rarely translates to better punch resistance or sustained stamina. If the extra weight dulls his hand speed or drains his work rate, Benavidez turns into a stationary target who lacks the one-punch eraser needed to keep giant opponents from walking him down.

If he slows down by even ten percent, he stops being a swarm puncher and turns into a flat-footed target. Without blistering hand speed, large heavyweights will simply time him with straight shots from the outside or tie him up in clinches, leaning on his shoulders to drain whatever legs he has left.

David Morrell already exposed how much damage Benavidez absorbs when a fight gets tough. Routine wins over Anthony Yarde and Gilberto Ramirez did not prove he can stand in the pocket against massive punchers and survive the return fire.

Careful matchmaking could hide some flaws. A washed-up Andy Ruiz Jr. gives him an accessible name, while Oleksandr Usyk showed clear signs of slippage at 39 years old against Rico Verhoeven, needing an eleventh-round rescue after trailing on one card through ten rounds.

Those soft targets might make the jump tempting, but they do not solve the fundamental issue. Benavidez could pack on thirty pounds, only to end up slower, easier to hit, and far less dangerous than the fighter who dominated at 168.

Sports.title: Tim Bradley Picks Abdullah Mason To Beat Schofield
Sports.content:
Floyd Schofield would lose his newly won lightweight belt to Abdullah Mason, according to Tim Bradley, who believes his movement against Lucas Bahdi exposed weaknesses a quicker opponent could exploit.

“Even Abdullah Mason is on an entirely different level than Schofield,” Bradley said on his channel in his post-fight breakdown. “You ain’t going to keep that belt that long, bro.”

That puts Bradley against the matchup Schofield’s father has been pushing for. His confidence in his son beating Mason faces a different reading from Bradley, who sees technical flaws beneath Schofield’s speed and athleticism.

Bradley’s main criticism concerns how Schofield controls distance. He believes Schofield moves too much without maintaining a stable punching position, leaving openings as he bounces around the ring. His proposed correction is a firmer jab, feints, and smaller steps that allow him to defend while remaining ready to punch.

Bahdi’s slower feet, in Bradley’s view, prevented him from consistently taking advantage. Being able to move away from Bahdi doesn’t establish that Schofield could do the same against an opponent who closes distance faster.

But Bradley’s own breakdown also offers reasons to question how emphatically he dismisses Schofield’s chances.

He praised the switch to southpaw, which disrupted Bahdi’s right-hand attacks and helped Schofield land shorter combinations. He also credited Schofield’s stamina and use of clinches to interrupt Bahdi’s momentum.

“That was a great technical and tactical shift,” Bradley said of the stance change.

Those adjustments deserve consideration when discussing Mason. Schofield showed he could change his approach when his initial offense wasn’t enough. Bradley identified weaknesses, but he also described a fighter capable of solving some of the difficulties in front of him.

A Mason fight would test whether Schofield can control distance with less movement and fewer openings. His speed gives him options; learning when to plant his feet and when to take a small step could make those options more effective.

Bradley favors Mason strongly. Schofield’s performance gives his camp plenty to work on before trying to prove him wrong.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia’s Catchweight Defense Overlooks Who Benefits
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia’s defense of catchweights leaves out who benefits when the more popular fighter dictates the conditions. He argues that flexible limits create bouts that otherwise could not occur, entirely skipping over how that dynamic forces concessions onto opponents.

“Impossible @Showbizz. That stops matchups that couldn’t happen without it. It will actually limit boxing and boxing is a sport without any [limits],” Ryan said on X.

Meeting between divisions can bridge weight classes, sure. Yet the marquee attraction can easily use contract terms to tilt the contest before either man touches a glove.

The B-side contender gets squeezed into a corner. Walk away, and he surrenders his career-high purse, elite visibility, plus a rare spotlight. Agree, and he secures the event while compromising his physical prime on fight night.

Ryan overlooks that reality. A signed contract proves agreement occurred, not that both sides wielded equal clout during negotiations.

His 2023 clash with Gervonta Davis proved the exact dynamic. The deal called for a 136-pound limit, paired with a morning check capping rehydration at 146 pounds. Davis wanted that second barrier.

Even when contract terms apply equally on paper, they rarely extract the same toll. One athlete cruises in comfortably while the other drains himself dry just to qualify.

Garcia also sidesteps rehydration stipulations altogether. These terms extend far past the opening weigh-in, policing how much bulk a fighter recovers before entering the ring. Paired with strict weight caps, they hand the A-side major leverage over an adversary’s preparation.

Nobody can claim Davis definitely loses without those rules in place. Still, simply getting two big names into the ring cannot stand as proof that the contract was balanced. Ryan loves talking about flexibility. His case still needs to account for contenders who must surrender their physical strength just to earn their shot against the bigger star.

Sports.title: Canelo Alvarez Sticks With Original Riyadh Fight Plan
Sports.content:
Canelo Alvarez plans to proceed with his October 31 bout against Christian Mbilli in Riyadh, Turki Alalshikh confirmed, standing by the Saudi boxing chief amid ongoing uncertainty around the event.

“Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens. He fears nothing,” Alalshikh wrote on X.

That commitment signals a fighter acting in full partnership with organizers. Instead of requesting a change of venue, Canelo gave private assurances that he will make the trip as scheduled. For someone working to hold the fight card together, receiving that backing from the main attraction carries serious weight.

Alalshikh made his appreciation unmistakable in his closing message.

“Thank you to everyone who checked in and showed support. Hard times reveal true friends.”

Canelo is displaying loyalty by keeping the original arrangement intact. Alalshikh has put substantial muscle behind major events featuring the Mexican superstar, and Canelo appears determined to return that backing when complications arise.

Turki Alalshikh is holding the deepest checkbook the sport has ever seen. For an aging superstar whose standard pay-per-view numbers in Las Vegas had begun to settle, maintaining direct favor with Riyadh Season is essential.

How prospective spectators respond to the situation remains less certain.

A promise from the headliner aids the promotion, yet it will not settle the concerns of traveling supporters. Individuals looking at plane tickets, hotel reservations, or seat prices will reach their own conclusions. Canelo’s willingness to compete does not guarantee their presence.

Sparse seating on fight night would still mean Alalshikh values the champion’s pledge. Still, empty sections would drain energy from the arena once Canelo and Mbilli step under the lights. Official ticketing numbers remain unconfirmed, making lower attendance an open risk rather than a settled fact.

The boundary is simple: the fighter controls his arrival, while paying fans decide if they make the trip.

At this point, Alalshikh holds the guarantee he needed most. Based on his statement, Canelo is staying the course in Riyadh.

Sports.title: Agit Kabayel’s Tyson Fury Pick Leans on Old Memories
Sports.content:
Agit Kabayel picks Tyson Fury to handle Anthony Joshua, but that pick relies on memories from a decade ago. Kabayel shared rounds with Fury back in 2016, sharing the ring with a fleet-footed heavyweight vastly different from the man competing today.

Kabayel credits Fury with superior ring IQ, even while respecting Joshua’s single-shot knockout power. His prediction leans on Fury having multiple paths to victory, yet those ancient gym sessions tell us very little about present-day form.

“The better boxer, the better boxing IQ [is with] Fury,” Kabayel told The Ring. “But only one guy in the heavyweight division can beat the guys with one hand. This is Anthony Joshua.” “I think Fury will win the fight. Points, KO, but we will see. My prediction is with Fury.”

The glaring flaw in Kabayel’s logic involves Fury’s faded mobility. The 2016 incarnation feinted opponents out of position, changed angles effortlessly, and slipped outside hitting range with ease. Combine that fluidity with his massive frame, and he became a nightmare to track down.

Recent outings show a far more stationary operator. Fury still knows how to manipulate range with his reach, yet recognizing open space is quite different from possessing the foot speed to claim it. Against someone carrying Joshua’s power, lingering in the pocket too long invites disaster.

Kabayel admits his sparring comparison carries an asterisk.

“For me, the hardest sparring was with Fury,” Kabayel explained, pointing out that he had logged three extra years of professional seasoning before testing Joshua in 2019.

That timeline skews the perspective. Kabayel met Fury as a raw prospect, then shared rounds with Joshua as a fully developed contender capable of holding his own.

Fury’s ring craft gives him a legitimate shot. Still, wondering whether his aging reflexes can execute his intentions remains the central issue. Kabayel’s glowing scouting report honors a long-gone fighter Joshua never has to face.

Looking at Fury across his recent outings, the double defeat to Oleksandr Usyk followed by soft recovery touches against plodding veterans like Arslanbek Makhmudov and Mariusz Wach, you are watching a fighter surviving on reputation and size rather than elite capability.

Beating Wladimir Klitschko in Düsseldorf was a psychological masterclass against an aging champion afraid to pull the trigger, and the 2020 demolition of Deontay Wilder was the absolute ceiling of Fury’s offensive bullying. Everything since has been a steady march into decline.

Sports.title: Fabio Wardley Expects Early Finish In Daniel Dubois Rematch
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley expects his rematch with Daniel Dubois to finish early, with either heavyweight capable of ending the fight before it reaches the later rounds. Their first meeting lasted 11 rounds, so Wardley’s prediction points to a quicker, more explosive second fight.

“It’s only going one way. It’s finishing early one way or another. It’s going to be a crazy night. Everyone, tune in,” said Wardley to Queensberry.

That “one way or another” qualification leaves room for both outcomes. Wardley knows the danger Dubois brings, even after beating him the first time. He is promising action without pretending that trading heavy punches comes without a cost.

Wardley’s overhand right gives him a clear weapon to take into the rematch. He has already described how he used it to counter Dubois’ jab in their first fight, making Dubois think about what could come back whenever he extended his left hand.

Dubois needs an answer to that punch. His jab can help him control the fight, but throwing it repeatedly without adjusting his defense could give Wardley the opening he is looking for. Wardley doesn’t need to change much if the same counter remains available.

Still, their first fight showed that hurting Dubois early and finishing him early are two different things. Wardley had success well before the stoppage, yet needed 11 rounds to complete the job. Chasing a quicker ending could also make him easier to hit if he becomes too eager after landing.

Wardley expects his supporters to add to the atmosphere on Saturday.

“It’s huge for me. Hometown boy, home grown. Had the club, the supporters, everyone behind me from the beginning,” he said. “So it does mean the absolute most and they’re going to make themselves heard on Saturday night.”

The crowd will be ready for the fireworks Wardley promises. Whether the finish comes early depends on how well Dubois adjusts, and whether Wardley can turn his next opening into something decisive.

Sports.title: Ricardo Sandoval Must Settle The Score With Mendoza
Sports.content:
Ricardo Sandoval must decide on his next fight after losing his WBA and WBC flyweight titles to Sergio “Yoreme” Mendoza last Saturday night in Chicago. The immediate rematch route is his only real play if Golden Boy has a return clause baked into the contract.

Mendoza was brought in as a late replacement, so Sandoval’s team likely secured rematch language. If they did, Sandoval has to trigger it immediately. He gave up all the leverage he built by beating Kenshiro Teraji in Tokyo, and nobody at 112 or 115 is going to offer him big money without those belts.

If there is no rematch clause, Sandoval is in no-man’s-land. The flyweight division moves fast. Unification bouts, big cards in Japan, and potential moves up to junior bantamweight are off the table for him. Those paydays belong to Mendoza now.

To rebuild, Sandoval has to face reality about his defense. Getting dropped three times inside five rounds by a guy coming off a second-round knockout loss shows Sandoval’s habits caught up to him. He relies on taking shots to give shots, but without elite sharpness, his punch resistance completely disappeared last night under Mendoza’s firepower.

Apart from a rematch, he needs a tune-up to see if his chin and punch resistance can hold up before trying to climb back into the top five of the sanctioning bodies. Sandoval should aim for spring 2027, ideally March or April.

That gives him roughly five to six months. He cannot afford another extended layoff, yet he took serious physical damage on Saturday night. Absorbing three knockdowns before getting stopped in the fifth round means mandatory medical suspensions and mandatory rest. He must keep his gloves off for at least sixty to ninety days to let his body recover. Rushing into hard sparring in November or December would be reckless.

Sitting out another year would kill what is left of his career, though. Inactivity was a major reason his timing, reflexes, and punch resistance betrayed him against Mendoza. At 112 pounds, fighters burn out quickly, and the division forgets former champions fast.

Flyweight is the wrong division to play the brooding, inactive contender. It is arguably the most unforgiving weight class in the sport because success relies almost entirely on twitch reflexes, hand speed, and conditioning. Those are the exact attributes that disappear when a fighter sits on the shelf.

Ghana News.title: Youth employment must remain central to Ghana’s economic reset – Joyce Bawah Mogtari
Ghana News.content:
Joyce Bawah Mogtari

Senior Presidential Advisor and Senior Aide to President John Dramani Mahama, Joyce Bawah Mogtari, has stressed the need for Ghana’s economic reforms and development investments to translate into sustainable jobs and meaningful opportunities for young people.

In a Facebook post on Monday, October 12, she acknowledged that youth unemployment, particularly among graduates, remained a serious national concern, noting that young people wanted jobs, dignity and opportunities to build meaningful lives.

She said government alone could not provide every job but had a responsibility to create conditions that allow businesses to invest, industries to expand and employment opportunities to emerge.

Ms Bawah Mogtari said investments in infrastructure, energy, agriculture and human capital were important because they could help establish the foundations for a stronger economy and greater employment opportunities.

She argued that such investments should be viewed not merely as projects but as building blocks for a more hopeful future for the country’s youth.

She called for patience, purpose and collective responsibility in pursuing the national development agenda.

According to her, Ghanaians should support initiatives that are working while holding government accountable where it falls short, stressing that the broader goal must be to build a country where opportunity is accessible to all rather than reserved for a privileged few.

Ghana News.title: Ethnic conflicts, land disputes and illicit drugs remain major security concerns – Muntaka
Ghana News.content:
The Minister for the Interior, Mubarak Mohammed Muntaka, has identified ethnic conflicts, land disputes and illicit drugs as major security concerns confronting Ghana, despite what he describes as an improvement in the country’s security situation.

Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Monday, October 12, 2026, the Minister said instability in the Sahel and Ghana’s porous borders added to the challenges facing security agencies.

Asked about his biggest security challenges and areas requiring further attention, he pointed to communal conflicts, disputes over land and narcotics trafficking.

He said the use of the West African coast as a transit route for illicit drugs remained a concern, citing findings by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

“You come and inherit a situation where the UN Office on Drug and Crime has consistently showed that in the last, probably, decade, the West Coast is being used as transit point for illicit drugs,” he said.

Mr Muntaka also expressed concern about insecurity in the Sahel, saying some countries in the region struggled to maintain control over substantial parts of their territory.

“I can tell you that, without mentioning specific countries, some of them don't control up to 60% of their area.”

He explained that regional security threats required close cooperation between Ghana and its neighbours, particularly through intelligence sharing.

“So there's no interior or national security minister in the sub-region that I don't have direct contact with,” he stated.

“You have to try and share intelligence, you have to work together. As difficult as it is, sometimes there's mistrust and all that.”

The Minister said the nature of Ghana’s borders complicated efforts to monitor movement, with some communities divided between neighbouring countries.

“So you could farm in one country and sleep in another country based on the way they've done it,” he said.

He disclosed that Ghana had more than 300 unapproved border crossing points, compared with 48 approved entry points.

“The legitimate crossing points are 48,” he said.

“We have over 300 illegitimate crossing points.”

On internal conflicts, Mr Muntaka recalled how violence linked to Bawku had spread beyond the immediate conflict zone in 2025, prompting security operations and mediation efforts.

He said retaliatory attacks, including the burning of buses along highways, had placed considerable pressure on the authorities.

“I mean, and I can bet you, these were periods that I could hardly sleep,” he said.

However, he maintained that the situation had improved, citing 150 days without gunfire in Bawku and a reduction in the number of curfews nationwide from about nine at the end of 2025 to three.

“Ghana is much safer even today than it was in 2025,” he said.

“We are doing everything possible to ensure that you can go about your duties without necessarily having to be watching your back.”

Ghana News.title: Ghana has 48 legitimate entry points but over 300 illegal crossing points – Interior Minister
Ghana News.content:
Ghana's border with Togo.

The Minister for the Interior, Mubarak Mohammed Muntaka, has disclosed that Ghana has 48 legitimate entry points but more than 300 unapproved crossing points, raising concerns about the challenges facing the country’s border security.

He said the numerous unapproved routes posed a security challenge that required stronger cooperation with neighbouring countries, particularly through intelligence sharing and coordinated efforts to address threats across the sub-region.

Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Monday, October 12, 2026, Mr Muntaka said cooperation among countries was essential to tackling security threats that could extend beyond national borders.

“You have to try and share intelligence; you have to work together,” he said.

The Minister’s comments come as he maintains that Ghana’s overall security situation has improved compared with 2025, despite continuing concerns about ethnic conflicts, land disputes, illicit drugs and border vulnerabilities.

“I can assure you that we are safer today than we were when we took over power,” he said.

“Ghana is much safer even today than it was in 2025.”

Mr Muntaka acknowledged that crime remained a challenge but said the government and security agencies were doing everything possible to protect the public and enable people to go about their daily activities without fear.

“We are doing everything possible to ensure that you can go about your duties without necessarily having to be watching your back,” he stated.

When asked to provide figures to support his assessment of the security situation, the Minister cautioned against measuring progress solely by comparing the number of deaths recorded in different years.

“Well, I always tell people that I hate the situation when I say, oh, last year, 200 people died; this year, 190 died.”

Instead, he pointed to a reduction in the number of curfews imposed across the country. According to him, Ghana began 2025 with about 11 curfews and ended the year with about nine.

“As we speak now, we have only three more curfews,” he said.

He cited developments in Bawku in the Upper East Region, where he said there had been no gunfire for 150 days.

“150 days, no gunshots,” he stated.

According to the Minister, the relative calm had allowed the authorities to ease restrictions in the town, including adjusting the curfew to between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. Residents had also been permitted to ride motorbikes between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m.

“They were not riding motorbikes for more than five years. Today, they are riding motorbikes from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.,” he said.

Mr Muntaka recalled that violence associated with the Bawku conflict had previously spread to other communities, triggering retaliatory attacks and the burning of buses along highways.

“I mean, and I can bet you, these were periods that I could hardly sleep,” he said.

He explained that the authorities had combined security operations with mediation and peacebuilding efforts to contain the conflict.

Despite the improvements he outlined, the Minister said Ghana continued to face security threats that required sustained attention, including ethnic conflicts, land disputes and illicit drug-related activities.

He said addressing these challenges also required effective border management, given the number of unapproved crossing points across the country.

The Minister stressed that Ghana could not tackle transnational security threats in isolation, underscoring the need for neighbouring countries to work together, exchange intelligence and strengthen their collective response.

His disclosure on the number of approved and unapproved crossing points highlights the scale of the border management challenge facing Ghana as the government seeks to sustain improvements in the country’s security situation.

“They were not riding motorbikes for more than five years. Today, they are riding motorbikes from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.,” he said.

Mr Muntaka recalled that violence linked to the Bawku conflict had previously spread to other communities, with retaliatory attacks and the burning of buses along highways.

“I mean, and I can bet you, these were periods that I could hardly sleep,” he said.

He explained that the authorities combined security operations with mediation and peacebuilding efforts to contain the situation.

Despite his assessment of improved security, the Minister identified ethnic conflicts, land disputes and illicit drugs as continuing concerns.

He also highlighted the challenges posed by porous borders, saying Ghana had more than 300 unapproved crossing points, compared with 48 approved entry points.

“The legitimate crossing points are 48,” he said.

“We have over 300 illegitimate crossing points.”

Mr Muntaka said cooperation with neighbouring countries remained essential to addressing security threats across the sub-region.

“You have to try and share intelligence; you have to work together,” he said.

Ghana News.title: Bawku has gone 150 days without gunfire – Interior Minister
Ghana News.content:
The Minister for the Interior, Mubarak Mohammed Muntaka, says the volatile Bawku area has gone 150 days without gunfire, describing the development as evidence of an improvement in the security situation.

Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Monday, October 12, 2026, he said security operations and peacebuilding efforts had helped contain violence that previously spread beyond Bawku to other communities.

“150 days, no gunshots,” he said.

According to the Minister, the improvement has allowed the authorities to ease the curfew in Bawku to between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m.

He recalled that restrictions had previously covered periods from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m., and, at one stage, from 4 p.m. to 6 a.m.

“When the curfew is 10 to 5, it tells you that it has largely eased,” he said.

Mr Muntaka said residents were also now permitted to ride motorbikes between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m., following years of restrictions.

“They were not riding motorbikes for almost five years. Today, they are riding motorbikes from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.,” he stated.

He indicated that the government was assessing the situation to determine whether the remaining restrictions could be lifted.

“And very soon, we'll be reviewing. Very soon, we may even lift it completely,” he said.

Asked whether he was considering lifting the Bawku curfew, he responded: “No, the curfew and then the motorbike riding. But we are obviously analysing the situation.”

Reflecting on the violence in 2025, Mr Muntaka said retaliatory attacks had spread beyond the conflict zone, affecting communities including Binduri, Nalerigu and Walewale, with buses attacked along highways.

He said the situation placed considerable pressure on the security authorities, particularly when the violence extended to students in secondary schools.

“I mean, and I can bet you, these were periods that I could hardly sleep,” he said.

The Minister explained that the response combined security interventions with mediation, including the involvement of the National Peace Council.

He also cited a reduction in the number of curfews nationwide as an indication of improving security, saying Ghana began 2025 with about 11 curfews and ended the year with about nine.

“As we speak, we have only three more curfews,” he said.

Mr Muntaka maintained that the country’s security situation had improved, while acknowledging that crime remained a challenge.

“Ghana is much safer even today than it was in 2025,” he said.

“We are doing everything possible to ensure that you can go about your duties without necessarily having to be watching your back.”

Ghana News.title: It still surprises me GAUA is on strike after signing MoU – Fair Wages CEO
Ghana News.content:
The Chief Executive Officer of the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission (FWSC), Dr George Smith-Graham, says he is surprised the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA) is still on strike after signing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Commission to allow further discussions on its concerns over salary disparities.

Speaking on the JoyNews AM Show on Monday, October 12, he said salary negotiations with GAUA had been concluded, and the association had been paid, but the Commission had agreed to examine fresh proposals to address its concerns.

Dr Smith-Graham explained that the government had prioritised efforts to address disparities in the Single Spine Salary Structure, with the FWSC and the Ministry of Finance working to correct the inequalities across public sector institutions.

The Commission, he said, had concluded negotiations with 58 institutions, including GAUA, as part of the broader effort.

“We have concluded negotiations with 58 institutions, including GAUA. We have signed an agreement with GAUA, concluded the negotiations with GAUA, and they have been paid,” he said.

Dr Smith-Graham attributed GAUA's decision to embark on strike to concerns that the University Teachers Association of Ghana (UTAG) had secured a more favourable deal in its negotiations with the government.

He said GAUA became dissatisfied after learning that UTAG had also negotiated with the government and believed the teachers' association had received better terms.

“Immediately they noticed that UTAG had also come for their negotiations, then they said UTAG got more than them; and because UTAG got more than them, they declared a strike,” he said.

The FWSC CEO disclosed that GAUA representatives had visited his office about a week earlier, where both parties signed an MoU to allow further discussions on the association's concerns.

“When GAUA raised the issue, GAUA came to my office about a week ago. They signed a Memorandum of Understanding with me,” he said.

“I said, give me some proposals on how we can resolve these inequities. We are also interested in resolving the inequities. We will study your proposal.”

Dr Smith-Graham stressed that the agreement to consider further proposals did not mean the earlier negotiations with GAUA remained outstanding.

Dr Smith-Graham said he had expected GAUA to call off its strike following the understanding reached at the meeting, which was intended to give the Commission time to examine the association's proposals.

READ ALSO :Education Ministry calls urgent talks to break GAUA strike deadlock

He said he was therefore surprised to learn on Friday that the industrial action was still ongoing.

“They signed that we are going to call off the strike, that they are giving us the time, only for me to hear on Friday that 'we are still on strike',” he lamented. “That really surprised me, because they came to sign an MoU with me.”

Dr Smith-Graham reiterated that the Commission would examine GAUA's proposals and respond by the end of October, while maintaining that the earlier negotiations had been concluded and the agreed payments made.

Ghana News.title: Kumasi Hospital removes 880-gram bladder stone in rare surgical case
Ghana News.content:
A team of doctors at Kumasi Hospital, a private health facility in the Ashanti Region, has removed an 880-gram bladder stone from a 49-year-old man in what the surgical team believes could be one of the largest such stones ever removed in Africa.

The stone measures 11.8 centimetres in length, 9.5 centimetres in breadth and nearly 8 centimetres in width.

At first glance, it resembles a ball of clay. However, the oval-shaped mass is a giant bladder stone — a hard, crystallised formation that developed inside the bladder of the patient, identified as Akoto, not his real name.

For nearly three decades, he endured pain, urinary difficulties and a gradual decline in his quality of life.

“It was really painful. Not being able to urinate is something I wouldn’t wish for anyone,” he said.

What may have begun as tiny mineral crystals gradually developed into an enormous stone, affecting his health and daily life.

The surgical team believes the stone is arguably the largest bladder stone documented as having been removed in Africa.

“We searched medical literature from the continent, but we couldn’t find any documented and removed bladder stone as big as this one. It was originally 980 grammes. But even after desiccating for over a day, the size is still the largest,” the Chief Executive Officer of Kumasi Hospital, Dr (Med) Samuel Koranteng Asante, told Luv FM’s Emmanuel Bright Quaicoe.

According to Guinness World Records, the largest bladder stone on record was removed from a patient in Brazil in 2003. It weighed 1.9 kilogrammes (4.2 pounds) and measured 17.9 centimetres (7 inches) in length.

Another record-breaking case was reported in Sri Lanka in August 2026, when doctors removed a 3.1-kilogramme bladder stone from a 55-year-old man.

How bladder stones develop

Bladder stones form when urine remains in the bladder for too long, allowing minerals in the urine to concentrate, crystallise and harden over time.

Dr Asante said underlying urinary tract problems could contribute to their formation.

“When one has prostate enlargement and urine consistently stays in the bladder, it can bring about bladder stones. But with this one, we realised there was a stricture in his ureter, which usually comes about when one has a urinary infection such as an STI, and it is not treated well, that can also contribute to bladder stones,” he noted.

Small bladder stones, sometimes as tiny as grains of sand, may pass out naturally. Larger stones, particularly those measuring more than one centimetre, can obstruct urine flow and may require medical intervention.

Stones measuring more than four centimetres are generally described as giant bladder stones.

Beyond the physical pain

For Akoto, the consequences extended beyond physical discomfort. The growing mass disrupted his social life, weakened his health and affected his sexual intimacy.

His experience highlights the importance of recognising urinary symptoms and seeking medical attention before an underlying condition progresses.

Doctors say early diagnosis and treatment of underlying urinary problems are important in preventing bladder stones from growing to such enormous sizes.

Dr Asante also advised people to drink adequate amounts of water to help reduce the concentration of minerals in their urine.

“Drink a lot of water. When you drink water, the urine becomes diluted. This means it will be difficult for the salt to crystallise and form a stone,” he advised.

For Akoto, the operation marks the end of years of suffering. His experience also serves as a reminder of the importance of seeking medical attention for persistent abdominal pain, difficulty urinating or other changes in urinary habits.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Delhi braces for more protests against election chief amid crackdown
World.content:
Opposition parties, joined by student groups, are hitting the streets, disrupting central New Delhi with flash marches.

Share Delhi braces for more protests against election chief amid crackdown on social media

New Delhi, India — India’s main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has returned to the streets of central New Delhi, leading dozens of members of parliament demanding the election chief’s resignation, as protests gather momentum.

Gandhi, heir to India’s most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn a summer youth uprising into a broader challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s decade-long dominance of Indian politics, putting the Hindu nationalist government under growing pressure.

In a press briefing on Monday, Gandhi said the Modi government had put the capital city “in jail”.

The youth-led “Cockroach” movement that forced out the education minister in July has also threatened to protest on Tuesday if it is not allowed to rally at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, which was the focus of summer demonstrations.

Joining Gandhi’s Congress party, other opposition forces and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) are thousands of students from left-wing organisations. As the government braces for further protests, security forces have been detaining thousands of students every day, with allegations of custodial violence casting a climate of fear over the capital.

‘No constraints on Modi’

India’s Election Commission, a supposedly autonomous body tasked with overseeing the world’s largest electorate, has been criticised after revelations that its chief, Gyanesh Kumar, frequently overruled concerns raised by the other two election commissioners about the integrity of changes to the voter database.



For months, India’s opposition parties have argued that the election commission is compromised, sabotaging elections at the behest of Modi’s Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) for its electoral benefit. The BJP denies the allegations.

Since June last year, the commission has been revising and updating statewide voter lists. It has since removed more than 130 million names, which critics say has disproportionately deprived minorities and other vulnerable groups in India of the right to vote.

Gandhi has called for the Chief Election Commissioner to be tried for treason. “We will not spare you,” he said, referring to Kumar, at his Monday press briefing.

Opposition politicians allege that protest rallies by leaders including Gandhi have been met with violent and brutal force, as seen in videos showing them being detained.

“[The protesters] came with love in their hearts, not hatred or anger,” Gandhi said, referring to a protest on Saturday. “They were beaten, both by cops and BJP goons.”

“Narendra Modi … cannot silence India’s voice. These cowards cannot intimidate us. They will have to step aside,” he wrote on X, calling on people from all walks of life to join the protest on Monday.

Analysts say circumstances this time around are starkly different to the summer protests, when CJP-led demonstrators demanded the resignation of then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Asim Ali, a political analyst in New Delhi, told Al Jazeera that the mobilisation of the wider opposition would not stop, but the Modi government was unlikely to back down.

“The crackdown this time on students is making it apparent that it would be tougher for young protesters this time, and students can’t get beaten up and dragged violently daily,” he said. “Going forward, the opposition parties stand to be the front face of the protests, and they need to lead from the front.”

Since 1975, when then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi imposed a state of national emergency suspending civil liberties, “India saw more civil politics grow into mainstream, where opposition parties were allowed space,” Ali said.

He added that after five decades, “those democratic gains have vanished – and there are no constraints on this government by independent institutions.”

Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst, said he has seen New Delhi at the centre of “several big opposition political rallies, held in areas near the parliament, hosting hundreds of thousands of people,” when the police did not interfere, unlike the crackdowns this year.



Kidwai said that the violent detention of members of parliament, in particular, was worrying.

“We are seeing a big change from when politicians were more tolerant of dissent,” he added.

Cat-and-mouse chases

With an unprecedented security deployment in central New Delhi designed to prevent protest, youth leaders are turning to new tactics.

Neha Bora, the president of All India Students’ Association (AISA), a left-wing group affiliated with the Communist Party of India, has often tricked Delhi police in order to stage protests.

Bora, a post-doctoral student of theatre, came to national prominence for her fiery speeches in the July protests, becoming a leading face of the Gen Z movement challenging Modi’s Hindu nationalist politics.

Aditi Thakur, a 23-year-old student in the capital, has turned on notifications for all of Bora’s posts on social media. “A call to protest can come anytime, anywhere,” she told Al Jazeera.

Bora does not reveal when or where she is going to stage a protest until just 30 minutes before, to avoid detentions by the police. Her supporters are alerted via social media to join her at a given location in the capital.

On Sunday, she picked a congested street near central Delhi — and was able to jump several barricades to reach the heavily secured Parliament Street, before being chased down and dragged into a police van.

Even Thakur couldn’t catch her, she told Al Jazeera, laughing. “These are guerrilla times, but peacefully. If the government cracks down on us, we also need to adapt,” she said. “It is a fun cat-and-mouse chase every day. I’m hooked on it.”

The Gandhi-led Congress is also adopting similar measures, holding flash rallies at unannounced venues, then running away from police.

The mood is changing

A defining feature of the July protests – a watershed moment for wrestling concessions from the government – was Gen Z’s humour in the face of police brutality.

Now, protesters are prepared for a more serious confrontation, even if demonstrations remain peaceful, say analysts.

“We are seeing that humour changing more into anger this time,” Asim Ali said.

The biggest challenge for the government is disruption in central New Delhi, which, Ali said, the government cannot allow on a daily basis. The area is home to most federal government offices, as well as being a major business hub.

Protesters know that too, and that gives them leverage.

“We are seeing this movement grow into a bigger anti-government, anti-Modi movement,” Ali said.

World.title: What do emergency and governor rule in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa mean?
World.content:
Pakistan has taken control of a province governed by Imran Khan’s PTI. Here is what the move means and what happens next.

Share What do emergency and governor rule in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa mean? on social media

Islamabad, Pakistan – Pakistan’s federal government has taken direct control of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the northwestern province until now governed by jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.

President Asif Ali Zardari signed a proclamation on Sunday, on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, imposing a state of emergency and declaring that the provincial government could no longer function in accordance with the Constitution, the legal basis for governor’s rule. On Monday, junior interior minister Talal Chaudhry said that the province’s chief minister Sohail Afridi had been placed under detention.

“The fundamental grounds for imposition of emergency are law and order, fight against terrorism, and to save innocent people from the dreadful consequences of terrorist activities,” federal Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said at a news conference in Islamabad on Sunday, alongside Information Minister Ataullah Tarar, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and other officials.

PTI, which has governed the province since 2013, has rejected the move. It came after talks collapsed between the federal government and the party over a planned to Islamabad demanding ex-PM Khan’s release.

Here is what the two measures mean, who now runs the province and how long the arrangement could last.

Who runs Khyber Pakhtunkhwa now?

Under the government’s decision, Governor Faisal Karim Kundi will assume the functions of the provincial government. Kundi belongs to the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), an ally of Sharif’s government.



Parliament — where Sharif’s Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz), the PPP and their other allies hold a majority — takes over the powers of the provincial assembly, where PTI has a majority. The chief minister, ministers, advisers, special assistants and advocate general “shall forthwith cease to hold office”, the proclamation says.

Hassan Abdullah Niazi, a Lahore-based lawyer and adjunct faculty member at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS), offered a different interpretation.

“However, this does not mean that the KP assembly or its elected Chief Minister have been permanently removed. It is more akin to thinking they are dysfunctional until the emergency is lifted, at which point they must be restored,” he told Al Jazeera.

Kundi will be assisted by an 11-member advisory council.

The army, already deployed in the province, is expected to assist the governor and his team maintain law and order.

A separate federal order has established a secretariat for 12 “designated districts”, most of them in the former tribal areas along the Afghan border.

It will be headed by an additional chief secretary, whose orders will carry the same legal effect as those of the provincial government.

“No province has been divided anywhere. It is only that these are the war-hit districts where more funding and more focus will be needed at this time, and for that this has been set apart,” Naqvi said at Sunday’s news conference.

The order also states that the constitutional provision requiring the judiciary to be separated from the executive “shall not apply” to the designated districts.

“The constitutional provision that mandates the separation of the judiciary from the executive has been suspended, allowing executive officers to perform judicial functions,” Rida Hosain, a Lahore-based constitutional lawyer, told Al Jazeera.

Why did the government invoke both measures?

Article 232 of Pakistan’s Constitution allows the president to declare an emergency when security is threatened by an “internal disturbance beyond the power of a Provincial Government to control”.

Article 234 applies when a governor reports that a province cannot be governed in accordance with the Constitution.

The proclamation cites “terrorist” attacks of “unprecedented level of violent intensity” and says the provincial government “has failed to demonstrate the ownership, will and intent to adequately deal with the menace of terrorism”.



According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based independent think-tank, militants carried out at least 1,066 attacks in Pakistan in 2025, up from 908 in 2024.

PICSS recorded 1,232 attacks nationwide in the first nine months of 2026, exceeding the total for all of 2025. The majority occurred in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, in the southwest.

“But this situation was so grave and exceptional that the requirements in both provisions, the conditions that demand them, were such that both provisions were exercised,” Tarar said.

Information Minister Ataullah Tarar went further, accusing the provincial government of links to armed groups.

“This was the carefully considered view, from start to finish, of all cabinet members that the PTI government in KP is hand in glove with the terrorists,” he said, without providing evidence.

Naqvi said the government had dozens of pieces of evidence against the provincial government. None has been made public.

PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan questioned why the measures applied across the province if the security concerns were concentrated in specific districts.

“If there is terrorism and an emergency is needed in 12 districts, then why is governor’s rule across the whole province?” he said at a news conference in Islamabad after the government’s briefing.

Taimur Jhagra, a PTI leader and former provincial finance minister, rejected the government’s allegations.

“Of course the provincial government was fighting terrorism. We own the fight against terrorism individually and collectively. If the issue was terrorism, then Balochistan should have had a state of emergency before KP,” he told Al Jazeera.

What has happened since Sunday?

PTI says that Sohail Afridi, the chief minister until Sunday, and other party leaders are under arrest.

“We know the CM, the provincial president Junaid Akbar, the Speaker Babar Swati, and some other leaders have been detained. The govt has not revealed where they are,” Jhagra said.

Naqvi had also indicated on Sunday that PTI figures could be detained.

“Definitely, them or whoever else is needed for law and order, to maintain it, we will take into protective custody. But those among them who are wanted will be arrested, and everyone else will be released as soon as law and order improves,” Naqvi said.

Tarar, relaying Naqvi’s position at the same news conference, said some PTI figures had already been taken into preventive custody.

PTI says several provincial ministers and lawmakers were detained even before Sunday.

Internet monitor NetBlocks reported late on Sunday that network data showed a major disruption to connectivity in parts of the province.

District administrations closed schools and colleges in Peshawar, Mardan, Swabi and Nowshera on Monday.

Meanwhile, in Punjab, Imran Khan’s sisters Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi have been held under arrest since September 20-21, under a public order law that allows detention for 30 days.

How long can the measures last?

Provinces have been placed under governor’s rule at least eight times since 1949. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, then known as the North-West Frontier Province, faced it in 1975 and 1994.



Because Zardari acted without a resolution from the provincial assembly, the Constitution requires both houses of Parliament to approve the emergency within 10 days, by October 21.

Sessions of the National Assembly and Senate have been called for Tuesday.

The emergency must also be placed before a joint sitting of Parliament within 30 days. It lapses after two months unless approved by the joint sitting.

Once approved, however, the Constitution sets no fixed end date. The emergency remains in force until it is revoked or a majority of the total membership of both houses votes against it.

Governor’s rule under Article 234 has a separate limit. Parliament can extend it in two-month increments, for a maximum of six months in total.

“The emergency provisions allow the executive to suspend certain fundamental rights, and there is no fixed time limit for how long an emergency can continue allowing for prolonged federal control,” Hosain said.

Gohar said PTI would challenge the measures in the courts and the assemblies.

“We have not formally called off the long march at all. Our struggle, as I told you, will absolutely continue,” he said.

World.title: Russia introduces drone classes in public schools
World.content:
NewsFeed Russia introduces drone classes in public schools

Russian public schools are now teaching children to assemble and fly drones as part of changes to the national curriculum brought in during Russia’s war with Ukraine. Al Jazeera’s Dmitry Medvedenko went to a Moscow classroom to see how patriotism is an increasing part of education.

World.title: Photos: Gaza mothers endure endless lines as famine fears persist
World.content:
Every morning, Palestinian mother Niyaha al‑Masri leaves her tent in Khan Younis and joins a long line outside a community kitchen, hoping that hours of waiting will end with a single meal for her family of 10.

More than a year after a “ceasefire” between Hamas and Israel was supposed to open the way for food into the devastated enclave, hunger still defines daily life for many Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

Without the kitchen run by humanitarian groups, al-Masri says, her family will have “nothing at all”. On a recent day, after six hours in the queue, she returned in the afternoon carrying four containers of rice, lentils and a small portion of chicken – the only meal the family would have that day.

World.title: Steve Smith breaks Test fielding record as Australia dominate South Africa
World.content:
Smith moves to 223 career catches, a record for fielders, as Australia bowl out South Africa for 284 in reply to 390.

Steve Smith has broken the Test record for the most career catches by a fielder as Australia have played themselves into a strong position on the third day of the first Test against hosts South Africa.

Smith held four catches on Sunday, taking his total to 223, as South Africa were bowled out for 284 in reply to Australia’s first innings of 390 at Kingsmead Stadium in Durban.

Nic Maddinson (17 not out) and Travis Head (10 not out) added 33 runs off just 5.4 overs to stretch Australia’s overall lead to 139 before bad light ended play for the third day in a row.

Maddinson, who laboured to a 33-ball duck in the first innings, hit two fours off Marco Jansen in the first over of the second innings and added a six off Wiaan Mulder before play was called off.

Australia’s bowlers applied relentless pressure on an easy-paced pitch and a succession of South African batsmen contributed to their own dismissals by playing poor shots.

Six Protea batters reached 30, but David Bedingham’s 49 was the top score.

Australian captain Pat Cummins took three for 54, and Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon claimed two wickets each as Australia’s long-serving bowling quartet combined with customary efficiency.

Smith special in the slips

Smith started the day on 219 catches, one behind Joe Root of England.

He equalled the record when he caught Temba Bavuma. Smith, playing in his 126th Test, broke the record when he lunged to his left from second slip to hold a sharp edge from Bedingham off Cummins.

Smith was in the action again with a spectacular catch to dismiss Verreynne, again anticipating well at slip as the South African wicketkeeper made good contact with a reverse sweep that Smith held in an outstretched right hand.



His fourth catch was from an edge to slip by last man Anrich Nortje off the bowling of Beau Webster.

Smith’s career haul of 223 catches exceeds the total of all but 11 specialist wicketkeepers.

World.title: India opposition plans New Delhi protest to demand election chief resign
World.content:
Thousands of security personnel have been deployed across New Delhi in advance of protest calling for the election chief’s resignation.

Authorities have closed half a dozen Delhi Metro stations and warned of traffic disruptions in New Delhi as opposition parties prepare to march to the Supreme Court to protest against a controversial revision of voter lists that has led to disruptions in the Indian capital.

Thousands of police officers and security personnel were deployed across central New Delhi on Monday for a third straight day, erecting heavy metal barricades and closing key metro rail stations in advance of a march called by Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in Lok Sabha, the lower house of Parliament.

Opposition parties and supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) youth movement have taken to the streets almost daily this month to demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over revisions to voter lists that critics say benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Police detained thousands of protesters over the weekend as supporters of the youth-led movement attempted to hold a protest march but were stopped by security personnel, with thousands of people detained.

The Election Commission of India (ECI), which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing.

Opposition figures have accused authorities of trying to suppress dissent through mass detentions.

Parliamentarian John Brittas of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) alleged he was “manhandled, dragged, assaulted” by police during the demonstrations on Sunday.



“This is not merely an assault on an MP. It is an assault on democratic freedoms and the rule of law,” he said.

Police did not respond to questions about the detentions or their actions during a news conference on Sunday.

Several journalists covering the protest said they were also detained despite prominently displaying their press cards.

International NGO Reporters Without Borders said at least 16 journalists were “brutally” detained while covering the protests over the weekend.

“Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police’s actions against the press are unacceptable,” it said in a statement.

Gandhi, a Congress party leader, urged supporters to join Monday’s march to the Supreme Court to press for Kumar’s resignation.

“Bring as much police as you want — 10 thousand, 20 thousand, 40 thousand, go ahead. Call as many BJP-RSS goons as you need,” he said in a post on X directed at Home Minister Amit Shah.

“We are not the ones to get scared. We are not the ones to back down. This fight is not going to stop now!”

The leaders of the youth-led CJP movement, which has millions of social media followers, have also pledged to continue their protests until Kumar steps down.

The protests have become one of the most significant political challenges for Modi in his 12 years in power, bringing together opposition parties, student groups and activists angered by the voter roll revisions.

The revisions resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say minorities, particularly Muslims, were disproportionately affected.

The ECI says the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

World.title: Alvarez vs M’billi boxing bout to go ahead in Saudi Arabia despite attacks
World.content:
Mexican boxer tells Turki Al-Sheikh he ‘fears nothing’ and will face M’billi in Riyadh on October 31 ‘no matter what’.

Share Canelo Alvarez ‘will fight in Riyadh’ despite attacks on Saudi airports on social media

The world title fight featuring Saul “Canelo” ‌‌Alvarez and Christian M’billi will go ahead this month in Saudi Arabia despite attacks on the country’s airports, which have killed at least 14 people in Riyadh in two days, Saudi sports promoter Turki Al-Sheikh confirms.

Alvarez vs M’billi is scheduled for October 31 in the Saudi capital, which has repeatedly come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis, but Al-Sheikh sought to allay the doubts over the bout on Sunday.

One person was killed and 11 were injured on Sunday when a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).

A Houthi strike on the same airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured more than 300, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
