World.title: Optics tell it all: Why William Ruto looks tell of a desperate politician
World.content:
President William Ruto has taken on a worrying look of late – sweating profusely, eyes wild and blazing, teeth bared in a rictus smile, absolutely furious, panicking and shouting, and with no apparent control of what comes out of his mouth. Things fall apart, and this is the look and sound of a desperate man. And optics matter.

World.title: Ruto wades into growing ODM-UDA conflict
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto marks Mazingira Day by planting trees in Elgon downs, Trans-Nzoia County. [PCS]

President William Ruto delved into the growing tension among Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and United Democratic Alliance (UDA) contenders in the Coast and asked them to tone it down during his recent tour of the region.

Speaking hours before he wound up his eight-day tour, Ruto appeared to notice the widening cracks and told politicians within the two parties to embrace a ceasefire and unite against the opposition.

The head of state, who is facing a formidable challenge from the united opposition, warned that divisions in the ODM and UDA could weaken their team, whose union gives it a chance to win the 2027 general election.

“ODM and UDA are one team, and you should accommodate each other under a broad-based government. We should not allow divisions in ODM and UDA to undermine our unity of purpose,” he stated.

His statement appeared to be directed at the growing tensions among contenders, particularly in Kwale, Mombasa and Kilifi counties where prominent politicians face challengers within the ODM and UDA political union.

President Ruto’s earlier attempt to zone the region in favour of sitting governors is also blamed for the cracks in the broad-based team at the Coast.

In Mombasa County, UDA secretary general Mr Hassan Omar has already rejected a plan by the so-called broad-based team to support governor Abdulswamd Nassir’s re-election.

Omar, who is also a member of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) insisted that he will challenge Mr Nassir.

Already, businessman and EALA member Mr Suleiman Shahbal has quit ODM after he left he could not get the party ticket as the president's allies favour Nassir, a deputy party leader.

Shhabal has since aligned himself to former Laikipia governor Mr Murithi Nderitu’s Kenya Reform Party even as he insisted that he will be on the ballot.

In Mombasa, Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs Cabinet Secretary Mr Hassan Joho and governor Nassir appeared to be handing over Coast which was the ODM leader late Raila Odinga’s political turf, to President Ruto.

“This region stands with Ruto because he has dignified us with title deeds and many other development projects. We however expect him to support us when we seek the presidential seat in 2032,” Joho said.

Joho’s elder brother Abubakar Joho, who is a prominent businessman, has also joined the campaign for President Ruto.

While touring Kwale, Ruto addressed the growing noise among the main contenders, Governor Fatuma Achani (UDA), Prof Hamadi Boga and Engineer Lung’anzi Chai (ODM) after the broad-based leaders appeared to settle for Ms Achani who has the backing of Sports CS and former Kwale governor Salim Mvurya.

After witnessing the rising political tension, Ruto changed tone and told the three contenders to directly seek support from the voters rather than relying on external political backing.

In a complete change of heart and political tact, Ruto emphasised that the power to choose leaders ultimately belongs to the electorate, who will evaluate candidates based on their track record and development agenda for the region.

“You should all seek votes from the people and not rely on external backing. What I need from all of you is your support,” he stated.

For long, Governor Achani has enjoyed unwavering backing of President Ruto, Mvurya and recently Joho, who had preferred Kwale to be zoned in favour of the governor and UDA.

But Prof Boga, who has been Mr Joho’s ally, described the broad-based government’s zoning arrangement as undemocratic and a coercion to the Kwale electorate who he said should be allowed to choose their leaders without external interference.

Boga has been critical about the attempt to stop some aspirants from contesting seats in the broad-based government, noting that it was possible to zone candidates and difficult to do so for the voters.

In a statement, Boga noted that former Gender CS and Kilifi governor aspirant Ms Aisha Jumwa’s recent departure from UDA to Wiper Patriotic Front (WPF) reflected a growing sense among a segment of coastal leaders that decisions about their political future are increasingly being made elsewhere, then handed down as settled outcomes rather than negotiated realities.

“Zoning at the Coast is a fantasy: You can zone candidates but you cannot zone the voters,” Boga had warned.

“And if UDA and ODM are not paying attention to that signal, they may be underestimating the political consequences of their emerging arrangements at the Coast. “There is a dangerous assumption taking root in the broad-based arrangement: that coastal politics can be settled around a table in Nairobi and then delivered to voters as a finished political package. You take this seat, we take that one, and the voters will follow,” he added.

Boga, who came second in the 2022 governor poll, warned that if the Coast is mishandled, the problem will not necessarily be that voters have suddenly embraced another political formation, but the greater danger is that voters may decide that none of the established arrangements speak for them, creating either a rebellion or apathy.

In Kilifi County, the broad-based team publicly worked with Governor Gideon Mung’aro, forcing Ms Jumwa, his main challenger, to quit the government team in protest.

Kilifi Senate aspirant Mr Stephen Kahocho and Ganze parliamentary aspirant Ms Zawadi Kingi have publicly warned that they might be forced to quit UDA and vie as independent candidates or join other political formations.

This is after it emerged that the broad-based arrangement was behind Mung’aro (ODM), Kilifi senator Stewart Madzayo (ODM) and Ganze MP Kenneth Kazungu Tungule of Pamoja African Alliance (PAA), an affiliate of UDA.

World.title: Kalonzo to Ruto: You have no numbers
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka speaks during launch of economic empowerment equipment distribution at Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos town on October 9, 2026. [John Muia, Standard]

The united opposition will deal President William Ruto a humiliating defeat in next year’s general election, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka has predicted.

Speaking Friday in his Ukambani backyard during an empowerment equipment handover ceremony hosted by Governor Wavinya Ndeti at the Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos, Kalonzo declared the opposition will defeat Ruto at the ballot ‘no matter what magic he (Ruto) deploys.

“Ruto has been cornered. We have heard him suggesting that they will import foreigners from neighboring countries to vote for him but even so, he will not secure the numbers. We in the united opposition have committed to produce a single candidate that will face Ruto at the ballot,” Kalonzo said.

Recognizing the need to consolidate his lower Eastern vote bloc, Kalonzo rallied the Akamba community to come out in huge numbers to register as voters in the upcoming voter listing initiative by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).

“It is the time to redeem this country. The IEBC will as from next month undertake the final leg of voter registration and I urge all eligible voters to apply for national identity cards and register as voters,” he said, vowing he will defeat Ruto in Luo Nyanza.

Kalonzo called out Ruto over what he termed as the president’s habit of making empty promises to Kenyans. “The other day I heard Ruto promising thousands of dams across the country. He should come for benchmarking in Machakos. Retired President Mwai Kibaki and I secured African Development Bank (ADB) funding for the construction of Yatta Dam and now he has ten months left in office. When will he build?” he posed.

Former Attorney General Justin Muturi, who flanked Kalonzo, declared time was fast running out for the opposition to identify and name its presidential flag bearer for the next year’s general election.

The DP party leader, who has gone public declaring his choice of Kalonzo as the presidential ticket bearer for the opposition expressed his frustrations for the opposition’s dillydallying in naming its flag bearer.

“We (the opposition) are tired of singing one song for years that we will produce and name one person to face Ruto. When you see us here another day, do not entertain such kind of talk. Demand that it is Kalonzo for State House,” said Muturi.

During the ceremony, Governor Wavinya Ndeti unveiled assorted empowerment equipment targeting about 6000 beneficiaries across the county.

Addressing residents during the forum, Wavinya jeered at UDA-allied politicians who have been dishing out cash handouts to residents, terming it untenable.

“It is time to demonstrate to those who are approaching our people with cheap hand-outs that when the people of Machakos are given the tools to work, they produce real wealth. My commitment is that I will continue allocating resources to asset-based empowerment until every household in Machakos enjoys economic dignity,” Wavinya said.

World.title: Revealed: 84 Kenyans killed, 52 missing in Russia-Ukraine war
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi. [File,Standard]

The government has records of 354 Kenyans linked to the Russia-Ukraine war, including 84 classified as killed or missing in action and five being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine.

Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign and Diaspora Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi gave the updated figures in a response to Parliament on the recruitment of Kenyans into the Russian military and the detention of Kenyans in Ukraine on Thursday, October 8.

The records show that 77 Kenyans remain on the front lines, 38 are in camps, 52 have an unknown or unclassified location and 34 are hospitalised.

Another 62 Kenyans have been repatriated, while one is in detention and another has completed a military contract.

The government said Russia has stopped the enlistment of additional Kenyans after Kenya secured the country’s placement on Russia’s ‘Stop List’ during Mudavadi’s visit to Moscow in March.

“The Embassy of Kenya in Moscow has since confirmed that no additional Kenyan nationals have been enlisted in the Special Military Operation following the implementation of the Stop List,” Mudavadi said.

Russian authorities have told Kenya that requests to terminate military contracts will be considered on a case-by-case basis by individual military unit commanders.

Mudavadi said Kenya continues to engage Russian authorities and affected families over the burial, cremation or repatriation of remains after Russia said its Defence Ministry could not meet the cost of repatriating the remains of deceased Kenyans.

Five Kenyans held in Ukraine

Five Kenyan nationals are currently being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine, according to information sent to Kenya by the Ukrainian Embassy in Vienna on September 3.

The government identified them as Evans Kibet, detained since May 2025; Willi Muniu Macharia, detained since November 2025; Haron Kibet Pachenge, detained since March 2026; Joseph, detained since April 2026; and Francis Ndarua Ndungu.

Kenya’s Honorary Consul in Ukraine visited the Zakhid 1 prisoner-of-war camp and reported that the detainees were being held in humane conditions, had access to medical services and were being treated under rules governing prisoners of war.

The government also said Ukraine was holding the remains of four other Kenyans.

They are Simon Gitau, Clinton Nyapara Mogesa, Dennis Bagaka Obwori and Eric Mwangi Nyambura.

Kenya is seeking the release and repatriation of the affected Kenyans through diplomatic channels, including engagement with Ukraine and the International Committee of the Red Cross.

The government wants Kenyans held as prisoners of war to be considered as possible victims of international human trafficking.

Mudavadi said many of the affected Kenyans reported that recruiters lured them with promises of employment before they ended up in military service.

The government says the circumstances surrounding their recruitment could fit the definition of trafficking under Article 3(a) of the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, also known as the Palermo Protocol.

It wants the issue considered during negotiations over their repatriation so the Kenyans can access assistance available to trafficking victims.

President William Ruto has also raised the matter directly with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a telephone conversation, according to the government.

Kenya has further received approval from Kyiv for its ambassador to Ukraine, with the government saying this will improve its ability to respond to cases involving Kenyans in the country.

The State Department for Diaspora Affairs said families should report cases to the government as soon as communication with relatives in Russia is disrupted.

Once a family reports a case, the department collects identification details, travel information and next-of-kin contacts before referring the case to the Kenyan Embassy in Moscow for verification.

The government has also facilitated the return of 62 Kenyans who had been involved in Russia’s military operations.

It has provided affected families with updates from diplomatic missions, information on compensation processes, psychosocial support and guidance on the repatriation or burial of remains.

The government said it is also expanding measures to prevent deceptive recruitment by providing pre-departure information, urging Kenyans to verify recruitment agencies and employment offers and strengthening emergency assistance through Kenyan diplomatic missions.

The scale of the recruitment first emerged publicly in February when Parliament was told that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been recruited to fight for Russia.

The National Intelligence Service report presented to lawmakers said recruiters targeted former security personnel and civilians with promises of lucrative employment, salaries and bonuses.

The figures at the time included 89 Kenyans on the frontline, 39 hospitalised, 28 missing in action, 35 in camps or bases, 30 repatriated, one detained and one who had completed a contract.

The government then stepped up diplomatic efforts. In March, Kenya announced an agreement with Russia to stop further enlistment of Kenyans into its military operations and to facilitate consular support and voluntary disengagement for Kenyans already serving.

The issue remains unresolved for many families. More than 30 families affected by the recruitment were reported this week to be seeking a meeting with President Ruto before Kenya's delegation travels to Moscow for the Russia-Africa Summit, demanding answers on missing relatives, repatriation of survivors and the return of remains.

World.title: Wajir patient isolated over suspected viral haemorrhagic fever
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The patient, a resident of Habaswein in Wajir South Sub-County, is currently admitted at Albadar Nursing Home. [File, Standard]

A 20-year-old man in Habaswein, Wajir County, has been isolated after presenting with symptoms consistent with a suspected viral haemorrhagic fever, following recent travel from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

The patient, a resident of Habaswein in Wajir South Sub-County, is currently admitted at Albadar Nursing Home, where he is being treated after developing fever, headache and cough. He was also found to have severe anaemia, with a haemoglobin level of 4g/dL.

According to a disease surveillance report filed at Habaswein Police Station, the patient told health officials that he had recently travelled to the DRC, where he worked as a “tan boy” on a cargo truck or trailer.

He reportedly developed fever and headache while still in the DRC on September 2, 2026, before traveling by trailer to Uganda, where he stayed for about five days and sought medical attention.

The report states that he was treated with antibiotics in Uganda before travelling by trailer to Malaba. From Malaba, he travelled by motorcycle to a relative's residence, where he stayed for approximately five days.

He later travelled by trailer to Nairobi and proceeded by bus to Isiolo, where he stayed for about 10 days before travelling to Habaswein by Probox vehicle. He arrived in the town around September 20.

Upon arrival, the patient sought treatment at Hilac Medical Clinic, where he was managed for pneumonia and septicaemia for about three days.

However, his condition did not improve and he was subsequently transferred to Albadar Nursing Home, where he remains admitted.

The report adds that the patient is receiving intravenous Augmentin and paracetamol and has been transfused with two units of whole blood.

“Despite the above interventions, the patient remains clinically unwell and sick-looking,” the report states.

Authorities have since placed the patient in isolation as investigations continue to establish the cause of his illness.

“Sample collection has been completed, and the specimen will be shipped to National Public Health Laboratories tonight,” the report states.

World.title: Complainant letters cannot be used to initiate judge's removal, court rules
World.content:
Chief Justice Martha Koome. [File]

A letter addressed to the Chief Justice seeking administrative intervention cannot form the basis for removing a judge, the Employment and Labour Relations Court (ELRC) has ruled.

Delivering a unanimous judgment in a case filed by Environment and Land Court Judge Anthony Ombwayo, a three-judge ELRC bench comprising Justices Jemimah Keli, Onesmus Makau, and Dr. Jacob Gikeri ruled that a letter written to the Chief Justice cannot simply be forwarded to the Judicial Service Commission (JSC) and treated as a petition for removal.

World.title: How KNEC plans to stop cheating in 2026 exams
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) Chief Executive Officer Dr David Njengere. [File]

The Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) will use smart padlocks to secure all examination storage containers as more than 3.6 million candidates sit the 2026 national examinations and assessments.

KNEC Chief Executive Officer Dr David Njengere said the council would monitor the containers from its headquarters to prevent anyone from accessing examination papers before the scheduled times.

“Last year KNEC piloted the use of smart padlocks in 250 containers. This year all containers will be secured using the smart padlocks which will be monitored from the KNEC headquarters,” said Dr Njengere.

Under the system, officials will open containers at designated times. Officials will access Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA) and Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA) papers at 6 a.m., while centre managers will collect Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) papers at 7 a.m. and 12:30 p.m.

However, Dr Njengere identified mobile phones as the biggest challenge in preventing examination malpractice.

“Mobile phones remain our biggest challenge in administration of KCSE examination,” observed Dr Njengere.

He warned that the council would not allow candidates or examination officials to have mobile phones at examination centres during examination sessions.

“Any contravention of this rule will constitute a malpractice as per the KNEC Act and the Rules and Regulations,” noted Dr Njengere.

The council will deploy 342,005 contracted professionals to administer and manage the examinations and assessments. They include centre managers, supervisors, invigilators, security officers and drivers.

For KCSE, KNEC will deploy 10,765 centre managers, 12,274 supervisors, 57,432 invigilators and 21,388 security officers. Each examination centre will have at least two police officers.

Centre managers will collect KCSE papers twice a day, and KNEC will place morning and afternoon papers in marked cartons to reduce mix-ups and unauthorised access.

KNEC has personalised question papers with candidates’ details, and examiners will receive anonymised scripts with those details removed.

The 2026 examination and assessment season will involve 3,634,846 candidates, a 6.13 per cent increase from the 3,424,836 registered in 2025.

KCSE rehearsals will take place on Friday, October 16. Examinations for papers with low candidature will run from Monday, October 19 to Friday, October 30, while papers with large candidature will run from Monday, November 2 to Friday, November 20.

KPSEA and KJSEA assessments will run from Monday, October 26 to Friday, October 30.

KNEC Chairperson Prof. Julius Nyabundi said the council was preparing for possible disruption from El Nino rains.

“As we start off the 2026 field administration season, one of the risks we contend with are the attempts to cheat in assessments and examination,” said Prof. Nyabundi.

He urged candidates, parents and examination officials to protect the integrity of the examinations, warning that malpractice could undermine public confidence in the education system.

“Cheating in examinations undermines public confidence in the credibility, fairness and quality of the entire education system,” noted Prof. Nyabundi.

KNEC will operate a 24-hour call centre with toll-free numbers for candidates, officials and members of the public to report incidents and seek assistance during the examination period.

The 2026 cycle will continue the implementation of Competency-Based Education assessments, including School-Based Assessments in primary, junior and senior school.

Grade 10 learners are undertaking their first School-Based Assessment, which will contribute 15 marks towards the Kenya Certificate of Basic Education.

World.title: PM reviews impact of urban development projects ahead of Egypt Forum 2026
World.content:
The government will use sessions at the Egypt Forum 2026 to present accurate data, address public concerns and answer citizens’ questions, while setting out clear priorities and timelines for the next phase of development, the Cabinet said Sunday.

The announcement came during a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly to review the main topics of a forum session on “Sustainable Urban Development and Its Impact on Improving Citizens’ Quality of Life.”

The forum is scheduled to take place in the New Capital from Oct. 19 to 24.

The meeting was attended by Minister of Local Development and Environment Manal Awad, Minister of Housing, Utilities and Urban Communities Randa al-Menshawy, Deputy Minister of Transport for Railways and Electric Traction Wagdi Radwan, Deputy Minister of Housing for Utilities Ahmed Omran, Assistant Head of the Armed Forces Engineering Authority Ahmed Zaki, and other concerned officials.

Madbouly said the session would review development in unsafe and unplanned areas, the construction of new cities, road and transport projects, infrastructure initiatives, and the presidential “Decent Life” initiative to develop Egyptian rural villages.

“What matters to us in this session is examining the impact of all these projects on citizens’ lives,” Madbouly said, adding that the discussion would address public concerns, challenges facing the sector, the state’s development targets for the coming period, and implementation timelines for strengthening urban infrastructure.

The government reaffirmed that the forum’s sessions would be based on accurate facts and data, with an emphasis on transparency and open discussion.

It said citizens would be treated as active partners in understanding current challenges and development efforts and in shaping a roadmap for the next phase, supported by clear objectives and specific timelines.

World.title: ‘Trump is dragging the party down’: GOP scrambles to stop steep midterm losses
World.content:
The Republican Party’s midterm campaign has turned into a triage operation just three weeks out from November, as officials race to avert losses in a string of once-safe seats that they increasingly fear could cost them total control of Congress.

The worsening landscape has alarmed GOP operatives across several battleground states, forcing the party to pour resources into traditionally red districts and states at the expense of their once-expansive ambitions in Democratic areas.

And after months of pressing President Donald Trump to ramp up his travel on behalf of key candidates, some Republicans now worry he’s grown so unpopular that his presence on the campaign trail may in some cases be doing more harm than good.

One House Republican running for re-election said of the president’s numbers: “Trump is dragging the party down.”

The grim outlook gripping the GOP follows weeks of polling showing Republicans on track to lose the House amid intense voter anger over the Iran war and rising cost of living — and at grave risk of losing their once-solid majority in the Senate as well.

A damaged port and storage warehouse facility is seen following a US military strike in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province on September 6, 2026. Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images

The widening number of competitive races has complicated Republican leaders’ plans to make up ground by unleashing hundreds of millions of dollars down the stretch. Despite a massive cash advantage fueled in part by pro-Trump super PAC, MAGA Inc., the spending so far has failed to significantly shift Republicans’ fortunes as more money gets diverted toward races once counted on as comfortable wins.

Already, the Senate Leadership Fund, the top GOP super PAC in Senate races, has suspended its ad reservations in North Carolina and plowed at least $10 million into Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. It also recently invested $5 million in South Carolina to boost incumbent Sen. Darline Graham amid concerns among some Republicans she’s losing ground to Democrat Annie Andrews in the deep red state.

That’s on top of the more than $100 million that the Senate Leadership Fund has spent in Texas to boost Ken Paxton, who is scrambling to shore up GOP support in his race with Democrat James Talarico after a bruising primary campaign. Trump himself has now traveled to Texas three times in one month to rally voters on Paxton’s behalf.

“We were all hoping the war was going to be over now, but it’s not,” said one Trump adviser. “We shouldn’t have a fight in a place like Texas, but obviously we do.”

Top Republicans steering spending on the House side are also expected to narrow their focus in the coming days, doubling down on races they see as winnable while slashing their investment in candidates whose fortunes are fading, multiple people familiar with the matter said.

That winnowing will mark the latest acknowledgment of the challenge facing Republicans — and an effort to concentrate resources on the select candidates capable of defending their seats, or flipping blue districts, and limiting Democrats’ encroachment overall.

The Cook Political Report dealt the latest blow on Friday, moving 18 House races toward Democrats. Those contests include five toss-up seats across Iowa, Pennsylvania and Washington that the closely watched analysis projects the Democratic candidates are now more likely to win.

The Senate map has also provided little reassurance for the GOP. Paxton is suffering a drip-drip of damaging audio leaks from a private fundraiser, further frustrating Republican officials who already believe he’s running a poor campaign. Democrats hold polling leads in swing states like Georgia and North Carolina, while making insurgent runs in solidly red states like Alaska and even Kansas.

President Donald Trump greets Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton at a campaign rally at the Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio, on Wednesday. Alex Brandon/AP

“I don’t know that the environment could possibly get worse than it is,” said Jason Roe, a Michigan GOP strategist advising Rep. Tom Barrett, who is in a neck-and-neck race against Democratic challenger Will Lawrence. “If we lose this, it couldn’t have been won.”

Inside the White House, Trump and his top advisers are clear-eyed about the difficult odds of keeping the House and the rising threat to the Senate majority, people familiar with the matter said.

But there is still optimism that Republicans can limit their losses and turn the prospect of a blue wave into little more than a ripple. Trump advisers expect the polls to tighten in swing races in the campaign’s final days, especially as more ads hit the airwaves and less-engaged Republican voters begin to tune in.

“I’m not saying we are going to f***ing win, it is going to be so great. No, I am not saying that. But do we get wiped out? No, we aren’t gonna get wiped out,” said another House Republican running for re-election.

Some strong GOP candidates are likely to outperform the generic ballot polling that shows Democrats favored by a healthy margin, the people familiar argued. At the same time, they’re counting on a handful of far-left Democratic candidates to underperform. And even at the current margins, they note, the difference between Republicans losing the House or expanding their majority is only a matter of a few percentage points across a handful of races.

“This election is going to come down to one side saying Republicans have not cleaned their mess up fast enough, and what we are saying is, ‘We know you are struggling, but these are the things we are doing to make your life better and, by the way, they are crazy,” another Republican told CNN.

For his part, Speaker Mike Johnson has vowed to do everything he can to hold the majority and is campaigning in more than 40 districts and 20 states leading up to the election.

“Speaker Johnson is not slowing down and helping to get resources to every district that will decide the majority,” Johnson’s political communications director, Greg Steele, said in a statement to CNN.

While Trump has largely steered clear of swing districts of late, he has shown newfound enthusiasm for the campaign trail that his advisers have rushed to take advantage of, sending him to favorable areas across the country where they believe he can help GOP turnout. They’ve shrugged off any talk of Trump needing to lay low given his sagging approval ratings, arguing that the midterms are going to be a referendum on his presidency no matter what.

“The panic is unwarranted and it’s unfounded,” one White House official said of the GOP’s midterm trajectory. “It’s all going to come down to who has the ability to turn out their low-propensity voters. … That’s why we’re going where we’re going: To jazz up the base.”

In a statement, White House spokesman Davis Ingle called Trump “the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party.”

National Republican Congressional Committee spokesman Mike Marinella said in a statement, “House Republicans have a more favorable map, a stronger ground game, historic fundraising and spending advantages and battle-tested incumbents while Democrats are stuck dragging their unelectable socialist nominees across the finish line.”

A senior Republican National Committee official argued that pollsters and strategists are writing off the GOP’s chances in the midterms too soon.

“The first ones to rush and get on the phone with you all in these times are not the ones in the fight,” the official told CNN. “They would rather just say nobody knows what they are doing and everything is doomed than take an objective look at what is happening.”

Trump’s rallies — which included a stop in Texas on Thursday and a trip to upstate New York on Friday to stump for gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman — have bolstered Trump’s mood and view of Republicans’ chances, the White House official and others familiar with his comments said.

Republican gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman visits a deli as he campaigns against New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on October 2, 2026, in New York. Spencer Platt/Getty Images

Nevertheless, Trump has tacitly acknowledged that his presence may not be helpful everywhere at a time when large majorities are frustrated with his economic policies and oppose the Iran war.

The president has declined to rebuke GOP candidates who have broken with him on the war and tariffs out of an understanding that they “need to run a campaign,” the White House official said — though those Republicans have still typically cleared the move with the White House ahead of time.

Trump has also stayed away from some races where vulnerable Republicans have tried to carve out an identity separate from him, such as Maine Sen. Susan Collins. The president isn’t currently expected to travel to Maine ahead of the midterms, people familiar with the matter said, though they cautioned his schedule fluctuates and that could change.

Still, there’s little expectation that any GOP candidate can fully escape the gravitational pull that Trump has exerted on the political landscape since returning to the White House.

And after nearly two years of demands for GOP unity, Trump advisers have counseled Republicans that their best hope in the final weeks is to make their own pitches for why they should get another term in Congress — and crucially, what they plan to do once they’re there to assuage voters’ frustrations.

“We’re fighting it out individually now,” the Trump adviser said. “It’s ugly out there for both sides, and it’s going to be hand-to-hand combat.”

World.title: Trump’s diesel deal with Putin drives a wedge through the Western alliance
World.content:
Moscow — By agreeing to open Russia’s taps and release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel into a starving global market, the Kremlin has achieved something that raw military might on the battlefields of eastern Ukraine could never deliver.

The deal, which involves suspending fuel export sanctions on Russia for six months to allow for diesel sales at market prices, will be a welcome boon for a Russian economy that is creaking under the strain of a war in Ukraine that has dragged on far longer than anticipated.

But for Vladimir Putin, Russia’s strongman president, the real benefit isn’t the billions of dollars in fresh revenue. It is the wedge this deal, and the rhetoric around it, drives right through the heart of the Western alliance, which has aimed to isolate Moscow over its war in Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump spelled out the new and extraordinary reality in stark terms as he mocked the angry reaction of Ukraine’s wartime leader, Volodymyr Zelensky, who derided the deal as a “weak decision by a strong partner” that provides “extra money for this war.”

“We said you can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused and he wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers,” Trump said before calling for a new Ukrainian leader, essentially blaming high global fuel prices, especially acute in the United States, on Ukraine.

Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney sided with Zelensky as the two leaders spoke on Sunday, saying that the agreement stands “in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe.”

In recent months, relentless Ukrainian drone strikes, flying deep into Russian territory with terrifying precision, have systematically crippled oil refineries that serve as both the economic engine and the fuel tank for Russia’s military.

Amid domestic fuel shortages and severe production cuts, the Kremlin suspended all diesel exports this month so that it had enough for its own needs — a stunning setback for a country that used to be the second-biggest diesel exporter in the world before the Ukraine war.

Whether Russia can actually provide the promised diesel or not, by framing the Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries as an assault on American interests, Washington is effectively aligning its economic priorities with Moscow’s survival — even as analysts have suggested the deal is unlikely to dramatically move the needle on diesel prices.

The US has powerful levers it can pull to get Ukraine to play ball.

Zelensky at a memorial ceremony to honor the victims of the Nazis during World War II in Kyiv on October 6. Genya Savilov/AFP/Getty Images Putin hosts a ceremony to present state awards to mentors and teachers of participants in Russia’s military action in Ukraine, at the Kremlin on October 5. Kristina Solovyova/AFP/Pool/Getty Images

Washington no longer provides money and weapons to Kyiv. But vital American intelligence sharing — the digital backbone of Ukrainian defense — risks being cut off if Ukraine now continues to strike at the Russian infrastructure Trump wants left untouched. The threat is real — the US did just that in the wake of the notorious Oval Office blowup last year.

Mindful of the risk , Zelensky has indicated he is willing to cooperate, but only if Russia does the same. “Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelensky said in a recent statement.

For Ukraine, this entire episode may seem like yet another bitter, existential betrayal by an American leader who has at times acknowledged a begrudging respect for Kyiv’s bold military tactics. Now, its most effective asymmetric weapon — relentless drone strikes on oil refineries — is being undermined and may be neutralized, not by Russian anti-air batteries, but by American diplomatic pressure along with Trump’s irrepressible urge to do a deal with the Kremlin.

In Moscow, on the other hand, the mood is upbeat.

“The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large,” Putin said in an official statement after a prearranged telephone call with Trump on Friday night.

“I am convinced this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy,” he added.

Privately, the Kremlin leader must be rubbing his hands with glee.

Both he and Trump want Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries to immediately stop.

Both want Ukraine’s president to be replaced with someone who will agree a quick deal.

Smoke rises from a drone attack on the area around Russian oil producer Gazprom Neft’s Moscow oil refinery as seen from Dzerzhinsky on September 20. AFP/Getty Images

And just a few weeks after Trump signed a bill into law, sponsored by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, allowing for punishing sanctions to be imposed on any country that bought Russian oil, Washington has now become a customer itself.

All at once, it seems, a battered but relatively unified Western front that has stood against resource-rich Moscow for more than four years looks like it is being dealt another powerful blow.

World.title: Saudi Arabia will have to respond to Houthi airport attack – but the choices are stark
World.content:
As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis continue to wreak havoc on the kingdom.

The kingdom launched a major offensive last week to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis, but the rebels have so far held their ground.

Instead, they have escalated their campaign against the kingdom, culminating in Saturday’s missile attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 13 people.

Drawing from Iran’s playbook in its conflict with the United States, the Houthis are vowing a painful escalation, targeting critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and imposing a global economic cost.

Members of the Saudi security forces take part in a military parade in Mecca on May 21, 2026. Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty Images

The Houthis have longstanding grievances against Saudi Arabia over Riyadh’s decade-long war against the group, which triggered the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. The recent Houthi escalation, however, is increasingly seen as an extension of Iran’s conflict with Washington.

After eleven years of trying to contain the Houthi advance militarily and through talks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khaled bin Salman, face limited options. Across the border, the rebels have grown more powerful, consolidating control over major cities and pushing to seize others, such as the densely populated Taiz.

“This threat has to be dealt with once and for all,” Ali Shihabi, an author and commentator on Saudi politics told CNN. “A lot will depend on the performance of the Yemeni government troops on the ground and Saudi is helping them extensively with air power.”

A plume of smoke rises during a reported airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital Sanaa. AFP/Getty Images

So far, Saudi Arabia has largely confined its role to providing air cover for the anti-Houthi Yemeni coalition, stopping short of any major deployment of its own troops on the ground. Whether that restraint will hold after Saturday’s strike on Riyadh remains an open question.

Sending large numbers of Saudi troops into Yemen would plunge the kingdom into a an expensive and grinding ground war across rugged terrain and undercut the image Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is carefully cultivating of a stable, investment-friendly kingdom and global tourism hub.

Better missile capability

Barely two decades ago, the Houthis were little more than a small religious revivalist movement. With Iranian backing, they have since grown into a formidable fighting force in possession of ballistic missiles and capable of striking as far away as Tel Aviv.

“They’ve developed their warfare,” a southern Yemeni official who fought the Houthis for years told CNN. “They’ve gotten more sophisticated in their attacks, they’re persistent and they’ve enhanced their intelligence.”

Yemen’s government alleges that Houthi rebels have worked with Iranian Revolutionary Guard experts to modify missiles into more effective weapons.

The new missiles fly faster and use a thermal-tracking system to home in on any heat source, Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemen’s armed forces, said. It remains unclear whether such missiles were used during Saturday’s attack on Riyadh airport.

The Houthis’ pursuit of more sophisticated weapons may now be extending into artificial intelligence.

AI company Anthropic said a group based in northern Yemen used its Claude AI tools to help develop guidance software for rockets and missiles – the systems that steer and stabilize the weapons in flight. The report did not identify those involved, but their location in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen suggests a possible link to the rebels.

Seeking international support

Saudi Arabia has sought support from partners across the world to counter the group. France, Britain and Pakistan have committed support, while other allies like Turkey are considering sending help.

Prince Mohammed has also reportedly turned to Syria for help. Its president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had led armed factions that successfully drove Iranian-backed groups from Syria after nearly a decade of civil war.

Yet Riyadh’s biggest ally, the US, has not supported air strikes on the Houthis, instead sending more than 100 military advisers to provide intelligence under a newly formed joint command.

US President Donald Trump shakes hands with Crown Prince and Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia Mohammed bin Salman. Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

Last year Washington reached a ceasefire with the Iran-backed group that reopened the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the maritime chokepoint through which global trade flows between Asia and Europe, to US vessels. Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month, urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but the president declined to intervene.

“Clearly, direct US involvement via air power would help because US aircraft can respond to US satellite intelligence more rapidly,” Shihabi said. “Saudi aircraft… are one stop removed from that loop so US involvement would be helpful.”

Saudi Arabia, one of the largest countries in the Middle East, remains vulnerable despite procuring some of the most advanced US air defenses. Its infrastructure, which carries rich resources across vast desert terrain, leaves it an easy target for the cheaper one-way drones developed by the Houthis.

Among those killed in the Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport was an American citizen, the Saudi civil aviation body said Sunday – an attack that might draw Trump further into the war.

“The Saudis are good fighters,” Trump told reporters following the attack. “But I think the attack was a terrible thing.”

Asked whether the US will join strikes on the Houthis, the US president said: “We may”

World.title: Buried bodies, cleared rubble, Israel’s yellow line: How war is hampering the search for Gaza’s missing
World.content:
Dusk had fallen in the northern Gaza neighborhood of Jabalya when an Israeli quadcopter broke the evening lull on November 1, 2024.

That evening, Mohammad Yousef Shalayel had settled into his in-laws’ home with his wife and children – after visiting 16 relatives displaced at his parents’ house nearby. He didn’t know that would be the last time they saw each other.

An “enormous explosion” rocked the area, “completely collapsing” the Shalayel house. When Shalayel returned to the site of the attack the next morning, “all four floors had fallen on top of one another, on the people who were inside,” he said.

Among them were his elderly mother, his two brothers and his sister, and their children and in-laws, too.

“I will never forget… I found dismembered remains of children and women,” he told CNN in late September. “I broke down, but I tried to hold myself together so that I could gather the pieces of flesh that were scattered around.”

Nearly two years later, Shalayel has been unable to return because the Israeli military has since occupied more than half of the shattered territory. He says almost all his family members remain unaccounted for.

Mohammad Yousef Shalayel (center), shown with two of his children, recalled the “horrific sight” of his relatives’ bodies after an Israeli strike in Jabalya, northern Gaza in November, 2024. Tareq El-Hilou/CNN

Amid the ruins of Gaza, Palestinians say they are trying to survive a conflict with no clear end in sight.

Three years after Hamas and other militant groups killed around 1,200 people in Israel on October 7, 2023 – and a year after a US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the ensuing war in Gaza – Israeli strikes remain a near daily occurrence. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 74,000 people have been killed in the coastal enclave during the Israeli offensive. And the number may still rise significantly.

Some 8,000 people are reported missing, according to Gaza’s Civil Defense, most of whom are likely buried beneath what the United Nations estimated last year to be 61 million tonnes of rubble.

And with each day that passes, the chances of identifying the dead grow slimmer as “crucial evidence” is lost, said Pat Griffiths, a spokesman for the International Committee of the Red Cross in Jerusalem.

Under international humanitarian law, the parties to an armed conflict “have an obligation to conduct search and recovery work” for the remains of those killed, missing or injured, and to collect, preserve and transfer that information to the other side, Griffiths told CNN.

Access blocked

Under the October 2025 ceasefire plan, Israeli forces were instructed to withdraw to the “yellow line,” which demarcated occupied areas. That shifting demarcation zone has blocked Palestinians from accessing swathes of land where their loved ones could be buried under the rubble, residents and aid workers say.

Several people in Jabalya told CNN they witnessed the Israeli military demolishing mosques, homes and buildings or clearing rubble near the yellow line.

“Where are the bones of our loved ones?” asked one resident, Yahya Odeh. “Where are their bodies? There are entire families beyond the yellow line who have been separated from their relatives.”

In September, the UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, warned against the clearance of rubble in areas under Israeli military control “by bulldozers with no respect for the dead,” after Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, a Geneva-based NGO, reported that such activity could erase evidence of war crimes.

Israeli forces use bulldozers east of Jabalya, northern Gaza, on April 13. Human rights groups have warned the use of heavy machinery to clear rubble could erase evidence of possible war crimes. Majdi Fathi/NurPhoto/Getty Images

Türk said the recovery of “what appears to be entire families” from under the rubble in areas accessible to Palestinians highlights the need for evidence of possible war crimes to be preserved, and called for international investigators to be given access to all of Gaza.

Meanwhile, Israel’s restrictions on heavy machinery entering Gaza have prolonged recovery efforts in parts of the enclave where Israeli troops are not currently present, Palestinian officials say.

In August, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a 15-point plan laying out a pathway to long-term stability in Gaza, insisting Israel’s forces would not withdraw “until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.” The militant group in turn demanded that the Israeli military stop striking Gaza and pull back to the yellow line, as set out in the ceasefire plan.

Last year, an independent UN inquiry found Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, a finding rejected by the Israeli government.

Gaza City’s sole excavator

In parts of Gaza accessible to Palestinians, Civil Defense members scour bombed-out homes for the remains of missing people.

Since last October, field crews have recovered around 1,000 bodies from the rubble, according to Mahmoud Basal, the Civil Defense spokesperson. But only one excavator is available in Gaza City, with another in central Gaza, said Basal, adding that operations could be “completed” if Israeli authorities were to provide the 10 excavators, 10 bulldozers and 30 trucks requested by Palestinian officials.

The Israeli aid agency tasked with facilitating the entry of aid into Gaza, COGAT, said Israel has allowed in “essential equipment” including engine oil, medical supplies and tents. However, COGAT insisted authorities would withhold heavy machinery and reconstruction materials until Hamas disarmed, according to Reuters.

Recovery efforts are made more dangerous by the presence of unexploded ordnance, said Griffiths. Many rescue workers are “literally scraping away, a few centimeters at a time,” he added.

When they do find buried Palestinians, some show signs of having been eaten by rodents or stray dogs, said Basal. Shalayel told CNN how he wrapped a blanket around his brother’s arm, which protruded from the rubble of their parents’ house, to try to protect it from an “enormous number” of roaming dogs. “It was a horrific sight,” he said.

“In the end, the family tries to comfort itself by believing that all of its relatives have been recovered from beneath the rubble,” Basal said. “But we cannot state (that) with certainty.”

Dr. Ahmad Dheir is one of only three remaining specialist forensic doctors in the enclave, he said.

Even before the war, doctors had no access to DNA testing facilities, Dheir said, after a years-long blockade imposed by Israel and Egypt limited the entry of medical supplies.

The slow eradication of Gaza’s medical infrastructure – following repeated Israeli strikes on health centers – has made medical workers even more reliant on elementary identification techniques, said Griffiths.

When rescue teams deliver unidentified bodies to hospitals, the lack of freezer storage, fuel shortages and frequent power cuts hasten the deterioration of samples, said Dheir.

With no DNA testing available, health workers have resorted to inconclusive blood typing and laboratory tests, condemning many relatives to a perpetual state of uncertainty, he said.

‘Deep human need for truth’

Suha al-Sharif’s son, Jihad, was supposed to care for his mother in old age. Instead, his absence is her only companion.

“When Jihad left, I realized that he was the one carrying me. He was my strength,” the 55-year-old told CNN.

Jihad, 33, was shot and killed on November 9, 2023 – when the family was displaced from Gaza City, Al-Sharif said. His body was taken to Al-Shifa Hospital, in the north, but Israel’s intensifying attacks meant health staffers could not bury people. Again, the family were forced to flee, journeying south. Nearly three years later, Al-Sharif has not been able to find him. “The hardest thing is that I couldn’t bury him; I don’t know where his body is,” she said.

“At night, when I put my head on my pillow, memories come back,” she added. “There is nothing left to cry for. My life feels over.”

People are forced to flee south after Israeli attacks in Gaza City, on September 16. Those with missing relatives are “trapped between hope and grief, waiting, and fear,” according to Israa Alqahwaji, a Palestinian aid worker. Habboub Ramez/ABACA/Shutterstock

Her sense of dispossession reflects that of many survivors in Gaza. Palestinians whose relatives are still missing have been presenting signs of “ambiguous loss” – a situational disorder where people feel lost, unable to concentrate, anxious, depressive or guilty, two aid workers told CNN.

Some people pray, preserve photographs or loved ones’ belongings to “keep their memory alive,” according to Israa Alqahwaji, the mental health program coordinator in Gaza for the UK-based NGO Medical Aid for Palestinians. Wanting to find a person’s body “reflects a very deep human need for truth,” Alqahwaji said.

“Continuing to live does not mean abandoning or forgetting the person they have lost,” she added.

The cemetery of the missing

Young men conduct burials at the cemetery of the missing in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza on February 13. Eyad Baba/AFP/Getty Images

In Deir al-Balah a cemetery of the missing, as locals call it, has become a totem for the unknown fate of hundreds of Palestinians.

About 1,000 unidentified people have been buried there, according to Gaza’s Civil Defense. Authorities have been working with international aid agencies to build a digital information sharing system, ascribing serial numbers to unnamed graves so that if DNA testing becomes possible, loved ones may be able to identify their relatives in years to come.

“We believe these people and their families have a right, as a matter of human dignity, to find their loved ones,” said Dheir.

Shalayel hopes that one day he will find his family and lay them to rest with dignity. “For us, the people of Gaza, there is a well-known saying: Honoring the dead means burying them. Our religion, customs and traditions teach us that when someone dies, they should be buried, and their burial place should be known.”

World.title: Trump says Putin wants settlement, urges Ukraine to elect new president
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said that his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, wishes to reach a settlement to end the war in Ukraine.

Trump accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being unwilling to strike a deal and called for a change in Ukrainian leadership to facilitate an agreement with Moscow.

Speaking to reporters, Trump added that Putin “very much wants to reach a settlement.”

US and international media reported that Trump’s remarks followed a roughly 90-minute phone call with the Russian president that covered the war in Ukraine and ways to achieve an agreement.

The US president criticized his Ukrainian counterpart for failing to hold elections since the start of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, arguing that elections could have been held at earlier opportunities.

His comments come amidst escalating disagreements between Washington and Kyiv regarding the course of the war, economic pressures linked to energy prices, and the terms for ending the conflict.

Trump calls for new Ukrainian president

Trump separately called for the election of a new Ukrainian president willing to reach a deal with Russia; he held Zelenskyy responsible for the war’s continuation and criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, stating that they contribute to rising diesel prices in the United States.

These statements coincided with the announcement of a US-Russian deal regarding Russian diesel supplies—a move that drew criticism from Ukraine and Europe due to its potential impact on the economic pressure exerted on Moscow since the war began.

Zelenskyy criticized the agreement concerning Russian diesel, arguing that easing restrictions on Russian supplies provides Moscow with additional resources to sustain the war.

The move sparked concerns in Kyiv and European capitals that easing sanctions could weaken the pressure on Russia, particularly as mutual attacks on energy infrastructure continue.

Attempting to contain the escalation, the Ukrainian president offered to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceased its strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities—a proposal linking mutual de-escalation to a halt in targeting critical infrastructure on both sides.

Recent statements reflect a widening rift between Trump and Zelenskyy regarding the conduct of the war and the terms of a settlement, particularly given Moscow’s insistence on retaining the Ukrainian territories it controls—a stance that remains a major obstacle to reaching a final agreement.

Several European nations have reaffirmed their support for Ukraine’s leader, stressing that the country’s political leadership must be decided by the Ukrainian people themselves.

World.title: Egypt and Malaysia elevate strategic relations
World.content:
Egypt and Malaysia reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the strategic partnership between the two nations and expanding cooperation across political, economic, investment, defense, and security sectors.

They also pledged to intensify coordination on regional and international issues of mutual interest, work towards enhancing stability in the Gulf region and West Asia, and ensure freedom of maritime navigation in the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with international law.

In a joint statement issued during Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s visit to Malaysia on October 9–10, 2026, the two countries announced the elevation of their bilateral relations to the level of a strategic partnership.

This move aims to bolster joint cooperation across various fields, support mutual interests, and contribute to international stability and prosperity.

The Egyptian and Malaysian leaders emphasized the importance of regular dialogue through existing bilateral institutional mechanisms and agreed to hold the second meeting of the Joint Commission, as well as the second round of bilateral consultations, at the earliest opportunity.

The leaders commended the growth of the economic partnership between Egypt and Malaysia, highlighting significant untapped economic potential.

Both sides agreed to boost trade and investment while encouraging business-led cooperation across several priority sectors.

These sectors include agriculture, the Halal industry, education, technical and vocational education and training (TVET), digital transformation, renewable energy, infrastructure development, the automotive industry, manufacturing, and semiconductors.

Economic hubs

Both sides emphasized that the strategic locations of Egypt and Malaysia position them to serve as economic hubs and gateways to regional and international markets.

Malaysia acts as a gateway for Egypt to the markets of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, while Egypt serves as a gateway for Malaysia to broader Arab, African, and European markets.

Regarding defense and security, the two leaders highlighted the strength of the friendly relations between their countries and the fruitful cooperation they share, underscoring the importance of further enhancing these ties.

The statement also stressed the importance of people-to-people exchanges in strengthening the bonds of friendship between the two nations, including through scholarship programs, human capital development, and academic cooperation.

On air connectivity, both sides emphasized its importance in supporting economic cooperation and encouraged their respective national airlines to explore opportunities for enhanced collaboration.

They also reaffirmed their commitment to facilitating reciprocal travel and strengthening people-to-people ties, recognizing the role these play in boosting tourism, trade, and cultural exchange.

World.title: Egypt’s foreign currency reserves rise to US$ 57.35 billion
World.content:
The Central Bank of Egypt’s net foreign currency reserves reached approximately US$ 57.35 billion by the end of September 2026—an all-time high—reflecting improved foreign currency indicators and a strengthened Egyptian economy capable of withstanding external pressures.

Foreign currency reserves continue to hit record levels, bolstered by increased foreign currency inflows into the Egyptian economy – edging closer to the $58 billion mark for the first time.

Central Bank data showed that the banking sector’s net foreign assets rose to $ 31.2 billion by the end of August 2026—marking the highest level since 2011—driven by an increase in foreign currency inflows.

These improved indicators come in spite of recent global economic developments and challenges.

It reflects the stability of the banking sector and the national economy, while showcasing Egypt’s ability to navigate external challenges.

World.title: Liberia: Investigators Find No Link Between Liberia’s US$19M and US$317M Cocaine Busts
World.content:
MONROVIA – For four months, Liberians have treated this year’s two great cocaine seizures as one story. The airport bust came first, the record haul followed six weeks later, and officials spoke of a single network that had burrowed into the state for more than six years.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Investigators now say that picture is wrong.



“We haven’t identified yet any connection between 19M and 317M,” investigators told FrontPageAfrica this week. “Leroy Harris doesn’t have connections to [the] 317M [case].”

If that holds, Liberia is not fighting one cartel. It is fighting two, with different suppliers, different routes, different customers and different methods. It also helps explain one of the stranger features of the State’s case: the disappearance of George Wah “Leroy” Harris, the Paynesville bar owner the government publicly charged in the US$317 million probe in August, from the indictment that followed.

It does not explain everything. A close reading of both indictments shows threads that still run between the two cases, and questions the Ministry of Justice has yet to answer.

Case one: the airport pipeline

The first case broke on June 8 at Roberts International Airport (RIA). Screeners flagged six cargo boxes declared as Maggi cubes and lappas. Inside were 198 compressed plates of cocaine, 237.6 kilograms in all, valued at about US$19.2 million.

The shipment was going out, not coming in. According to the indictment, a logistics manager arranged for the boxes to fly Brussels Airlines to London Heathrow, consigned to Usman Ali at an address in Birmingham, England. Prosecutors say a similar four-box consignment, also declared as Maggi cubes and lappas, left on May 20 for US$1,400 in fees.

This is the network investigators describe as running Sierra Leone–Liberia–United Kingdom/Netherlands. FPA sources now tie it to Jos Leijdekkers, the Dutch fugitive whom authorities believe has been sheltering in Sierra Leone. A senior security official had earlier linked Leijdekkers to Liberia’s drug trade in general terms; investigators now place him with the airport pipeline specifically. Leijdekkers has not been charged in Liberia.

A Montserrado County grand jury indicted 10 defendants in the August Term of Criminal Court “C”: Harris; Paul Jamaal King; Philip Yeoh Jr.; Mohammed O. Gbowrah; former LDEA airport deputy commander Moses Jallah; Michael U.S. Brown, alias Rahim Bah; Polo Bah; Oscar J. Brown; Usman Ali; and an unidentified “private bar” entity or person.

Harris sits at the centre of the bribery allegations. Prosecutors say that after the seizure he offered LDEA agents US$100,000 to return the boxes, handed US$5,000 to Jallah at Private Bar, offered a warehouse in Sayon Town for storage, and told Jallah he owned a quarter of the drugs. Harris is in Monrovia Central Prison and is presumed innocent.

Case two: the sea route

The second case is a different animal. On July 21, a joint security team raided a compound on Cement Road in the VOA Community, off the RIA Highway. They found 3,971 plates of cocaine in 157 bags, which the State values at US$317.68 million.

Two foreigners were arrested on the spot: Johann David Garces Grajales, who holds Spanish and Colombian passports, and Srdan Seles, a Serbian. A third man, known only as Tom, allegedly slipped away before the raid.

This cocaine came in by sea. Prosecutors say it was landed from the Atlantic in May, carried by canoe up the Po River at Royesville through ground the group had secured in Bomi County, then trucked to the VOA house. The cover was a fishing business on the riverbank and a front airline, Afri-Connect Airlines, whose aircraft was bought in August 2025 and flew into Spriggs Payne.

Investigators describe this pipeline as Colombia–Brazil–Liberia–Ghana–Eastern Europe (Serbia, Croatia, Ukraine)–Dubai. The 55-page indictment, issued with an October 7 writ, names Nikola Ivancic as the cartel’s paymaster and puts the network’s political recruitment in a Dubai meeting.

Its reach is far wider than case one. The defendants include former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, former NSA deputy director Gerald Folley Smith, former airport operations chief Mark Kuiah, and a string of security officers. The charges run to 11 counts, including money laundering and weapons offences.

Where the two cases part

The differences are not cosmetic. They go to how each network made money.

* Direction. Case one was an export: cocaine already in Liberia leaving by air for Britain. Case two was an import and storage operation: a mother shipment landed by sea and held near the airport road.

* Scale. The VOA haul is nearly 17 times heavier and about 16 times more valuable than the airport seizure.

* Method. The airport network used ordinary commercial airfreight, false cargo declarations and small cash payments to handlers. The sea network bought land, boats, a plane and, prosecutors say, protection at the highest levels.

* People. Case one’s defendants are mostly Liberian logistics workers, airport hands and a UK consignee. Case two is run by foreign operators with Latin American and Balkan links, allegedly shielded by senior Liberian officials.

* Markets. One route ends in Britain and the Netherlands; the other fans out to Eastern Europe and the Gulf.

On that reading, the State’s treatment of Harris makes some sense. His alleged conduct — the US$100,000 offer, the US$5,000 payment, the claim to a quarter share — concerns the airport boxes. Prosecutors may simply have charged him where their evidence lies.

The Harris gap

But the record does not move in a straight line.

In early August, the Ministry of Information announced that Harris had been charged in the US$317 million probe. Security forces sealed Private Bar and searched it three times; management says nothing illegal was found. Harris was arraigned at the Monrovia City Court. Police said at the time that he had called security officials in the hours after the seizure to try to free the shipment.

On August 27, Criminal Court “C” issued its writ in the airport case, naming Harris. On October 7, the US$317 million indictment arrived. Harris is not in its caption, its counts or its narrative.

No one has told the public whether the August charge was withdrawn, merged into the airport case, or left pending.

That matters for a man in pre-trial detention: he is entitled to know which case is holding him.

The threads that remain

Investigators may be right that the two networks are distinct. Yet the 317M indictment itself keeps brushing against the smaller case.

Private Bar appears in both. The new indictment places the cartel’s introductory meeting for its front airline at Private Bar in Paynesville — Harris’s venue — while charging no one over it. Witnesses separately told FPA that Usman Ali, the airport case’s UK consignee, attended a birthday party for Harris and Michael Browne at the same bar on May 17.

The “19” in the voice notes. Among the State’s evidence against Howard-Taylor are WhatsApp exchanges with co-defendant Sheik Bashiru Kante. In them, prosecutors attribute to Kante references to “the 19 kilos” and “19 million.” If those words point to the airport seizure, the larger case’s own evidence invokes the smaller one.

The airport in the middle. Both cases run through RIA. The June boxes were caught there. The sea cartel allegedly paid Kuiah, then RIA’s operations chief, US$50,000 to smooth its path. Kuiah is named in the big indictment, though no count lists him, and he was dismissed after the airport seizure.

Leijdekkers and Sierra Leone. If the Dutch fugitive stands behind the airport pipeline, has Liberia asked Freetown and The Hague for help? The Inspector General promised in July to pursue suspects abroad through extradition and mutual legal assistance. The public has seen no request.

The 2022 shadow

Liberia has been here before. In 2022, a jury acquitted all four defendants in the US$100 million Freeport case, then the country’s largest, and all four left the country within a day.

Two indictments now stand where one case once seemed to. Whether they are two cartels or two halves of one is a question for evidence, not press briefings. But a prosecution that cannot say clearly who belongs in which case will hand defence lawyers their opening — and risk repeating 2022.

All defendants named in this report are presumed innocent unless proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: Liberia: What Judge Ousman Feika’s Ruling Against Attorney Gbawou Kowou Does, and What It Leaves Unanswered
World.content:
MONROVIA – Judge Ousman F. Feika of Criminal Court “C” did not suspend Atty. Gbawou Kowou’s law license. That distinction matters.

By Rodney D. Sieh

In a ruling dated October 9, Judge Feika dismissed a complaint in which Kowou accused the State’s prosecutors of tampering with defense witnesses. He then referred Kowou to the Supreme Court’s Grievance and Ethics Committee, “with a strong recommendation that his law license be suspended for one calendar year for unethical and unprofessional conduct unbefitting of a lawyer.”



Kowou remains a licensed lawyer. Whether he stays one is now a question for the Committee and, ultimately, the full bench of the Supreme Court.

How it started

The dispute grows out of the economic sabotage prosecution of former officials including Varney Sirleaf and Dee Maxwell Saah Kemayah. The case is brought by the Assets Recovery and Property Retrieval Task Force (AREPT), chaired by Cllr. Edwin K. Martin. Kowou represents co-defendant Wayfa Ciafa.

On Sunday, October 4, members of the Group of 77 went to AREPT’s offices. Some of them had already testified for the defense. That night, Kowou went live on Facebook and called in to the Spoon Talk Show. He alleged that AREPT had summoned his witnesses to intimidate them into recanting.

The next day he filed a Bill of Information asking the court to investigate. The court halted the trial, sent the jury back to quarters and opened an inquiry that afternoon.

What the court found

The ruling rejects Kowou’s account on almost every point:

• Why the witnesses went. The witnesses went at the instance of Raymond K. Zarby, the Group’s senior administrator. Zarby testified that he misread AREPT’s invitation, which was meant for rebuttal witnesses.

• What happened when they arrived. AREPT asked them to leave once it realized some had already testified for the defense. Witnesses for both sides said no one was threatened, though their phones were taken at the door. AREPT described that as routine for all visitors.

• Kowou’s prior knowledge. Kowou knew of the visit in advance. A witness had called him, and he advised them to go. That undercut his claim that they went without his knowledge.

• Martin’s whereabouts. Martin was not on the premises. Kowou had testified that Martin ordered him beaten and dragged out.

• The scuffle. The video showed a scuffle that began when AREPT staff tried to stop Kowou from filming and live-streaming inside the compound.

The court called the tampering allegation “absolutely false and misleading.”

The real charge: going public

The ruling says plainly that raising witness tampering is not misconduct. Counsel who has credible information, the court said, “should promptly bring the matter before the Court.”

The court’s objection is to the order of events: the Facebook live stream and the talk show came first, and the formal filing came after. It also points to a gag order issued at the start of the trial, barring lawyers from discussing the case with the media.

The judge found that Kowou breached Rules 1, 18, 20 and 22 of the Code of Moral and Professional Ethics. Those rules cover:

• Rule 1: undermining the courts

• Rule 20: publicity about pending litigation

• Rule 22: asserting unproven matters as fact

“Criticism of a judicial decision and denigration of the judicial institution are not synonymous,” the ruling says.

Where the ruling is on firm ground

On procedure, Judge Feika did what the law asks. Article 75 of the Constitution gives the Supreme Court authority over the legal profession. The Judiciary Law gives it the power to censure, suspend, or remove lawyers. Judicial Canon 21, which the ruling cites, tells trial judges to correct unprofessional conduct and, where necessary, refer it to the Grievance and Ethics Committee.

A trial judge who believes a lawyer has misbehaved before him is expected to make that referral. Feika did.

The questions it leaves open

The ruling still raises issues the Committee and the public will weigh.

Proportionality. A one-year suspension is a severe penalty. It would take Kowou out of every case he handles, not just this one. The conduct the ruling describes is publicity during a gag order and an allegation the court found unproven. Breach of a court’s own gag order is ordinarily a matter for contempt, and the ruling does not say why the court went straight to recommending a year off the roll.

Who judged the complaint? Kowou’s complaint was against the prosecuting party in a case the same court is trying. Courts routinely rule on such Bills of Information. Still, when a defense complaint against the prosecution is dismissed, and the complaining lawyer is then recommended for suspension, it raises a concern. Other defense lawyers may hesitate before raising similar complaints.

The “extreme circumstances” exception. By the ruling’s own account, Rule 20 allows that extreme circumstances may justify a public statement. Kowou will likely argue that a lawyer who believes his witnesses are being pressured faces exactly such circumstances. The court found the belief unfounded. The Committee will decide whether that makes the conduct sanctionable.

Where the ruling and Kowou agree. The ruling confirms that the witnesses’ phones were taken at AREPT’s door. It also confirms that AREPT staff physically tried to stop Kowou from filming. Neither amounts to tampering, but both help explain why a defense lawyer might have feared the worst.

What comes next

The Grievance and Ethics Committee must now conduct its own investigation, with Kowou entitled to be heard. Its recommendation then goes to the full bench of the Supreme Court. Judge Feika’s recommendation does not bind the Committee, and the Supreme Court is not bound by the Committee’s.

Kowou is also on the defense team for former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor in a separate case before the same court. How the Supreme Court handles his referral will be watched closely by lawyers on both sides of Liberia’s most politically charged prosecutions.
