World.title: Liberia: Lack of Transparency Clouds Government’s Street Child Program as Officials Concede Funds are Inadequate to Address the Exploding Numbers
World.content:
Some of the children removed from the streets under the Boakai administration’s “Support a Child, Save the Future” program.

Summary

The Boakai government’s flagship program to get children off the streets is falling behind. The program promised to move 73,000 children back to families in five years, but two years in, the project is not on track, and there is little transparency.

flagship program to get children off the streets is falling behind. The program promised to move 73,000 children back to families in five years, but two years in, the project is not on track, and there is little transparency. The government has received little of the $15 million projected budget from donors and has put up just $1.3 million.

Advocates say the project falls far short of the exploding numbers of street children. A 2024 report found 366,00 Liberian children living in “street situations.” The number has likely grown as poverty rises.

By Augusta S. Lafalay, senior reporter with New Narratives

WEST POINT, Monrovia – When school lets out here in this informal settlement on the seashore, 15-year-old Stanley does not go home to rest or study for the next day. He picks up a bundle of plastic bags and walks towards the traffic, selling until dark. He then carries whatever he makes back to his mother and grandmother.



His classmates see him out there and laugh at him. He has cried over it before, he says, but he keeps coming back because the family needs the money. His mother sells cooked creamy wheat in a wheel barrow but her income is not enough to cover their needs.

“I want people to know me as a student, not the boy selling plastic bags in traffic,” he said. “But if I don’t sell plastic bags in the street, I won’t carry recess to school or get other things like my friends.”

Even still, Stanley is luckier than many of the hundreds of thousands of children found to be living on the streets in a 2024 government-backed survey, supported by UNICEF, that said more than 366,000 were children living in “street situations” nationwide. A Front Page Africa/New Narratives report found many of the children were forced into drug use, selling, and prostitution and had given birth to babies who also lived on the streets. As climate change and price rises have tipped more people into poverty since then, the number has certainly risen.

The survey prompted the Boakai administration to launch its flagship “Support a Child, Save the Future” initiative to remove 73,000 children like Stanley from Liberia’s streets over five years through school enrollment, family reunification and support grants for caregivers. The first two phases of the program alone were estimated to cost $15 million. But that was almost entirely dependent on support from donors. The government committed just US$300,000 when the program was first launched and followed it with US$500,000 the next year. Since it was announced, donors have slashed hundreds of millions in annual support for the country. The project is now 95 percent funded by the government, according to a ministry official.

A 16-year-old girl living in the streets and forced into drug selling and prostitution talked to FrontPage Africa/New Narratives in 2024. Credit: Ricardo Partido/New Narratives

The project’s progress is unclear. Sylvesterus Armand Johnson, the project’s coordinator at the Ministry of Gender, said nearly 24,000 children have been reached so far and just over 4,000 of them have been placed in school. Johnson did not provide supporting evidence for the figure beyond a screenshot of a factsheet shared via WhatsApp.

Abraham M.T. Sagi Jr. and Ellen Sagi, both 18, are two of the children who have been helped by the project. Both now attend Picoli Academy, Gardnerville. Both used to beg on the streets to help their families, whose fathers live with disabilities. Abraham’s father is visually impaired.

Abraham said he spent long days begging from morning until night instead of focusing on school. “It was stressful and discouraging, especially seeing other children going to school while I was trying to help my family survive,” he said.

People sometimes made hurtful remarks as Ellen begged, telling her that instead of asking for money, she should be selling something. “Those experiences were painful and made life even harder,” she said.

The project identified the two children’s families and helped enroll her in school. It now pays their school fees and provides books, uniforms, shoes and bags. “Now I can stay in the classroom, study, and concentrate on building my future. I no longer have to return to the streets to beg,” Abraham said. The program “has changed my life and given me hope for a better future,” said Ellen.

Both are already looking beyond school. Ellen’s dream is to learn tailoring so she can become self-reliant. Abraham wants to pursue business skills training so that he can build a better future for himself and his family.

Johnson K. Dorbor, president of the Hoping God Association of the Blind, said it has brought meaningful change to many families, especially those of people with disabilities and other vulnerable households. Children from those families are enrolled at schools including Perfect Grace, Daniel Memorial and Picoli, where the program covers tuition and provides school uniforms, bags, shoes and other learning materials.Parents get help too. Some received small livelihood grants of between US$100 and US$120 to start or strengthen a small business, Dorbor said. His own wife uses their grant to support the household and their children’s education. Social workers regularly visit the community to encourage children to stay in school and to support parents, he said. About 62 children in his association are currently benefiting.

Teenage girls share a bed in a shack near Redlight area after selling sex all night in 2024.

A limited project without transparency has advocates calling for an overhaul

But advocates say they have no way of knowing if the project has achieved measurable success. There has been no independent audit as would be required in a donor-funded project “to know as to whether the very children that they are claiming to take off the street are not going back in the street,” Kalifala Kromah, chairperson of the Child Protection Network of Liberia, a government-led coalition of ministries, civil society groups, UN agencies and other partners working to coordinate efforts to protect children.

Getting a child into a classroom does not settle what comes next. Dorbor said many families still struggle to pay rent and put food on the table, and some parents work long hours just to provide the next day’s meals.

“Children learn best when their basic needs are met,” he said. He asked the government and its partners to bring in school feeding programs, help vulnerable families with housing, and keep funding the program beyond its five years, so that more children stay in school and away from the streets.

Johnson acknowledges the project is dramatically underfunded compared with the original plan. There is a direct 2026 budget line of US$296,000, topped up with a US$200,000 supplementary allocation, according to Johnson, putting the year’s funding close to US$500,000.

Cumulative government commitments since the launch come to just under $1.3 million against the US$15 million estimated for the first two phases alone. That is less than nine cents of every dollar the program’s own architects said it needed, with two of the five years already gone.

“Even if we were going at a pace of $500,000 [a year] … in five years’ time, it’s not going to even equate to $15 million,” said Andrew Tehmeh, former county director of Street Child Liberia, “Resource mobilization is far below the targeted amount.”

Keifala Kromah, chairperson of the Child Protection Network of Liberia, at an event marking the first phase of the project. Photo credit: Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon

The funding gap has led to a staffing shortage. Johnson said the ministry deployed around 50 social workers for the pilot phase to track thousands of children nationwide. That forced civil society groups to step in and undertake documentation work the ministry could not keep pace with alone.

Tehmeh said the hardest cases remain the ones the program struggles most to resolve: children with disabilities or those whose disabled parents, who rely on them to beg.

“Every time you got them all, you kind of saw them back again,” he said.

Johnson confirmed that the ministry only recently began a targeted approach with the National Commission on Disability, acknowledging that some caregiver grants intended for small businesses were instead diverted to other uses. He maintains that the program is on track and hopes it will eventually be absorbed into permanent ministry operations rather than ending when its five years run out.

A Children’s Rights Law that has been ignored

Experts said the whole program was unnecessary from the start. Liberia already has a legal tool designed to address exactly this problem: the Children’s Rights Law of 2011 – which provides a range of policies to reduce the number of street children, but which has never been enforced. The law calls for a standing Child Rights Advancement Fund meant to pool government and donor money and a Child Well-Being Council to coordinate child protection efforts across the government permanently. Neither has been established more than a decade on. Advocates said that failure, more than any single funding shortfall, explains why the country is falling behind.

“The law is better than whatever intervention is being done,” said Kromah. “That will be a statutory and holistic means of protection for children instead of short-term projects.”

Kromah said the funding shortfall is exactly why a legally mandated fund matters more than a project budget line. A standing Child Rights Advancement Fund, he said, provided by the bill, could pool government and donor contributions in one place instead of leaving the program dependent on whatever a single ministry can secure in each budget cycle.

“If the fund is established, partners can come in and support the fund,” he said. Without it, “everybody will want to own their own project, and there will be no coordination.”

“Help me feed my family, pay my rent, and survive with dignity”

Seven-year-old Alice attends school, but her mind is often not on her studies. When classes end, she returns to the traffic at 72nd Junction, where she moves between cars to raise money for school expenses and food for her family. She says she knows the street is dangerous but feels she has little choice.

“If somebody wants to help me,” Stanley said, “I’m asking for two things: pay my school fees and help my family. If that happens, I will leave the street the same day. I want to stay in school and learn. I don’t want to grow up begging between cars.”

Patience, Alice’s mother, keeps her daughter in school at a painful cost. The 40-year-old, who has a disability, begs at 72nd Junction alongside her daughter. She says removing children from the streets without supporting the families they depend on will not solve the problem.

“I am not asking the government to leave my child on the street,” Patience said. “I am asking them to give us a way to live. Send my child to school, yes, but help me feed my family, pay my rent, and survive with dignity.”

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency in Liberia. The funder had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: Koon’s Own Allies Join Revolt as 41 Lawmakers Boycott House Reopening, Raising Stakes for Leadership
World.content:
The rebellion within the Speaker’s own ranks exposes growing discontent over lawmakers’ benefits and legislative support, reviving memories of the bitter Koffa-Koon leadership crisis.

MONROVIA — House Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon is confronting a fresh challenge to his leadership, with about 41 lawmakers reportedly boycotting the reopening of the House of Representatives and holding a separate meeting to discuss grievances against the chamber’s leadership.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh



The development is significant not simply because of the number of lawmakers involved, but because several reportedly associated with the emerging Reformist Movement are political allies of Koon who occupy influential positions on key House committees.

Their participation suggests that the discontent may extend beyond the familiar divisions that have shaped the Legislature in recent years. It also raises questions about whether Koon can maintain the support of lawmakers whose cooperation is essential to the functioning of the House.

The immediate dispute, according to lawmakers who spoke publicly, centers on benefits, legislative support funds and other resources they allege have been withheld under the current leadership. But reports that the group is seeking signatures on a proposed 12-count resolution targeting the House leadership have introduced a more consequential possibility: a renewed contest over who controls the chamber.

The precise contents of the proposed resolution have not been publicly established, and the lawmakers who addressed the meeting did not openly confirm that removing Koon and Deputy Speaker Thomas P. Fallah was their objective.

For now, the central question is whether the Reformist Movement represents a coordinated effort to force administrative and financial concessions or the early stages of another leadership struggle.

A Rebellion From Within

The lawmakers gathered in Schefflin, Margibi County, on Friday, while Koon and a small group of legislators attended the formal reopening ceremony at the Capitol following the legislative break.

The reported boycott was striking: only 13 of the House’s 73 members reportedly attended the ceremony, including the Speaker.

The gathering outside Monrovia also brought together lawmakers who hold influential committee positions, including chairs and co-chairs responsible for scrutinizing public procurement, government contracts, natural resources, the judiciary and public expenditure.

Among those reportedly associated with the Reformist Movement are Jeremiah Garwo Sokan Sr. of Grand Gedeh County District #1, chairman of the House Committee on Mines, Natural Resources and Environment; Prince K. Koinah of Bong County District #1, chairman of the Committee on Contracts, Monopolies, Public Procurement and Concessions and co-chair of the Public Accounts and Expenditure Committee; and Sam P. Jallah of Bomi County District #3, co-chair of the Hydrocarbon Committee.

Other lawmakers reportedly linked to the movement include Bernard Blue Benson Jr. of Montserrado County District #17, chairman of the Committee on Information, Broadcasting, Culture and Tourism; Anthony Williams of Maryland County District #2, co-chair of the Peace, Religion and National Reconciliation Committee; Augustine B. Chiewolo of Lofa County District #5, chairman of the Committee on Resettlement, Repatriation, Relief and Readjustment; and Johnson S. N. Williams Sr. of River Gee County District #3, chairman of the House Committee on Judiciary.

Their reported involvement gives the agitation institutional significance. These are not merely lawmakers expressing dissatisfaction from the margins of the chamber; several occupy positions that place them at the center of legislative oversight and administration.

However, committee positions alone do not establish the intentions of individual lawmakers, and the full membership and objectives of the Reformist Movement remain unclear.

What is evident from Friday’s gathering is that a substantial number of lawmakers chose to meet separately rather than participate in the official reopening ceremony.

Benefits Dispute or Leadership Challenge?

The lawmakers’ public statements have focused primarily on financial and administrative grievances.

Representative Frank Saah Foko of Montserrado County District #9 said Friday’s meeting was intended to give lawmakers a collective platform to express their concerns. He indicated that another meeting had been scheduled for Sunday, October 11, when the group was expected to determine its next steps.

Representative Matthew Joe of Grand Bassa County said the discussions centered on demanding benefits and legislative support funds that he alleged had been denied under Koon and Fallah.

Joe described the concerns as recurring and said lawmakers intended to engage the relevant authorities to press their demands. Asked whether the gathering was intended to organize the removal of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, he said he was unaware of such a plan.

Representative Samuel Enders of Montserrado County District #6 similarly said the discussions concerned benefits and district support, adding that he knew of no effort to remove the House leadership.

Representative Abu Kamara of Montserrado County District #15 described the meeting positively but offered little detail about its outcome.

These explanations leave an important gap between the public grievances and the reported effort to circulate a 12-count resolution.

If the dispute is principally about benefits and district support, the movement could be pursuing financial transparency, the release of resources or changes in administrative procedures. If the proposed resolution formally targets Koon and Fallah, however, the confrontation could move from a dispute over entitlements to a contest over the leadership itself.

The distinction matters because a demand for financial accountability is not necessarily equivalent to a motion to remove legislative officers. The resolution’s text, the signatures supporting it and the demands accompanying it would help establish the movement’s actual objective.

Neither the full resolution nor a detailed account of the alleged financial and administrative irregularities has been publicly established in the information available.

That leaves the allegations unverified and makes a response from the Speaker’s Office particularly important.

Why Koon’s Own Allies Matter

The political significance of the agitation lies partly in the reported involvement of lawmakers who have worked alongside Koon and occupy senior committee positions.

Leadership in the House depends not only on formal authority but also on the ability to maintain working relationships with members, coordinate legislative business and secure cooperation across committees.

When discontent emerges among lawmakers associated with the leadership, it can complicate that process even if no formal removal motion is ultimately pursued.

The reported involvement of lawmakers overseeing procurement, public accounts and other major portfolios also places questions about financial administration at the center of the dispute. Their allegations, however, should not be treated as proof of misconduct without supporting documentation or findings by an appropriate authority.

The movement’s leverage will depend on more than the number of lawmakers attending a meeting. Its members would need to demonstrate sustained coordination, agreement on their demands and a willingness to pursue a common course of action.

The next meeting could therefore be an important test of whether Friday’s gathering was a temporary show of discontent or the beginning of a more organized challenge.

The Koffa-Koon Crisis Offers a Warning

The confrontation inevitably recalls the prolonged leadership dispute that preceded Koon’s emergence as Speaker.

During that earlier crisis, lawmakers aligned with what became known as the Majority Bloc boycotted sessions and held parallel meetings. They subsequently declared Koon Speaker and Fallah Deputy Speaker while Cllr. Fonati Koffa remained the sitting Speaker.

The dispute eventually reached the Supreme Court, which ruled that actions taken outside the House chamber while the Speaker remained in office and present were ultra vires.

Koffa later resigned, clearing the way for Koon’s election as Speaker, while Fallah retained the deputy speakership.

That episode exposed deep divisions within the House and demonstrated how disagreements over legislative leadership can disrupt institutional operations and raise questions about the validity of decisions taken during a political confrontation.

The current agitation does not automatically mean the House is headed for a repeat of that crisis. The circumstances may differ, and the Reformist Movement has not publicly confirmed that removing Koon and Fallah is its objective.

Nevertheless, the earlier dispute provides an important institutional backdrop. Any attempt to change the leadership would have to be assessed against the House’s rules and applicable constitutional requirements, rather than simply the strength of a faction’s public declarations.

The previous crisis also illustrates the risks of parallel meetings and competing claims to authority when lawmakers fail to resolve disputes through established legislative procedures.

The Speaker’s Office Keeps Its Distance

When contacted about the reported effort to remove the Speaker, Vehzelee Sumo, head of communications for the Speaker’s Office, declined to comment, saying the office would respond at the appropriate time.

The office had previously said it was unaware of any plan to remove Koon and would not comment on rumors.

The limited response leaves unanswered questions about the allegations involving benefits, legislative support funds and administrative irregularities.

A substantive response from the leadership could clarify which resources have been requested, what has been disbursed and whether disagreements exist over the procedures governing legislative support. Such information would help distinguish a political dispute from a documented administrative failure.

For the lawmakers, the publication of their proposed resolution and a clear statement of their demands would similarly help establish whether their campaign is directed at financial administration, the leadership’s conduct or both.

What Comes Next?

The Reformist Movement’s reported follow-up meeting on Sunday, October 11, is expected to provide a clearer indication of its direction.

Several developments will be worth watching: whether the group releases the proposed 12-count resolution; whether the reported signatures translate into a formal legislative initiative; whether its members present documentary evidence for their allegations; and whether Koon’s office responds to the concerns over benefits and support funds.

The number of lawmakers who continue to participate will also matter. A large turnout at a single gathering demonstrates discontent, but sustained coordination and a clearly defined objective would provide stronger evidence of an organized leadership challenge.

For Koon, the immediate issue is not simply whether a motion to remove him emerges. It is whether the House can restore sufficient cooperation to conduct its business without another prolonged confrontation.

For the Legislature as an institution, the dispute raises broader questions about financial transparency, the distribution of legislative resources and the accountability of its leadership to members.

Those questions remain unresolved, and the public statements made after Friday’s meeting do not establish that a leadership change is inevitable.

What the boycott does establish is that the House is facing a serious internal dispute at the start of its renewed legislative business. Whether that dispute ends in negotiated concessions or develops into a formal challenge to Koon and Fallah will depend on what the lawmakers decide, what evidence they produce, and how the leadership responds.

World.title: Liberia: Rev. Reeves Tells Liberia Peace Must Go Beyond the End of War
World.content:
Providence Baptist pastor says revenue milestones and quiet guns are no substitute for justice, trust and character

MONROVIA – Liberia’s leaders and churches must not mistake the end of the war for the arrival of peace. That was the charge Rev. Dr. Samuel Reeves delivered from the pulpit of Providence Baptist Church on Sunday.

By Rodney D. Sieh

“Listen, church, listen, Liberia, the first generation after conflict must not be satisfied merely because the guns became silent,” Reeves said. “Silence is not the same as reconciliation. Stability is not the same as justice.”



In a sermon billed as “A Message for the Nation,” Reeves went further, singling out the economic yardstick the country has been using to measure progress. “Economic growth, and raising 1 billion dollars in revenue is not the same as human flourishing,” he said. “Institutional survival is not the same as institutional excellence.”

“A nation can rebuild roads and still need to rebuild trust”

Preaching from Philippians 3:9-11 on the theme “The Power of Resurrection Living: Living Beyond Our Fears,” Reeves framed Liberia’s recovery from civil war as a story of death and resurrection. He said the country “knows what it means to pass through a Friday.”

He pointed to the 2003 Comprehensive Peace Agreement, which called the nation toward reconciliation, democracy and good governance. “That is resurrection language,” he said. But he warned that resurrection “does not mean pretending the grave never existed. It means refusing to let the grave have the final word.”

“Healing is not amnesia. Reconciliation is not denial. Peace is not the absence of memory,” Reeves told the congregation.

He laid out what he called the nation’s unfinished work. “A nation can rebuild roads and still need to rebuild trust. A nation can construct buildings and still need to construct character. A nation can hold elections and still need to deepen citizenship.”

A call to ordinary citizens

Reeves credited Liberia’s peace not to any single leader but to many hands: women who pressed for negotiations, faith and traditional leaders, teachers who returned to classrooms, and health workers who served through crisis. “God rarely raises a community through spectators,” he said.

He painted a picture of what he called “faith with skin on it.” He described a teacher telling children their circumstances do not determine their possibilities, and a young entrepreneur creating jobs rather than waiting for them. He also pointed to “a civil servant refusing corruption because righteousness matters more than personal gain.”

He also challenged the church itself, calling for “a church that refuses to compete for influence while communities struggle for hope.” He urged universities to teach young people “not simply how to find employment, but how to think, serve, lead, create, and rebuild.”

“Resurrection requires participation”

Reeves closed with a message aimed at both the nation and individuals in the pews. “Your history is real. Your wounds are real,” he said. “But your history is not your destiny.”

“God may open the tomb, but somebody has to walk out of it,” he said. “God may give the vision, but somebody has to build.”

His final words were addressed to the country: “So stand, Liberia. Stand in righteousness. Stand in grace. Stand in truth.”

World.title: From Rwanda’s Experience to Liberia’s Quest for Justice: Delegation Seeks Partnerships For War Crimes Court
World.content:
KIGALI, Rwanda — For thousands of Liberians still waiting for justice for atrocities committed during the country’s brutal civil conflicts, the establishment of a court to prosecute war and economic crimes represents more than a legal undertaking. It is a long-awaited opportunity to confront the past, hold perpetrators accountable and give victims and survivors a greater sense of justice.

By Patience M. Jones,[email protected]

Against this backdrop, a high-level Liberian delegation is looking to Rwanda for lessons, technical support and strategic partnerships that could help shape Liberia’s transitional justice process.



The delegation, comprising representatives of the Office for the Establishment of War and Economic Crimes Court for Liberia (OWECC-Liberia), the Press Union of Liberia (PUL) and the Liberia National Police (LNP), has undertaken a series of engagements with Rwandan institutions working in transitional justice, law enforcement, academia, civil society and the media.

The engagements, which began following the delegation’s arrival in Rwanda on October 2, are aimed at identifying practical lessons and opportunities for collaboration as Liberia moves toward establishing and operationalizing its proposed War and Economic Crimes Court (WECC) and National Anti-Corruption Court (NACC).

For Liberia, where questions of accountability for past atrocities remain central to national reconciliation, the initiative presents an opportunity to learn from another African country’s experience in confronting a violent past and pursuing justice.

LOOKING BEYOND THE COURTROOM

Led by Cllr. Professor Jallah A. Barbu, Executive Director of OWECC-Liberia; Julius Kanubah, President of the Press Union of Liberia and Ezekiel E. Fayia, Superintendent of the Liberia National Police, the delegation has held discussions across Kigali, Musanze and Rubavu.

The delegation is also scheduled to visit Kibuye and Nyamata before returning to Liberia.

The discussions have focused on transitional justice, reconciliation, accountability, national healing, memorialization, digitalization and support for victims and survivors of Liberia’s armed conflicts.

These issues extend beyond the creation of judicial institutions. They also raise questions about how victims can access justice, how survivors can have their experiences acknowledged, how evidence can be preserved and how society can confront the consequences of violence without abandoning accountability.

For the Liberian delegation, Rwanda’s experience offers an opportunity to examine approaches that could inform the country’s own efforts, while recognizing that Liberia must develop solutions suited to its history, institutions and national circumstances.

During engagements with Rwandan transitional justice actors, Barbu and Kanubah emphasized the importance of cross-cultural learning, technical assistance and institutional capacity-building in strengthening Liberia’s transitional justice process.

The delegation includes Simeon J. Lomah, Head of Information and Communications Technology at OWECC-Liberia; Edmond S. Kamei, Assistant Director for Operations at OWECC-Liberia; and Patrick Niyongabo, Escort and Adviser to the delegation.

Media Partnerships To Strengthen Accountability

Beyond judicial institutions, the delegation is also exploring opportunities to strengthen cooperation between Liberian and Rwandan media organizations.

Kanubah expressed confidence that discussions with the Rwanda Journalists Association (ARJ) and the Rwanda Media Commission (RMC) would lead to a memorandum of understanding to promote collaboration between the two countries’ journalism communities.

The proposed partnership is expected to create opportunities for professional exchange, knowledge-sharing and stronger media solidarity.

For Liberia, where public understanding of transitional justice will be essential to meaningful national participation, stronger journalism partnerships could help expand public education and improve reporting on accountability, reconciliation and the work of institutions responsible for addressing past and present injustices.

A well-informed public is critical to ensuring that transitional justice is not treated solely as a government or legal-sector initiative, but as a national process in which citizens understand their rights, responsibilities and opportunities to participate.

Turning International Lessons Into National Action

The delegation’s engagements come as Liberia continues efforts to advance the establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court and the National Anti-Corruption Court.

While international exchanges can provide valuable insights, their significance will ultimately depend on how those lessons are translated into practical action at home.

For victims and survivors of Liberia’s civil conflicts, the promise of transitional justice will be measured not simply by international partnerships or institutional announcements, but by whether credible mechanisms emerge to pursue accountability, recognize suffering and contribute to national healing.

The delegation’s ongoing engagements in Rwanda therefore represent an opportunity to build relationships and strengthen institutional knowledge that could support Liberia’s justice and accountability agenda.

The ultimate test, however, will be whether the knowledge gained and partnerships developed can help move Liberia closer to a transitional justice process that responds meaningfully to the needs of victims, survivors and the wider public.

World.title: Liberia’s YEIB, Diaspora Affairs Office Explore Partnership to Boost Youth Businesses, Expand Exports
World.content:
The Proposed partnership seeks diaspora investment, business expertise and export opportunities for Liberian entrepreneurs. – Erasmus Williams (far left), head of ODA and Joseph Fatorma Sando (second from right), CEO of YEIB-MANCO.

MONROVIA — The Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO) and the Office of Diaspora Affairs (ODA) are exploring a strategic partnership aimed at connecting young Liberian entrepreneurs with diaspora investors, professional expertise and international markets to expand businesses and create jobs.

The discussions, held Thursday, October 8, at the Office of Diaspora Affairs at the Executive Mansion in Monrovia, focused on potential areas of cooperation to strengthen micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), promote Liberian products abroad and improve access to investment and business networks.

The proposed collaboration seeks to leverage YEIB-MANCO’s enterprise development and financing mechanisms alongside ODA’s connections with Liberians abroad to help locally owned businesses expand beyond the domestic market.



Participants included Erasmus Williams, head of the Office of Diaspora Affairs; Emmanuel B. Kollie, the office’s chief administrative officer; Joseph Fatorma Sando, chief executive officer of YEIB-MANCO; Hillary B. David, director for enterprise development; and Marcus B. Zarway, YEIB-AfDB project coordinator.

Diaspora Markets Offer Opportunities for Liberian Products

A major issue discussed was the potential to increase exports of authentic Liberian food products to markets in the United States, Europe and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) region.

Participants identified palm oil, gari, dried fish, pepper and other traditional food products as items with potential demand among Liberian diaspora communities.

However, Liberian producers are reportedly missing opportunities to supply these markets, while some products marketed as Liberian abroad are said to originate from countries such as Ghana and Malaysia.

The discussions highlighted the need for local businesses to improve production capacity, packaging, branding and compliance with international quality standards to compete more effectively in overseas markets.

Through the proposed partnership, ODA’s diaspora networks could help connect youth-led enterprises with buyers, distributors, investors and potential business partners abroad.

The initiative could also help businesses establish more reliable supply chains and position authentic Liberian-made products for broader international distribution.

Investment, Training and Business Connections

The two institutions identified several potential areas of collaboration, including diaspora-backed investment and co-financing for youth enterprises, mentorship from diaspora professionals, technical assistance, skills transfer and business-to-business partnerships.

Other proposed areas include export development, market access, trade facilitation and the promotion of Liberian small businesses on international platforms.

The discussions emphasized the potential to connect diaspora capital and expertise with the needs of emerging businesses in Liberia.

YEIB is a government initiative developed with the African Development Bank (AfDB) to support youth entrepreneurship and financial inclusion. Its three core instruments are the Technical Assistance Facility, which provides business development support and capacity building; the Enterprise Investment Facility, which provides investment financing; and the Credit Guarantee Facility, which helps reduce lending risks and improve young entrepreneurs’ access to credit.

ODA, operating under the Ministry of State for Presidential Affairs, works to mobilize the expertise, investment and partnerships of Liberians abroad and the wider African diaspora in support of Liberia’s development.

Proposed Link to Diaspora Initiatives

The meeting also explored potential links between the partnership and two ODA initiatives under development: the Diaspora Professional Service Corps (DPSC) and the iLiberia Platform.

The DPSC is intended to connect diaspora professionals with skills and expertise needed in Liberia, while the iLiberia Platform is designed to facilitate information sharing, matchmaking and connections between Liberians at home and abroad.

Participants also discussed the upcoming 2026 Diaspora Annual Return, which ODA is organizing with government institutions, business leaders, cultural organizations and international partners.

The event could provide an opportunity for eligible Liberian businesses to showcase their products and innovations while engaging directly with diaspora investors, professionals and prospective commercial partners.

MoU Proposed to Formalize Cooperation

To advance the discussions, the institutions identified two initial follow-up steps: drafting a memorandum of understanding (MoU) outlining potential cooperation in enterprise development, export guidance and business promotion; and identifying areas where YEIB’s existing programs and budget allocations could align with ODA’s activities.

The proposed alignment is intended to improve coordination and cost-effectiveness as the institutions explore ways to support youth-led businesses.

Although the discussions represent an initial step toward formalizing the partnership, the institutions have yet to announce a finalized agreement or specific implementation timeline.

If formalized, the collaboration could provide young Liberian entrepreneurs with improved access to financing, professional mentorship and international markets. Its impact will depend on the eventual terms of the agreement, the resources committed and the mechanisms established to help businesses meet export requirements and secure overseas buyers.

World.title: Tengbeh Urges Sweeping Financial, Personnel and Academic Audits at University of Liberia
World.content:
Labour advocate calls on GAC, IAA and university administration to strengthen oversight, verify faculty credentials and enforce promotion standards ahead of 2027

MONROVIA — Labour advocate and University of Liberia adjunct faculty member George Sahr Tengbeh has called for comprehensive financial, personnel and academic credentials audits at the country’s premier public university, urging authorities to strengthen accountability, transparency and academic standards ahead of 2027.

Tengbeh is calling on the General Auditing Commission (GAC), the Internal Audit Agency (IAA) and the university administration to undertake an independent review of the institution’s finances, verify employee records and qualifications, and ensure that faculty appointments and promotions comply with established academic requirements.

In a statement addressed to University of Liberia President Dr. Layli Maparyan, GAC Comptroller General Garswa P. Jackson and IAA head David A. Kemah, Tengbeh urged the relevant authorities to prioritize a comprehensive external financial audit beginning in January 2027.



He said the exercise would establish a clearer picture of the university’s financial and administrative position while identifying weaknesses requiring corrective action.

According to Tengbeh, the university’s last financial audit was reportedly conducted during the 2023/2024 period, with no subsequent external audit of the current administration identified in his statement.

“We want to see a different version of institutional integrity at the University of Liberia in 2027,” Tengbeh said, emphasizing that accountability and academic excellence should remain central to the institution’s governance.

Tengbeh Calls for Semester-Based Financial Audits

Beyond an external financial review, Tengbeh proposed internal financial audits every semester under the supervision of the Internal Audit Agency.

He argued that the university’s public funding and internally generated revenues require consistent monitoring to ensure proper accounting, effective expenditure controls, and responsible resource management.

Regular audits, he said, would help identify potential financial irregularities, improve financial reporting and strengthen the university’s internal control systems.

Tengbeh also acknowledged President Maparyan’s reported initiative to station IAA representatives at the university as independent internal auditors. However, he argued that their presence should be supported by regular reviews, effective follow-up mechanisms and implementation of recommendations arising from audit findings.

He maintained that internal auditing should produce measurable improvements in financial oversight rather than remain a procedural arrangement.

Personnel Records and Academic Credentials Under Scrutiny

Tengbeh also called for periodic personnel and academic credentials audits to verify employees’ records, qualifications, appointments, and related expenditures.

He recommended annual or biennial reviews, with the university’s Human Resource Management Department working alongside the IAA to maintain accurate and regularly updated personnel records.

According to him, such reviews would help establish whether appointments are properly documented, academic qualifications are verifiable, and personnel expenditures comply with established procedures.

He stressed, however, that the process should be conducted professionally and fairly, with respect for institutional regulations, employee rights and appropriate verification procedures.

Challenges GAC to Commission Independent Audit

Tengbeh directly challenged the General Auditing Commission to prioritize an independent audit of the university, referencing Jackson’s previous experience in the institution’s financial administration, internal auditing and comptrollership.

He also pointed to Jackson’s record of commissioning audits under his leadership at the GAC, arguing that the University of Liberia should receive similar attention.

“The GAC under your watch must respond to the University’s request for an audit and take the necessary steps to commission one under this new administration,” Tengbeh said.

He emphasized that an external audit should not be construed as an accusation against the current administration but as a standard governance measure for public institutions entrusted with managing public resources.

An independent review, he argued, would provide a clearer assessment of the university’s financial position and help strengthen public confidence in its management.

Faculty Promotions and Research Standards

Tengbeh’s proposed reforms extend beyond financial and administrative management to the qualifications, research records and promotion standards of faculty members.

He urged President Maparyan to enforce existing policies requiring the verification of academic credentials, research outputs and qualifications corresponding to faculty members’ respective ranks.

He expressed concern about cases in which faculty members holding master’s degrees may occupy senior academic positions without demonstrable research experience or peer-reviewed publications, where such qualifications and outputs are required by university standards.

Tengbeh said the institution should consistently apply its approved requirements and ensure that promotion decisions are supported by verifiable evidence of scholarly competence.

He also called on the university’s Board of Trustees to establish clear and transparent promotion criteria for academic staff if such provisions are not already in place.

Under his proposal, promotions to Assistant Professor and Associate Professor should follow the university’s approved requirements, including terminal degrees where required, peer-reviewed publications, demonstrated research capacity and the ability to attract competitive external research grants where applicable.

Tengbeh argued that transparent promotion standards would strengthen the university’s academic credibility, encourage research productivity and improve its prospects of securing international academic partnerships and donor support.

Calls for Broader Institutional Reform

Tengbeh framed the proposed audits as part of a broader effort to strengthen the university’s financial management, administrative systems and academic standing.

He said regular financial reviews, accurate personnel records and credible academic promotion procedures would help ensure that public resources are properly managed and academic standards are consistently enforced.

He cautioned that the proposed exercises should follow established institutional procedures and should not be used to target individuals or undermine any administration.

“As we enter 2027, our goal should be to build a University of Liberia that is financially accountable, administratively transparent, and academically competitive,” he said.

He urged the university administration, the GAC and the IAA to treat the proposals as an opportunity to reinforce public trust and advance institutional development.

“The time is now. Let us make 2027 a year of accountability, credible academic standards, and meaningful institutional reform at the University of Liberia,” Tengbeh added.

The statement did not include responses from the university administration, the GAC or the IAA regarding the proposed audits.

World.title: Mundubile’s Detention Is A Criminal Matter, Not A Barrier To Reconciliation, Says State House
World.content:
State House rejected claims that President Hakainde Hichilema’s call for national reconciliation cannot succeed while opposition leader Mr Brian Mundubile remains in detention. The President’s Political Advisor, Mr Levy Ngoma, said reducing Mr Mundubile’s incarceration to a political issue is misplaced because he is accused of committing a crime.

Mr Ngoma was responding to Mr Davies Mwila, National Chairperson of the BM8-ECL Movement and a former Patriotic Front (PF) Secretary General. Mr Mwila said on Saturday that there can be no reconciliation in the country as long as Mr Mundubile, Mr Makebi Zulu and 16 others remain in prison.

The exchange goes to the heart of the President’s message since he opened the 14th National Assembly. In a prayer posted on his Facebook page, President Hichilema asked God to guide public servants to serve with humility, gratitude and love.

“May we cherish our peace and remember with gratitude the quiet sacrifices that sustain it. May we all place service to our country and her interests above our own,” the Head of State wrote.

The opposition reads the same moment very differently. Mr Mwila earlier called on Government to establish an independent, credible and transparent inquiry into the death of former Transport Minister Mr Mutotwe Kafwaya, who was killed during a security operation at Mr Mundubile’s residence after the August polls. He also demanded the release of the detained opposition leaders.

Governance expert Dr Neo Simutanyi took a similar line. He said the President’s call for unity could not carry weight because of what happened during the elections, including the raid on Mr Mundubile’s house that ended in Mr Kafwaya’s death.

“There is no way the head of state can say we need to heal when people have a lot of questions like what happened during the elections,” Dr Simutanyi said.

He urged the President to convene a truth and reconciliation commission where citizens could air their grievances freely, without duress or intimidation. He also questioned why a full Cabinet had not been appointed a month after the President’s re-election.

State House’s position is that the detentions belong to the justice system. Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu face treason charges and were later also charged with seditious practices. Director of Public Prosecutions Mr Gilbert Phiri has said complex cases such as treason require time to investigate before they can be taken to court.

The detained leaders’ lawyers dispute that approach. They are seeking the court’s intervention over the prolonged detention in a hearing scheduled to run from 26 October to 6 November.

The reconciliation language has also spilled into the row over the National Day of Prayer. Tonse Alliance spokesperson Dr Lawrence Mwelwa said Government could not confidently stand before God in prayer while questions about Mr Kafwaya’s death and the treason detentions remained unanswered.

“What exactly would the government be celebrating? On its head there is Kafwaya’s blood. On its shoulders there is the incarceration of opposition leaders on trumped-up treason charges,” Dr Mwelwa said.

Church mother bodies said in August that they were considering a broader, longer-term national healing and reconciliation process. That process would be separate from their earlier role in facilitating Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu’s departure from United Nations premises.

For now, State House maintains that the President’s appeal for peace stands on its own and that the treason case must run its course in the courts.

World.title: Let The Opposition Hold The Executive To Account, British High Commissioner Says
World.content:
British High Commissioner to Zambia Ms Rebecca Terzeon said the opposition in Parliament must be allowed to operate effectively so that it can hold the Executive to account. She also urged that recommendations from election observation missions be taken seriously.

Ms Terzeon was speaking shortly after President Hakainde Hichilema officially opened the First Session of the 14th National Assembly in Lusaka on Friday, 9 October.

Her remarks come as the composition of the new House is being contested. Opposition voices say the governing party’s strength and recent decisions on proportional representation seats have left them with less room in the Chamber.

National Democratic Congress (NDC) president Ms Saboi Imboela said the current Parliament was basically a one-party state because members of other political parties had been compromised. She said Zambia now has an increased Parliament with a reduced voice, and she called on MPs to speak for the people rather than along partisan lines.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) is defending its decision to redistribute proportional representation seats belonging to the opposition National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) to the United Party for National Development (UPND). The Commission says the NRPUP failed to submit a full list of nominees within seven days, as the Electoral Process (Amendment) Act No. 12 of 2026 requires. It has dismissed claims of collusion as untrue and unfounded.

The President, in his address to the House, pledged to protect democratic institutions. “We will continue to protect our democracy, uphold the rule of law, and safeguard the peace and stability that Zambia has worked so hard to preserve,” he said.

He said his administration had worked since 2021 to restore confidence in democratic institutions and strengthen respect for the rule of law. He also warned that no lawlessness would be tolerated regardless of political affiliation.

Ms Terzeon’s reference to observer recommendations connects to a long-standing gap in the country’s electoral reform record. Several international missions, including a European Union mission that deployed 100 observers, monitored the August elections and committed to issuing recommendations for consideration by Zambian authorities once post-election processes conclude.

The opposition has said much of the post-election period remains unresolved. Its leading figures, Mr Brian Mundubile and Mr Makebi Zulu, remain in detention on treason charges, and governance commentators have called for a fuller account of what happened during the polls.

The opposition’s limited footprint in the House is also being contested in the courts. Election petitions in Kwacha, Zambezi East and Zambezi Central are due for judgment in November, with one of them challenging the election of an NRPUP MP.

For now, the British envoy’s message places the health of parliamentary oversight on the table at the start of the new term. Her central point is that an opposition able to scrutinise the Executive’s decisions is part of how democracies function.

World.title: Government To Cut Next Year’s CDF As Maize Overspend Squeezes Treasury
World.content:
Government will reduce next year’s Constituency Development Fund (CDF) allocation below the level initially budgeted, Finance and National Planning Minister Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane said. The Treasury is moving to contain overspending recorded this year, including heavier-than-planned maize purchases for the strategic food reserve.

Dr Musokotwane said the Treasury would communicate the revised allocations to local authorities. The aim, he said, is to prevent councils from over-procuring and building up arrears on the strength of figures that will no longer hold.

The cut lands on one of the administration’s most visible programmes. CDF has risen from K1.6 million per constituency in 2021 to K40 million in 2026, a national envelope of about K6.245 billion. Constituencies have used it for classrooms, boreholes, bursaries and local empowerment schemes.

The Minister said Government had exceeded its planned spending on strategic food reserves after buying larger quantities of maize than it had budgeted for. The pressure on that line is already showing. A front-page report quoted Dr Musokotwane as saying there would be no Treasury funds for the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) next season. In Northern Province alone, the agency has bought 234,000 tonnes of maize this marketing season.

The squeeze does not end with CDF. Dr Musokotwane said Government’s limited cash position could also affect funding for road construction, as the Treasury tries to manage available resources and meet its financial obligations.

He warned that spending must urgently be aligned with available revenue. Limited revenue, he said, could affect funding for priority sectors, including free education.

The September Treasury figures show how tightly the budget is already drawn. Of the K14.6 billion released that month, K5.4 billion went to the public service wage bill. Another K5.4 billion went to debt service and arrears: K4.1 billion to domestic debt, K625.1 million to external debt and K674.2 million to clear domestic arrears. Capital expenditure received K526.9 million, of which K459.9 million went to roads.

Transfers, subsidies and social benefits took K1.8 billion. This covered K857 million for grant-aided institutions such as hospitals and universities, K435.8 million for the Social Cash Transfer, K200 million for the Food Security Pack and K120.8 million for the Local Authorities Equalisation Fund.

Dr Musokotwane said credible budgeting requires reliable revenue inflows, disciplined expenditure, sustainable debt management and stronger domestic revenue mobilisation. He tied the recent restoration of excise duty on fuel directly to that pressure.

“The excise duty on fuel has been restored to help ease fiscal pressures arising from the war in the Middle East,” the Minister said. He added that the measure would help sustain free education, school feeding and the Social Cash Transfer.

The planned CDF reduction comes days after President Hakainde Hichilema opened the 14th National Assembly. In that address, he cited the rise in CDF from K1.6 million to K40 million per constituency as evidence of development decisions moving closer to communities.

Public submissions on the 2027 national budget and the 2027 to 2029 Medium-Term Budget Plan have closed. The Treasury says it will analyse them to strengthen expenditure prioritisation and value for money.

“The 2026 budget remains under implementation. The detailed revenue and expenditure measures for 2027 will only be announced when the 2027 National Budget is presented to Parliament,” Dr Musokotwane said.

The exact size of the CDF reduction will therefore be confirmed only when the 2027 Budget is tabled. Councils will receive their revised allocations from the Treasury before then.

World.title: ZPL suspends midweek fixtures
World.content:
The Zambian Premier League (ZPL) has suspended all midweek matches under its umbrella scheduled between Monday, 12th October and Friday, 16th October 2026 for reasons yet to be disclosed.

The suspension affects key fixtures, including the Stream A top-of-the-table clash between leaders Nkana and NAPSA Stars which was scheduled for Wednesday, 14th October 2026.

In Memo 115 of the 2026 Transition Season dated 11th October 2026, the League announced the immediate suspension of all midweek league matches covering competitions from Monday to Friday until further notice.

ZPL Chief Executive Officer Joseph Chimpampwe said new dates will be assigned to the suspended matches.

“With immediate effect, all midweek matches (Monday to Friday) in the MTN Super League, the Women’s Super-Division, the Men’s National Division and the Women’s National Division are suspended until further notice. This includes rescheduled and postponed matches allocated to midweek dates,” Chimpampwe stated.

Chimpampwe warned clubs against making independent arrangements to play the affected fixtures.

“Suspended matches will be rescheduled to dates to be announced by the League. Clubs must not make their own arrangements to play any suspended fixture. Clubs must immediately inform their players, officials, supporters and service providers,” he said.

Meanwhile, league matches scheduled for the weekend of 17–18 October 2026 remain unaffected and will proceed as planned, although clubs have been advised to remain on standby for further developments.

“Matches scheduled for the weekend of 17th to 18th October 2026 are not affected and will be played as scheduled. All clubs must, however, remain on standby for further developments,” Chimpampwe added.

World.title: Seriousness Of Treason Charges Does Not Justify Prolonged Detention, Says COF, As Food Is Seized At Mukobeko
World.content:
Rights group Chapter One Foundation (COF) said the seriousness of an offence does not justify prolonged detention without judicial oversight. The challenge to the State’s handling of the treason case comes as lawyers for the detained opposition leaders say prison officers blocked food sent by their families.

COF Executive Director Mr Josiah Kalala was responding to Director of Public Prosecutions Mr Gilbert Phiri. The DPP attributed delays in prosecuting cases to ongoing investigations and said complicated matters such as treason take time.

Mr Phiri has previously defended the pace of the case against Mr Brian Mundubile, Mr Makebi Zulu and others. He said investigators must gather witness statements, medical reports and other evidence before a fully supported case can go to court, and he cited the historic treason trial of Mr Edward Jack Shamwana as an example of how long such cases can take.

Mr Kalala’s position is that time spent investigating cannot be time spent in prison without a court overseeing the detention. The detainees have yet to appear before a court on the treason charge.

The question of how they are being treated in custody has now sharpened. Senior counsel Mr Sakwiba Sikota appealed to President Hakainde Hichilema to intervene after authorities at Mukobeko Maximum Security Correctional Facility in Kabwe allegedly blocked food meant for Mr Mundubile and 17 others.

Mr Sikota said the families sent the food to the prison through the Anglican Cathedral of the Holy Cross on Wednesday. He said it was confiscated at the gate without explanation and never reached the detainees, who include retired Anglican bishop Mr Trevor Mwamba.

“Visitors to the 18 detainees were turned away, with all food parcels seized by prison warders,” Mr Sikota said.

He described the seizure as inhumane, unconstitutional and politically motivated. “These are persons presumed innocent until proven guilty. Denying them food from their families is cruel and degrading. This is an embarrassment to the State,” he said.

Mr Sikota urged the President to order the Zambia Correctional Service (ZCS) to stop the practice. “The President said he would restore the rule of law. This is a test of that commitment,” he said. The ZCS had not responded to queries at the time of publication.

The length of detention varies across the group. Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu had been held for 51 days without appearing before a court, and Lusaka businessman Mr Valden Harry Findlay for more than 68 days.

The detainees have petitioned the State over violations of their constitutional rights arising from detention without trial. The petition also cites the alleged torture of three detainees, Mr Brazil Soko, Mr Jackson Mutyoka and Mr Bernard Chanda Chewe. They were allegedly moved to Mwembeshi Correctional Facility and back on 7 September without their lawyers’ consent.

The food seizure is not the first dispute over meals. In September, Mr Sikota said Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu had asked to receive food from outside the facility rather than eat what was prepared internally, a request prison authorities turned down.

The Law Association of Zambia has also called for the release of the detainees who have not been taken to court. Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu were separately charged with seditious practices on 11 September.

The detainees are now looking to the courts. Their application seeking intervention over the prolonged detention is scheduled to be heard from 26 October to 6 November.

World.title: ECZ Defends Handing NRPUP’s Vacant Proportional Representation Seats To UPND
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has rejected claims that it unlawfully handed proportional representation (PR) seats belonging to the opposition National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) to the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND). The Commission says the opposition party lost the seats by failing to submit a full list of nominees within the period set by law.

The row began with allegations by former diplomat Mr Emmanuel Mwamba, who accused the Commission of unlawfully allocating the NRPUP’s seats to the UPND. Mr Mwamba claimed the reallocation was the product of political collusion or deliberate manipulation of the PR process.

In a statement responding to the claims, Chief Electoral Officer Mr Brown Kasaro dismissed any suggestion of wrongdoing. He said the Commission had acted strictly within the Electoral Process (Amendment) Act No. 12 of 2026, which clearly sets out the procedures every qualifying political party must follow once PR seats have been allocated.

“The redistribution of seats arising from a failure to submit a party list is a requirement of the law and not an act of political favouritism or manipulation,” Mr Kasaro said.

The electoral chief pointed to Section 36C(1) of the Act, which requires a qualifying party to submit its party list within seven days of the distribution of PR seats. Section 36C(9) then directs the Commission, where a party misses that window, to redistribute the vacant seat to another qualifying party using the formula laid down in Section 36B.

The Commission’s defence rests on what it describes as the NRPUP’s own shortfall. The ECZ said the party knew how many seats it was entitled to but submitted fewer nominees than required. That left seats unfilled once the statutory period had run its course.

Mr Kasaro said the Commission had met both qualifying political parties, and the requirements governing the PR process were explained at that meeting. He said the duty to submit the required names within the statutory deadline rested with each qualifying party. The Commission, he added, could not be held accountable for a party’s failure to meet the legal requirements.

The ECZ said the redistribution was a direct consequence of that failure, not an attempt to favour the UPND. It also rejected claims that applying the law amounted to electoral misconduct.

Under the electoral framework, the PR system allocates seats to qualifying political parties. The provisions cited by the Commission deal specifically with vacant seats left when a party does not submit its list within the required period.

The dispute concerns seats in the new National Assembly. President Hakainde Hichilema officially opened its First Session in Lusaka on Friday, 9 October. Addressing the House, the Head of State highlighted the role of women, young people and persons with disabilities under the Mixed-Member Proportional Representation System. Allocations under that system include 20 women, 15 youths and five persons with disabilities.

The NRPUP’s parliamentary standing is also being tested in the courts. In Kwacha Constituency, losing UPND candidate Mr Crispin Chomba is challenging the election of NRPUP MP Dr Brian Chirambo, alleging violence and vote-buying. The ECZ is cited as second respondent in that matter, which continues before Judge Bonaventure Mbewe in Kitwe.

Opposition unease over the make-up of the new House goes beyond the PR dispute. National Democratic Congress (NDC) president Ms Saboi Imboela said the current Parliament was basically a one-party state because members of other political parties had been compromised. She said Zambia now has an increased Parliament with a reduced voice.

For now, the Commission is standing by its decision. The ECZ urged political stakeholders and members of the public to disregard the allegations, describing them as untrue and unfounded.

World.title: When repentance is merged with a party: why the State got the prayer day wrong
World.content:
When repentance is merged with a party: why the State got the prayer day wrong

By Amb Emmanuel Mwamba

Some days a nation keeps because they are holidays, and some it keeps because it needs them. The 18th of October was the second kind. Government has now erased it from the calendar and folded what was left of it into the 29th of December, as if fasting and feasting were the same act on different dates.

The decision was announced by Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa, the most senior civil servant in the land and the official voice of Government on such matters. In a statement issued in Lusaka, he said Statutory Instrument Number 78 of 2015 had been revoked and replaced by Statutory Instrument Number 73 of 2026, and that the merger followed consultations with the church mother bodies.

The two days are not the same, and anyone who has ever prayed knows it.

Consider what the 18th was for. Its full name was the National Day of Prayer, Fasting, Repentance and Reconciliation, and every word in that name points inward and downward. People fast to empty themselves and repent because they have done wrong. They reconcile by going to the person they have wounded and asking for forgiveness. It was a day for sackcloth, not for a stage.

The 29th of December is a different occasion. It marks the day in 1991 when President Frederick Chiluba declared Zambia a Christian Nation, a declaration later written into the preamble of our Constitution. It honours a heritage that runs back through the churches that walked with this country from Kaunda’s time. It is a day of thanksgiving, choirs and ceremony, a day to rejoice.

So where, in a day of prayer and reconciliation, do celebration and commemoration come in? No one can fast on their knees in repentance while marching in a ceremony for a historic declaration. No one can weep for the nation’s sins and toast its heritage in the same breath. Reverend Godfridah Sumaili said it plainly: “I am wondering how a day of weeping and repentance could be combined with a day of celebration.” Government has yet to answer her.

If the real concern was the cost of another public holiday, the solution was simple and in plain sight: keep the day and drop the holiday. When the 18th falls on a Thursday, observe it on the Saturday or Sunday that follows, when churches are already full and offices already closed. The nation would keep its altar and the Treasury its working day, and nobody would lose anything.instead Government chose to remove the day altogether, and that choice tells us something.

Look at what was cut. The commemoration survived and so did the heritage. What disappeared were the repentance and the reconciliation, and the timing makes that hard to ignore.

This country has just come through a bitter election. Constituencies such as Mandevu are going back to the polls because the 13 August vote there was inconclusive. Opposition leaders sit in maximum-security prisons while churches plead for a national round table. Many Zambians still carry questions about how the counting ended, and about the elder statesmen this nation has buried along the way.

That is the atmosphere the 18th would have arrived in, with a whole nation gathered around one word: reconciliation. And reconciliation is exactly what our own official record now demands.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia stopped counting, and the reason it gave the nation was violence. Yesterday the President stood before Parliament and declared that the same elections were “peaceful, free and fair”. One arm of the State says there was violence, while the Head of State says there was peace.

Both cannot be fully true. If counting had to stop because of violence, the polls were not entirely peaceful. If the polls were entirely peaceful, the nation is owed a different explanation for why the counting stopped. Either way, Zambians have been handed two official accounts of one election, and a nation holding two truths is a nation split down the middle.

That is precisely what a day of prayer and reconciliation exists for. It is the one day on the calendar built to bring the two sides of a divided country to the same altar, to name what went wrong and to ask for healing. This year, of all years, the country needed the 18th of October more than ever.

Yet this is the year it was abolished. A day of national repentance would have carried those contradictions onto every pulpit in the land, and perhaps that is exactly what someone did not want. Removing the day instead of facing it is not reform. It is cowardice dressed up as administration.

There is one more fair question. The 18th of October was declared under Statutory Instrument Number 78 of 2015, during the time of the late President Edgar Lungu. Does the day simply remind this administration of a political rival it never made peace with? Zambians are entitled to wonder whether a sacred observance has been treated as part of an old regime’s furniture and cleared out with the rest.

It would fit a pattern, because this administration treats everything as a first. Free education, we are told, is a first. Yet Zambians remember free basic education long before 2021. Many of us remember the school milk and biscuits, the free exercise books and the pencils handed out in classrooms when we were growing up.

School feeding is also called a first, and it is not. The Constituency Development Fund is called revolutionary, yet it existed for years before this Government arrived. The President himself told Parliament the fund stood at K1.6 million when his administration took over.

Raising that figure to K40 million on paper is welcome. Zambians, however, judge a fund by what they can touch. In too many constituencies the classrooms, clinics and teachers’ houses that K40 million should have built are still missing, and announcing big numbers is not the same as building with them.

A government that respected the past would have built on the 18th of October rather than buried it. Imagine what the day could have become: the nation’s annual moment of healing after a divisive election. The President, the opposition and the churches could have knelt in one cathedral, with the families of prisoners in the front pews, before the God named in the preamble of our Constitution. No budget line can buy that kind of national cohesion.

The Ministry of National Guidance and Religious Affairs, however, was dissolved soon after this Government took office in 2021, and the day of repentance has now gone the same way. Each step can be explained away on its own. Taken together, they suggest that the Christian character of this nation, written into our founding law, is being emptied out one quiet decision at a time.

It is the no-look pass of football: the ball moves while the player looks elsewhere, and by the time the crowd notices, the goal has gone in. Zambians do notice. They have been watching since 2021, and a merger announced in a Friday evening statement does not fool them.

That brings me to the church. Government says it consulted the church mother bodies, so let the mother bodies speak.

Where is Dr Nevers Mumba on this? Where are Bishop Joe Imakando and Bishop H.K. Banda? Where is Bishop Mususu, and where is Billy Mfula? Where is the United Church of Zambia? What is the position of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, whose members keep the Sabbath and understand better than most what it means to set a day apart? Where are the traditional churches that were praying in this land long before any political party existed?

And who exactly was consulted? Name them. If the decision is sound, publish the minutes of the consultation and let the faithful judge. If it cannot survive being explained, it should never have been made.

Above all, what does the ordinary Zambian think? Nobody asked the woman who fasted every 18th of October for her family and her country.

A nation that declares itself Christian in its Constitution cannot quietly retire its day of repentance and expect neither God nor the people to notice. Zambia’s Christian identity seems to make some in power uncomfortable, because repentance demands that the powerful be humbled too.

Restore the 18th of October. Keep it as a day even if it is no longer a holiday. Let the nation fast, pray and reconcile, and let those in authority kneel alongside everyone else.

World.title: Wedson named coach of the month in Malawi
World.content:
Former Chipolopolo coach Wedson Nyirenda has won the coach of the month accolade in the Malawian FDH Bank Premiership.

Nyirenda, the FCB Nyasa Big Bullets head coach, has been named the August Coach of the Month, securing his second monthly honour since taking charge in June.

According to the Bullets website, Nyirenda received the award at half-time during Sunday’s league encounter against Blue Eagles at Mpira Stadium, where Bullets went on to secure a 2-0 victory and move to the top of the standings.

Having also claimed the June award following a winning start to his tenure, Nyirenda earned his latest recognition for a four-match unbeaten run covering August and the final first-round fixture in September before the mid-season break.

Bullets began the run with a 2-0 victory over Chitipa United at Mpira Stadium, where Blessings Mpokera broke the deadlock from the penalty spot before Clever Kalambo doubled the advantage two minutes later.

Another narrow victory followed a week later as we travelled north to face Karonga United, with Ephraim Kondowe’s 37th-minute finish proving enough to secure a 1-0 win at Karonga Stadium.

The unbeaten run continued at Dedza Stadium, where Bullets were held to a goalless draw by Luanar Mitundu, maintaining their record of not conceding during the run.

Nyirenda’s side then signed off the first round in emphatic fashion on 5 September, sweeping aside Silver Strikers 5-0 at Mpira Stadium.

Kondowe struck a hat-trick, with Wongani Lungu and Misheck Billiat also on target as Bullets completed their league commitments before the mid-season break.

Across the four matches, Bullets collected 10 points from a possible 12, scoring eight goals without conceding and keeping four consecutive clean sheets.

Nyirenda claimed the award ahead of fellow nominees Declerk Msakakuona of Blue Eagles and Abbas Makawa of Civil Service United.

Sunday’s victory over Blue Eagles took The People’s Team to 33 points, one ahead of Mighty Wanderers, as the second round of the FDH Bank Premiership got underway.

Nyirenda has in the past coached inZambia, South Africa and Mozambique.

Meanwhile, Nyirenda is encouraged by the progress of our three midseason signings but insists they still have plenty to prove as competitive football resumes.

Zimbabwean forward Tinaye Tsimba, Liberian midfielder Sheku Sheriff and defender Alihaji Mnjale joined us during the transfer window, with the five-week break giving Nyirenda and his technical panel an opportunity to assess them through a series of friendly matches ahead of the second round.

“The break was well planned and allowed us to closely assess the players we signed during the transfer window,” said Nyirenda during a pre-match press conference, adding that the trio had shown in the friendlies that they could fit well into his squad.

Despite their encouraging performances, the Zambian stressed that adapting to his playing system is only the first step, with competition for places remaining high.

“When it comes to game time, they still have to prove themselves. It is one thing to show that you can fit into the system, but it is another to secure a place in the team. They have to demonstrate that they are capable of playing for Bullets.

“It will not be easy because competition for places is high, and they must fight for their positions,” he added.

Tsimba and Mnjale underlined their progress by scoring their first goals for Bullets in the 4-2 victory over Extreme FC in Mchinji, our final friendly of the midseason break.
