World.title: Popcaan gets US visa, Belizean fans in America celebrate
World.content:
Popcaan gets US visa, Belizean fans in America celebrate

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Good news for dancehall lovers. Popcaan has secured his US visa.

The Jamaican star, known as the Unruly Boss, has cleared a major hurdle that could finally allow him to perform for his American fans, according to The Shade Room.

Popcaan, who is signed to Drake’s OVO Sound label, has a huge following across the Caribbean, including right here in Belize, where his music is a staple at parties, on the radio and in vehicles across the country.

The news could be especially exciting for Belizeans living in the US. Communities in cities like Los Angeles, New York and Chicago may soon get the chance to see him perform live.

No US performance dates have been announced yet.

World.title: China sanctions Belize Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca over Taiwan ties
World.content:
China sanctions Belize Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca over Taiwan ties

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): China has imposed sanctions on Belize’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Francis Fonseca, over Belize’s diplomatic relationship with Taiwan, according to Al Jazeera.

The report, citing AFP and Reuters, says China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the measures on Monday, October 12. They took effect the same day.

Paraguay’s Communications Minister Gustavo Villate was also sanctioned.

According to Al Jazeera, the measures include freezing the ministers’ assets in China and denying them entry visas to Hong Kong and Macau. Chinese organizations and individuals are also barred from doing business or cooperating with them.

Beijing said the sanctions were about safeguarding China’s national sovereignty and opposing what it called Taiwan separatist activities. The Chinese Foreign Ministry claimed the ministers had made statements and taken actions damaging to China’s core interests.

These are China’s characterizations. Belize and Paraguay are among the 12 countries that maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, a relationship Belize has held for 37 years.

It was not immediately clear whether the Government of Belize had responded to the sanctions.

World.title: Home movers raise safety concerns after crash that killed Sgt. Ponce
World.content:
Home movers raise safety concerns after crash that killed Sgt. Ponce

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Belize Home Movers Group says it has serious concerns about the circumstances of Saturday night’s crash on the George Price Highway that claimed the life of Police Sergeant Jovanni Ponce.

Sgt. Ponce, 50, died after his SUV collided with a house being transported on a flatbed truck between Miles 42 and 43 in Cotton Tree Village.

In a statement on Sunday, the group said it was devastated by the tragedy and extended condolences to the family and loved ones of the deceased.

The group said its members recognize the added risks of moving houses on weekend nights and have consistently tried to avoid moves on Saturdays and Sundays. It said it is deeply disappointed that a house was being moved on a Saturday night.

It also pointed to what it called apparent shortcomings in the safety lighting on the house involved.

“Public safety must always take precedence,” the group said. “These precautions exist for one reason: to protect human life.”

World.title: Social media influencer Benjamin Garcia, Mexican businessman formally charged following shooting incident in Belize City
World.content:
Social media influencer Benjamin Garcia, Mexican businessman formally charged following shooting incident in Belize City

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Social media influencer Benjamin Eduardo Garcia, 27, and Mexican businessman Sergio Martinez Ramirez, 36, have now been formally arrested and charged with discharging a firearm in public following an incident on the Philip Goldson Highway early Saturday morning.

The Belize Police Department confirmed the development in an update issued at 11:35 a.m. Sunday, putting to rest earlier uncertainty surrounding the status of the two men.

The charges follow earlier media reports that Garcia, who has been publicly associated with newly appointed Minister of National Security Michel Chebat, had been released without charges after police detained both men in connection with gunshots heard near Social Lounge at approximately 1:45 a.m. on October 10. The Belize Police Department subsequently disputed those reports.

According to the initial police report, officers conducting business checks heard several gunshots and observed a grey Ford F-250 pickup truck leaving the area. A pursuit ended near the Pallotti roundabout, where police intercepted the vehicle and detained both occupants.

During a search, Garcia informed officers that he had a licensed 9mm firearm in the glove compartment. Police recovered the weapon with one round in the chamber and 11 rounds in the magazine.

Earlier Sunday, police issued a clarification disputing media reports that Garcia had been released, maintaining that the individual concerned remained in custody while investigators prepared charges.

The department has now confirmed that both Garcia and Ramirez have been formally charged with discharging a firearm in public.

The incident has attracted public attention because of Garcia’s previously documented association with Chebat, who assumed responsibility for the Belize Police Department less than a week ago. There is no verified evidence or suggestion by BBN that Minister Chebat intervened in the investigation or influenced the handling of the case.

The two men are now facing criminal proceedings in connection with the incident. The charges remain allegations, and neither man has been convicted.

The police statement does not indicate whether either man has appeared before a magistrate or whether bail has been considered.

World.title: Belize Police mourn Sergeant Jovanni Ponce
World.content:
Belize Police mourn Sergeant Jovanni Ponce

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Saturday night drive ended in tragedy for Sergeant Jovanni Ponce and his family.

The 50 year old police officer was travelling along the George Price Highway near Cotton Tree Village when his SUV collided with a house being moved on a flatbed truck heading the other way.

The impact left his Chevrolet Equinox trapped under the structure. First responders found Sgt. Ponce unresponsive at the wheel. He was rushed to the Western Regional Hospital but did not survive.

His wife and a child travelling with him escaped without serious injury.

The 58 year old driver of the flatbed truck was served with a Notice of Intended Prosecution, and a urine sample was taken as part of the investigation.

Sgt. Ponce’s death is a heavy loss for his family, his colleagues and the Belize Police Department.

BBN extends condolences to his loved ones and fellow officers.

World.title: Police dispute reports that Benjamin Garcia was released following shooting incident; Say he is still detained pending charges
World.content:
Police dispute reports that Benjamin Garcia was released following shooting incident; Say he is still detained pending charges

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Police Department has issued a clarification disputing media reports that a social media influencer was released without charges following a shooting incident on the Philip Goldson Highway early Saturday morning.

In a statement issued Sunday morning, police said that, contrary to reports circulating in the media, particularly those published by Channel 7 News Belize, the individual at the centre of the investigation remains in police custody.

“The individual in question remains in police custody and is presently being processed as investigators prepare to lay the appropriate charges,” the department stated.

The clarification follows reports concerning the detention of 27-year-old social media influencer Benjamin Eduardo Garcia and 36-year-old Mexican businessman Sergio Martinez Ramirez, who were intercepted near the Pallotti roundabout after police heard several gunshots in the vicinity of Social Lounge at approximately 1:45 a.m. on October 10.

According to the initial police report, officers pursued a grey Ford F-250 pickup truck after hearing the gunfire. During a subsequent search, Garcia reportedly disclosed that he had a licensed 9mm firearm in the glove compartment. Police recovered the weapon with one round in the chamber and 11 rounds in the magazine.

The initial report indicated that both men would be jointly charged with discharging a firearm in public. Subsequent media reports, however, suggested that no charges had been laid and that Garcia had been released.

In its clarification, the department urged media houses to ensure their reporting reflects the current status of the investigation and that accurate, verified information is disseminated to the public.

Police also reaffirmed their commitment to transparency and professionalism, adding that further updates would be provided as appropriate.

The department did not identify the individual by name in its clarification, specify which charges investigators intend to pursue, or explain the circumstances that led to the earlier reports of a release.

The incident has drawn attention because of Garcia’s publicly documented association with a known Minister of Government, and comes amid growing concern over a recent spate of deadly shootings in Belize City.

As of Sunday morning, police have not announced any formally laid charges in connection with the incident.

The police clarification follows the department’s initial report, which expressly stated that both men would be charged with discharging a firearm in public.

While police now maintain that the individual remains detained and charges are being prepared, they have not explained the discrepancy between that account and the earlier reports of his release.

World.title: Social media influencer reportedly released without charges after shooting incident
World.content:
Social media influencer reportedly released without charges after shooting incident

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Less than a week after a reshuffle of Cabinet, questions are emerging over the reported alleged release without charges of a social media influencer, following a shooting incident in Belize City early Saturday morning.

Benjamin Eduardo Garcia, 27, and Mexican businessman Sergio Martinez Ramirez, 36, were detained after police responding to gunshots along the Philip Goldson Highway pursued and intercepted a grey Ford F-250 pickup truck. Although an initial police report indicated that both men would be jointly charged with discharging a firearm in public, a Channel 7 report indicated that Garcia was subsequently released without charges.

According to the police report, officers assigned to the P4 Support Team were conducting business checks at Social Lounge at approximately 1:45 a.m. on October 10 when they heard several gunshots. Officers observed the pickup truck leaving the area and initiated a pursuit that ended near the Pallotti roundabout, where additional police units intercepted the vehicle.

Garcia, who was travelling as a passenger, and Ramirez, the driver, were detained. During a search, Garcia informed officers that he had a licensed 9mm firearm inside the glove compartment. Police recovered the weapon and found one live round in the chamber and 11 rounds in the magazine.

Both men were cautioned in connection with the alleged offence of discharging a firearm in public. Scenes of Crime personnel were called to process the relevant locations, and the report expressly stated that both men would be taken to the Belama Police Station to be jointly charged.

Garcia’s reported release without charges raises questions about what transpired between the initial police investigation and his alleged release, including whether ballistic evidence was examined, whether either detainee was found to have discharged a weapon, and who may have authorized the alleged decision not to proceed with charges.

The incident comes at an especially troubling time for Belize City, where a fresh wave of deadly gun violence has claimed several young lives in recent days. On Thursday, October 8, 17-year-old Kaylon David was fatally shot on Iguana Street Extension, while 20-year-old Shamar Smith was murdered on Pelican Street later that evening. Another victim, 27-year-old Jory Bowden, was killed on Central American Boulevard on Friday night. The three killings have heightened public concerns about escalating firearm violence and the police department’s ability to contain it.

The Garcia incident also places renewed attention on how the police department handles high profile cases and Belizeans are hopeful that this matter will not be shrugged under the rug. The police department underwent leadership changes on October 6, when Michel Chebat was appointed Minister of National Security, replacing Julius Espat, who had served as interim Minister of Home Affairs since June. The Cabinet reshuffle placed both the Belize Police Department and Belize Defence Force under Chebat’s leadership.

In July, during Espat’s short stint as Police Minister, he had handled a politically sensitive police matter. Following allegations that Stoney Ferguson, the son of Agriculture Minister Rodwell Ferguson, assaulted a police officer and damaged a police vehicle in Placencia, Espat reportedly directed police to pursue his arrest despite his family connections. Ferguson had initially been released without charges, reportedly following telephone calls made on his behalf. Espat subsequently made clear that police officers were expected to act according to the law rather than political considerations.

The question now is whether that same standard of accountability will be upheld under the police department’s new leadership. The fact that Garcia possesses a licensed firearm does not, by itself, establish that he discharged it unlawfully. Equally, the initial police report’s stated intention to charge both men does not establish their guilt. However, the apparent reported reversal warrants an explanation, particularly given the seriousness with which firearm offences are ordinarily treated in Belize.

As of publication, BBN has not independently established who fired the shots, whether ballistic testing linked Garcia’s firearm to the incident, or the official grounds for his reported release. There is also no verified evidence that Minister Chebat intervened in the police investigation or influenced the decision not to charge him.

With Belize City confronting another deadly surge in gun violence, the circumstances surrounding the incident raise broader questions about consistency, transparency and equal treatment under the law.

World.title: Greed does not run the world, envy does, the old man’s verdict and the Belizean books
World.content:
Greed does not run the world, envy does, the old man’s verdict and the Belizean books

By Horace Palacio:

A quote has been moving across Belizean timelines this week, and readers know the house ritual. Before we discuss any famous line, we check the signature.

This one, for once, is genuine. Charlie Munger, the late vice chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, said it plainly at his shareholder meeting in 2022, at ninety eight years of age. The world is not driven by greed. It is driven by envy. His partner Warren Buffett spent decades quoting the line on his behalf. So this is not an internet orphan. It is the considered verdict of a man who spent a full century watching money move through human hands, delivered a year before he died, still worth billions, still unimpressed.

When a witness that qualified files a report that strange, a Sunday is well spent examining it. So let us make the old man’s case, and then bring the books home to Belize.

Start at the kitchen table with the distinction, because the two sins are commonly confused and they are entirely different machines.

Greed is wanting more. Envy is wanting what he has. Greed is absolute, a bigger number on your own page. Envy is relative, a smaller gap between your page and your neighbor’s. And that difference changes everything, because an absolute hunger can be fed. A relative one cannot, ever, because the reference point walks. Researchers once famously found that people would accept a smaller salary, provided it exceeded their neighbor’s, over a doubled salary that fell short of the man next door. Read that twice. Human beings will pay real money, out of their own pockets, purely to win a comparison. That is not greed. Greed would take the bigger check. That is envy, and it is the stronger force.

Now the case for Munger’s verdict, and it stands on three legs.

First, universality. Greed, in its grand form, is a specialist’s sin, the engine of the tycoon, the hoarder, the few. Envy is issued to everyone at birth. The man with nothing feels no greed for a yacht he has never imagined, but he feels envy for his cousin’s pickup truck by Tuesday. Greed drives the top of the pyramid. Envy drives every floor of it. A force that operates in every heart will always move more of the world than one operating in a handful.

Second, the oldest evidence on record. Open the Book our grandmothers kept by the bed. The first crime scene in human history had no money in it. Cain did not rob Abel. He envied him, and a brother died over a comparison. And study the Ten Commandments with an economist’s eye. Nine of them ban actions, stealing, killing, lying. The tenth bans a feeling. Thou shalt not covet. The ancients legislated against envy itself, the only commandment aimed directly at the heart’s bookkeeping, because they understood what Munger confirmed three thousand years later. The other sins are envy’s employees.

Third, the modern proof, and this one Belize carries in its pocket. The entire advertising industry is an envy refinery, selling not products but comparisons. And the feed, the algorithm this column has dissected all year, is envy at industrial scale. Your grandmother compared her life with one village. You compare yours, hourly, against the curated highlight reel of the entire planet, and the machine profits precisely from the width of the gap it manufactures. The richest companies in history run on harvested attention, yes, but ask what holds the attention. Munger answered. The scroll is a mirror rigged to lose.

Now bring the books home, because Belize runs some of the most envy-leveraged accounts on earth.

Count the household entries. The loan taken not for the land but for the show, the rims before the roof, the September splurge calibrated to the neighbor’s September, the funeral and wedding spending that bankrupts families in the name of appearances. This column begged you months ago, land before car. Understand today who writes the opposite purchase order. Envy does. Envy is the silent co-signer on half the bad debt in this country.

Count the political entries. The ham economy works because the gift is relative, visible, comparative. The deepest cry in our politics is rarely build it for all of us. It is why did he get it. And both parties farm that crop expertly, aiming each tribe’s resentment sideways at neighbors, never upward at ledgers, exactly as the unpaid bodyguards column described. Envy is the cheapest fuel in Belizean politics, and the tank is always full.

And count the oldest entry of all, the one this column named long ago. The crab bucket needs no lid, and now you know the engine underneath it. The crab does not dream of climbing. He dreams of the climber falling. That is envy’s signature move, it prefers leveling down to building up, because leveling down closes the gap without requiring a single day’s work. Every mocked student, every slandered success, every whispered must be connections is the bucket doing envy’s accounting.

Very well. The diagnosis is Munger’s. The medicine, mercifully, is also his, and he left three doses.

Dose one, see the sin’s absurd economics. Envy, the old man loved to say, is the one sin with no fun in it whatsoever. Gluttony at least offers the meal. Envy is all pain, zero pleasure, a trolley ride consisting entirely of the fare. Why, he asked, would anyone board that trolley?

Dose two, retire the race you cannot win. Someone, Munger taught, will always be getting richer faster than you, and this is not a tragedy. The only comparison that compounds is you against your own yesterday. The farmer measuring his field against last season grows. The farmer measuring it against his neighbor’s seethes, and seething has never fertilized an acre.

Dose three, and this is the conversion that turns the poison into fuel. The safest way to get what you want, Munger told a graduating class, is to deserve what you want. So when the burn rises in your chest at another Belizean’s success, run the test this column gave you once, and then go further. Do not merely refuse to stone the climber. Enroll with him. Envy, interrogated honestly, is just unprocessed information about what you actually want. Convert every pang into one question, what did he do that I have not done yet, and envy becomes a curriculum. The bad mind becomes a reading list.

Close the books, then, with the national arithmetic. Belize runs a chronic envy surplus and a building deficit, and the two lines are connected, because every hour spent minding the neighbor’s progress is an hour unavailable to your own. Imagine this country converting its envy budget, the whispering, the clawing, the comparison scrolling, into the builder’s question this column planted weeks ago. What are you building. That single currency exchange, performed in enough Belizean hearts, is worth more than any foreign loan.

The old man watched money for a hundred years and left us the finding free of charge. The world runs on envy, and envy runs on us.

It is Sunday, Belize. The trolley is at the stop, doors open, fare ready, no fun aboard, same as every day.

Let it leave without you.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: WALK AWAY!
World.content:
West Indies’ Sherfane Rutherford (right) walks back to the pavilion after his dismissal during the 2026 ICC Men’s T20 Cricket World Cup Super Eights match between hosts India and West Indies at the Eden Gardens in Kolkata on March 1, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

FORMER Cricket West Indies (CWI) president, Jamaica’s Dave Cameron believes CWI should consider pulling out from international cricket if its financial struggle continues, in a bid to force the International Cricket Council (ICC) to take notice.

The region’s governing body is undergoing major changes to its structures and competitions as it battles significant financial challenges, with chief executive officer (CEO), Jamaica’s Chris Dehring saying, “West Indies cricket is at an important crossroads.” Among the changes is a 25 per cent cut in retainer fees for international players’ contracts, which the players are expected to accept or decline this week following the conclusion of the tour of India.

Cameron, who served as CWI president from 2013 to 2019, says he anticipated the current situation, in part because of what he considers an unfair ICC revenue-sharing model that favours cricket’s biggest nations, led by India.

“[This is] something I wrote about 10 years ago, and was championing in the ICC, and got them to create committees.

I got so upset in meetings [to the point] where I challenged people that we would stop playing with them because it was just unfair that you would get all the resources,” he said on The Mason and Guests talk show in Barbados.

“This series we’re [playing] in India, [India] are probably making north of about $100- $200 million dollars in the series, and it’s costing West Indies Cricket to go and play in India.

It just doesn’t make sense. “No matter if you are the best team in the world, you can’t improve your revenues. The model has to change. In 2016, we proved that.

[Some] 10 years ago we were the best team in every format of the game, and we weren’t able to move our revenue needle. Those were the concerns that we had and, unfortunately, my successors didn’t think it was important.” He added, “There are two issues with West Indies cricket.

One, and Chris Dehring outlined it, is that the West Indies Cricket Board funds the entire development of West Indies cricket.

That needs to change, [but] I’m not going to offer any model here. And secondly, how the revenues in international cricket is shared …

needs to change for us to be relevant going forward.” Dehring believes the changes will help to stabilise West Indies cricket for the future but Cameron is far less optimistic about the prospect.

“I’m not sure how you get out of this,” said Cameron. “If you’re not in any of the World Cups [or] if you’re not hosting any of the World Cups, I’m not sure if there is a path to get out of this situation.

With revenues from broadcasts going down — and that’s a huge item that is now affecting us and so sponsorship revenues are increasing, revenues from broadcasts is going down — so if you don’t have a big market for sponsorships, then you’re in trouble.” Several stakeholders have raised concerns about the current state of West Indies cricket.

Earlier this month, former Australia Captain Michael Clarke, who won the 2007 and 2015 World Cup, said the ICC, along with India, Australia and England, “need to come together to save West Indies cricket”.

Cameron, however, believes CWI should consider the more drastic step of stepping away from international cricket to force the ICC’s hand.

“Nobody has ever given us anything without a fight,” he said. “[That’s how] we got independence, how we got emancipation. Nobody gets anything by just asking and sitting down and hoping that it happens.

What I’m hearing now is, ‘ICC should look at us because we’re important.’ No, no, no, that will never work.

“We need to be more forceful about it, and if it means withdrawing from the cricket, I would be as dramatic as that to say, ‘India, play yourself if you’re not willing to share the resources with us.’ Maybe that would be a little bit dramatic but I think that would get everybody understanding how serious the situation is.” Cameron told the Jamaica Observer in May that he wouldn’t be interested in returning as president, despite Dr Kishore Shallow’s tenure coming to end in 2028.

Cameron is currently president of the Jamaica Obstacle Sport Federation and chairman of the Private Sector Organisation of Jamaica’s Sports and Entertainment Development Committee.

World.title: Back on top!
World.content:
Montego Bay United’s Dwight Merrick (right) gets away from Dunbeholden FC’s Tyrese Gowe in their JPL first-round game played at Jarrett Park on Sunday, October 4th. MBU won the game 1-0. Merrick got among the goals as MBU defeated Cavalier yesterday to return to the top of the standings. (Photo: Paul Reid)

TURNERS, Clarendon — Montego Bay United reclaimed the lead in the Jamaica Premier League after dominating Cavalier 3-1 in their first-round game played at Turners Oval in Clarendon on Sunday.

Despite conceding for the first time this season MBU improved to 13 points — three more than Waterhouse who play tonight — while Cavalier, who were losing for the first time this season, stayed in sixth place on seven points.

Dunbeholden got their first win of the season after four straight losses, edging Molynes United 1-0, while Humble Lion got their second- straight point, holding Chapelton Maroons to a 0-0 draw.

After back-to-back 1-0 wins MBU exploded with three goals — the most they have scored in one game this season — maintaining in the process their unbeaten start to the season.

Deonjay Brown and Dwight Merrick both scored their second goal of the season and Richardo Ramsey scored his first, with Christopher Ainsworth scoring for Cavalier, ending MBU’s run of not conceding a goal at 412 minutes.

Brown was well placed at the far-right post to volley home a cross in the 17th minute and give MBU the lead.

Merrick doubled the lead 20 minutes later with a spectacular left footer from about 27 yards away, beating Cavalier’s goalkeeper Taywaine Lynch at his left post.

Ainsworth was well placed to tap home a cross in the 52nd minute to cut the deficit but Ramsey — who had replaced the injured Jourdain Fletcher and who missed an easy scoring chance just minutes earlier — made the points sure when he wormed his way past two defenders and fired past Lynch in the 80th minute.

At Dunbeholden Sports Complex, Tuwain Merrick scored the hosts’ second goal of the season.

his first, when he finished off a good combination by curling the ball past the Molynes goalkeeper into the far -eft corner in the 66th minute.

World.title: West Indies fall short in another high-scoring contest
World.content:
West Indies Shimron Hetmyer (right) reacts after getting clean-bowled by India’s Naman Dhir during the third Twenty 20 International cricket match between India and West Indies at the Holkar Cricket Stadium in Indore on October 11, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

INDORE, India (CMC) — India’s bowlers held their composure this time around to deny a gutsy run chase by West Indies and take the third Twenty20 International (T20I) by 14 runs at the Holkar Cricket Stadium here on Sunday, in another high-scoring affair.

For the first time in the series the team batting first prevailed, with Abhishek Sharma’s blistering 69 off 30 balls along with several other crucial cameos from their middle- and lower-order batters propelling India to 223 in their 20 overs.

The visitors were then unable to replicate Friday’s record-breaking performance, only managing to get up to 209 for seven before running out of overs.

With the win, India took a 2-1 lead in the five-match series and will have a chance to close it out when they travel to Hyderabad for the fourth match on Wednesday.

The Windies actually did well to restrict the home side to their eventual total, following an impressive display by their top order batters that saw them bludgeon 87 runs in the opening six overs after the early loss of Sanju Samson for three.

Sharma and Ishan Kishan sent the West Indies’ bowlers to all parts of the ground in a brutal attack, with the former bringing up his half-century off just 18 balls — inclusive of five fours and four sixes — inside the power play.

At one point India was scoring at over 14 runs an over, until Roston Chase got the breakthrough by having Kishan stumped for 37 off 18 balls to leave the score 115 for two in the ninth over.

Three balls later the offspinner trapped Captain Shreyas Iyer lbw for one, and when medium pacer Shamar Springer had Sharma caught and bowled, and Naman Dhir hit spinner Gudakesh Motie into the hands of long off, the Windies were in the driver’s seat at 135 for five in the 11th over.

The visitors took wickets regularly thereafter, but cameos by Tilak Varma, who made 28, Nitish Kumar Reddy (21), Axar Patel’s 20, and an unbeaten 13 off six balls by Prince Yadav, got India up to a competitive total.

Chase was the pick of the Windies’ bowlers with 2-38 while Springer (2-50) and Shamar Joseph (2-54) provided support.

The West Indies suffered an almost immediate setback in their chase, with left-arm pacer Arshdeep Singh bowling their inspirational Captain Shai Hope with just seven runs on the board.

Shimron Hetmyer dominated a 60-run partnership with Kamil Pooran for the second wicket, which carried the Windies to 67 for one until India struck two blows to stamp their authority on the match.

Hetmyer looked good for his 43 off 26 balls before he was bowled off his pads by Dhir, and spinner Axar Patel had Rovman Powell caught at long off for five to reduce the West Indies to 82 for three in the 10th over.

From thereon the required run rate continued to spiral out of control, reaching 15 runs an over at one point as India’s bowlers put a clamp on the Windies’ scoring.

Sherfane Rutherford tried his best during his innings of 32 off 25 balls but Singh made crucial strikes by bowling him, and also accounting for the wicket of Keemo Paul, to effectively end the contest.

Shamar Springer belted an unbeaten 35 off 11 balls, with 22 runs coming off the last over and the West Indies needing 36 runs to force a Super Over.

Player of the Match Singh claimed 3-44 and Dhir took 2-39.

World.title: Little London stars resist big transfer offers
World.content:
Little London High football player Orlando Reid speaking with the Jamaica Observer last Friday.

LITTLE LONDON, Westmoreland — Two student athletes at Little London High School, both recently called up to represent Jamaica at the national level, have declared they will not leave the institution that nurtured their talent — despite being bombarded with transfer offers, some of which allegedly include money, from competing schools.

“I’m not really fighting to go to a different school or caring if a school is bigger than ours, or if people say, ‘That school is dunce, and this school is bright.’ I’m not that type of person; I keep myself where I was spotted first,” stated Little London High football player Orlando Reid in an interview with the Jamaica Observer on Friday.

Reid was recently called up to the Jamaica Under-17 national team, and he and the school have already received 30 transfer inquiries for him.

A similar sentiment was shared by 16-year-old Negril native Ashanti Guthrie, a member of the Jamaica Under-19 Women’s Cricket team.

Guthrie made the national side at age 15 and has already received three transfer offers from other secondary institutions.

“I don’t want to go to their school.

I’m not going to leave my teammates, the girls I know here, and the people who push me and motivate me.

I prefer to stay at this school until I graduate and go to college,” stated Guthrie, who aspires to become a physical education teacher or nurse while continuing her cricket career.

Both students became emotional as they reflected on the personal setbacks that drive their determination to succeed.

At age three Reid lost his father.

Two years ago he suffered another tragic loss when his uncle — his primary mentor — died in a crash on his way to the Sangster International Airport in St James.

“I was very emotional about it but I decided to keep my head up.

That motivated me,” said Reid, whose main support system now includes his mother and stepfather.

“He [deceased uncle] taught me how to be a goalkeeper.

That’s the reason why I’m doing this — for him and my dad.” In addition to coping with grief, Reid, who wants to become a soldier and a professional footballer, lost his personal belongings and missed out on a potential scholarship following the passage of Hurricane Melissa last October.

Guthrie’s drive is similarly rooted in family adversity.

Her father lost two fingers during a domestic dispute, an incident she uses as fuel to excel.

“Sir, I don’t want to cry but… the reason I want to push myself on the cricket team is because of what happened to my father last year,” shared Guthrie.

“I want to become the next Stafanie Taylor [national player and former West Indies women’s captain] so I can make my father proud…” added Guthrie.

Principal of the 56-year-old institution, Garfield James, expressed immense pride in the students’ accomplishments and the school’s role in developing raw talent.

“I always encourage my teachers and staff to understand that parents send the best that they have,” relayed James.

Reflecting on Guthrie’s growth, James noted that while she didn’t initially display this level of determination, her talent was carefully nurtured.

“Those talents that she has were nurtured, and here today we are happy to highlight the fact that she is on the right path towards success,” stated James.

He added, “On behalf of the Board of Governors, all the stakeholders, all the students, classmates, and teaching staff who are here, we are right behind her and we’ll be supporting her all the way.” James spoke with equal pride regarding Reid’s resilience.

“[He is a] young man who would have suffered a lot emotionally, physically [and] mentally.

[He] lost his dad at an early age [and] lost the other father figure in his life, which was his uncle, in a very tragic situation where he witnessed that accident.

Despite that, he found the intrinsic motivation to drive the passion, and he allows that passion to be driven by sheer determination which has allowed him today to be called up by the national team for training,” stated James.

However, James — who also serves as councillor for the Sheffield Division under the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) banner — expressed deep frustration over what he describes as predatory recruitment tactics by competing institutions.

“It’s really disheartening to know that every time you build these talents or realise these opportunities, some other institution is ready to take the students out of their space.

And then it sets back these specific institutions because you have to start all over,” argued James.

He noted that despite prior measures by the Intersecondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) to curb the practice of athlete student recruitment, aggressive approaches and backdoor offers persist.

James called for stronger national policy intervention from all stakeholders, including the Ministry of Education.

“We need input from all stakeholders to come on board to see if we can refine something that can work for the best interest of the students and the schools,” stated James.

World.title: Curfew imposed in St Elizabeth amid threat of double murder reprisals
World.content:
Head of the St Elizabeth police, Superintendent Coleridge Minto

ST ELIZABETH, Jamaica — Police have imposed a 48-hour curfew on eight communities amid the threat of reprisals in relation to Saturday’s double murder in Luana.

The communities of Hodges Land, Luana, Speculation, Cambridge, Spring Park, Brompton, Fyffes Pen and Crawford are under curfew as at 6:00 pm on Sunday, October 11, until 6:00 pm, on Tuesday, October 13.

Head of the St Elizabeth police Superintendent Coleridge Minto said the threat of reprisal stems from the murder of one of two men in Saturday’s gun attack identified as Shadrick Watson, a resident of Hodges Land.

READ: Double murder in St Elizabeth

Police also theorised that Watson’s killing stemmed from another murder committed on August 22, 2025 in Hodges Land.

“The intelligence is that persons aligned to [Watson] are planning reprisals and as such a curfew is now in effect,” said Minto.

The boundaries of the curfew are:

North- Along an imaginary line from the Hodges Land Basic School to the Luana to Sandy Ground

Road and Central Road Intersection.

East- Along Central Road and then an imaginary line from the Luana to Sandy Ground Road and

Central Road Intersection to another cul-de-sac at Galleon Beach, Crawford District.

South- Along an imaginary line from the cul-de-sac at Galleon Beach, Crawford District to

Darlintober Church of God of Prophecy.

West- Along an imaginary line from the Darlintober Church of God of Prophecy, back to the Hodges Land Basic School.

World.title: Dunbeholden grab first win of JPL season
World.content:
Coach Alex Thomas (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Dunbeholden FC earned their first win of the Jamaica Premier League season on Sunday, edging Molynes United 1-0 at the Dunbeholden Sports Complex to move off the foot of the points table.

After four straight losses, the Alex Thomas-coached team got their first points after Tuwain Merrick’s 66th minute goal eased the pressure on the St Catherine based club.

Meanwhile, despite conceding a goal for the first time this season,

Montego Bay United (MBU) reclaimed the lead in the standings after beating Cavalier SC 3-1 at Turners Oval.

MBU improved to 13 points, three more than Waterhouse FC who play on Monday, while Cavalier FC stayed in sixth place on seven points after their first loss this season.

In the other game played on Sunday, Humble Lion earned back-to-back points after holding Chapelton Maroons 0-0 at Wembley Centre of Excellence.

Dunbeholden jumped four places to 11th place on the points table after Merrick finished off a superb team move by curling the ball past the Molynes goalkeeper into the far left corner in the 66th minute, his first goal of the season and his team’s second.

At Turners Oval, Deonjay Brown and Dwight Merrick both scored their second goal of the season and Richardo Ramsey scored his first with Christopher Ainsworth scoring for Cavalier, ending MBU’s run of not conceding a goal at 412 minutes.

Brown was well placed at the far right post to volley home a cross in the 17th minute to give MBU the lead and Merrick doubled the lead 20 minutes later with a spectacular left footer from about 27 yards away, beating Cavalier’s goalkeeper Taywaine Lynch at his left post.

Ainsworth was well placed to tap home a cross in the 52nd minute to halve the deficit but Ramsey, who had replaced the injured Jourdain Fletcher, and who had missed an easy scoring chance just minutes earlier, made the points sure when he dribbled his way past two defenders and fired past Lynch in the 80th minute.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Heroy Clarke nominated as JLP Area Council 4 Deputy Leader
World.content:
The newly nominated deputy leader of the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP), Heroy Clarke who was nominated during an Area Council 4 constituency meeting held at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James on Sunday, October 11, 2026.

ST JAMES, Jamaica — The Member of Parliament for St James Central, Heroy Clarke has been nominated as deputy leader for the Jamaica Labour Party’s (JLP) Area Council 4.

Clarke, who was the lone nominee after nominating himself, accepted the position during an Area Council 4 constituency meeting hosted by St James East Central at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in Rose Hall, St James, on Sunday.

While his nomination is set to go to the JLP’s National Conference for official ratification in November, Clarke noted that additional nominations remain open up to the 14th of this month.

Expected to succeed JC Hutchinson in the role, Clarke expressed confidence and readiness to begin his duties immediately.

“I do understand that the work is cut out for me because, as the saying goes, anywhere the West goes, the rest goes. Therefore, I cannot afford to allow the West to fall out of the winning column,” said Clarke in an interview following his nomination.

He emphasised that strong family support will be crucial as he balances his political obligations.

“I know the work is there for me to do, and I will continue in light of what is happening. One thing I am grateful for is that my immediate family is very political — they understand what it means when I say I am going into the trenches, into every nook and cranny, to get the job done. Most of the time, they will be accompanying me to those areas,” stated Clarke.

Clarke added that his immediate focus will align with the strategy of the party’s senior leadership.

“I know what the work requires, and we have to deliver because elder statesmen like Dr Horace Chang, Edmund Bartlett, and JC Hutchinson have vowed that the West must return to where it was,” noted Clarke.

With local government elections scheduled for 2028, Clarke identified leading the party through that campaign as his first major task in his new post.

— Anthony Lewis.

World.title: CAFFE in crisis
World.content:
Voters queue outside a polling station during the 2025 General Election. CAFFE had initially intended to recruit 1,000 volunteers on a budget of approximately $15 million for the 2025 poll, but a funding freeze forced the observer group to cut that number in half. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

AFTER almost 30 years of monitoring elections in Jamaica, the internationally acclaimed agency Citizens Action for Free and Fair Elections (CAFFE) is now cash-strapped and desperately in need of assistance from the private sector to continue observing the country’s democratic process.

CAFFE is still navigating the financial fallout from the Donald Trump Administration’s 2025 withdrawal of United States Agency for International Development (USAID) funding from non-governmental organisations globally.

Speaking at a Jamaica Observer Press Club at the agency’s New Kingston office last Thursday, CAFFE Chair Grace Baston said its financial position has deteriorated further since the September 2025 General Election.

For that poll, CAFFE had initially aimed to recruit 1,000 volunteers on a budget of approximately $15 million.

Frozen funding, however, forced the organisation to halve its target to about 500.

The shortfall has heightened concerns about its capacity to monitor future local government elections, by-elections, and the country’s next general election.

Baston warned that such a setback could erode the democratic gains the country has made.

“There is no doubting the work of the ECJ (Electoral Commission of Jamaica) and the EOJ (Electoral Office of Jamaica).

There has been remarkable progress in those electoral processes; we are the first to give credit.

That being said, we believe strongly [that a] democracy not monitored is democracy threatened.

“CAFFE’s presence has made a huge difference.

The respect people have for the CAFFE observer entering a polling station; the confidence they have in what we are going to say, or what we pronounce about the quality of the conduct of the poll — it is extremely important.

[If] you ease up on that you are inviting a return to what was before,” she insisted.

The election watchdog was established in 1997 amid lingering political strife and fears that Jamaica’s democratic process could be undermined, based on the experiences in the 1980s and early 1990s.

Although the country has moved beyond those dangers, Baston said new threats have emerged, demanding continued vigilance.

“Once, the big threat was overvoting in a polling station — [you have] 100 people on the list and 150 people voting — or the stuffing of a box.

There are other threats now, and we are working hard to make sure we can monitor those.

They are difficult.

One of the new things coming on that we have to think about is going to be precisely this AI (artificial intelligence) that you hear talked about so much,” Baston said.

“How are elections going to be free and fair if campaigning is going to involve the use of deepfake videos? How are we going to hold politicians accountable to make sure that is not happening? The public is being duped because of the power of artificial intelligence in political campaigning.

I am saying not only do we need to be there to prevent the recurrence of the old things that used to threaten our democracy, but there are new threats that we must be prepared for,” charged Baston.

CAFFE Deputy Chairman Anton Thompson also named voter apathy as a major threat to democracy, noting that the agency had established clubs in schools on a $5-million annual budget to foster political awareness and engagement among young people.

However, he told the Sunday Observer that budget cuts have since forced approximately 85 per cent of more than 40 clubs to close.

“We have about half a dozen active clubs, which is far less than we had when we launched this.

And when we launched this with some funding we were able to hire somebody to energise the schools, talk to them, arrange for them to meet.

I met with several schools online — because it was still COVID time — encouraged them, and told them what we were trying to do,” he said.

Thompson added that turnover among school and student leaders had also contributed to the closure of some clubs.

Additionally, many of CAFFE’s volunteers are sixthform students who are trained by the agency at their respective schools and receive a stipend for their civic service.

Baston added that the enthusiasm and dedication that she had seen from engaged students emphasised the need to keep the programme going.

“This is 2026.

The average young person can’t take himself or herself away from their phone for five minutes,” she said.

“When you see these young people making their way to polling locations at six o’clock in the morning because they take so seriously their duty to be there to observe the set-up of the poll.

Once you engage them; once you begin raising their awareness and their consciousness of how precious, how hard-won our democracy was, how fragile it is; once you begin engaging them, their energy and their interest levels are so impressive.

That is why the lack of the resources to have the clubs active is so painful, so difficult,” lamented Baston.

For his part, former Chairman Dr Lloyd Barnett warned that the volunteer count, having been reduced for the September 2025 General Election, could shrink further unless the organisation secures additional funding.

“We are not going to get it from the European Union or USAID anymore.

It’s clear that just like the election monitoring, it has to be Jamaicans.

And as we have said, we have been grateful to Jamaicans…

the commercial interests have been helpful [but] we need more help because of the absence of a major part of our funding from the international sources,” he explained.

“That is why we have been appealing to them.

We have a strong programme in which we are trying to convince them that it’s in their interest, and in the interest of all Jamaica, that they should participate,” added Barnett.

He maintained that the right to choose the country’s leadership is a cornerstone of democracy, and urged the private sector to help ensure that CAFFE’s election-monitoring work does not disappear.

“The electoral system is at the foundation of democracy, and democracy means the Government is of the people, by the people, for the people…

It is in everybody’s interest that democracy should be preserved, and the preservation of elections is the first step in preserving democracy.

You can’t have a democracy without free and fair elections, and that’s why we can’t afford to have CAFFE die,” charged Barnett.

World.title: Berechenbare Risiken – unberechenbare Politik? Warum Deutschland jetzt aus Worten Gesetze machen muss
World.content:
In der Ökonomie gibt es eine fundamentale Unterscheidung, die für das Verständnis unternehmerischer Entscheidungen zentral ist: Das Risiko und die Ungewissheit. Risiko lässt sich berechnen, einpreisen, managen. Man kennt die Spielregeln – auch wenn man nicht weiß, wie das Spiel ausgeht. Ungewissheit hingegen entzieht sich jeder Formel, weil sich die Spielregeln selbst immer wieder verändern.

Dr. Daniel Steiners, © Roche Pharma AG

Wer neue Technologien entwickelt, Produktionskapazitäten aufbaut und langfristige Zukunftsprojekte anstößt, ist bereit, Risiken einzugehen. In kaum einer Branche zeigt sich das deutlicher als in der forschenden Pharma- und Biotech-Industrie. Denn bis ein neues Medikament bei Patientinnen und Patienten in der Versorgung ankommt, vergehen 10 bis 15 Jahre milliardenschwerer Forschung und Entwicklung. Und die Wahrscheinlichkeit, auf dem Weg zu scheitern, liegt bei über 90%. Mit diesem Risiko können wir umgehen. Es ist fester Bestandteil unseres Geschäftsmodells, das auf Innovation ausgerichtet ist. Es ist auch Voraussetzung für die bahnbrechenden Fortschritte, die in der Medizin in den letzten Jahren erzielt wurden.

Was Zukunftsentscheidungen jedoch lähmt: Ungewissheit durch politische Sprunghaftigkeit.

Wer Zukunftsversprechen formuliert, im Alltag der Gesetzgebung aber vor allem den Rotstift an Innovation und Fortschritt ansetzt, konterkariert jegliche Industriepolitik und erstickt Vertrauen im Keim – da hilft das stärkste Signal nicht mehr.

Genau diese erleben wir in der politischen Diskussion zuletzt zu oft. Genau diese Sprunghaftigkeit haben wir als forschende Gesundheitsindustrie in Deutschland in den letzten Monaten in aller Deutlichkeit zu spüren bekommen. Auf der einen Seite ein ambitioniertes Bekenntnis zum Pharmastandort Deutschland im Koalitionsvertrag – eine Pharmastrategie unter der Regie des Bundeskanzleramtes. Ein starkes Signal!

Auf der anderen Seite dann aber gravierende Eingriffe in bestehende Spielregeln. Eine Gesetzgebung, die einzig und allein darauf abzielt, wieder einmal Finanzlöcher auf Seiten der Kassen zu stopfen – maßgeblich auf Kosten der Industrie durch künstliche Preisdeckel und Zwangsrabatte. Wer Zukunftsversprechen formuliert, im Alltag der Gesetzgebung aber vor allem den Rotstift an Innovation und Fortschritt ansetzt, konterkariert jegliche Industriepolitik und erstickt Vertrauen im Keim – da hilft das stärkste Signal nicht mehr.

Ein gefährlicher Dominoeffekt

Wenn Vertrauen schwindet, explodiert ein Industriestandort nicht mit einem lauten Knall. Vielmehr setzt eine leise Kettenreaktion ein, bei der ein Dominostein den nächsten umwirft. Und klar ist: Die ersten Steine des Gesundheits- und Forschungsstandorts Deutschland sind längst gekippt – mit direkten Folgen für Wirtschaft, Versorgung und Sicherheit:

Abfluss von Risikokapital: Milliardenschweres Risikokapital ist global mobil und fließt in jene Märkte, in denen Innovation ein erfolgreiches Geschäftsmodell sein kann. Schon heute vereinen die USA über 50 Prozent des weltweiten Pharmamarktes auf sich, auf Deutschland entfallen lediglich 4-5 Prozent. Mit Regulierung, die Innovation entwertet, verliert Deutschland weiter an Attraktivität und private Investitionen fließen in Zukunft noch häufiger in jene Märkte, die mit strategischer Konsequenz innovationsfreundliche Rahmenbedingungen schaffen.

Verlust an Forschung und Innovationskraft: Wo Kapital abwandert, schrumpft auch die wissenschaftliche Substanz. Der europäische Anteil an der globalen Pharma-Forschung ist in den letzten Jahrzehnten drastisch von über 40 auf knapp 30 Prozent gefallen; der Anteil an klinischen Studien hat sich binnen einer Dekade auf 9 Prozent halbiert. Auch Deutschland ist längst zurückgefallen: Im Global Innovation Index der WIPO zählen wir erstmals nicht mehr zu den zehn innovationsstärksten Volkswirtschaften der Welt.

Gefährdung der medizinischen Versorgung: Ein Markt, der Innovation nicht fair honoriert, ist unattraktiv für medizinische Durchbrüche. Schon heute sehen wir, dass Deutschland seine Rolle als globaler Versorgungspionier verliert: Jedes dritte in den USA neu zugelassene Medikament erreicht Patientinnen und Patienten in Deutschland nicht mehr. Besonders alarmierend: Bei zwei Dritteln dieser Therapien handelt es sich um Präparate mit anerkannt hohem Innovationsstatus.

Verlust von Souveränität: In Zeiten geopolitischer Umbrüche und fragiler Lieferketten sind medizinische Schlüsseltechnologien längst zu einer Währung für nationale Resilienz geworden. Wer Forschung und Produktion im eigenen Land vernachlässigt, gibt Handlungsspielräume auf und gerät bei der Versorgung der eigenen Bevölkerung in gefährliche Abhängigkeiten.

Chance auf einen Perspektivwechsel

Zukunftsfähigkeit, Innovationskraft und Souveränität lassen sich nicht durch kurzsichtiges Flickwerk verteidigen. Um den Dominoeffekt, der unseren Gesundheitsstandort erfasst hat, zu stoppen, braucht es jetzt ein Umdenken; weg von Verteilungsdebatten hin zu einem verlässlichen Bekenntnis zu Innovationen.

Erstmals wird medizinischer Fortschritt nicht mehr einseitig von der Kostenseite gedacht, sondern daran gemessen, was die forschende Gesundheitsindustrie durch Forschung, Entwicklung, Produktion und hochwertige Arbeitsplätze für unser Land leistet.

Dazu gehört auch, dass wir uns ehrlich machen: Die finanzielle Schieflage der Kassen entsteht durch strukturelle Ineffizienzen im System, nicht durch medizinischen Fortschritt. Ganz im Gegenteil: Innovative Medizin ist kein Kostenfaktor, sondern eine Investition in die Zukunft. Der konsequente Einsatz modernster Diagnostik, digitaler Prozesse und innovativer Therapien könnte schon heute jährlich über 40 Milliarden Euro freisetzen – direkt im Gesundheitssystem und indirekt als positiver Effekt auf Wirtschaft, Wachstum und Wohlstand.

Die Politik hat jetzt die Chance, einen Perspektivwechsel einzuleiten. Eine Expertenkommission hat jüngst konkret vorgeschlagen, wie Unternehmen, die in Deutschland investieren, von einem Teil – wohlgemerkt: nur einem Teil – jener zusätzlichen Belastungen ausgenommen werden können, die mit dem GKV-Beitragssatzstabilisierungsgesetz eingeführt wurden. Diese Vorschläge zur Verknüpfung des Herstellerabschlags mit einer sogenannten Standortklausel liegen nun auf dem Tisch. Und sie sind schon bemerkenswert: Erstmals wird medizinischer Fortschritt nicht mehr einseitig von der Kostenseite gedacht, sondern daran gemessen, was die forschende Gesundheitsindustrie durch Forschung, Entwicklung, Produktion und hochwertige Arbeitsplätze für unser Land leistet. Ein Ansatz, der Industriepolitik, Sozialpolitik und Geopolitik endlich zusammendenkt.

Denn erst dann sendet die Bundesregierung die notwendige politische Verbindlichkeit.

Dabei wird uns keineswegs etwas geschenkt: Die Kassen werden mit einem erhöhten Herstellerabschlag von 15,5% weiterhin auf Rekordniveau durch die Industrie gestützt – Unternehmen, die nachweislich vor Ort Werte schaffen, Arbeitsplätze sichern und Forschung verankern, erhalten lediglich die Chance, die zusätzlichen Belastungen zu reduzieren. Das ist kein Geschenk – sondern die Korrektur einer massiven Fehlsteuerung. Eine vorausschauende, ressortübergreifende Standortstrategie hätte von vornherein auf positive Anreize gesetzt, statt bestehende Strukturen zu schwächen. Umso wichtiger ist es, dass daraus nun schnell ein wirksames, unbürokratisches Gesetz wird – und dass weitere Schritte folgen. Denn erst dann sendet die Bundesregierung die notwendige politische Verbindlichkeit. Denn milliardenschwere Investitionsentscheidungen in die Zukunft Deutschlands folgen keinen Kommissionspapieren – sondern verlässlichen Taten, die die Grundlage für eine Pharma-Strategie werden können, die Deutschlands Wettbewerbsfähigkeit wiederherstellt und den internationalen Herausforderungen gerecht wird.

Hinweis

POLITISCHE WERBUNG

World.title: Revealed: The chancellor’s plan to survive the budget
World.content:
With the budget barely a fortnight away, Chancellor John Healey is warning of mounting economic headwinds. Can he ease the pressure on the public finances without loosening the purse strings?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy test the tightrope Healey is attempting to walk ahead of a major speech to the International Monetary Fund.

Elsewhere, is Donald Trump’s energy deal with Vladimir Putin putting the UK’s support for Ukraine to the test? And why has Andy Burnham chosen now to confirm Russian interference in the Brexit vote?

Plus, Sam has an exclusive on how the promise of more money for regional mayors might not be worth as much as they were hoping.

World.title: The EU budget battle just got nastier
World.content:
Germany has rejected Ireland’s proposal for the EU’s next seven-year budget, despite €159 billion in cuts. And it’s not alone: Governments are divided over where the cuts should fall, while the European Parliament is threatening to block the deal.

Plus, Zoya interviews Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner about Europe’s efforts to curb irregular migration and plans to tighten restrictions on Russian visitors and former soldiers.

World.title: Wie Trumps Ölkrise zur Ukraine-Frage wird
World.content:
Donald Trump verkündet eine „Energie-Waffenruhe“ zwischen der Ukraine und Russland an. Fraglich allerdings ist, was die beiden Länder davon wirklich wissen. Um den heimischen Druck durch steigende Ölpreise abzufedern, lockert Trump zuvor die Sanktionen gegen Russland. Weil er dafür von Wolodymyr Selenskyj kritisiert wird, fordert er, die Ukraine brauche einen neuen Präsidenten. Währenddessen ringen die EU-Außenminister in Luxemburg um ein neues Sanktionspaket gegen Russland. Hans von der Burchard ordnet zusammen mit Rixa Fürsen ein, wie Europa die russische Schattenflotte stoppen will und welche Konsequenzen der Drohnenangriff von Leipzig wirklich hat.

Im Konrad-Adenauer-Haus herrscht derweil Krisenstimmung bei herbstlichem Wetter. Angesichts verheerender Umfragewerte sucht die CDU-Spitze nach einem Ausweg aus dem Tief. Rasmus Buchsteiner analysiert die Strategie des CDU-Präsidiums, das sich in Klausur befindet, und wie Parteichef Friedrich Merz in seiner Position stabilisiert werden soll.

Im 200-Sekunden-Interview warnt Dennis Radtke, Vorsitzender der Christlich-Demokratischen Arbeitnehmerschaft (CDA), vor einer inhaltlichen Schieflage seiner Partei. Er fordert echte Strukturreformen bei Rente und Gesundheit statt reiner Sparprogramme und erklärt, warum die Union dringend Antworten auf die alltäglichen Sorgen der Menschen finden muss.
