World.title: How can Europe leverage laws to secure cloud sovereignty?
World.content:
Europe should not wait for CADA to take effect before acting, though. European cloud service providers (CSPs) have been partnering with established technology providers to deliver real sovereign capability, without rebuilding the entire technology stack from scratch.

The best time to plant the sovereign tree was 10 years ago

If Europe wants to grow its industrial base, it has to support the ecosystem as it is now, not as it may in 10 years’ time. CADA’s own roadmap assumes roughly five to seven years to triple the EU’s data-center capacity. Providers who have already built capacity by blending EU capabilities with proven non-EU technologies would have to spend the intervening years relinquishing their growth. It is scale, not a shortage of skills or innovation, that is the biggest practical obstacle facing a stronger European cloud market. This is precisely why partnership with proven technology sources deserves a central place in the sovereignty debate rather than being treated as a second-best option.

Partnership shortens that timeline considerably, letting European CSPs deliver sovereign, scaled services now instead of waiting for domestic capacity to catch up organically. In Italy, IPZS, owned by the Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance, is using this model to build a modern Digital Application Platform for the Italian EUDI wallet, a foundational EU digital identity initiative. It provides a live example of that model working in Europe today, at the scale and speed the policy window demands.

It is through scale that the local industrial base can deliver sovereign capabilities, compete, capture market share, and invest in developing and integrating home-grown technologies. Hoping for the alternative to happen, that is for a European technological stack to fully emerge and be adopted, is the equivalent of putting the cart before the horse.

The rules need to allow for a model that’s already working

World.title: EU lacks influence(rs): No content creators at leaders’ summit
World.content:
Why? Seems they just haven’t got around to it. “Mainly logistical problems and budget constraints,” said one of the diplomats, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, as were others quoted in this piece. Another said they’d not had a chance to discuss it with their capital, but hadn’t ruled out the idea for future summits.

“There is no appetite for this,” said a third diplomat. “If my leader wants an influencer [they] would take one” with them, the diplomat said, adding that countries “don’t need the Council for that.”

Council spokesperson Romain Sadet confirmed that “we won’t be having content creators at the upcoming European Council.”

When the plan was unveiled, a Council official said the influencers would be granted access to areas of the Council’s Brussels HQ that are currently open only to journalists accredited by the EU institutions — though they would be banned from asking ministers and leaders questions.

“Content creators will be accompanied at all times and will not be treated as media,” the Council official continued. “We are working on the basis of about 10 content creators per event max, accompanied by Council staff.”

In June, the Council sent guidance for choosing influencers to national governments, seen by POLITICO.

World.title: Independent wins Kraków mayoral race in setback for PM Tusk
World.content:
“The people of Kraków have just regained their city! Now let’s put aside our differences and show that we can work together,” Gibała said, appearing to acknowledge that he will have to cooperate with Civic Coalition and its national coalition partner, the Left party, which together control 23 of the city council’s 43 seats.

This was Gibała’s fourth shot at the mayoralty. A local councilor and former national lawmaker, Gibała narrowly lost to Miszalski in 2024 in his previous attempt.

This time around, he campaigned on breaking with the political establishment, riding a wave of public discontent over Kraków’s huge debt and attempts to establish a low-emissions zone.

Gibała won the Sept. 27 first round with 36.4% ahead of Piątkowska on 29.9%. The candidate of the main opposition Law and Justice party finished third with 17.5%.

Piątkowska, backed by Civic Coalition, tried to distance herself from Miszalski while arguing that close ties with the national government would benefit Kraków, pop. 800,000.

Nationally, Civic Coalition remains ahead in opinion polls, but current voting intentions suggest that Tusk’s coalition will fall short of a majority in scheduled fall parliamentary elections.

World.title: Ireland’s budget cuts weaken EU, Commission warns
World.content:
The Commission is “very concerned about cuts to flexibility,” said one of the EU diplomats.

As a result of the changes, “we will have no ways left to help farmers and regions when crises hit, because of climate change or geopolitical tensions,” they added.

EU ambassadors gathered to discuss the Irish plan, which envisages cuts of €159 billion in current prices from the Commission’s nearly €2 trillion proposal. Of that amount, €38 billion was cut from foreign aid, €75 billion was axed from competitiveness, and at least €22 billion was slashed from rainy-day funds.

But even those reductions were criticized as insufficient by a German-led group of states pushing for cuts of several hundred billion. During the closed-door meeting, a rival bloc of 17 countries, known as the Friends of Cohesion, welcomed the fact that the Irish presidency had spared agriculture and regional payments from cuts.

EU governments are racing to finalize a deal on the budget among themselves by the end of the year — before elections in France, Italy and Poland that threaten to disrupt the negotiations.

A leaders’ summit on Thursday and Friday will give early signals as to whether the end-of-year deadline is achievable — or whether leaders should start preparing contingency plans.

World.title: ‘We still love you’: NATO envoy seeks to reassure Europe over US military pullback
World.content:
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker told European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius that Washington remains committed to Europe’s defence, amid an ongoing US military review withdrawing thousands of troops and key strategic assets from the continent.

 

“We still love you,” Whitaker said at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday in the Polish capital.

“I keep telling our European allies… the United States isn't stepping back.”

His remarks came during a panel on NATO 3.0 — a US-backed model that calls for Europe to take the lead with its conventional defences as American forces draw down from the continent and shift their attention elsewhere.

Kubilius said NATO 3.0 did not mean the United States was saying, “We don’t love you anymore, Europeans, so you should do your own job”. Rather, he argued, Europe needed to develop the capabilities to deter aggression on its own territory.

“Europe needs to take responsibility in our hands,” he said.

Kubilius has previously estimated that replacing US strategic military assets could cost Europe up to €500 billion. Experts have also suggested that Europe could need 300,000 additional troops to defend itself against Russia in a scenario in which Washington continues to withdraw its military support.

Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, Washington has sought to redirect military resources towards other regions, including the Indo-Pacific, to counter China’s growing influence.

The Pentagon’s review of US military deployments in Europe is expected to conclude by December, with its findings to be presented to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. The assessment could pave the way for further reductions in America’s military presence on the continent.

However, separate force reductions are already under way. In May, for example, the Pentagon ordered the withdrawal of approximately 5,000 troops from Germany and cancelled a planned deployment of a long-range fires battalion.

Whitaker said he did not want to “preview” further measures under the review because “it is not ready”, but argued that Washington’s push for a more European NATO was “working”.

“The proof is in where we're sitting today, here in Poland, spending 4.7% on core defence and leading really the alliance to a stronger, more capable military,” he said.

Allies agreed to raise their core defence spending target from 2% to 3.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035 at the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, alongside a further 1.5% for broader security and defence spending.

"That is what the United States is expecting from all of its allies," Whitaker said of the overall 5% defence spending target.

Poland is among NATO’s highest spenders on core defence as a share of GDP, according to the alliance’s latest estimates.

The effort to increase defence spending also comes as the European Union seeks to strengthen its military capabilities by 2030, amid warnings from European intelligence agencies that Russia could pose a more direct threat to NATO in the coming years.

But the rearmament drive is facing significant hurdles. A leaked version of the European Defence Agency's landmark report — aiming to assess the progress — reveals major capability gaps, most notably in drone defences and maritime warfare.

World.title: Zelenskyy says Russia ignored Trump's 'energy ceasefire' and kept attacking Ukraine
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia on Monday of violating an energy ceasefire announced by Donald Trump, saying Kyiv had not even been consulted about the purported agreement and had only learned of it through the media.

 

"We did not know about that. We've learned that from the media as well, that the president of the United States has secured an energy ceasefire," Zelenskyy said.

Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelenskyy questioned whether Moscow had agreed to the proposal at all, saying he had seen neither a public endorsement from Russia nor any let-up in its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

"We have not seen that they support this ceasefire anywhere," he said, pointing to continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities.

Large parts of Kyiv were without electricity and water when Trump made his announcement, as repair crews struggled to restore power following Russian strikes. Shortly afterwards, Russia launched another targeted attack on a power plant in Kharkiv, Zelenskyy said.

"It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," he remarked, referring to Trump's social media platform.

People watch Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on a large screen as he speaks at the Warsaw Security Forum in Warsaw, 12 October, 2026 AP Photo

Zelenskyy also accused Russia of striking a Ukrainian gas production facility and a petrol station overnight, while Ukraine had refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries.

Despite the continued attacks, he said Kyiv remained willing to observe a reciprocal halt to strikes on energy infrastructure.

"We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree if they agree," he said.

Zelenskyy offered to sign formal guarantees if Washington considered them necessary, but stressed that the US would have to secure Moscow's compliance.

Trump-Putin diesel deal sparks backlash

Zelenskyy's remarks followed several days of mounting tensions with Washington, beginning on Friday when Trump announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to US and global markets, in an attempt to bring down soaring fuel prices ahead of November's US midterm elections.

The US Treasury subsequently issued a six-month licence easing sanctions on Russian diesel already loaded onto tankers, allowing deliveries until April 2027 — a sharp reversal of Washington's efforts to restrict Moscow's energy revenues.

The move drew criticism from European leaders and US lawmakers, including a bipartisan group of senators who urged Trump to reverse course, warning that the deal could provide Moscow with fresh revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.

Trump, meanwhile, blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising fuel prices and demanded that Zelenskyy halt them. On Saturday, he went further, suggesting Ukraine needed a new president and accusing its wartime leader of obstructing efforts to end the war.

On Sunday, Trump announced on Truth Social that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire, although neither side had publicly confirmed an agreement.

It was not the first such declaration. A similar announcement in September failed to halt the strikes.

Against this backdrop, Zelenskyy used his Warsaw address to make a pointed appeal for Washington to change course.

"We need American pressure on Russia, not sanctions relief, not concessions, but real pressure," he said.

He argued that Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries and exports were a response to Moscow's sustained campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure, and that both sides would have to halt such attacks for a ceasefire to work.

Zelenskyy offers elections if Trump secures 60-day ceasefire

Responding to Trump's renewed pressure to hold presidential elections, Zelenskyy said voting remained impossible under current security conditions, with Russian attacks now taking place around the clock.

"From a security standpoint, that's completely impossible. We have attacks day and night," he said.

He also pointed to the logistical challenges of organising a vote for more than a million Ukrainian military personnel, including those serving on the front line.

Nevertheless, Zelenskyy signalled that he was prepared to seek changes to Ukraine's legal framework if Washington could secure a comprehensive ceasefire with Moscow.

"If there is a ceasefire and if the Americans reach such an agreement with the Russians, I'm ready to engage with our Parliament and find difficult solutions," he said.

He suggested this could involve changes to legislation and even the constitution, although constitutional amendments are prohibited under martial law.

Zelenskyy then turned Trump's own diplomatic engagement with Moscow into a challenge to the US president, arguing that Washington should be able to use its influence over Putin to secure a complete halt to hostilities.

"And if we have at least a 60 day full ceasefire, then I'll be ready to work on holding elections," he said.

A residential building burns following a Russian air attack in Kharkiv, 12 October, 2026 AP Photo

Zelenskyy warns of Russian hybrid attacks

Beyond the dispute with Washington, Zelenskyy warned that Ukrainian intelligence had uncovered further Russian plans to destabilise European countries.

"Our intelligence services know that Russia is planning many, many aggressive hybrid operations against Europe, against different countries, against your countries," he told the forum.

"There is no such thing as a small act of destabilisation," he added, urging European governments to remain vigilant and united.

Zelenskyy also appealed for continued military assistance, including ammunition for Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets, air-defence interceptors and funding for domestic weapons and drone production.

He called for closer defence-industrial cooperation with Poland, arguing that joint production and technological partnerships could strengthen both countries' security.

A residential building burns following a Russian air attack in Kharkiv, 12 October, 2026 AP Photo

The Ukrainian president also urged European leaders to prevent further delays in Ukraine's EU accession negotiations, saying progress was essential not only politically but also for the morale of Ukrainians living through another winter of war.

"Please do not allow any pauses in Ukraine's European integration," he said.

Zelenskyy said Kyiv expected to open two negotiating clusters and wanted another two opened by the end of the year.

"Our people need to feel that despite all the difficulties, Ukraine's European future is close," he said.

He concluded by urging European leaders to ensure Washington understood that an energy ceasefire, de-escalation and credible security guarantees were urgently needed in practice, rather than simply being announced on social media.

"In reality, not just on Truth Social," he said.

World.title: IEA urges additional diesel releases ahead of key meeting
World.content:
Ahead of the International Energy Agency's (IEA) governing board meeting this Thursday, its executive director Fatih Birol has written to member governments calling for further action as global diesel markets face tight supplies.

 

Birol suggested that members that have not yet released all the oil they pledged in March, when the IEA agreed to release 400 million barrels, should speed up their remaining releases, prioritising diesel. Some countries have already released more than they initially pledged.

All members were also asked to assess whether additional diesel releases are necessary and, if so, explain how much they could release and when.

The governing board will review these efforts at its meeting on 15 October.

“As we did in March, I believe we can once again demonstrate the IEA’s capacity to act together in support of energy security and economic stability,” Birol said in the statement published on Sunday.

The G7 previously announced plans to release up to 100 million barrels of oil to curb soaring energy prices. However, an internal document seen by Euronews showed that these volumes would fulfil outstanding March commitments, rather than add to the original 400-million-barrel pledge.

"Of its 400 million barrels, 326 million have been released. Because some members over-delivered, the 100 million barrels in the G7 statement can be covered within the existing action if everyone fulfils their commitments," the document states.

Diesel prices have been soaring amid global fuel shortages. The Iran war disrupted crude oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, while damage to refineries has also restricted fuel supplies.

Related Italy lets diesel tax cut expire as Europe tackles fuel costs

According to Kpler, crude oil and condensate exports from the Middle East Gulf, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September. However, much of that oil now travels through alternative routes or is transferred between tankers offshore.

The IEA statement comes two days after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia. Washington temporarily eased sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing its sale and delivery, including imports into the US, until 7 April 2027.

Moscow said it was ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets following a telephone conversation between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"I am convinced this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy," Putin said, according to the Russian statement.

European sanctions remain in place, but additional Russian supply to the global market could help lower diesel prices. The impact will depend on how much fuel Russia can deliver, with damage to its refineries limiting production.

Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, remained above $100 a barrel on Monday morning. European diesel futures fell about 3% to around $1,437 a tonne.

World.title: Chinese carmaker BYD considers opening a factory in France
World.content:
BYD wants French drivers to see it as a local company — and a factory in France could be its next step.

 

"France is on the shortlist," vice-president Stella Li said at the opening of the Paris Motor Show. "We are looking very closely at the possibility of setting up a plant in France."

Li said her objectives were simple: she wants "people in France to think that BYD is a French company. I want them to like it".

She added that BYD "will try to open a second and a third plant in Europe".

a recent electric car model from Chinese manufacturer BYD, shown at the Auto China 2026 motor show in Beijing on 25 April 2026. (AP Photo/Andy Wong, file) AP Photo

The group's vice-president spoke as BYD prepares to open a plant in Hungary by the end of this year, she said.

China agreed on Friday to "moderate" exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the EU, according to European trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič.

According to Li, the Chinese group "has a strong commitment in Europe" and intends "to become a local company in every region of the world".

A dealer network gaining ground in France

BYD is already relying on a well-established distribution network in France. The Chinese manufacturer has forged partnerships with major French automotive groups such as Bymycar, Emil Frey and Bodemer. These dealers handle sales and after-sales service for its vehicles in the country's main cities.

In July, BYD said it had around 115 dealerships in France. The brand is continuing to expand through established local dealers. BYD registered 13,935 passenger vehicles in France in the first half of 2026, up 136% from a year earlier, according to the company.

BYD’s expansion comes as electric car registrations across the EU rise sharply, against a backdrop of record fuel prices.

World.title: Independent Gibala beats Tusk’s party to win Krakow mayoral run-off
World.content:
Independent candidate Łukasz Gibała has been elected mayor of Krakow, Poland's second-largest city, declaring that "after 24 years, the people of Krakow have got their city back".

 

Gibała won Sunday's run-off with 62.12% of the vote, against 37.88% for Monika Piątkowska of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), the main party in Prime Minister Donald Tusk's governing coalition.

Turnout was 44.27%.

He made his first remarks after the National Electoral Commission announced the exit poll results. In a speech at his campaign headquarters, he also thanked voters who had backed his rival.

"The election has just ended. Let us put all disputes aside. Let us show the whole of Poland that, despite what divides us, what unites us matters more, and that together we are capable of working for the good of our city," he said.

He warned that the city faced a difficult situation and that the next two years would be very challenging. "Krakow's budget situation is disastrous. There are many things that need fixing. There are many things that need to be changed, cleaned up, so that life in Krakow can return to normal. But I believe that together, with all of you, we will manage."

Certificate confirming the election of Łukasz Gibała as Mayor of the City of Krakow facebook.com/LukaszGibalaOfficial/

Who is Łukasz Gibała?

Gibała, a city councillor, entrepreneur and founder of the residents' association Kraków dla Mieszkańców (Krakow for Residents), ran as an independent. He was backed by Jan Hoffman, head of the Old Town district council and one of the organisers of the referendum that removed Civic Coalition mayor Aleksander Miszalski from office in May.

Gibała made his name as a critic of the city's leadership. He opposed both Jacek Majchrowski, who ran Krakow for 22 years, and his successor Miszalski, who served two years before being ousted.

This was his fourth bid for the post, after standing in 2014, 2018 and 2024 at the head of his own independent electoral committees. Early election after the referendum

Early election after the referendum

In May, residents voted in a grassroots recall referendum to remove Miszalski from office. Because he belonged to the country's main governing party, the dispute quickly took on national significance.

Voters picked the two run-off candidates on 27 September. In his speech, Gibała noted that the southern city of Częstochowa faces a recall referendum of its own in two weeks: "in two weeks' time, the residents of Częstochowa will also be trying to win back their city, because they too have a referendum coming up".

World.title: Cute cats and street fighters: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
World.content:
What makes you feel better during the colder months? If the answer includes cats, spooky TV, 90s video games or more cats, we've got good news.

 

The Louvre-Lens in France has become an explosion of pastel pink cuteness for its latest exhibition, which celebrates all things wide-eyed, fluffy and glittery. It's ideal for families and the perfect antidote to any October gloom.

Meanwhile, Irish rockers Fontaines D.C. have created a sonic mood board for their fifth studio album 'Dopamine Chamber', which swirls with synths, psychedelia and the sudden urge to disappear on a dance floor.

For those looking to embrace Halloween's approach, look no further than the new Friday the 13th TV adaptation, Crystal Lake. But if campy kung fu and martial arts are more your thing? Street Fighter, based on the legendary arcade game franchise, is about to "hadoken" onto the big screen.

Keep scrolling to find out more about what's coming up this week.

Exhibitions and events

So Cute! The Art of Happiness

Jules Le Roy, Chats dans une commode, 1900, huile sur bois. Roubaix, La Piscine.

When: Until 18 January 2027

Where: Louvre-Lens (Lens, France)

In a world that can often feel overwhelmingly scary, we've never needed the calming reprieve of cuteness more. From sculptures of chubby babies to pastel plushes and Internet cats, the Louvre-Lens explores the many manifestations of mignon throughout history in this joyful new exhibition. There are nearly 300 works in total, including Egyptian animal figures, renaissance portraits, trendy toys and bedazzled reinterpretations of masterpieces — all displayed within an adorable-maxxed space of pastel pink walls and cat-eared archways. It not only asks visitors to reflect on the happiness such aesthetics give us, but also their use for rebellion — and manipulation. Anyone that owns cute cats can certainly attest to the latter!

Book tickets right n'aaaaaaw.

Ruth Asawa: Retrospective

Ruth Asawa amidst several of her looped-wire sculptures, November 1954. Photo: Nat Farbman/The LIFE Picture Collection/Shutterstock Artwork © 2026 Ruth Asawa Lanier, Inc., Courtesy David Zwirner

When: 18 October 2026 - 10 January 2027

Where: Fondation Beyeler (Riehen, Switzerland)

Japanese American artist Ruth Asawa remains a pioneer within the world of abstract art, best-known for her intricate wire sculptures that captured the geometry of organic matter. However, her career was so much more than just these — incorporating everything from figurative drawings to life casts and even outdoor fountains. This diversity is captured at the Fondation Beyeler's retrospective; a comprehensive exploration of Asawa's ability to transform materials into reality-bending marvels that still inspire profound contemplations. Find out more here.

Bonus highlight: One not to be missed for photography enthusiasts and historians: ‘Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography’ opens at Tate Modern in London from 14 October 2026 until 21 February 2027.

Movies

Street Fighter

Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji in 'Street Fighter'. Courtesy of Paramount Pictures.

Where: Cinemas

When: 16 October

It's Showtime! After two rival martial artists are recruited for a World Warrior Tournament, so begins a collision course with violent criminals, inner-demons — and each other. Based on the legendary 90s video game series of the same name, it's the latest in a long line of previous adaptations that have spanned everything from live-action features to anime web series. For fans and wannabe warriors this is an ideal outing that packs all the (rising dragon) punches while not taking itself too seriously.

Bonus highlight: Russian-language thriller Minotaur (which is also France's choice for the 2027 Oscars) is out at French cinemas from 14 October, with a staggered release across the rest of Europe to follow in November.

TV series

Crystal Lake

Linda Cardellini in 'Crystal Lake'. © 2026 Peacock TV LLC. All Rights Reserved.

Where: SKY/NOW

When: 19 October

Dim the lights, burrow under a blanket and prepare to enter Camp Crystal Lake. Set in the summer of 1972, shortly after a young Jason Voorhees drowned, this new prequel show unravels the events that took place eight years before the first Friday the 13th film. Linda Cardellini (Freaks and Geeks, Scooby-Doo, DTF St. Louis) stars as Jason's mother, Pamela, whose grief unleashes dark secrets from her past — and fuels a slow descent into madness. Much like Mike Flanagan's recent Carrie adaptation, the episodic format allows for a deeper origin story that explores the psychology behind one of horror's most legendary villains.

Bonus highlight: Sylvester Stallone returns for season four of crime series Tulsa King, out on 16 October on Paramount+.

Music

Fontaines D.C. - Dopamine Chamber

When: 16 October

More than two years since the release of 2024's Romance (one of our favourite albums that year), Irish post-punk band Fontaines D.C. have returned with Dopamine Chamber — a mood board of synth-driven sounds that explore societal issues. There are eleven tracks in total, with lead single 'Marianne' setting the tone for something cinematic and psychedelic through its mesmerisingly trippy dirge.

Bonus highlights: Two other notable albums this week include 'Cookie Happened' by Eels and 'No Bad Memories' by The Avalanches — both out on the 16 October. Find out more about them in our fall album previews list.

World.title: EU leaders face budget showdown as Germany leads revolt over spending plans
World.content:
EU leaders are heading for a bruising battle over the bloc’s next long-term budget this week, after a German-led coalition of net contributors rejected the latest compromise proposal as insufficient.

 

On Saturday, the Irish presidency of the EU Council proposed cutting €141 billion from the overall budget, bringing it to €1.622 trillion in 2025 prices for the seven-year period from 2028 to 2034.

But Berlin and its allies insist the cuts do not go far enough, while other member states and EU institutions have criticised the proposal for lacking ambition.

“We are still far from an agreement. The size of the new proposal is not a basis for agreement. The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the brunt of financing it,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a statement.

“Everyone must contribute to the necessary adjustments, because prioritising and modernising EU spending is a task for us all,” he added.

Germany and its allies object not only to the overall size of the budget but also to how the cuts are distributed, with emerging priorities such as competitiveness and defence bearing the brunt.

“Defence, research and new technologies are being hit disproportionately hard. Europe needs to strengthen itself in these areas. Savings need to be found in a balanced way across the entire budget,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement.

The Irish proposal concentrates the deepest cuts on programmes favoured by the so-called “frugals”, who prefer to call themselves “modernisers”. Competitiveness funding would fall by 13% and global cooperation by 17%.

By contrast, traditional policies such as agriculture and cohesion are largely spared, with a mere 3% reduction. They are backed by the “Friends of Cohesion”, a group of 17 southern and eastern European countries including Italy and Romania.

It is not the first time the frugals’ own priorities have borne the brunt. In June, the then Cypriot presidency proposed cutting the European Competitiveness Fund and the Global Europe programme by almost 4%.

“There is an urgent need to strengthen the link between the political realities of the European leaders and the negotiations on the MFF [Multiannual Financial Framework],” an EU diplomat told Euronews.

“The Netherlands cannot accept this proposal. At this rate, there will be no deal by the end of the year,” warned Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen.

Sweden’s Minister for EU Affairs Jessica Rosencrantz likewise called the proposal “unreasonable,” adding that “we are therefore nowhere near an agreement.”

The frugals are not alone in their disappointment. The Friends of Cohesion welcomed with a sigh of relief that funding for their farmers and poorest regions was spared significant cuts. But they also say the next budget looks unambitious given the challenges facing the bloc.

Excluding the repayment of NextGenerationEU, the post-pandemic recovery instrument, the budget would amount to a mere 1.02% of EU gross national income. According to leading MEPs, that is a 10% cut to the current budget in real terms.

“The choice before us is not between a cheap and an expensive Europe. It is between an underfunded Europe at the mercy of the next crisis, and a properly funded Europe that can tackle challenges and respond to Europeans’ needs,” said MEP Carla Tavares (Portugal/S&D).

Meanwhile, the Commission’s Director-General for Budget, Stéphanie Riso, told EU ambassadors on Sunday that she had severe concerns, not only about the lack of ambition but also because the proposal risked making the EU much more rigid.

She singled out the cuts to Brussels ' public administration, largely supported by the member states, and the EU Facility, an instrument meant to give the budget room to react to shocks, which the Irish proposal drastically cuts by 40%.

The long-term budget will be discussed at the European Council summit on Thursday and Friday, when EU leaders are expected to provide political direction to break the deadlock.

“We are hearing more of the same arguments. We are getting to a point where we need leaders to advance the discussion,” a second EU diplomat told Euronews.

World.title: What is ‘pilgra-merch’? The travel trend turning souvenirs into trip inspiration
World.content:
Long gone are the days when your souvenirs were limited to whatever you could hastily grab from the airport gift store before rushing to your gate.

 

Nowadays, buying something you can only get in that specific destination has become a key part of the travel experience, at least according to Skyscanner’s latest travel trends report.

Dubbed “pilgra-merch”, the trend is the latest iteration of the millennial phrase “pics, or it didn’t happen”, says fashion psychologist Shakaila Forbes-Bell.

“Fashion brands have been leaning into this trend by providing more sensation-seeking style experiences from mystery bags to pop-ups, all of which you have to be ‘tapped in’ to know about,” she said.

“This community-driven aspect is key to creating a coveted pilgra-merch item. When a bag, a tote, or a mug becomes sought after, it’s often positioned as something only a ‘real traveller’ would know about. This positioning taps into our ingrained desire to belong and fear of being othered, which ultimately heightens the item’s desirability.”

Some 23% of travellers have made a trip in the past year to buy something they couldn’t purchase online, with 28% of Gen Z saying they are most proud to buy a limited-edition grocery tote, while 22% of Millennials are showing off their branded robes or caps from luxury hotels.

Where to embrace the ‘pilgra-merch’ trend

Skyscanner’s trends report focused on two ‘pilgra-merch’ examples – the Trader Joe’s tote bag, and Ritz Paris’ merchandise – but we think you can do better than that.

If you want supermarket merch that not everybody has, Family Mart in Japan has you covered. Last month, the chain released 47 different pairs of socks to represent the country’s prefectures.

Exclusively available in Family Mart stores within the prefecture in question, you’ll be able to flex on people about all the under-the-radar places you’ve visited.

While the “pilgra-merch” trend is more about instantly recognisable items that show off how well-travelled you are, we think buying a unique item you’ll use everyday that isn’t necessarily branded is a much better use of your cash.

With autumn finally upon us, it’s time to start thinking about upgrading your wardrobe – so why not head to one of the Handknitting Association of Iceland’s stores to pick out 100% wool, locally-made jumpers and cardigans?

Alternatively, if you’re all sorted for jumpers, you could head to Riga, where SENĀ KLĒTS sells mittens knitted in traditional Latvian designs which are filled with symbolism.

For when the weather warms up again, there are several places on the continent where you can get custom-made sandals, the most famous of which is probably Melissinos Sandals in Athens.

World.title: Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff
World.content:
The escalating clash between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia now threatens to ignite the already tense rivalry between Israel and Turkey in the Horn of Africa. This week, Turkey threw its military weight behind Saudi Arabia, while Somaliland – a self-declared state recognised only by Israel – is urgently seeking Israeli military support.

Advertising

Somaliland, a breakaway state from Somalia, is calling on Israel to provide military hardware. “We need air defence systems,” Mohamed Osman Fadal, a senior foreign affairs adviser to Somaliland’s president, said in a Middle East Eye interview this month.

Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi made a similar request last month for Israeli military support.

Last December, Israel became the first nation to recognise Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991. Because of its close ties to Israel, Somaliland now fears it could become a target for the Houthis, who operate from Yemen just across the Gulf of Aden and have previously targeted Israel.

“The Houthi threat is growing; it’s a major issue,” said Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

“Access to the Red Sea and Somaliland’s location just across from Yemen are very important, and I think this is where Israel recognises that it’s difficult to deal with the threat only from afar, and it’s important to have allies in the Horn of Africa,” she added.

Israel, which is in the midst of an election campaign ahead of the 27 October vote, has not commented on the request. But Lindenstrauss predicts a favourable response. “Obviously, if you look at the location, there should be some military support," she said.

Turkey’s backing for Somalia

Yet Somaliland’s call for military aid is fuelled by more than just anxiety over the Houthis. Somalia’s government is still intent on reclaiming Somaliland, branding it a rogue state. At the same time, Turkey has stepped up its military support for Somalia, deploying F-16s and advanced drones in January, and running its largest overseas military base to train Somali troops.

Somaliland president makes 'historic' visit to Israel

“Turkey has strong defence cooperation with Somalia; Somaliland sees that as an issue for them. It sees them as a potential future threat down the road. And so that’s why they’re calling for Israeli security support,” explained Horn of Africa analyst Omar Mahmood of the International Crisis Group.

“I think what’s happening is both sides, Somalia and Somaliland, are drawing external actors into their local dispute,” added Mahmood. “So it’s elevating what has been an unresolved but a local dispute for quite some time into something broader, something more regional.”

Tensions between Turkey and Israel have also been mounting, fuelled by Israel’s ongoing wars in Gaza and Lebanon and Ankara’s vocal support for Hamas. Both nations now see each other as an increasing threat.

“There is a security dilemma evolving between Turkey and Israel,” warns Lindenstrauss. “What Turkey does for its security, Israel sees as threatening. What Israel does for its defences in [Syria] is seen as threatening.”

Soli Ozel, an expert on Turkey at the Institut Montaigne in France, warns that because Somalia holds such strategic value for Turkey, any Israeli military involvement in Somaliland could dangerously escalate the situation.

“They may consider the deployment of Israeli missiles in Somaliland another destabilising factor,” said Ozel. “But I don’t think that the F-16s or the drones would be used against Somaliland, honestly; at least for the moment, I wouldn’t expect that to happen.”

Lebanon becomes latest battleground in Turkish-Israeli tensions

Containment, not conflict

Ozel argues that while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan are trading increasingly bellicose rhetoric, both countries are engaged in a high-stakes battle of containment rather than conflict.

“The theatrics and the realities of Turkish-Israeli relations may not be exactly the same,” explained Ozel. “I don’t think they will fight, but they are both showing their colours, right? Israel sent missiles to Somaliland; the Turks send F-16s and drones in order to set limits to what the other party will do.”

Turkey is preparing to expand its military footprint in the region. This week, Turkey and Pakistan pledged armed support to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August, a pact binding the three nations to mutual defence.

While the specifics remain unclear, Lindenstrauss notes that despite rising friction between Turkey and Israel, both countries may still find common cause in confronting the Houthis.

“I think the recognition that the Houthis are not something that is seen as only Israel’s problem, and it’s not just a minor proxy of Iran, but it’s a major problem that many states have to join together to deal with. I think that’s actually good news,” said Lindenstrauss.

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Yet Mahmood cautions that as clashes in the Red Sea escalate, Israel’s possible deployment of military hardware to Somaliland points to a worrying new trend.

“Horn actors need to realise that while they’re inviting external actors in to support their own ambitions locally, to get one step over their political adversaries, they risk turning their theatre into a wider proxy battleground. And so certainly, I think there’s a risk that those types of tensions can spill over,” he warned.

World.title: India news: Rahul Gandhi to march to Supreme Court
World.content:
10/12/2026 October 12, 2026 INDIA bloc to hold protest march demanding CEC's resignation

Leader of the opposition and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi-led INDIA bloc is going to march to the Supreme Court today at 4 p.m. local time (10:30 UTC), intensifying their agitation against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Gandhi urged people to join his "march for democracy" and "march for justice" in a post on X, as he gave the "Chalo Dilli" (Let's go to Delhi) call ahead of the INDIA bloc's planned march to the Supreme Court.

The call for the protest march came a day after forceful, mass detentions of protesters, journalists and lawyers were reported in Delhi on Saturday.

The Cockroach Janta Party has also expressed support for the planned march.

The Congress Party had sought a meeting with the Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant to raise the issue of alleged vote theft.



However, the CJI declined the meeting, reportedly citing the matter being sub judice in the Supreme Court.

World.title: Germany's women: Ena Mahmutovic makes her case to become Germany's next No.1 goalkeeper
World.content:
Germany's win against Australia saw Ena Mahmutovic excel in goal. The 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper is considered the successor to Ann-Katrin Berger and is making a name for herself.

With determination, pace, and four beautifully crafted goals, Germany's women won its friendly against Australia, thrilling not only the fans but also head coach Christian Wück.

"You can see how fired up the girls are, how well they're already playing together, and that we have an incredible amount of talent on the field and on the bench," said a delighted Wück after his team's well-deserved 4-2 victory.

Since there were several notable absences, including captain Giulia Gwinn and top scorer Lea Schüller, others had to step up and fill the gaps. And they did so with flying colors. Melissa Kössler made a strong case for herself as a striker by scoring her first two international goals. Center back Camilla Küver and Sjoeke Nüsken were also on the scoresheet.

Mahmutovic seizes her chance in goal

Much like it was with the men's team during Jürgen Klopp's first international break as Germany head coach, the question as to who will emerge as the next number one goalkeeper for the women was also a hot topic.

The understudy and the current No.1: Ena Mahmutovic and Ann-Katrin Berger Image: Madeleine Fantini/HMB Media/picture alliance

The difference is that unlike Manuel Neuer, who has retired from international football, Ann-Katrin Berger is sticking around for at least one more tournament cycle.

However, with just three matches to go before the start of the playoffs in the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), where she plays for Gotham FC, Berger is giving these two Germany friendlies a miss.

Parallels to men's goalkeeping situation

This means 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper Ena Mahmutovic, who is seen as a potential successor to Berger, took her her chance.

"Ena deserves to play the next match," Wück said ahead of the game. "We must not forget that she already kept a clean sheet in Slovenia (Germany's last World Cup qualifier). And I hope she can repeat that tomorrow."

Some will draw parallels to Jonas Urbig, who many see as a future number one for Germany's men. Both he and Mahmutovic were born in 2003 in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, and both are seen as up-and-coming stars for their club and country.

Manuel Neuer remains the first choice at Bayern, while Jonas Urbig looks set to become Germany's No. 1 Image: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

The difference is that while Urbig remains an understudy to Neuer at Bayern, Mahmutovic is already the first-choice keeper at her club, having won the starting job over Maria Luisa Grohs prior to the start of the season.

For Germany, though, Mahmutovic still has to bide her time, while there are already strong indications that Klopp intends to make Urbig his number one.

'The future of the national team'

"I'm obviously delighted," Mahmutovic said ahead of the games.

"It's always something special, of course – especially playing against a team from another continent. I think testing ourselves against them is very helpful as we look ahead to the World Cup."

Bayern director Bianca Rech recently described Mahmutovic as "the future of the national team," calling on Wück not only to give her a callup, but also regular playing time.

Wück still sees Berger as slightly better than Mahmutovic, but he is also full of praise for the young keeper.

"Ena's performances have been very good," he said. "She will get her playing time."

When Ena Mahmutovic lost control of the ball after a backpass, Italy's Sofia Cantore took full advantage Image: David Inderlied/dpa/picture alliance

Costly mistake in Germany debut

The match against Slovenia was just Mahmutovic's second appearances for Germany. Her first, which came almost two years ago, was memorable for the wrong reason. In the dying minutes of a friendly in December 2024, she lost control of the ball after a back pass, allowing an Italian forward to score the winner in a 2-1 defeat for Germany. Still, Mahmutovic was included in Germany's squad for the 2025 Euros.

Had it been up to her father – who is from Montenegro – Mahmutovic would never have become a goalkeeper.

"He still says I would have been better as an outfield player because I'm good with both feet," she said.

Unusual Bundesliga debut

That's a quality that evidently wasn't lost on Thomas Gerstner, when her coach at her then-club Duisburg, gave her her Women's Bundesliga debut in May 2020. With the team coping with several absences, the then-16-year-old, who had been on the bench as backup goalkeeper, came on as an outfield player.

"The coach brought me on during stoppage time," Mahmutovic recalled. "I got to make two sprints – that was my debut."

That, however, was a one-off, and nobody questions Mahmutovic's strengths as a goalkeeper.

"She is one of the most talented goalkeepers in the world," said Bayern coach Jose Barcala, noting that she is the kind of player who can decide a match.

Mahmutovic will be hoping she gets many more opportunities to do just that for Germany.

This article was originally published in German.

This article was updated on October 12 after Germany's friendly against Australia.

World.title: Frankfurt Book Fair: Rights lawyer Sands awarded peace prize
World.content:
Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands was awarded the German Book Trade's Peace Prize this weekend. Accepting the award, Sands criticized Germany's "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel.

The 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair concluded on Sunday with the awarding of the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade to the Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands.

Sands was honored in the presence of German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier as a committed humanist "who, despite growing resistance, fights tirelessly for human rights, justice and mutual understanding."

The jury said that his work was based on a "commitment to the universal rights of every human being, evidenced in his advocacy for victims of war crimes, racism, torture and colonial injustice."

Sands criticizes Germany's 'silence' on Israel

Sands, a professor of law at University College London and human rights lawyer at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, used his acceptance speech to criticize Germany for what he called its "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel and its actions in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.

Sands said human rights abuses should be clearly named, especially among allies, stating: "It's not antisemitic. It's not anti-Israel. It's the truth."

Philippe Sands: Peace through law To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sands, himself a descendent of Jews driven out of what is now Lviv in western Ukraine during the German occupation in the Second World War, became known to a broader audience through his 2016 book East West Street: On the Origins of Genocide and Crimes Against Humanity.

The work, which details the lives of two Jewish lawyers, Hersch Lauterpacht and Raphael Lemkin, and the origins of international criminal law, was translated into dozens of languages, including German as Rückkehr nach Lemberg (Return to Lviv) in 2018.

"Germany knows all about ethnic cleansing," Sands said in Frankfurt, referring to criticism leveled at Israel by many states over its treatment of Palestinians.

"So why the silence? Silence is not the way. Not for a family. Not for a community. Not for a country."

Sands also condemned the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, as "appalling" and "a monstrous crime against the norms of international law" and acknowledged that Israel, like any state, has a right to defend itself.

"[But] this right is not unlimited and must be practiced within the boundaries of international law."

World.title: Germany news: Söder demands CDU supports of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt reveal themselves
World.content:
Skip next section Söder: Those who voted for AfD speaker should show 'backbone'

10/12/2026 October 12, 2026 Söder: Those who voted for AfD speaker should show 'backbone'

"Do you want to go somewhere else? Then just say so," Bavarian leader Markus Söder said during an interview with public broadcaster ARD.

As a member of the CSU, the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), Söder was referencing bloc members in the state of Saxony-Anhalt who are believed to have voted for a member of the far-right in a secret ballot.

Last week, Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — whose chapter in Saxony-Anhalt is classified as right-wing extremist — was elected state parliamentary speaker.

This marked the first time the AfD has seen a member elected to such a position, and the first time in postwar Germany that a right-wing extremist has risen to this rank.

AfD lawmaker elected speaker in Saxony-Anhalt To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The populist BSW party had declared their intention to support Rausch's nomination alongside the AfD, but his win with 48 votes means that other lawmakers must have voted for him too. It is strongly suspected that these were members of the conservative CDU.

Rausch's election prompted outrage across Germany, including from CDU members who have accused their colleagues of abandoning the so-called "firewall" — the agreement amongst the country's mainstream parties not to support the AfD.

Söder called it "pretty poor form," from the CDU members in Saxony-Anhalt, saying they should "at least have the backbone" to make their decision public.

World.title: How green is Europe's urban public transport? A data-driven reality check
World.content:
Greener buses and cleaner fleets are reshaping public transport across Europe. But are cities moving fast enough to meet their zero-emission goals?

An electric plug icon on their windows makes them easy to spot in cities like Brussels and Madrid. Quietly navigating the streets, electric buses have become an increasingly common sight on Europe's streets in recent years.

Michela Le Pira, assistant professor of transportation at Italy's University of Catania, says removing tailpipe emissions — the gases and particles generated when a combustion vehicle is running — might be "the easiest strategy to improve public transport."

Most Europeans live in urban settings, and road transport harms air quality. In 2023, almost 300,000 deaths across the EU were caused by air pollution levels exceeding the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended thresholds.

Of all fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations in European urban areas, about 14% come from road transport, including public, private and freight transport. Additionally, towns and cities account for nearly a quarter of the European Union's transport greenhouse gas emissions (GHG).

DW and the European Data Journalism Network evaluated more than a decade's worth of data from more than 100 reports and sources on public transit and the emissions it causes, and identified 148 sustainability commitments by local authorities and transport operators in 33 cities across Europe. The analysis focuses on motorized mass transit, leaving out bikes and pedestrians as well as taxis, shared vehicles and e-scooters.

More electric buses, thanks to EU funds

The EU wants to become the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. A key part of that plan is cutting transport-related GHG emissions by 90% from 1990 levels.

As DW's analysis shows, Copenhagen is the only EU capital that has almost electrified its entire bus fleet — its vehicles do not have combustion engines and therefore do not produce tailpipe emissions. In cities like Rome, Lisbon and Nicosia, more than 90% of buses still run on diesel, and metros and trams account for less than 10% of their public transport fleet.

Although cars still dominate European streets, "electric buses are one way to reduce local air pollution," said Martin Baierl, data analyst with Transport & Environment, an advocacy non-profit for clean transport.

EU funds enabled many cities to increase their electric and alternative fuel bus fleets from 2021 on.

Electric buses comprise 20% of the total fleet in EU capitals and selected cities. Their number increased by 55% between 2021 and 2025 — equivalent to 1,234 more such vehicles on the road. The number of diesel-only buses has been declining since then, although they still outnumber those running on alternative fuel.

Slow road to sustainability in some cities

In addition to decarbonizing the bus fleet and helping to reduce air pollution, embracing electric models can help to lower noise and public transport operating costs. All the more so if the city produces its own electricity, explains Baierl. However, the outlay for e-buses is higher than for diesel models. In 20 out of the 31 cities with data to analyze, over 50% of the bus fleet is made up of traditional vehicles.

Brussels, for example, was an early adopter of moving away from traditional diesel-powered buses, switching to hybrids instead. Now the Belgian capital is in the process of electrifying its fleet, but at a slower pace. "It's not easy to know what the right technology will be in the end," Baierl said.

Another example is hydrogen-powered buses, which also produce zero emissions but are more costly to operate than their electric counterparts.

Many cities have not fully committed to zero-emissions despite EU targets

Transportation is the only major sector where greenhouse gas emissions remain above 1990 levels, despite the EU's ambition of a 90% reduction by 2050.

On average, public transport — including buses, trams and metros — is used for more than a quarter of trips in the 10 largest EU capitals, according to recent data from the non-profit group Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP). In Stockholm, the share is 49%, while in the smaller Slovenian capital of Ljubljana, it's 11%. DW analysis of transport sustainability pledges reveals that only four cities have explicitly committed to achieving zero emissions in buses or all public transport.

Rail transport is climate-friendly, but scarce

Yannis Papadimitriou lives 85 kilometers (about 53 miles) away from Athens, the EU capital with the highest air pollution mortality risk. He travels to work by commuter rail, a means of transport he'd like to see promoted more.

"For me it is a very conscious choice to use electric public transport, especially trains, which are the safest, most environmentally friendly and quickest way of transport."

Though trains, trams and metros run on electricity, there are more buses within city boundaries, and in many urban areas the majority still run on diesel.

Public transport's emissions go beyond the tailpipe

In Northern Europe, 15 kilometers away from Copenhagen, Poul Kattler also used to commute to work. He is now retired and takes the bus more frequently with his grandchildren. Despite Copenhagen having an almost completely fossil-fuel-free public transport system (only one bus runs on biomethane), the metro expansion, which is responding to the city's growth, comes with its own set of concerns.

"The whole construction phase [of the new metro line] is extremely environmentally demanding," Kattler said. If the construction emissions are considered, "the CO2 balance would be very poor for the metro now."

But in the long run, the benefits of a new metro line in reducing CO2 emissions outweigh its construction-related emissions, Le Pira said.

Combustion or exhaust emissions are not the only way transport pollutes the air and the environment. Indirect emissions, like those coming from electricity generation or fuel production, add to transport's CO2 footprint. Brakes and wheels release non-exhaust particle matter when wagons or vehicles slow down.

Since 1992, buses and any vehicle running on fossil fuels in the EU have been subject to stricter emissions standards. Fine particle emissions from buses and heavy-duty vehicles had dropped by 92% in 2022 according to the European Environment Agency . Yet overall road transport non-exhaust emissions from tire wear have increased 58% in two decades, as cars have become heavier.

Shifting from cars to a multimodal transport system

With a few exceptions, EU member states are not close to cutting greenhouse gas transport emissions by 90%, as envisioned by the EU's 2050 target.

Zero-emission public transport is one step toward decarbonizing transport in cities and meeting GHG reduction goals. The next challenge is to get people out of their cars.

"If we talk about sustainable mobility in general and not only clean public transport, the main problem is the model shift from private cars to public transport," Le Pira said.

On average, private automobiles account for more than a third of transport in the largest EU capitals, according to CDP data.

Cheaper ticket prices for groups, like students, and disincentives for car use, such as low-emission zones, are two complementary ways of attracting more passengers while reducing private transport.

In her research work, Le Pira investigates how public transport can be more efficient and appealing for city dwellers, for example, by combining transport modes where people step off their bikes and onto a train. This kind of solution could be particularly relevant for small cities "where cars are still the main transport mode."

According to Baierl, places with good public transport draw people in. "Cities where not everybody has to use a car are just more livable," he said.

Edited by: Gianna-Carina Grün and Sarah Steffen

Fact check: Eva Lopez

For data, code and methodology behind this analysis, see this GitHub repository . More data-driven stories from DW can be found here.

World.title: UK students call for school uniforms to be banned in pornography
World.content:
Short skirts, knee-high socks, white blouses: Girls' school uniform items are widely used as costumes in pornographic videos. As students experience harassment, a group wants to change that.

Aylin and Mae, both age 15, are members of their school's Little Feminist Book Club in Bicester, Oxfordshire, England.

During a group discussion, the club learned that teenagers at other schools were trying to have the sale of school uniforms banned in sex shops.

Schoolgirl costumes are also widely used in pornographic videos.

"All of us unanimously agreed. We wanted to take it a step further; we wanted to ban school uniform from all pornography," Aylin told DW. As a result, they started a petition to raise awareness of the issue.

Many of their fellow students, as the petition states, have already had unpleasant experiences while wearing their uniforms. Some reported being harassed as early as the age of 11. Many of these experiences had left them feeling frightened, ashamed and insecure. "I don't wear my school uniform outside of school," said Mae. "I don't like wearing it out."

One in three schoolgirls reports harassment

In their petition, the girls also refer to a 2018 report by the charity Plan International . According to a survey in the report, 35% of the 1,004 respondents aged 14 to 21 had experienced unwanted sexual attention while wearing a school uniform. Eight percent said they had been filmed or photographed by a stranger without their permission, or that someone had taken a photo under their school skirt, known as "upskirting."

"Something that should actually be innocent, something that is supposed to symbolize a community, has now become discredited in society," said Mae. "And our perception of what a school uniform represents has been distorted by this disgusting media."

School uniforms are also iconic symbols of Japanese culture Image: Michael Bihlmayer/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

School uniforms often mandatory

School uniforms are common in many countries around the world. They are meant to make class and financial divides less visible, which is also supposed to prevent bullying while strengthening a community feeling.

In the United Kingdom, uniforms are mandatory at almost all schools and preschools, which means essentially all children between the ages of 4 to 16 wear them.

Outside school, children have no way to escape unwanted attention.

"We just want to prevent people from thinking about children and school uniforms in that way," said Mae. "Hopefully, we'll be able to actually turn the ban into legislation."

Until that happens, they still have a long way to go, but the girls are optimistic. As of October 5, 2026, the petition has garnered more than 24,000 signatures. Thanks to an article in the English newspaper The Times, it's also gotten plenty of attention.

Now, Mae and Aylin hope to get parliament to debate the issue. Two Members of Parliament have already voiced their support.

But the girls also know some people believe longer skirts are the solution. "I believe that's wrong," explains Aylin. "We shouldn't blame the victims. We should blame those who think it is acceptable to sexualize them."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Hurricane Simon batters Mexico's Pacific Coast
World.content:
Hurricane Simon is currently running parallel to Mexico's Pacific Coast, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds to vulnerable towns.

Hurricane Simon lashed vulnerable resorts and towns along Mexico's Pacific Coast on Sunday as it moved parallel to the shoreline, despite weakening to a category 3 storm.

"Additional weakening is forecast but Simon is still expected to be a strong hurricane as it passes near the coast of west-central Mexico tonight," the US National Hurricane Center's advisory said.

Simon is expected to move farther offshore on Monday before turning back towards Mexico's coast on Wednesday, it said.

On high alert

Mexican authorities have placed 28 municipalities across the states of Jalisco and Colima under the highest cyclone alert level. Another 93 municipalities were under high ‌alert, according to civil protection bulletins.

Strong winds are battering the coastal states on the Pacific end of Mexico Image: Daniel Becerril/REUTERS

The hurricane's center closed in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rains were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Puerto Vallarta is a popular tourist destination in Jalisco. Apart from the resorts, several Mexicans live in communities inland and uphill, in houses that may not be able to weather the storm.

How to protect houses from natural disasters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Experts believe the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.

"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin said.

"They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."

heavy rainfall overnight has increased the risk of flooding and muslides Image: Daniel Becerril/REUTERS

In Manzanillo, residents waded through flooded streets on Sunday morning as soldiers helped rescue locals from the overnight rainfall.

"The beds, the refrigerators, the stoves, all the furniture got wet. The whole house flooded," Cecilia Palomar told Reuters outside her home.

How do tropical storms form? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"My mother doesn't want ‌to leave. We took her to my brother's, to higher ground. She's an elderly woman, but ‌she doesn't ​want to leave. She doesn't want to be away from her home."

Airport closed, authorities urge caution

Puerto Vallarta International Airport was closed temporarily while authorities suspended non-essential activities.

They also established emergency shelters in threatened coastal communities.

Earlier on Sunday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum had urged residents of coastal communities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain indoors ahead of the storm.

Hurricane Simon has come days after Hurricane Polo struck Mexico's Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, knocking down power lines and flooding the streets.

World.title: Germany: Bas quits as SPD co-chair amid coalition friction
World.content:
Bärbel Bas has resigned as labor minister and as co-leader of the Social Democrats as tension grows with Chancellor Merz's CDU.

Bärbel Bas, a longstanding top official with Social Democrats (SPD), resigned from her post on Monday citing the death of her stepdaughter and "open attacks" within Germany's ruling coalition of the SPD and Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrat (CDU) bloc.

"I am currently unable to muster the strength to fully carry out my government and party duties on short notice, I have decided to step down from both offices,” the 58-year-old said.

She is to be replaced by Alexander Schweitzer, the former SPD premier of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate.

Who is Bärbel Bas?

A member of the parliament since 2009, Bas' star began to rise when she became president of the Bundestag in 2021 under the SPD-led coalition of former Chancellor Olaf Scholz.

Within her center-left party, Bas has been among its more progressive members.

Following the collapse of Scholz's government, the SPD became the junior coalition partners to Merz's conservative bloc.

She served as president of the Bundestag until 2025, when she became Merz's labor minister as well as co-leader of her party alongisde Lars Klingbeil.

Why is she resigning now?

After being widowed in 2020, Bas said her stepdaughter recently passed away. The outgoing labor minister said she needed time to process her grief, and that her party deserved strong leadership.

She added that recent infighting between the SPD and CDU over various policy matters hastened her decision.

The CDU has accused Bas of delaying or blocking several reforms the conservatives are keen to pass, including changes to Germany's struggling pension system and employment laws.

Bas said that she informed both Chancellor Merz and Lars Klingbeil before issuing her public statement.

Merz thanked Bas for her "trustworthy cooperation" and said he respected her decision.
