World.title: La fórmula perfecta para triunfar en la industria de la cósmetica
World.content:
Con un crecimiento que le ha permitido llegar al 1,03% del PIB, el sector del cuidado de la piel, la higiene personal, la perfumería y el maquillaje recompensa a los emprendedores que apuestan por la innovación, la funcionalidad y la especialización

La industria de la cosmética y del cuidado personal se mueve a dos velocidades. Una es la del mercado, que exige novedades constantemente; la otra, la del laboratorio, donde es la paciencia la que impera para el desarrollo de nuevas fórmulas. Y en medio se encuentran los empresarios que realizan malabarismos para encajar ambos ritmos en uno de los mercados más competitivos y al alza. En los últimos cinco años, la industria ha crecido un 44,3% hasta alcanzar el 1,03% del producto interior bruto español. España es el segundo exportador mundial de perfumes, por detrás de Francia, de acuerdo con el informe anual de la Asociación Nacional de Perfumería y Cosmética (Stanpa), organización que reúne al 90% de las empresas del sector.

El cuidado de la piel es uno de los campos en auge dentro de esta industria, destaca Juan Matji, presidente de Cantabria Labs, una compañía farmacéutica que elabora productos, tanto cosméticos como medicamentos, para el cuidado dermatológico. “Ahora se habla del concepto one health, que significa una única salud, fenómeno que combina el hacer deporte con las rutinas de la piel: limpiarla, protegerla, hidratarla... Antiguamente, la cosmética era solamente para un cierto grupo de mujeres que contaban con recursos económicos, pero hoy se ha democratizado”, explica el empresario en un nuevo capítulo de El poder de las empresas, el pódcast de los que hacen, de Banco Sabadell.

Matji llegó a la dirección de la empresa con 27 años, mientras trabajaba en el proceso de cierre ordenado de un laboratorio farmacéutico en 1994. Entonces vio su potencial y decidió comprar la empresa. “Llegué sin plan, pero tenía ilusión, y sabía que tenía que rodearme de gente con talento”, cuenta el empresario. Hoy es una compañía que vende en 100 países.

Crear un buen equipo resulta también clave para Estefanía Ferrer, ingeniera química y fundadora de LICO Cosmetics, un laboratorio de ingeniería cosmética 100% digital, que coprotagoniza el pódcast junto a Matji. “Los principios fueron duros, porque abrirse camino en este sector no es fácil, pero tuvimos claro que queríamos trabajar desde Sevilla. Esto podía ser un obstáculo para captar talento, pero nos hemos encontrado que es todo lo contrario. Hay mucho talento fuera de las grandes ciudades”, celebra Ferrer. Ambos empresarios ofrecen consejos para emprender en este sector en plena expansión.

Invertir en formulación antes que en ‘marketing’

El mercado de la belleza y el cuidado personal es un sector competitivo impulsado por tendencias cambiantes y consumidores cada vez más exigentes. Por eso, señala Matji, el éxito de esta industria, aunque pueda resultar obvio, es que el producto funcione. Así es como el consumidor apuesta por una marca: encuentra algo que le soluciona un problema. “Un fabricante puede generar mucho ruido en redes y desaparecer si el producto no convence. La innovación y la eficacia tienen que estar detrás de la promesa”, explica el empresario. De hecho, las compañías de este sector invirtieron en I+D+i, de media, el 3,4% de sus ingresos en 2025. Muy por encima de la media general española, que es del 0,9%, de acuerdo con el Instituto Nacional de Estadística.

Consejos de Empresario Tener una comunidad en redes es importante, pero un seguidor no equivale a una venta Estefanía Ferrer, fundadora de LICO Cosmetics

La investigación es una carrera de fondo con el fin de dar con nuevas soluciones para los problemas de las personas, como cremas solares o antiacné más efectivas y, sobre todo, baratas. Esto, afirma Ferrer, de LICO Cosmetics, se consigue destinando recursos desde el principio. Su empresa, explica, comenzó con una inversión inicial de 15.000 euros, que le dio la posibilidad de desarrollar sus dos primeros productos (hoy cuentan con 42 artículos en su catálogo). “Nos permitió fabricar un pequeño lote y sostenernos, aunque con un sueldo muy bajo”, agrega.

La presentación del producto marca la diferencia

Una vez que se cuenta con un producto, ambos empresarios coinciden en que se debe presentar de manera atractiva. Va a competir con cientos en los lineales y en los buscadores de internet y va a configurar la primera impresión. Pero, puntualiza Ferrer, además de atractivo, ha de resultar útil. El envase construye la experiencia de uso. Un envase efectivo es intuitivo, es decir, que nada más tenerlo en la mano permite entender cómo se abre y cómo se dosifica. Pero, sobre todo, añade la directora ejecutiva de LICO Cosmetics, tiene que preservar bien el contenido. “Lanzamos nuestros dos primeros productos con una imagen sencilla y funcional: dos botes blancos de un cristal duro que preservaban muy bien, cumplían al máximo la función”, describe Ferrer.

Los seguidores en redes no son clientes

Una de las lecciones más importantes que Ferrer reconoce haber aprendido con su empresa, que nació como nativa digital, es que es necesario promocionarse en redes sociales, plataformas que ofrecen un amplio escaparate con pocos recursos. Pero eso, advierte, no se traduce directamente en ventas. “Tener una comunidad en Instagram o TikTok no significa tener un negocio. Un seguidor no equivale a una venta”.

Consejos de Empresario Una web está bien y es necesaria, pero si quieres que te conozcan coge el teléfono y haz que los clientes te reciban Juan Matji, presidente de Cantabria Labs

Matji defiende una forma más tradicional de buscar clientes. “No se puede transmitir toda la ilusión que uno tiene en sus productos a través de una web o un power point, hay que hacerlo como se ha hecho siempre, saber quién es quién y cómo llegar hasta las personas”, argumenta el empresario. El trabajo de los comerciales es insustituible. “Yo sinceramente pienso que muchas veces los emprendedores gastan mucho dinero en la web. Pero, ¿el tráfico cómo se genera? Cogiendo el teléfono y haciendo que te reciban, conociendo a los clientes”, completa Matji.

Gracias a esa manera de trabajar, cuenta Matji, Cantabria Labs logró su colaboración con la universidad de Harvard a mediados de los años noventa. El empresario envío un fax al especialista Thomas B. Fitzpatrick, una figura de gran prestigio en dermatología y profesor de Harvard Medical School. En él, le hablaba de un extracto de origen vegetal que estaba investigando por sus posibles propiedades frente al daño producido por la radiación solar en la piel. Poco después, empezaron a desarrollar la línea central de la compañía, Heliocare, que incluye productos orales y de uso tópico para la fotoprotección.

En una industria tan amplia... hay que especializarse

La industria de la higiene y el cuidado personal no es un único mercado. Incluye el cuidado facial, el del cabello, la higiene, la fotoprotección y la perfumería. Intentar abarcar todos de primeras es el error que comenten muchos empresarios, argumentan Ferrer y Matji. Además, tienen ritmos de compra, canales de distribución y niveles de competencia muy diferentes. Ferrer señala que el sector del maquillaje, especialmente el de bajo coste, ha experimentado un bum tan grande en la última década que se encuentra saturado. “Hay una batalla tremenda para encontrar un espacio”, puntualiza.

Matji señala el campo de los productos fotoprotectores como el más competitivo en este momento. “Es un sector muy agresivo”, describe. La preocupación de los españoles por el cuidado de la piel frente a la radiación solar ha crecido notablemente en los últimos años, lo que se ha reflejado en el consumo de protectores solares, que ha crecido un 55% entre 2020 y 2025, de acuerdo con un estudio sobre hábitos de consumo de fotoprotectores, realizado por Stanpa en colaboración con la agencia de investigación de mercados Kantar. Un campo con muchos competidores, pero en el que aún hay margen para la innovación, señala el empresario. Ese es el fin último de esta industria que no para de crecer.

World.title: De Bilbao a A Coruña, una vuelta por el norte de España para disfrutar del mejor arte
World.content:
Las aperturas del Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao y Faro Santander se añaden a los centros culturales nacidos las últimas décadas entre el País Vasco y Galicia. Excusa perfecta para recorrer una zona que se ha convertido en uno de los epicentros mundiales del arte contemporáneo

Con la aportación del genio de arquitectos de la talla de Frank Gehry, Norman Foster, Renzo Piano, Oscar Niemeyer y David Chipperfield, las recientes aperturas del Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao y de Faro Santander confirman el interés cultural que ofrece el norte de España.

Para demostrarlo, trazamos una singular ruta cultural que se extiende desde el País Vasco hasta Galicia, una zona que se ha convertido en uno de los epicentros mundiales del arte contemporáneo. Un viaje con mucho arte que se inició hace 29 años con la apertura del Guggenheim Bilbao.

Más información Por los lugares de Goya: de Fuendetodos a Madrid pasando por Zaragoza

Guggenheim Bilbao

Levantado hace 29 años en una zona degradada del Nervión, el arriesgado edificio de Frank Gehry no ha perdido su aura. Todo lo contrario. La creación el arquitecto canadiense-estadounidense está considerada el edificio contemporáneo de mayor trascendencia. Su influencia ha sido tal que ha impulsado la transformación de una ciudad industrial en declive, hasta ser referente mundial de innovación urbana. Es el llamado Efecto Bilbao.

Antes de entrar en esta ágora del arte contemporáneo, hay que echarle un vistazo desde el puente de La Salve. Sus arcos rojos, del artista Daniel Buren, son contrapunto de los fríos tonos del titanio del Guggenheim. Desde sus alturas, la vista pasea por las escamas metálicas del enorme pez —“lata de Sardinas”, lo llaman los bilbaínos—, doradas por la luz del otoño bilbaíno.

El Guggenheim Bilbao y, a la izquierda, los arcos rojos del artista Daniel Buren en el puente de La Salve. m. subirats (Alamy / cordon press)

En el inicio de la escalinata que conduce a la entrada del muso pocos resisten la tentación de tirarse unas fotos a los pies de Puppy, gigantesco ramo de flores al que Jeff Koons dio forma de entrañable Westie. Ya en el centro del esbeltísimo atrio central se impone doblar el cuello y vislumbrar sus alturas. “La Flor” lo bautizó el arquitecto por la disposición de sus láminas de cristal. En la distancia, los visitantes que transitan por las aéreas pasarelas asemejan hileras de hormigas. Es parada obligada el mirador sobre La materia del tiempo, desmesurada instalación de Richard Serra para la que Gehry tuvo que diseñar un espacio suficiente para albergar su inmensidad.

'La materia del tiempo', de Richard Serra, en el museo Guggenheim de Bilbao. ilyas Ayub (Alamy / cordon press)

Alrededor del museo y en lo que fue un espacio industrial que olía a abandono, una sucesión de zonas verdes invita al paseo. Por ellas transita el tranvía de Bilbao, que sigue el viejo trazado ferroviario de los trenes cargados de productos y desechos de siderurgias y astilleros. Recorrer la línea entre las estaciones de Atxuri y la del nuevo estadio San Mamés es buena manera de conocer cómo le ha cambiado la cara al Botxo. No lejos aguarda Azkuna Zentroa, la impactante restauración de la vieja alhóndiga que la magia de Philippe Starck convirtió en centro de ocio y cultura.

Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao

No hay que abandonar Bilbao sin la visita a su última gran novedad: la reapertura del Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao, inaugurado el 5 de octubre después de una reforma a cargo de Luis María Uriarte y Norman Foster que se ha prolongado cuatro años. Son 6.900 metros cuadrados donde destacan el impresionante atrio de entrada y el transgresor nuevo cuerpo Agravitas, rematado por una terraza de 700 metros cuadrados de vistas impagables.

El Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao, un edificio diseñado por Norman Foster y Luis María Uriarte. Nigel Young (BILBAO MUSEOA)

Con 150 nuevas obras, se incluyen trabajos de 55 mujeres, como un lienzo de Frida Kahlo. Destaca el centenar de piezas aportadas por el mecenas Plácido Arango. Obras de Eduardo Chillida, Cristina Iglesias, Susana Solana, Jorge de Oteiza, Juan Muñoz y Richard Serra, entre otros, ocupan los nuevos espacios. No opacan el severo fulgor del Guernica de Agustín Ibarrola, a propósito del cual Miguel Zugaza, director del museo, advirtió a los periodistas en la presentación de la ampliación: “Estamos satisfechos con nuestro Guernica. Aquí (en el montacargas) el de Picasso no entra ni en diagonal”, disipando la polémica sobre el traslado de la obra del malagueño, hoy en el Reina Sofía, en Madrid.

La reapertura del Bellas Artes confirma el esplendor cultural de Bilbao iniciado con el Guggenheim. Desde ahora inseparables, ambos museos ofrecen una entrada conjunta a precios ventajosos.

Faro Santander

Exterior del Faro Santander. BELÉN DE BENITO (FARO SANTANDER)

La rehabilitación del británico David Chipperfield de la antigua sede del Banco de Santander despierta admiración desde su inauguración, el pasado 7 de septiembre. Faro Santander es la primera obra museística realizada en España por el arquitecto premio Pritzker. Se ha transformado por completo el histórico edificio Pereda, que tiene su origen en dos bloques independientes. El primero se construyó en 1795 para viviendas, el segundo llegó en 1921. Albergaron un hotel, el club de regatas de la ciudad, hasta que pasó a ser la sede bancaria en 1923. Se unieron en los años cincuenta con un gran arco.

Las obras se han prolongado ocho años. Vaciado el conjunto por completo, solo se han respetado las fachadas. La novedad más reseñable está en el citado arco. Concretamente en el cubo de cristal encajado en su interior. Ha permitido unir las plantas de ambos bloques, logrando una continuidad de la que carecían, sin ocultar las vistas al exterior. “El arco es un potente gesto que conecta el edificio con su entorno”, señaló Chipperfield en la inauguración.

Dos esculturas en una de las terrazas del nuevo Faro Santander. JUAN BARAJA

La cuarta planta alberga uno de los puntos fuertes del museo: las obras maestras de la Colección Banco de Santander. De momento se exponen 69 piezas de las más de 1.200 que la componen. No son demasiadas, pero apabullan. El Sansón y el león, de Rubens, enfrentado a tres obras contemporáneas: Niña sentada en la sala con bancos, de la santanderina María Blanchard, un Tàpies y una pieza de Ángela de la Cruz de idéntico rojo al del perizoma que cubre la desnudez del héroe. Resumen de la vida que quiere darse al proyecto expositivo, en las siguientes salas conviven Velázquez, El Greco, Murillo, Goya, Lucas Cranach el Viejo, Alonso Cano, Tintoretto y Zurbarán con Barceló, Millares, Picasso, Miró y Chillida, entre otros.

Algunas de las obras de la Colección Banco Santander expuestas en Faro Santander. BELÉN DE BENITO (FARO SANTANDER)

El morbo de Faro se encuentra estos primeros meses en las exposiciones temporales. La consagrada a la surrealista Leonora Carrington (hasta el 31 de enero de 2027), en la que se recogen las terribles experiencias que sufrió en España. Otra ofrece una selección de las obras de la Colección Gelman Santander. Se trata del conjunto de 161 obras maestras de artistas mexicanos reunidas por Jacques Gelman y Natasha Zahalka, pareja de origen ruso establecida en México en la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Catalogadas Monumento Artístico por el Gobierno Mexicano, 93 de ellas se muestran en Faro. Esta muestra estará abierta hasta el 10 de enero de 2027, razón suficiente para visitar Santander estas semanas y contemplar las obras de Diego Ribera, David Alfaro Siqueiros, José Clemente Orozco, Rufino Tamayo, Graciela Iturbide, Tina Modotti… y Frida Kahlo. Absolutamente de moda la mexicana, el público hace cola para admirar, retratar y tirarse selfis ante Diego en mi pensamiento, Autorretrato con monos, El abrazo de amor de entre el Universo, la Tierra, yo, Diego y el señor Xólotl, Autorretrato con trenza y el resto de sus 18 obras expuestas.

Centro Botín

Exterior del Centro Botín, inaugurado en junio de 2017 en Santander, con diseño de Renzo Piano. Stéphane ABOUDARAM (CENTRO BOTÍN)

Al otro lado de los jardines de Pereda destaca el inconfundible hermano de Faro, el Centro Botín. Si en el primero se tuvo especial cuidado en conservar su imagen neoclásica, en el Centro Botín no fue necesario, pues se construyó en un espacio vacío. Inaugurado en junio de 2017, con diseño de Renzo Piano, este rompedor edificio de dos volúmenes se sitúa en el borde del muelle de Albareda. Unidos por terrazas, escaleras y pasarelas que se adentran en la bahía, tiene piel de cristal, acero y 270.000 piezas cerámicas que otorgan al edificio un aspecto inconfundible, causa de que los santanderinos le llamen “el Radiador”.

Se reparten su espacio exposiciones temporales —hasta el 25 de octubre puede verse la de la poco conocida Marisol, enigmática artista encuadrada en el pop— y una selección de piezas de la colección del Banco de Santander.

Una de las obras expuertas en 'MARISOL: Cuando todo está por comenzar', muestra que se puede ver en el Centro Botín. CENTRO BOTÍN

Es buena idea darse un paseo por el muelle de Calderón, que conserva muestras del patrimonio de la ciudad, como el Palacete del Embarcadero y la Caseta de Bombas. No puede pasarse por alto el homenaje a los raqueros: cuatro entrañables figuras de bronce del escultor José Cobo que recuerdan a los niños de la clase humilde santanderina, que esperaban en la orilla de la bahía a que los paseantes arrojaran una moneda al agua para zambullirse y sacarla a la superficie entre los dientes.

El Palacete del Embarcadero, en Santander. NATALIA PEREVERZIEVA (GETTY IMAGES)

Más allá, a los pies del Palacio de Festivales, se alzan las Naves de Gamazo. Antiguos talleres navales, datan de 1908. Quedaron en desuso a finales del siglo XX, hasta que Puertos del Estado las cedió a la Fundación ENAIRE, del Ministerio de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible. Tras una profunda transformación, abrieron en 2021 como primera sede permanente de la fundación fuera de Madrid. Hasta el 17 de enero acoge Persona, que reúne más de 80 retratos realizados por Estela de Castro a animales rescatados de centros de recuperación y entidades protectoras.

El Palacio de Festivales de Cantabria, en Santander. Andrzej Rostek (GETTY IMAGES)

Centro Niemeyer, en Avilés

Sorprende que una pequeña ciudad como Avilés tenga algo tan mayúsculo. Todo se inició en 1989, cuando el premio Príncipe de Asturias de las Artes recayó en el arquitecto brasileño Oscar Niemeyer. En agradecimiento, este regaló al Principado el proyecto de un centro cultural, con la única condición de que se construyese cerca del mar. Se escogió Avilés para recuperar su degradada zona industrial. El centro abrió en la primavera de 2011, despojando a la urbe de la triste grisura que la cubrió décadas para vestirlo con la optimista blancura de Niemeyer. Recorrer su amplia plaza es entender las palabras del brasileño, que señaló su obra como “una plaza abierta a todo el mundo, un lugar para la educación, la cultura y la paz”.

El exterior del Centro Niemeyer, en Avilés (Asturias). Carranza

La singular forma del auditorio le han hecho ganarse el sobrenombre con el que algunos lo conocen y que evita su descripción: “el huevo duro”. La Cúpula es una semiesfera en cuyo interior destaca una voluptuosa escalera. El arquitecto aseguró que la diseñó inspirándose en las curvas de la mujer carioca. El edificio polivalente alberga cafetería, sala de cine y oficinas. Sobre el resto de construcciones destaca la torre. En sus alturas aguarda el deleite de la gastronomía convertida en un bien cultural, que ofrece el exclusivo restaurante Yume.

Fundación MOP (A Coruña)

Antes de 2022, A Coruña daba la espalda al muelle de Batería. Cerradas a cal y canto, las verjas impedían ver poco más que el tránsito de los grandes cruceros internacionales que atracan a diario en el puerto de la capital gallega. Desde entonces, el Centro MOP ha barrido el polvo de la vieja cementera aquí situada, transformando el lugar en destino de cabotaje obligado del circuito de las grandes exposiciones internacionales.

La Fundación MOP, ubicada en el muelle de Batería de A Coruña. THE MOP FOUNDATION

Ha sido posible por el empeño de Marta Ortega, presidenta de Inditex, en impulsar la difusión del octavo arte y su relación con la moda. La nómina de artistas que ha desfilado por el estandarte de The MOP Foundation confirma su calado: Peter Lindbergh, Steven Meisel, Helmut Newton, Irving Penn, David Bailey, Annie Leibovitz, Paolo Roversi y, a partir del 21 de noviembre, David Sims.

No solo son estos artistas la razón de que el MOP se haya convertido en referencia mundial. También lo es el exquisito proyecto de recuperación de la arquitecta coruñesa Elsa Urquijo, que ha logrado fusionar la espesa esencia industrial que reinó en el pasado con un minimalismo contemporáneo. Sin cambiar el exterior, donde se ha creado una irresistible terraza, el silo mantiene sus ásperas formas. En su interior, las mesas de la cafetería comparten espacio con la vieja maquinaria y en los racks de almacenamiento reposan libros de fotografía. Sentarse aquí a tomar un café con un libro entre las manos frente al Atlántico es buena manera de entretener una tarde.

Interior de The MOP Library. YAGO CASTROMIL (THE MOP FOUNDATION)

Al lado se abre una de las salas más formidables de la instalación: la librería. Adaptada al volumen circular del interior del silo, sus anaqueles colman las paredes hasta el techo. Una rampa asciende hasta los libros situados en lo más alto. Especializada en fotografía, permite una consulta gratuita de sus más de 5.500 libros, revistas, catálogos y otras publicaciones, sin descuidar una esmerada sección infantil. La vecina nave acoge las exposiciones, todas gratuitas. Sus montajes son auténtico espectáculo. Instalaciones inmersivas, proyecciones, rincones que reproducen el universo donde trabajan los artistas… muchos repiten la visita solo para disfrutar otra vez las puestas en escena. Da pena que la estricta programación del centro impida prolongarlas.

World.title: Las cajas de ahorro islámicas están de moda en Turquía
World.content:
Sus sucursales se han multiplicado en los últimos años, especialmente en las capitales de provincia del interior de Turquía, donde ocupan los puestos de honor de las principales avenidas. Sus lustrosos y modernos escaparates prometen hacer realidad los sueños de sus clientes: adquirir una casa, un automóvil o una tienda “sin necesidad de créditos” o “sin pagar intereses”. Son las Empresas de Financiación mediante Ahorro (TFS, en turco), una suerte de cajas de ahorro islámicas basadas en los principios de las finanzas islámicas, como el rechazo a los intereses —aunque esto, como mucho en las finanzas islámicas, tiene truco— y la mutualización del riesgo: un grupo de ahorradores aporta cuotas mensuales a un fondo común y, por turnos o por sorteo, cada miembro recibe el capital solicitado para adquirir la propiedad elegida.

Algunas, como Eminevim o Fuzul, se han convertido en grandes grupos empresariales. Comenzaron su existencia como sociedades de ahorro colectivo creadas durante los años noventa por empresarios del entorno del islamismo político deseosos de financiarse fuera de unos bancos controlados por la —entonces dominante— élite laica del país. Otras quebraron o fueron liquidadas, pues operaban en un vacío legal. Su historia cambió en 2021, cuando el Gobierno del conservador Recep Tayyip Erdogan endureció los requisitos de solvencia, profesionalizándolas y poniéndolas bajo el control de la Agencia de Regulación y Supervisión Bancaria. Pero sobre todo, su verdadera explosión se ha dado desde que, en 2023, Mehmet Simsek fue nombrado ministro de Finanzas con el mandato de reducir una tasa de inflación que había llegado a superar el 100% interanual. Aplicó el manual más ortodoxo e instó al Banco Central a elevar el precio del dinero, lo que ha supuesto que los bancos restrinjan los créditos y eleven los intereses de sus préstamos hipotecarios por encima del 40% anual (la inflación sigue sin bajar del 30%). “Debido a las medidas de macroprudencia financiera, se ha hecho muy difícil acceder a créditos bancarios. Aunque, al inicio, las TFS se dirigían a personas de bajos ingresos, ahora les interesan a trabajadores de cuello blanco e incluso a gente de ingresos altos que no puede acceder a créditos bancarios”, explica Ahmet Büyükduman, analista financiero.

Una comisión fija por adelantado

Frente a los elevados intereses que demandan los bancos —y que implican que se termine pagando casi cuatro veces el capital inicial en préstamos a diez años—, las TFS cobran una comisión fija por adelantado, equivalente a entre el 7% y el 10% del capital solicitado. La pega es que solo se puede acceder a la casa, el automóvil o el negocio que se va a adquirir cuando se ha aportado al fondo el 45% de su valor, lo cual puede ocurrir pronto —si se adelanta parte del capital o se eligen cuotas de pago mensuales elevadas— o tardar varios años. La TFS, luego, hipoteca el bien hasta que el cliente ha terminado de pagar los plazos, pero entretanto puede hacer uso de él. Otro de los problemas es la protección de los ahorros contra la inflación galopante, ya que la cantidad solicitada por un cliente al inicio del programa puede haberse convertido en insignificante cuando llega a ejecutarla. Así que las TFS han tenido que establecer programas de inversión de estos ahorros en oro, bonos del Estado acordes con las finanzas islámicas (sukuk) o fondos.

De los apenas 370.000 usuarios que las TFS tenían hace tres años en Turquía se ha pasado a más de 1,5 millones en la actualidad, y su tamaño en activos se ha multiplicado por diez hasta superar los 9.000 millones de euros. Aun así, apenas suponen una fracción de la banca tradicional, y es que muchos turcos mantienen cierta suspicacia: por el carácter islámico de este sistema y porque algunos lo acusan de ser un esquema piramidal, debido a la necesidad de que lleguen nuevos ahorradores para mantenerse. Pero Büyükduman atribuye estas críticas a falta de información: “También los bancos pueden quebrar si los depositantes se retiran”. Para este experto, lo más importante es que estas entidades “promueven el ahorro antes de ofrecer un préstamo” y permiten a personas que trabajan en sectores informales acceder a financiación.

World.title: Fire that damaged cables under railway bridge is suspected arson
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Police are investigating a fire under a railway bridge in Rotterdam that led to trains being cancelled over the weekend as a suspected act of sabotage.

The door to a technical area in Rotterdam-Delfshaven was forced open and a fire was started that damaged around 35 cables, 15 of which were destroyed, network operator ProRail said.

All trains between Rotterdam Centraal and Delft Campus were suspended until 9.15pm on Sunday as engineers worked to repair the damage.

The stretch of line is one of the busiest in the Netherlands, carrying long-distance trains from Amsterdam to Zeeland and Limburg via Holland Spoor station.

Junior infrastructure minister Annet Bertram said she was shocked by the incident. “I find it appalling and worrying that this appears to be arson and a deliberate act,” she told NOS.

In a separate incident, trains to Schiphol airport were disrupted for several hours by problems with an overhead power line, but ProRail has ruled out arson as a cause.

More than 20 sprinter trains between Amsterdam and Hoofddorp were cancelled between 1.30pm and 9pm as engineers worked to repair the fault at Riekerpolder. “It is an intersection, which means trains are not running in a large area,” a spokesman said on Sunday.

International services were also affected, with trains to Brussels starting and ending in Rotterdam.

World.title: Utrecht weighs tougher measures on landlords after lack of fines
World.content:
Utrecht fined only 1 landlord last year despite receiving almost 200 complaints for breaking rules designed to protect tenants. The city is now considering a tougher approach modelled on Rotterdam, which issued 25 penalties in the second half of the year alone.

The figures were reported by regional broadcaster RTV Utrecht. Rotterdam received 667 complaints in 2025, and its fines ranged from €1,000 to tens of thousands per offence.

The threat of a fine is often enough to resolve a dispute since many renters are too scared to even report illegal or abusive practice for fear of losing their homes amid the housing crisis, but the city showed that when tenants did make reports, rents fell an average of €350 for private tenants.

Under the “good landlord law”, which came into force in 2023, landlords cannot discriminate against or intimidate tenants. Deposits are capped at 2 months’ basic rent, and service charges may only cover actual costs.

Unlike Rotterdam, Utrecht gives landlords a warning before handing down a penalty. It says it wants to avoid having fines overturned in court for being too heavy.

Research published by the Federation of Private-Sector Tenants (FHCS) in December last year found that Utrecht lacked the resources to look for abuses itself and relied entirely on complaints from tenants. Only around half of those complaints were taken further, usually because of a lack of evidence.

Fines are also rare in other big cities. In The Hague, around 600 complaints in two and a half years led to dozens of penalty orders but only 3 fines, which are being contested, according to the FHCS.

Amsterdam’s public list of sanctions showed only 1 fine, for intimidating tenants, which could still be challenged. Last October, the city warned a landlord who would only rent to working Dutch women that he faced a fine of up to €10,000.

Utrecht has not yet decided whether to follow Rotterdam’s lead, but believes fines could deter landlords and prevent repeat offences. It aims to introduce a rental permit in 2028, so that rents can be checked before a home is let.

The city also plans to do more to inform tenants about their rights and its complaints hotline. Every council is required by law to run a hotline for complaints about landlords.

World.title: Feyenoord top Eredivisie as AZ left seething over denied penalty
World.content:
Feyenoord climbed to the top of the Eredivisie after a 2-0 win over AZ Alkmaar took them above their opponents for the first time this season.

Nacho Ferri continued his strong start to the season by putting the Rotterdammers ahead in the 13th minute as he capitalised on a poor defensive header by Wouter Goes.

Fellow Spaniard Javi López scored the second from a corner in the second half to make sure of the points.

Coach Giovanni van Bronkhorst played down the significance of the result, telling NOS: “We have a long way to go and need to keep both feet on the ground.”

AZ were aggrieved that they were denied a penalty just before half-time when Mexx Meerdink appeared to have been brought down by Tjark Ernst.

Meerdink called the decision by referee Danny Makkelie “disgraceful”, but coach Leeroy Echteld refused to linger on the incident. “I’m not interested in being dragged into that kind of story,” he said.

PSV blank

PSV kept their first clean sheet of the season to beat Heerenveen 2-0 in the Friday night game, but the result owed much to the visitors’ wastefulness in front of goal.

Guus Til, playing as a stand-in striker, headed in the first after half an hour after good work by Esmir Bajraktarevic on the right wing, while the second was an own goal by Marcus Linday.

Twente and Fortuna Sittard, two teams enjoying strong starts to the season, shared the points in Enschede. Anthony Descotte headed in an inswinging cross by Mo Ihattaren to give Fortuna the lead in the ninth minute, before Robin Pröpper tapped in the equaliser before half-time.

Ajax stay fifth after they had to settle for a point against NEC Nijmegen. Tjaronn Chery equalised for NEC from the penalty spot after Tolu Arokodare had given the hosts an early lead.

Groningen hit five

Groningen put on a dominant second-half display to win 5-1 at Excelsior, but the turning point came at the end of the first period when Excelsior goalkeeper Stijn van Gessel fumbled a cross by Tika de Jonge into his own net.

Go Ahead Eagles and Sparta shared six goals in Deventer, but only after Sparta’s Andrej Kostic squandered a golden chance for a last-minute winner when he blasted the ball over the crossbar.

Utrecht managed their second win under coach Anthony Correia thanks to two outstanding goals by Yoanne Cathline against Willem II, while a late Nicholas Bindner goal earned Cambuur their first away win of the season at PEC Zwolle.

Telstar played most of their match against ADO Den Haag with an extra man following the dismissal of Milan Hokke in the 13th minute, but still only managed a draw as Tyrone Owusu scored twice.

World.title: Albert Heijn app and deliveries down after “IT incident”
World.content:
Albert Heijn has been hit by an “IT incident” according to a company statement released on Monday morning, which notes that cosmetics chain Etos and alcohol shop Gall and Gall are also affected. All three chains are owned by Ahold Delhaize.

Albert Heijn has switched off part of its IT systems, leaving its website, app and home delivery service unavailable.

“We immediately took measures to protect our IT environment,” the company said in a statement on Monday. “Part of that is temporarily switching off a number of systems as a precaution.” Customer services and logistics systems are offline, and online order cannot be delivered until further notice.

AH has not said what caused the incident or when services will return. It said only that protecting the data of customers, staff and partners is its priority.

Shops are open and tills are working, but personal discounts and app-linked savings schemes are paused. Electronic shelf labels may also show last week’s offer prices, the chain said, so the prices at the till can be higher than shown on shelves.

World.title: Inburgering with DN: 10 Dutch words every foreigner in NL uses
World.content:
There are some Dutch words which all foreigners in the Netherlands seem to adopt as soon as they get off the plane, train or ferry. So here’s a list of some of them.

Lesson 63: First words

Lekker: means tasty and is the first Dutch word everyone learns. Lekker describes just about everything which is positive: from a lekker broodje with lekker weer and lekkere sex.

Borrel: For some reason, we don’t go for drinks; we always have a borrel. And if you work in an office you may well have a vrijmibo (vrijdagmiddagborrel) on Friday afternoon.

Btw: Always pronounced bay-tay-vay in the Dutch way and meaning sales tax, not “by the way”.

Belasting: Closely associated with btw is, of course, tax in general. Given that we pay so much of it in NL, it is hardly surprising everyone gets to know the word very quickly.

Gemeente: Perhaps it is because internationals have so much to do with the good folks at the town hall, but everyone talks about the gemeente, never the council or city hall.

Apotheek: Another word that just sneaks in, even though there are plenty of respectable foreign-language equivalents for pharmacy.

Makelaar: Those other good folk who find houses for extortionate fees.

Bel: When you have been in the Netherlands a few weeks, everyone seems to stop phoning. We bel, as in “I’ll bel you tonight”. NB: when the Dutch say “we bellen” it means they will ring you sometime, or never.

Horeca: As in working in the horeca. A terrifically handy term derived from hotel, restaurant, cafe – and one which the rest of the world could easily adopt.

Agenda: Almost instantly, the English diary becomes an agenda – there is no escaping it. You will make appointments in your agenda and you will consult your agenda to see if you can have a meeting in three weeks’ time at 2.30pm.

Wintersport: Once you are settled in the Netherlands you will stop going on skiing holidays. You will go on wintersport instead – even if you spend more time on the après-ski than on the slopes.

Storing: If your train does not arrive, your tram is late, the internet is down and you can’t pay for your groceries with your phone, this is probably due to a storing. If you are a frequent rail user, you will probably get to know it very well.

Gezellig: Cosy, fun, warm, inviting… one of those words which are so crucial to understanding the Dutch that we wrote an entire lesson around it.

World.title: Trump administration sanctions International Criminal Court
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The United States has announced sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), escalating Trump’s war on the international tribunal.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” US secretary of state Marco Rubio said in an announcement.

The Trump administration has previously pledged to dismantle the court “brick by brick” and has sanctioned 13 current and former staff members, but this is the first time it has levied sanctions against the institution itself.

Ahead of the announcement, prime minister Rob Jetten said the Netherlands will protect the ICC “stone by stone”.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said the country would stand behind the court. “The announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court are an undesirable new escalation,” Berendsen said in a statement. “I deeply regret this new step.”

The sanctions will cut the court off from any US company or organisation, including providers of financial and technology services.

The announcement came hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the ICC and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

Trump has long coveted the prize, telling reporters earlier this week that he deserved the award for what he said was ending eight wars.

World.title: Russia wants NL to hand over ICC judges
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Russia has asked the Netherlands to hand over nine International Criminal Court (ICC) officials who were convicted in absentia last year.

The prosecutor’s office in Moscow requested the extradition of the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and other staff members for their involvement in the arrest warrant of Russian president Vladimir Putin.

The ICC issued the warrant for Putin’s alleged involvement in “the war crime of unlawful deportation of children” from occupied Ukraine.

The ICC has also issued an arrest warrant against Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights.

In December, a court in Moscow convicted Akane and others in absentia, sentencing them to prison terms ranging from 3.5 to 15 years.

Japan, Akane’s home country, said the request was regrettable. “Measures targeting individuals connected to the ICC are unjust and unacceptable,” Masanao Ozaki, the country’s deputy chief cabinet secretary, said.

The United States has also sanctioned 13 staff members, including Akane, over the investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

World.title: Unions call regional transport strike, threaten weekly walkout
World.content:
Regional bus services across the Netherlands will be heavily disrupted on Wednesday, after the FNV and CNV unions called a nationwide 24-hour strike in a dispute over a new pay and conditions deal.

If Wednesday’s strike does not shift the employers, the unions say they will hold an action day every week, and will only announce the dates shortly beforehand. Earlier this month they said they were considering weekly strikes in the run-up to Christmas.

Some 13,000 workers, mainly bus drivers, are covered by the public transport collective agreement, which expired on July 1. Staff at Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Keolis, Transdev and RET’s regional services are involved. City transport in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague is not affected.

Talks broke down after eight rounds of negotiations. This week an ultimatum to the employers’ organisation VWOV expired without a response.

“Employers are holding on to drastic cuts in working conditions,” FNV negotiator Marijn van der Gaag said in a statement. “In doing so, they are forcing their staff to take action.”

The unions say employers want to reduce sick pay, add more unpaid breaks to shifts and give staff less say over their rosters. Rosters are currently fixed about eight days in advance, and employers want to cut that to four days or less, Van der Gaag said.

The FNV wants a 6% pay rise. The CNV is calling for 9.5% over two years, as well as better arrangements for older workers and faster access to permanent contracts.

“We will not let employers sabotage the action by drawing up emergency rosters at the last minute,” CNV negotiator Niels Rook said, explaining why dates will not be announced in advance.

World.title: Independent beats PM Tusk’s candidate in Kraków mayoral election
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Łukasz Gibała, an independent, has won the mayoral election in Kraków, Poland’s second-biggest city, beating Monika Piątkowska, the candidate backed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. With all votes counted by just after 1 a.m. on Monday morning, Gibała had 62.1% against 37.9% for Piątkowska, who had already conceded defeat shortly after 9 p.m. on Sunday night, when exit polls showed a large margin of victory for her opponent. “Today in Poland, more and more people realise that we don’t have to live in the reality that politicians in Warsaw project upon us,” declared Gibała as it became clear he had won. “More and more people realise that we, in our own towns and cities, know better what’s good for us than they do in Warsaw.” The victory marks a blow for Tusk – whose Civic Coalition (KO) party has its strongest support in large cities – just a year before he seeks to win another term at parliamentary elections. The prime minister had visited Kraków to campaign alongside Piątkowska. Dziś 11 października 2026 roku, po 24 latach, mieszkańcy odzyskali swoje miasto. Chciałbym podziękować wszystkim Krakowianom, którzy mi zaufali i zdecydowali się oddać ma mnie głos. To nasze wspólne zwycięstwo. Dziękuję mojej partnerce Adzie, sztabowi i współpracownikom ze… pic.twitter.com/0FsNYwjPkj — Łukasz Gibała (@LukaszGibala) October 11, 2026 For Gibała, a wealthy businessman who has largely funded his own political career, this was victory at the fourth attempt, having stood in every mayoral contest since 2014, obtaining a growing share of the vote each time. He stood as an independent, promising to sort out the city’s finances, end cronyism in the appointment of municipal officials, improve public transport and reverse ticket-price increases, and hold a referendum on Kraków’s controversial clean transport zone for vehicles. He also pledged to favour residents over developers in planning decisions and to counteract the negative effects of tourism in what is Poland’s most-visited city, including by restricting short-term-rental properties. Gibała’s victory had been expected after he came top in the first round two weeks ago with 36.4% of the vote among the seven candidates who stood. Piątkowska trailed on 29.9%. The top two candidates then met in today’s run-off. Piątkowska was the joint candidate of Tusk’s centrist KO party and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), which are both part of the national government. She has, since last year, been a member of the Senate in Warsaw. Previously, she worked in Kraków city hall during the mayoralty of Jacek Majchrowski, who held office from 2002 to 2024. Piątkowska received the personal backing of Tusk, who announced her candidacy in June alongside PSL leader and deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (though critics noted that they held the event in Warsaw rather than Kraków). Tusk also visited Kraków before the first round to support his candidate. Among her campaign promises were to seek to locate an AI “gigafactory” in Kraków, to boost the availability of housing for young people, and to implement a package of policies for women, including free mammograms, pram-friendly infrastructure, free menstrual hygiene products, and safer nighttime public transport. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb. Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026 Kraków’s election was held in unusual circumstances after the previous mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, also from KO, was removed from his position in May, just two years into his term. He had faced accusations of cronyism and poor financial management, as well as criticism over the introduction of the clean transport zone. A petition to hold a recall referendum received more than the 58,355 signatures required. In the subsequent referendum, 97.3% supported removing the mayor (Miszalski had appealed to his supporters not to vote in an unsuccessful effort to keep turnout below the 27% needed for the result to be binding). Before today’s election, both Miszalski and Majchowski had called on Cracovians to vote for Piątkowska. After his victory had become clear, Gibała declared that “11 October 2026 will be remembered as the day when, after 24 years, the inhabitants of Krakow regained their city”. The vote had been particularly closely watched as it came just a year before the parliamentary elections. Gibała’s victory has been celebrated by figures from the right-wing opposition, though the new mayor is not politically aligned with them (and indeed previously served as an MP in Tusk’s party). World.title: Polish security services report alleged assassination plot against PM Tusk
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. At the time of writing, no details have been released regarding where and how the alleged attacks were expected to take place, who might be behind them, or what the source of the information was. W związku z informacją, która wpłynęła do @PolskaPolicja i dotyczy możliwego zamachu na premiera @donaldtusk oraz wicepremiera, ministra obrony narodowej @KosiniakKamysz, minister koordynator służb specjalnych @TomaszSiemoniak oraz minister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji… — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 11, 2026 On Sunday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for the security services, first announced that the police had received “information…regarding a possible assassination attempt” on Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz, who, as well as serving as defence minister, is also a deputy prime minister. Dobrzyński revealed that the Internal Security Agency (ABW), police and State Protection Service (SOP), which provides security for high-ranking officials, would meet to discuss the potential threat. Speaking after that meeting, interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka confirmed that the threat had first been identified by SOP, which passed the information on to the police. “We are taking this matter extremely seriously,” added Dobrzyński, speaking alongside her. He criticised “pseudo-experts” in the media who had expressed doubt about the announcement of a possible assassination attempt. “We’re talking about threats directed at the most important people in the country,” he added. “This information is so serious and credible that we’ve decided to share it with you now…We are talking about a high probability that these threats will be carried out.” Dobrzyński did not divulge any details about the nature of the attack or where the warnings had come from, but said that he would be able to provide further information once the police and security services had carried out further investigation. "Sprawę traktujemy śmiertelnie poważnie. Mówimy o dużym prawdopodobieństwie spełnienia tych gróźb" Rzecznik prasowy ministra koordynatora służb specjalnych o możliwym zamachu na premiera i szefa MON. pic.twitter.com/2xoWrZJT2w — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 11, 2026 Government spokesman Adam Szłapka, speaking to broadcaster TVN, acknowledged that the authorities constantly receive a “cascade of indications” regarding potential threats. However, “this signal was more disturbing than previous” ones, he added. Szłapka also indicated that one element of the warning had come via email, but added that “it was not just an email” that had raised concern. Like Dobrzyński, he said that further information would be released in due course. Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reports that an unnamed “official close to the prime minister” had said that the threat came from “right-wing extremists” and that the perpetrators were Poles. Another source within the intelligence services told the newspaper that the threat was treated more seriously than others because it contained information about addresses linked to Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz. Poland has charged a 17-year-old with planning neo-Nazi terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school. Two other Polish teenagers who were part of the same online community promoting neo-Nazism and violence have also been detained https://t.co/86AnIHWFe8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 22, 2026 Last month, police detained a 56-year-old man in the city of Przemyśl after he posted a video on social media threatening Tusk. Earlier in September, a 52-year-old man in the town of Oława was likewise arrested for making criminal threats against the prime minister online. Also in September, the security services detained three teenagers who were accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them was additionally charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school. This week has also seen Poland facing an unprecedented security challenge after three knife attacks took place on schools, leaving one person dead and many injured. In response, the police have since Friday carried out checks at over 64,000 locations, including many schools, and detained over 100 people, most of them teenagers found to have made threats or been in possession of weapons. World.title: Polish prosecutors seek to drop case against South Asian men who slaughtered goat in kebab bar
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar. They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time. 🔴Ubili kozę na zapleczu. Wkrótce decyzja sądu, zastanawia ruch prokuratury Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026 The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar. After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time. The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”. However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.” Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska. The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Not all cases involving illegal animal slaughter have been treated as causing low social harm. Last month, a court in the town of Limanowa convicted three men for carrying out illegal halal ritual slaughter and selling unapproved meat. The main suspect, a Polish man, was found guilty of overseeing the operation, while two Azerbaijani nationals were convicted of helping distribute the illegal meat. The verdicts can still be appealed. Although it has relatively small Muslim and Jewish populations, Poland is one of Europe’s biggest producers and exporters of kosher and halal meat. Almost a third of Poland's meat exports are halal and kosher, making it one of Europe's leading producers. Having fought off attempts by the ruling party to ban ritual slaughter, the industry is now hoping to expand further to cater to a growing market https://t.co/duOJTfHoLT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2022 However, the country has itself been experiencing growing levels of migration in recent years. Most of the new arrivals are from neighbouring Ukraine and Belarus, but there are also growing numbers from outside Europe, too. Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients. Poland’s current government has blamed some immigrant groups for a rise in crime and has stepped up deportations of those found to have broken the law. However, data show that, overall, immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than Poles themselves. World.title: Polish police detain more teens following school knife attacks amid fears of further incidents
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Following this week’s two knife attacks on schools in Poland, police have today carried out security checks on over 10,000 schools and detained at least 10 more people, many of them teenagers found to have made online threats or been in possession of weapons. Meanwhile, many parents decided not to send their children to school today, as rumours swirled online that this week’s attacks were somehow coordinated and that further incidents were planned on Friday. The issue has also sparked a political dispute, with the government criticising opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for previously vetoing laws intended to improve children’s safety. The opposition in turn accuses the government of failing to protect schools properly. 🚨 Ponad 10 tysięcy skontrolowanych placówek i 10 osób zatrzymanych w całym kraju. Bezpieczeństwo w szkołach priorytetem Policji ⬇️ Tragiczne zdarzenia, do których doszło w ciągu ostatnich dni na Mazowszu, wywołały w przestrzeni medialnej falę nieprawdziwych informacji,… pic.twitter.com/WVkYUdVO9C — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) October 9, 2026 On Thursday, a 39-year-old school caretaker was killed in an attack by a 15-year-old former pupil on a primary school. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that the assailant had been wearing a head-mounted camera intended to broadcast the attack. That came a day after a 19-year-old student carried out a knife attack on another school, leaving eight people injured. Two other teens were also detained on suspicion of planning attacks in other locations. In response, Tusk announced on Thursday that police would carry out regular checks on schools. However, on Friday, many parents in the Masovia province around Warsaw, where both of this week’s attacks took place, decided to keep their children at home. Some districts closed schools entirely. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school by a 15-year-old former pupil. Yesterday, a knife attack by a 19-year-old at another school left eight people injured. The assailant also had a homemade explosive that failed to detonate https://t.co/xJAzhT6u3U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 Concern was stoked by claims circulating on social media that this week’s school attacks were part of a coordinated action by a group of teenagers, who were planning further incidents on what they were calling “Bloody Friday”. Two schools in the town of Legionowo, just north of Warsaw, were closed on Friday after local authorities said they received “unconfirmed information that they were on a list” relating to the alleged group. Poland’s national police headquarters issued a statement on Friday morning saying that they were aware of the rumours but that “so far nothing indicates such an event is actually happening”. They urged people to remain calm, not share unverified information, and rely only on credible sources. At the same time, police and local authorities stepped up security in schools. At 9 a.m. on Friday, the national police headquarters announced that checks had been conducted at over 10,000 schools around the country and that ten people had been detained. Among those to be arrested was a 17-year-old in the town of Ełk, who had reportedly made online threats to attack other students, and a 13-year-old in Sochaczew who wrote in a chat that he would bring a machete to school. The boy later said it was a “silly joke”. In Bartoszyce, a school principal saw that an 11-year-old student had posted a photo of a knife alongside a statement indicating a threat. Police detained the boy and found an “imitation knife” in his backpack. In Ostrów Mazowiecka, police announced they had arrested a 15-year-old boy who had sent out images of himself in a Guy Fawkes-style mask, saying that he planned to take people’s lives. In Warsaw, police detained a 14-year-old who was found to be in possession of a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers. 🚨 Policjanci z Mokotowa niezwłocznie po otrzymaniu informacji o zagrożeniu bezpieczeństwa zatrzymali na terenie szkoły 14-latka, który posiadał nóż z ukrytym ostrzem. Nastolatek miał przy sobie także 11 petard hukowych. W sprawie prowadzone są dalsze czynności. Dokumenty… pic.twitter.com/lbQrqe2pgl — Policja Warszawa (@Policja_KSP) October 9, 2026 The situation has also taken on a political dimension. On Thursday, Tusk criticised Nawrocki for earlier this year vetoing a government bill intended to improve online safety by blocking harmful content. The president had argued that the measures were an “Orwellian” threat to free speech. In a hastily called vote in the lower-house Sejm on Thursday evening, Tusk’s ruling coalition passed a new version of the bill that will now be sent to the upper-house Senate. Once it receives final parliamentary approval, the legislation will return to Nawrocki for his signature or veto. Meanwhile, education minister Barbara Nowacka also noted that Nawrocki had vetoed a bill introducing new rights and responsibilities for school pupils, including greater powers to confiscate dangerous items. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Mieliśmy jedną z najmocniejszych propozycji zmiany prawa w Europie, która miała chronić w internecie przede wszystkim dzieci i młodzież. pic.twitter.com/dyxY6prGzB — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 8, 2026 In response, presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz criticised those who were “exploiting this issue for political purposes”, saying that “a political argument is the last thing we need right now”. Meanwhile, Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of focusing on “political warfare” instead of ensuring security in schools. “There is no coordination or top-down directives on what to do, where it is safe, and where there is risk or threat,” he wrote on social media, calling the situation “chaos”. World.title: Polish parliament approves ban on nighttime alcohol sales in shops
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours. The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved. #PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6 — tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026 The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package. The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently. Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales. In the first six months following the implementation of its restrictions in 2023, Kraków saw a nearly 50% decrease in nighttime police interventions, with other cities reporting similar improvements. The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400). Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage. The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 zloty for stronger drinks. Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops. The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026 In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show. The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005. They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 1, 2026 In June, an IBRiS poll for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 55% of Poles support some form of ban on nighttime alcohol sales while 43% are opposed. A survey by IBP for Super Express published today showed even stronger support, with 67% in favour of a ban and only 26% opposed. Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. World.title: Polish man suspected of helping Russian plot to assassinate Zelensky sentenced to 5.5 years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding. The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024. Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers. Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine. “These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year. Poland and Ukraine have revealed further details of a foiled plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa at Poland's Rzeszów airport. A Polish man was last month indicted in relation to the incident, which he is accused of seeking to carry out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/Lrp99vH4s2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2025 Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim. However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities. Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet. In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison. However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP. “Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz. Poland has charged three of its own citizens with working on behalf of Russian intelligence. They are accused of spreading disinformation, conducting reconnaissance of NATO troops, and undergoing firearms training in preparation for acts of sabotage https://t.co/maYd0kb9HW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 20, 2026 Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia. In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers. The AWB last year launched 48 investigations related to espionage, more than twice as many as in 2024. Over those two years, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 In January, Polish prosecutors indicted five people – four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian – accused of carrying out a plot on behalf of Russia to plant explosives in packages that were then dispatched by courier services across Europe. In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops. In July this year, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb. A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it. The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack. “We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters. “So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.” Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000. Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP. However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.
