World.title: Young Croatian Men Ending Up in Court Over Military Service Obligations
World.content:
October the 12th, 2026 – Young Croatian men are ending up being taken to court over no responding to calls for medical examinations for military service.

Multiple young Croatian men, including secondary-school students, have faced court proceedings recently because they failed to respond to calls for an examination to determine fitness for military service. Index reports that while some were fined, others were acquitted because the summons had not been properly delivered.

fined for failing to appear

The Municipal Court in Čakovec last month issued a final fine of 250 euros to a secondary-school student from Međimurje. The young man, who is training to become a car painter, did not appear in mid-June for a medical examination and psychological testing at the Čakovec Health Centre. In court he admitted the misdemeanour. Since he had not previously been fined for a misdemeanour and is supported by his parents, the court imposed a penalty lower than the statutory minimum, which ranges from 500 to 5,000 euros.

Similar cases also occurred at the Municipal Misdemeanour Court in Zagreb, which handed down several non-final judgments. A 19-year-old was fined 120 euros plus 30 euros in court costs because he overslept the examination appointment. In a written defence he explained that the previous night he had returned from a trip with his mother and grandmother. He said he immediately contacted the competent office, but was told he could only come if he appeared within five minutes, which was impossible for him. The same court also fined a student born in 2007 with 120 euros plus 30 euros in costs. In his defence he admitted the misdemeanour and explained that he had remembered the wrong examination date and was therefore one day late.

not all cases ended in fines

Not all cases, however, ended with fines. Last month the Municipal Misdemeanour Court in Zagreb acquitted a young man of the charge that he had failed to appear for an examination at the beginning of May. In court the young man stated that he had never received or signed the summons. He explained that four families live in his house. The court checked the return receipt and established that the shipment had been placed in the letterbox without the recipient’s signature, so there was no proof that the summons had been properly served.

In mid-September the Municipal Court in Varaždin handed down a similar non-final judgment. A young man born in 2007 was acquitted after telling the court that he had not personally received the summons because he was working in Germany at the time. He stated that it was possible that a family member or neighbour had collected it and disputed that the signature on the delivery note was his mother’s, whom he described as illiterate. The court compared the signatures and concluded that it had not been proven that the young man had personally received the summons. At the beginning of September the Municipal Misdemeanour Court in Zagreb acquitted another young man. He had not appeared for the examination back in July and in his defence stated that he could not have received the summons because he was working seasonally in a shop on the island of Čiovo. In this case too, the court established that the signature on the delivery note differed from his. It was concluded that the summons had not been properly served and the young man was acquitted of the charge.

World.title: Rijeka Receives New Infrastructure to Strengthen its Gateway Position
World.content:
October the 12th, 2026 – Rijeka has received brand new infrastructure that should further strengthen its position as a gateway to the markets of eastern and southeastern Europe.

In 2025, the Croatian transport and logistics sector was deeply marked by major infrastructure projects, growth in road and maritime transport, and a strong investment cycle in transport infrastructure. Nevertheless, overall freight traffic did not grow: during the year 132 million tonnes of goods were transported in Croatia, 1.1 percent less than in 2024. Ana Roksandic reports for Poslovni that road transport remained dominant with 94.8 million tonnes, with growth of one percent, while the largest drop was recorded in rail transport, where the quantity of goods transported fell by 21.2 percent, according to the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS).

The most important event of last year was the start of commercial operations of the Rijeka Gateway container terminal in September. The terminal, worth around 380 million euros, in the first phase has a capacity of 650 thousand TEU per year, with planned expansion to more than one million TEU. With this, Rijeka has received infrastructure that should further strengthen its position as a gateway for the markets of Central and Southeast Europe. A key precondition for realising that potential is the development of railway infrastructure and quality connection of Rijeka with Central European markets.

“With the commercial start of operations in September, Rijeka Gateway operated for only four months in 2025, which is why it can primarily be viewed as a year of launching and stabilising operations, and not as a full business year. That year laid solid foundations for further growth and development of the business. The first phase of terminal construction exceeds a value of 200 million euros, and with the planned expansion the total value of the investment in Rijeka Gateway will exceed 380 million euros.

Together with the value of the transport infrastructure, from roads to the railway interface in and around the port, the total investment reaches 600 million euros. More than the business results, we are proud of the entire team that, through dedicated work, togetherness and readiness for cooperation, achieved what only a year ago seemed like a major challenge – the successful launch of the terminal and an excellent start of operational work,” said Peter Corfitsen, President of the Management Board of Rijeka Gateway.

World.title: Will Croatian Pantheon Project be Completed Within the Deadline?
World.content:
October the 11th, 2026 – The massive and controversial Croatian Pantheon project has been a hot topic for a multitude of reasons, but will it actually be completed within the prescribed deadline?

The controversial Croatian Pantheon project is a data centre with a capacity of one gigawatt which would enable the employment of several thousand people during construction and later on. Poslovni reports that the Pantheon project is proceeding according to the planned schedule and should be completed within the set deadline, entrepreneur Jako Andabak revealed on Friday. Together with American partners, he stands behind the realisation of the Pantheon data centre in Topusko, worth a staggering 50 billion euros.

A solid and high-quality network

Andabak made the statement as part of the third edition of the Master Business Forum (MBF), a platform that brings together leaders of the business community, experts and institutional representatives from the region and beyond, which was held in Rovinj and gathered more than 80 speakers from the public, private and academic sectors. It is a data centre with a capacity of one gigawatt that would enable the employment of several thousand people during construction and later. In addition to the technological components, the construction of a 500-megawatt solar power plant is planned. With the project whose start is planned for 2027 and the start of the centre’s operation in 2029, Croatia will rank at the very top of the European and world technology industry because the latest solutions open up the possibility of development in wider application, Andabak said.

“We decided on putting it in Topusko because there we have land where it’s possible to realise a project that will not harm nature and the environment. By building a solid and high-quality network we will create the conditions for stable and safe power supply without impact on the environment, which has also been confirmed by a study,” Andabak emphasised. He added that the centre will exploit its own wells and use its own water sources and its own solution for cooling the system.

The potential of empty land

“There are solutions that I carry from childhood which say that when everyone does their part of the work, then everything is done simply,” Andabak said. He added that he has dealt with many things, and only a year ago he began to think about data centres. He also explained how the whole idea came about, and it started with livestock farming and sheep. “Back during the nineties, Croatia was home to a million sheep, and now that number is in the thousands. When you see data like that, you ask yourself how to utilise that empty land and potential,” Andabak said and added that solar first came to mind. As he stated, the area is very interesting in all segments, from cooling to energy supply.

Locals in Topusko have been vehemently against the giant Pantheon data centre, however, and concerns remain for the environment and for water usage regardless of reassurance that no harm will be done.

World.title: Why Do Croatian Motorways Cost So Much When There are Constant Disruptions?
World.content:
October the 11th, 2026 – Croatian motorways cost a lot to use, but why is this the case when there are constant road works and extensive disruptions?

Drivers in Croatia pay the full price of tolls even on motorway sections where, due to road works, traffic is slowed, doesn’t flow, is full of bottlenecks, closed traffic lanes and speed restrictions. It’s very clear that such conditions can prolong the journey, but the price of the toll remains the same. Index’s text problematised the introduction of an expensive and complex toll collection system instead of simpler vignettes, such as those used by neighbouring Slovenia. It also warned about the very high costs of using Croatian motorways, opening the question precisely opened of why drivers need to pay the full fees even when, due to works, they cannot use the motorway under normal conditions.

Vedran Salvia reports that anyone who regularly uses Croatian motorways knows very well how frequent the works are, because of which queues form that prolong the journey itself. On individual sections, these burdensome works last for many months. For example, on the A3 motorway between Nova Gradiška and Lužani, works on doing up the carriageway have been ongoing since September, with completion scheduled for mid-November. On the A1 motorway between Gornja Ploča and Sveti Rok, the rehabilitation of two bridges began at the beginning of October and is due to last until the beginning of December. In both cases traffic on part of the motorway is two-way on one carriageway. Those are only some of the works currently being carried out on Croatian motorways.

hac remains silent

According to the applicable Toll Collection Act, the possibility of granting discounts exists, but the regulations do not provide for a reduction in price due to works or difficult driving conditions. Neither do HAC’s General Terms of Use of the motorway and toll collection provide for a special refund of money in cases when, due to works, traffic takes place on a narrowed carriageway or with speed restrictions. HAC was asked for additional clarification on whether there is a legal possibility of reducing the toll during works and under what conditions such a discount could be introduced.

In addition to asking HAC for a legal clarification of that possibility, they were also asked whether they have ever considered introducing temporary discounts. We also requested data on the scope of works and the total kilometrage of motorways affected by bottlenecks and the closing of traffic lanes during 2025 and 2026. By the time the text was closed we had not received an answer.

croatia charges enormous tolls

The question of charging the full toll during works gains particular importance when the high prices of using Croatian motorways are taken into account. Drivers for non-small amounts expect corresponding quality of service, which also opens the broader question of the relationship between the price and what they receive in return. The toll Zagreb – Split for a passenger car amounts to 26.40 euros in one direction, or 52.80 euros for a return trip. Even with the ENC discount of 21.74 percent, three return trips cost around 124 euros. As a counter-argument, it could be said that the toll is paid according to the kilometres travelled, and not according to the time spent on the motorway, so road works should not affect the price. But that does not mean that it is all the same under what conditions one drives. One takes the motorway precisely in order to travel faster and with fewer delays. In Croatia, however, works and bottlenecks are very frequent, so it isn’t remotely unreasonable that drivers expect normal driving conditions when paying such sums.

slovenia smartly extends the validity of vignettes during such works

That it is perfectly possible to compensate drivers for difficult driving conditions is also shown by the example of neighbouring Slovenia. The Slovenian parliament in November last year adopted a law by which, due to numerous works and reduced motorway throughput, it extended the validity of annual electronic vignettes by four months, without additional costs. The measure applied to all annual vignettes that were valid on the 1st of December 2025, and the extension was carried out automatically. The Slovenian Ministry of Infrastructure explained that the aim of the measure was a fairer relationship towards drivers who, due to works, suffered worse travel conditions on the roads.

additional road users could be attracted by lower fees

However, does that mean that they should not pay the full price of the toll? Marko Ševrović, associate professor and vice-dean of the Faculty of Transport and Traffic Sciences in Zagreb, told Index that he understands drivers’ dissatisfaction, but warns that the problem must also be viewed from the perspective of traffic planning. “I understand that users look from their perspective and ask themselves why they pay the full price when the driving conditions are worse. But imagine that on a section we already have a jam due to reduced capacity and then we also lower the price. What will we achieve by that?

I believe that a reduction of the toll during works would be unusual, but also counterproductive. A lower price could attract additional traffic precisely to the sections on which traffic capacities are already reduced due to works. The goal in such situations should be to reduce traffic on those sections, and not to further encourage it. If there is an alternative road, it would make more sense to reduce the price of its use and thus encourage drivers to avoid the section on which works are being carried out,” our interlocutor believes.

road works go on for much too long in croatia

He emphasises that the problem is that the works last too long in Croatia, and become a constant source of irritation to all road users as a result.

“That’s partly a consequence of the situation in the construction sector. Contractors do not have enough workers, the costs of labour and materials have risen significantly, so savings are made on the number of employees and work shifts. The works could be completed significantly faster, but that is the current situation. We have a public procurement system that in practice favours the lowest price. In doing so, it is not calculated how much society loses due to long-lasting works. Because of such an approach deadlines are often exceeded and the works drag on. That is not only a problem of HAC, but also of state roads and city thoroughfares, which we also see in Zagreb,” he says.

neighbouring italy also does things differently

That it’s possible to regulate toll collection during works differently is also shown by the example of neighbouring Italy, which, similarly to Croatia, charges tolls according to the distance travelled. There drivers on the network of the largest Italian concessionaire Autostrade per l’Italia and related companies can obtain a partial or full refund of money if works significantly impede or prolong their journey. Such a system has existed for several years, and from June this year new rules are applied that have expanded drivers’ rights, as also reported by the Italian news agency ANSA.

An interesting example also comes from Spain, where courts sided with drivers over the charging of the full toll during works on a motorway in Galicia. The Supreme Court in 2025 ruled that charging the full amount during major delays was an unfair practice, thereby opening the way for a refund of money to the affected drivers.

In a separate procedure, about which the local newspaper La Voz de Galicia wrote, the court recognised a group of 21 plaintiffs, mostly craftsmen and local carriers, the right to a refund of half of the paid toll amount due to significantly worse driving conditions. The same question that was raised was also opened back in 2023 in the French Senate, where it was problematised why drivers pay the full toll when works prolong the journey and reduce the quality of service. The French Government replied that the prices are determined by concession contracts and that their reduction would require legislative changes or changes to the contracts, with possible financial compensation to the concessionaires. It also warned that such costs could be compensated by a later increase in tolls.

World.title: Croatian Geophysicist Explains What Sort of Winter Awaits Croatia as El Niño Bites
World.content:
October the 11th, 2026 – A Croatian geophysicist has explained what sort of winter awaits Croatia this year as what is perhaps the strongest El Niño takes hold.

The well known climate phenomenon El Niño is rapidly strengthening and could become the strongest since measurements began. Index reports that according to the latest forecast by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the peak is expected to arrive in December, and it’s almost certain that El Niño will last until February next year. Croatia could, as a direct result, expect an above-average warm and rainy winter.

Academician Mirko Orlić from the Department of Geophysics of the Faculty of Science in Zagreb explained for Dnevnik Nova TV what the strengthening of this phenomenon could mean for Croatia and warned about the combination of an extremely warm Adriatic and atmospheric disturbances.

croatia can expect an above-average warm winter

“We have two sources of information. One is what happened during previous similar El Niños – and three such have been recorded since the middle of the last century – and each time it was above-average warm. Second, the models that provide seasonal forecasts show the same: it will be above-average warm. Therefore, that is realistic to expect,” Orlić said. El Niño occurs when the surface layer of the sea in the central and eastern part of the equatorial Pacific warms above usual values. This changes atmospheric circulation and weather patterns around the planet and in certain regions increases the risk of droughts, floods and extreme temperatures.

According to the WMO, the average deviation of the sea surface temperature in the key Pacific area during the period from October to December could reach 3.7 degrees above normal, which would surpass the previous record.

a warmer adriatic could increase precipitation

Orlić warned that the winter in Croatia could also be above-average when it comes to rainfall. A considerably warmer Adriatic Sea plays an important role in this.

“Both sources of information, previous cases and forecast models, say that it will be above-average wet, with above-average amounts of precipitation this winter. But there is also another reason – the exceptionally warm sea. This summer on the open Adriatic we recorded temperatures of 28 and 29 degrees, that is, significantly higher than the usual 27 degrees back in August,” he said. He explained that the sea has accumulated a large amount of heat, which can contribute to strong atmospheric instabilities when colder and moist air arrives over the area. “If moist and cold air arrives over such a surface, that is a real recipe for great instability and heavy precipitation,” Orlić warned.

Weather conditions in Croatia will not be influenced only by El Niño. Orlić also warned about processes in the Arctic, where warming is more pronounced than in the rest of the world. Due to the reduction of the temperature difference between the Arctic and the equator, patterns of atmospheric circulation can change, including the position and waviness of the jet stream, which plays an important role in shaping the weather over Europe. “Figuratively speaking, this winter above our heads we’ll have a battle – El Niño on one side and Arctic processes unfolding on the other. If El Niño prevails, the changes will probably be milder and will alternate more quickly. If the Arctic processes prevail, the disturbances will be greater and will pass more slowly,” he explained.

potential food production disruption

A strong El Niño could also have consequences for world agriculture because it changes the distribution of precipitation and increases the risk of droughts in certain production regions. Orlić recalled the previous El Niño from 2023 and 2024, when a weaker cocoa harvest contributed to a large rise in chocolate prices.

“Since this El Niño is significantly stronger, it’s only logical to expect disruptions,” he concluded. Nevertheless, seasonal forecasts do not mean that every part of Croatia will have an equally warm and rainy winter, nor do they enable reliable prediction of individual storms or floods several months in advance. They indicate an increased probability of certain weather patterns, and their development will also depend on other atmospheric factors.

World.title: Croatian Geothermal Wells Explored in Four Areas
World.content:
October the 11th, 2026 – Croatian geothermal energy potential is enormous, with wells currently being explored in four different areas.

Velika Gorica, Osijek, Vinkovci and Zaprešić could be heated with geothermal energy by as early as 2030, it was announced at the signing of the Grant Agreement “Investment in the Development of Geothermal Energy”, worth 35 million euros. Ana Blaskovic reports for Poslovni that geothermal energy should serve for heating households, schools, kindergartens and other public buildings, and a total of 86 million euros will be invested in the project in two phases.

Geothermal deposits have so far been confirmed by research in the mentioned four cities. The contract that represents the basis for the construction of additional wells was signed by Minister of Economy Ante Šušnjar, Director of the Central Agency for Financing and Contracting Dragan Jelić and President of the Management Board of the Croatian Hydrocarbon Agency Marijan Krpan.

Above-average potential

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković pointed out that Croatia has a significantly greater geothermal potential than is commonly thought. Geothermal energy, he said, will be very useful for heating, and the state is approaching it strategically in order to improve the conditions for the use of this energy source in the long term. “This is domestic, renewable and low-carbon energy,” Plenković emphasised, stressing that, unlike energy that depends on the sun or wind, it is available regardless of weather conditions and that geothermal equipment does not take up much space. In the first phase geothermal deposits have been confirmed, while in the second technical preconditions for their sustainable use will be created. For the construction of additional geothermal wells 30 million euros of non-repayable funds from the European Regional Development Fund have been secured. The total value of that project amounts to 35 million euros, while more than 50 million euros have already been secured through the NRRP for the exploration of geothermal potential.

Pannonian Basin

“Croatian geothermal potential is not the future; it’s a reality that the country still needs and must fully utilise. In the Croatian part of the Pannonian Basin the geothermal gradient is as much as 60 percent higher than the European average,” said Minister of Economy Ante Šušnjar. The geothermal gradient denotes the increase in temperature in the Earth’s interior with increasing depth and is a key indicator for assessing the potential for exploiting geothermal energy.

In Zaprešić, geothermal energy should enable the heating of sports halls, schools, kindergartens, swimming pools, the municipal company and a new business zone. Vinkovci are planning a central heating system that would meet the needs of 1,700 households as well as the heating needs of schools and other public institutions. In Velika Gorica geothermal energy should cover more than 60 percent of the population, while Osijek has assessed the project as strategic for the city’s economy, agriculture and energy independence. According to Marijan Krpan, if everything goes according to plan, works should begin in 2028 and the project be operational in 2030.

World.title: Ukraine's deputy culture minister: Culture a key component in resistance
World.content:
Ukrainian culture is at the heart of the war because Russia is seeking to destroy Ukrainian identity and claim Ukraine's cultural heritage as its own, Ukrainian Deputy Culture Minister Ivan Verbytskyi told ERR.

When a country is fighting for its survival, culture may seem like something that can wait. At the same time, culture is at the center of the battlefield. The Kremlin is trying to destroy Ukrainian identity, while Ukrainians are defending it. How do you see the relationship between war and culture?

As you rightly said, culture is at the heart of this war because the reason the war began was not territory or people, but Ukrainian identity, our right to be ourselves, with our own culture and history.

They claim that Ukraine, Ukrainian culture and Ukrainian history do not exist. They want to destroy them or claim them as Russian. Culture is always a target of attack. At the same time, we are defending our culture.

Culture is also important as a source of resilience. It is not so much about what you do, but who you are. When your identity is attacked, you defend yourself, your country and your culture. Culture is important here because it is how our identity is formed and developed within society.

Culture is at the heart of the war. It is a matter of national security because culture can be used as a weapon. We see this with Russia, which uses social media, films, exhibitions, museums and various cultural spheres to influence other societies and peoples, spreading its narratives to wider audiences. That is why culture is extremely important.

I also want to thank the Estonian people and government for standing with us in defending Ukrainian culture. You support us in other areas of the war as well, but particularly when it comes to culture.

Hundreds of cultural heritage sites in Ukraine have been damaged by Russia.

How are you protecting or restoring these sites? What resources do you have?

Our main goal is to protect and preserve as much as possible. This means evacuating museum collections from war zones. They are at risk because museums and cultural treasures are being targeted for destruction. We are trying to evacuate as much as possible from the front lines.

Another important issue is damaged and destroyed sites. When buildings have been damaged, our first step is to stabilize and preserve them. It is important to prevent further deterioration from wind, rain or snow.

Our priority is to salvage as much as possible from damaged buildings, but also to document everything and digitize inventories of cultural objects. Otherwise, the Russians will claim that everything belongs to them.

We are also creating 3D models of buildings. In several cases, this is already the only way to preserve a record of a building so that it can eventually be restored.

For example, at the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, one of Kyiv's most important cultural monuments, which also has a long history of destruction, we created several 3D models over the past few years.

Now that the cathedral was damaged in a Russian attack on June 15, with its roof almost completely destroyed, we have a 3D model that will allow us to restore and rebuild the building and show it to the world again.

You said that culture is part of resilience. To what extent are you consciously using it to mobilize society?

We are not using it that way. Society is doing it on its own. For example, it is difficult to get tickets to theaters or concert halls in Kyiv because people want to maintain their connection to culture.

Culture has a healing effect. This is extremely important during a crisis when there is so much stress. People need something to lean on and culture provides that safe environment. It offers a safe space in which to reflect on what is happening around them.

One visible aspect of cultural policy is the shaping of public spaces and the removal of monuments. Ukraine has taken down numerous monuments to Soviet leaders, but also monuments to writers such as Alexander Pushkin and Mikhail Bulgakov. Could you explain some of the background? Where do you draw the line in deciding which monuments to remove, and why?

Culture is part of politics. Every artistic gesture is also political. We ask ourselves why there are countries and places where monuments to Pushkin stand, while elsewhere there are none.

Strangely enough, the dividing line coincides with the borders of the former Soviet Union. It was not because people loved Pushkin so much. There was no enormous following for Russian literature. It was a symbol of imperialism, a way for Russia to try to turn these places into Russian spaces. Into the "Russian world," as they called it.

They used culture, religion and other means to achieve this. They used them as weapons to gradually, subtly, though sometimes not so subtly, exert power and make these places their own.

Today, it is difficult for Ukrainians to appreciate such literature or art amid the aggression and suffering we experience every day. For Ukrainians who witness death, tension and pain every day, it is unbearable to see these monuments and symbols in their surroundings.

That is why it is important to create a psychologically safe environment where people can live in peace and do not have to see things that bring back painful memories. Symbols of the very culture being used to kill us.

Another issue is Russian and Belarusian athletes who are increasingly returning to international competition. What do you think of this development? How should other athletes, including Estonian athletes, behave toward them or interact with them?

We know that Estonia has a very good policy on this issue. Thank you very much for that.

From our perspective, there are several dimensions to this issue. The first is the human dimension.

When Russian athletes meet Ukrainian athletes at a competition, those Ukrainian athletes may have lost relatives or siblings in Russian attacks. They may have had to sit in bomb shelters instead of training in sports halls.

It is not safe for them to be alongside Russian athletes, some of whom are members of the Russian military or military sports clubs. Some have received medals and awards from the Russian Defense Ministry.

For the Russian Defense Ministry, sport is part of its power. It is one of the ways Russia demonstrates its strength to the world. They use these opportunities to display Russian influence, including the Russian flag.

A national flag does not represent only sport or culture. It is also political.

This is not a political symbol we can share. For us, it is a political symbol of our suffering, of the deaths of Ukrainians. It is unbearable for us to treat this as something normal, because going to kill your neighbor is not normal.

What do you think Ukraine will look like after the war?

I hope we will be able to rebuild on the foundations of what we have today. That means a flourishing culture and a desire to be ourselves and live normal lives.

And with the support and solidarity we have received from around the world, especially here in Estonia, I hope that when the war finally ends, we will have tremendous creative potential to build a better world together and live in peace, solidarity and mutual support.

We would like to invite everyone to Ukraine after the war to see and experience it for themselves and so that we can thank everyone who is standing by our side today.

World.title: Hiiumaa residents can no longer give birth on the island
World.content:
Women on Hiiumaa haven't been able to to give birth on their home island since July. However, no clear arrangements have been made for transporting expectant mothers to the mainland and back or covering the associated costs.

Kärolyn Kivistik, who lives in Kärdla, is expecting her fifth child on November 8 and her hospital bag is already packed. This time, however, packing it was more complicated than before.

Kivistik said that in the past, her husband had been able to quickly bring her anything she needed. "Now I have to think everything through carefully because I'll be in the city and there won't be any way for someone to bring me things I've left at home," she explained.

Since Hiiumaa Hospital stopped providing maternity services on July 1, Kivistik will have to travel to the mainland to give birth and she does not want to make the journey while in labor. As a mother of a large family, she wants to stay home as long as possible, but she will likely have to head to the capital a week before her due date.

"These children like to be born at night," Kivistik said, adding that ferries do not operate at night, making it difficult to wait for labor to begin on Hiiumaa.

The family has budgeted nearly €1,000 in additional expenses, as renting an apartment near a Tallinn maternity hospital alone costs almost €500. But what bothers her even more than the extra expense is the uncertainty surrounding the arrangements.

Staff shortage to blame

In fact, Hiiumaa Hospital has all the facilities needed to provide maternity services. What it lacks is staff. A pediatrician retired on July 1, there was no gynecologist available on four days in September and in October the hospital will have to manage for about a week without an anesthesiologist. Yet all of these specialists are essential to ensuring that childbirth is as safe as possible.

On Monday, a proposed plan outlining what the journey to give birth might look like was presented to the board of the hospital in Kärdla. According to Hiiumaa Hospital Director Riina Tamm, these are still only preliminary recommendations and do not address the main concern: how expectant mothers will get to the mainland and back and who will cover the costs.

"Where will she stay in Tallinn? Who will pay for her accommodation? She travels to Tallinn, gives birth, but how does she get back? Who will bring her home? Does she have to make her own way back? Should the municipality arrange it or should the hospital? And again, who pays for it all?" Tamm asked. She acknowledged that these are important questions that must be resolved before such a change can be implemented.

As a midwife, Tamm has helped deliver hundreds of babies on Hiiumaa, but she now admits frankly that she would no longer want her own loved ones to give birth on the island. Complications during childbirth can become critical within minutes and the hospital is not equipped to handle such emergencies. This is also why women with high-risk pregnancies have been sent to the mainland for years. But what awaits women on Hiiumaa who do not want to travel to the mainland ahead of time to await labor?

"If everything goes smoothly — the woman arrives, we have an ambulance available and a ferry is just about to depart from Hiiumaa — the patient can reach the Women's Clinic at East Tallinn Central Hospital in three hours and 45 minutes. The ferries are already operating on their winter schedule, with three hours between departures," Tamm explained.

Transport by helicopter would take two hours to reach the hospital, but only if weather conditions permit flying, a helicopter is available and its allotted flight hours have not been exhausted.

A problem of regional policy

Tamm believes this is not just a problem for the small Hiiumaa Hospital or Hiiumaa Municipality. "This is actually a regional policy issue," she added.

In Tamm's view, the state has failed to do its job. The possibility of closing maternity units was first discussed back in 1998, yet the decision on whether to close them has ultimately been left to individual hospitals.

Vivian Arusaar, head of midwifery at East Tallinn Central Hospital, said women who have already gone into labor will not be turned away, but the hospital cannot offer extended accommodation. However, if maternity services continue to be concentrated in larger centers, a solution will have to be found.

Arusaar suggested that the Estonian Health Insurance Fund could be given the option of funding hotel-style accommodation at hospitals. "It is common elsewhere in the world for people to travel hundreds of kilometers to receive healthcare and many large hospitals of regional importance actually have patient hotels," she explained.

According to Heli Paluste, a healthcare network expert at the Ministry of Social Affairs, the decision to close a maternity unit rests with the hospital's board, not the ministry, because hospitals operate autonomously. To ensure high-quality maternity care, a hospital should handle at least 300 births a year, a threshold met only by hospitals in Tallinn, Tartu and Pärnu.

Paluste did not rule out similar decisions being made in the near future. Time will tell whether this happens and which counties might be affected.

Hospital boards in charge of decisions to close wards

Hospital board leaders met at the ministry on Friday where, according to Paluste, it was again emphasized that decisions on any potential maternity unit closures would remain the responsibility of hospital boards.

Where maternity services have been discontinued at Estonia's general hospitals, it has been due to declining birth numbers. The closures have been driven either by financial considerations or staff shortages.

Paluste said patient hotels had been discussed before, but funding them would come at the expense of already scarce healthcare resources. The ministry believes that providing financial assistance to expectant mothers facing economic hardship should be the responsibility of local governments.

World.title: Estonia's August goods exports rise 3% as imports jump 10%
World.content:
Estonia's goods exports rose 3 percent on year in August while imports increased 10 percent, widening the trade deficit to €360 million.

August exports totaled about €1.5 billion euros and imports exceeded €1.8 billion euros at current prices, Statistics Estonia reported Monday. Finland, Latvia and Lithuania were Estonia's main foreign trade partners.

Imports of mineral products rose 30 percent year over year, including a 67 percent jump in automotive fuel.

"This was mainly influenced by the rising prices of petroleum on the global market," said Jane Leppmets, a foreign trade statistics analyst at the agency.

Electrical equipment accounted for 15 percent of commodities exports, followed by agricultural and food products at 11 percent.

Exports to Finland, Estonia's largest export market, made up 17 percent of the total, followed by Latvia at 13 percent and Lithuania at 10 percent.

Shipments to Latvia grew the most at 19 percent, mainly due to increased exports of mineral products, including natural gas and electricity.

Imports grew most in value from Lithuania, rising €50 million euros, or 28 percent, as deliveries of mineral products, including automotive fuel, increased.

Lithuania tied with Finland to account for 12 percent of Estonia's imports, while Latvia made up 11 percent.

World.title: Telia to cut 100 jobs in Estonia as telecom group plans 900 layoffs
World.content:
Telecommunications and IT provider Telia is cutting around 100 jobs in Estonia, with 900 positions slated for elimination across the group as it seeks to remain competitive.

The company aims to make the necessary decisions by the end of 2026, it said in a press release, noting that Telia has already begun consultations with the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund (EUIF).

The restructuring comes as Telia increasingly adopts artificial intelligence (AI), digitalization and automation to reduce costs and remain competitive.

Telia Eesti CEO Andre Visse said the goal is to build a more efficient organization that can adapt to changing customer needs and rapid technological advances.

"Customers increasingly expect more personalized, digital solutions, and technology is evolving faster than ever," Visse said. While these changes create new opportunities, he noted, rising costs still threaten the company's ability to invest and grow.

Telia group seeks stronger localized operations

"To strengthen our competitiveness, we need to make our organization more efficient," the CEO said, adding that the changes should also help ease growing pressure on service prices.

In a press release issued in Sweden, Telia said it "intends to localize its operations further and strengthen the role of its country units in meeting evolving customer needs and delivering profitable growth."

The company, it added, aims to transfer around 220 positions primarily from its central Technology unit to its country-level operations.

World.title: Registered unemployment falls below 40,000 as labor market improves
World.content:
Estonia's labor market showed signs of improvement in the third quarter, with fewer registered unemployed people, more job openings and less competition for available jobs.

Estonia averaged 38,000 registered unemployed in the third quarter of 2026, down 5,600, or 13 percent, from a year earlier. The share of the working-age labor force registered as unemployed fell from 6.3 to 5.5 percent.

The number of registered unemployed has remained below 40,000 for two consecutive quarters, reaching a level last seen in the first quarter of 2020.

The Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund (EUIF) had an average of 5,250 job openings to fill during the quarter, up more than 25 percent on year. Vacancies grew most in manufacturing, professional, scientific and technical activities, trade and construction.

EUIF board member Brit Rammul said the figures point to a modest recovery.

"There are fewer registered unemployed people and more job offers," she said. But opportunities vary by sector, and finding work still depends on applicants' skills and which workers employers need.

Competition for jobs, meanwhile, has also eased. There were an average of seven registered unemployed people per vacancy in the third quarter, down from 11 a year earlier.

Registered unemployed profile largely unchanged

Competition was steepest in finance and insurance, with 255 registered unemployed people per vacancy, followed by information and communications at 66. By contrast, there were four unemployed people per vacancy in administrative and support services and three for craft and related trades jobs.

The profile of registered unemployed in Estonia changed little from a year earlier. The shares of older people, university graduates, managers and senior specialists rose slightly, while the shares of young people, those lacking vocational qualifications and unskilled workers declined.

There were also fewer registered unemployed who did not speak Estonian and fewer long-term unemployed. The gender breakdown, however, was largely unchanged on year.

World.title: President Alar Karis loved by the people but foreign policy possibly a stepping stone
World.content:
President Alar Karis spent his final week as head of state at Kadriorg. Journalists say foreign policy was his weak point.

"Sometimes laws are drafted in great haste and certain things are simply overlooked. Sometimes the political desire to achieve something is so strong that the Constitution is forgotten. And that's what has led to all the decisions I've had to make," Outgoing President Alar Karis said, commenting on his decisions to initially refuse to promulgate 11 separate pieces of legislation.

"But I don't consider it something to boast about, saying, look how many laws I've rejected. Rather, it's a cause for concern. And I've always emphasized that parliament, the Riigikogu, could do its job better and examine things more thoroughly," Karis said in an interview to ERR.

Indrek Kiisler, deputy editor-in-chief of Postimees, said Karis did not come from a political background and therefore is not the kind of political operator that politicians tend to be.

"His primary aim was to guide the Riigikogu by sending a signal. He was doing exactly what the president is actually supposed to do," Kiisler added.

According to Kiisler, Karis tried to provide a counterbalance to the Riigikogu and the turmoil within it.

"That also applied to the legislation it passed, such as the motor vehicle tax," he noted.

Motor vehicle tax veto

President Karis initially refused to promulgate the motor vehicle tax law in 2024, arguing that it violated the principle of equal treatment. The Riigikogu amended the law and the president promulgated it six weeks later.

Erik Moora, head of Delfi's opinion section, said a debate emerged suggesting that every tax should have only one purpose.

"On the contrary, very few taxes have just one purpose and it is clear that the purpose of every tax is to raise revenue for the state budget," he said.

Critics began suggesting that there was something wrong with the motor vehicle tax having multiple objectives.

"It is clear that many taxes are intended to influence certain consumer behaviors and achieve other objectives, as was also explained in the case of this tax," Moora said. "Jumping on that bandwagon seemed a little populist to me."

The most politically contentious decision was Karis' veto of amendments to the Churches and Congregations Act, mainly concerning the status of the Estonian Christian Orthodox Church. The president referred the law to the Supreme Court, seeking to have it declared unconstitutional because it would not bring about any substantive change.

Karis said the law and the churches' statutes could be amended, but the ties would remain.

"That's why I repeatedly asked for the law to be reconsidered. And as you saw, when it reached the Supreme Court, quite a few judges there also expressed dissenting opinions," he said.

Karis said the case has now reached the European Court of Human Rights.

"I said, think through what the next steps will be and how this law is going to be implemented," he explained.

Tõnis Leht, an editor of the "Poliitikaguru" podcast, said Karis had not managed to change the approach toward the Russian Orthodox Church.

"Nevertheless, his criticism was fundamentally valid and substantive and the Supreme Court's ruling did take significant account of the arguments put forward by the president and his legal adviser," he said.

Russia's full-scale war

The defining event of Karis' presidency was Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine. Karis met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy just two days before Russia launched its full-scale invasion. He subsequently visited Ukraine several times and the two presidents also met at Kadriorg. Karis describes his approach to foreign policy as soft diplomacy.

Moora said Karis' presidency coincided with a period when Kaja Kallas, as prime minister, enjoyed an exceptionally high international profile, attracting considerable attention, airtime, quotations and media coverage. In his view, Estonia's message had an extraordinarily strong international presence.

"Karis was inevitably overshadowed by that," Moora said.

"I recently read that President Karis wasn't interested in foreign policy, which is an outright lie.," Karis said.

He noted that foreign policy can be conducted in different ways.

"In a sense, people are barking up the wrong tree here," he said. "Because the main responsibility, particularly in the context of the war in Ukraine, lies with the prime minister and the foreign minister."

Karis said they are the ones who take the lead because they attend NATO meetings and European Council summits.

Karis said he has always considered soft diplomacy important and believes its impact is much longer-lasting. He cited the Kazakhstan incident as an example.

"When I ask what actually happened there, I don't get an answer because nothing happened.," Karis said.

Kiisler said that once events had unfolded, Karis struggled to explain them clearly.

"He consistently had difficulty explaining his positions," Kiisler added.

"I can see how much the Kazakhstan scandal still weighs on him. He simply hasn't been able to move past it," Kiisler continued.

He noted that although considerable time has passed, Karis keeps returning to the issue because many people in Estonia still do not understand why he acted as he did.

"I get the impression that over those five years, he never really managed to develop a thick skin," Kiisler said.

Popular with the people

Despite the criticism of his foreign policy, Karis' greatest achievement was maintaining a high level of public support.

Leht said people like Karis because he comes across as smart and articulate, but also open and warm. He added that Karis is not dismissive, does not appear arrogant or condescending and never seems bored when interacting with people.

However, the mild-mannered Karis also showed that he could be quite sharp.

Kiisler said Karis did make pointed remarks, sometimes indirectly and sometimes explicitly, such as when he said Kaja Kallas should resign during the scandal over her husband's business ties to Russia.

Kiisler noted, however, that the kind of sharp rhetoric associated with former presidents Toomas Hendrik Ilves and Kersti Kaljulaid was largely absent during Karis' five years in office.

One of Karis' best-known quotes, however, comes from this year's Independence Day speech.

"We've overheated our beloved sauna and become dizzy from the intense steam."

Moora believes the remark will stick in people's minds. He said Karis often delivered good speeches, although they tended to be even better when read than when heard.

In closing, the president said it is ultimately the happy moments that he will remember most from his years in office.

"The occasions when I've presented state decorations have always been moving, seeing the emotions people experience. It's so wonderful to watch, all that surprise. It's genuine," Karis said.

President Ülle Madise will take over the presidency from Karis in the Riigikogu on Monday.

World.title: Police detain 10 illegal immigrants in Tallinn's Nõmme district
World.content:
Police apprehended 10 illegal immigrants in Tallinn's Nõmme district on Sunday evening. Nine were taken directly to a detention center, while one was transported to a hospital by paramedics for further medical treatment.

At around 7:30 p.m. Sunday, police received a tip that two dark-skinned men who appeared lost were standing outside an apartment building on Valdeku tänav in Tallinn's Nõmme district. Police responded to the scene and detained both men. Checks revealed that they were Sudanese nationals staying in Estonia illegally. During conversations with the men, police learned that several other people were hiding in the area.

Kevin Kohver, field commander at the Lääne-Harju Police Station, said police launched a search of the area based on the information they had received, involving police patrols, service dogs and personnel from the Rescue Board.

"The area was searched using drones and ATVs. A drone also detected people moving in the forest and dog patrols and other search teams were dispatched to find them. Those hiding in the forest initially tried to flee from police officers, but with the help of service dogs and patrols, they were soon apprehended in various wooded areas. A total of eight additional men of Sudanese origin were found in the forest," Kohver explained.

He added that paramedics assessed the health of all 10 men after they were detained. "Nine of the 10 men did not require additional medical attention and were subsequently taken to a detention center. However, one of the men who had been hiding in the forest and attempted to flee from police had fallen while running away and injured his arm. He was taken to a hospital for further medical treatment. After receiving treatment at the hospital, he was also transferred to the detention center," Kohver said.

All of the detained men were in Estonia illegally and only one was carrying identification documents.

World.title: Ülle Madise assumes office as president on Monday
World.content:
Ülle Madise will take the oath of office before the Riigikogu on Monday and assume office as president.

At 2:15 p.m., President-elect Ülle Madise and her husband will arrive at the Office of the President in Kadriorg where they will be welcomed by President Alar Karis and his wife, Sirje Karis.

From there, they will proceed together to the square in front of the Riigikogu building. President Alar Karis will greet the Guard Battalion's honor guard assembled in Lossi plats, after which the two presidents will enter Toompea Castle.

At the ceremony, which begins at 3 p.m., President Alar Karis will deliver a speech, President-elect Ülle Madise will take the oath of office and deliver her first address as president.

The presidential oath-taking ceremony and speeches will be broadcast live on ERR channels.

Born and educated in Tartu, 51-year-old Ülle Madise is a lawyer by training. She has previously worked at the Ministry of Justice, on the Riigikogu's Constitutional Committee, as chief auditor at the National Audit Office, as legal adviser to the president and, since 2015, as chancellor of justice. She was reappointed to the latter position for a second term in late 2021.

Ülle Madise is married to Lauri Madise, who works as a judge at the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg. The couple have no children. Ülle Madise's father is former politician and Supreme Court justice Tõnu Anton.

Madise was nominated as a presidential candidate by 75 members of the Riigikogu. Representatives of the Reform Party, Eesti 200, Isamaa, the Social Democrats and unaffiliated MPs submitted the relevant documents to the National Electoral Committee.

The Riigikogu elected Madise president in a secret ballot with 71 votes.

World.title: Al Quwa Al Jawiya hosts Al Ain in Basra
World.content:
Basra (IraqiNews.com) – Basra International Stadium is set to host a high-stakes continental encounter on Monday evening, October 12, 2026, as Iraqi powerhouse Al-Quwa Al-Jawiya welcomes UAE champions Al Ain for the second round of the AFC Champions League Elite.

Scheduled for kick-off at 9:15 PM Baghdad time (+03:00 GMT), the fixture represents a pivotal opportunity for “The Falcons” to rebound from their opening-day defeat against Uzbekistan’s Neftchi Fergana and open their points account in the expanded league phase.

The hosts enter the tie backed by strong home support and a fully fit roster. Having parted ways by mutual consent with Tunisian tactician Fathi Al-Jabal earlier this season, the club turned back to Omani manager Rashid Jaber, who famously guided Al-Jawiya to the Iraq Stars League crown last season.

Monday night’s clash marks Jaber’s first continental appearance in his renewed tenure, with the coaching staff focusing on tactical discipline and defensive compactness to neutralize Al Ain’s attacking trident while capitalizing on swift transitional play.

Al Ain arrives in Basra holding three points from their first outing and carrying significant continental pedigree as former Asian champions. With the Emirati side seeking to solidify their standing near the top of the group standings, Al-Quwa Al-Jawiya faces an intense tactical battle where securing maximum points on home soil is critical to sustaining their qualification momentum.

World.title: Iraqi judiciary recovers 4 billion dinars
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council announced on Monday, October 12, 2026, the recovery of four billion Iraqi dinars (approximately $2.66 million) in misappropriated public funds tied to a major financial and administrative corruption case.

The clawback of state capital was executed through specialized judicial intervention on behalf of the state-owned Rafidain Bank.

According to a formal statement received by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the Rusafa Investigation Court Specialized in Integrity and Money Laundering Cases successfully traced and seized the funds following forensic financial tracking.

The presiding investigative judge affirmed that the restitution forms part of ongoing judicial proceedings targeting administrative corruption schemes designed to siphon liquidity from state commercial banking accounts.

The competent magistrate stated that rigorous interrogations and judicial audits conducted by the anti-graft court resulted in the full recovery of the four-billion-dinar sum into Rafidain Bank’s institutional accounts.

The judiciary underscored its steadfast resolve to pursue criminal enforcement and statutory penalties against individuals exploiting illicit mechanisms to generate unlawful personal gains at the direct expense of sovereign assets.

World.title: Australian engineer Robert Pether leaves Iraq after five-year ordeal
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Australian engineer Robert Pether departed Iraq on Monday, October 12, 2026, ending a five-year ordeal that began with his arrest in Baghdad over a commercial contractual dispute tied to the construction of the Central Bank of Iraq’s landmark headquarters.

His departure was officially confirmed by Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong, marking the resolution of an extensive bilateral and multilateral diplomatic effort.

Speaking to Australian media, including The Canberra Times, Wong announced that the Iraqi federal government formally lifted the travel ban that had restricted Pether’s movement following his conditional release from prison in June 2025.

The Foreign Minister stated that Pether is now free to resume his life and reunite with his family in Ireland, highlighting that the outcome followed persistent representations by Australian consular officials alongside coordinated diplomacy with Irish authorities. Wong welcomed his exit from the country, reaffirming Canberra’s commitment to supporting him and his family through the transition.

Pether was initially detained in April 2021 alongside his Egyptian colleague Khaled Radwan after traveling to Baghdad for what was intended to be a commercial resolution meeting between their employer, Dubai-based engineering consultancy CME Consulting, and Iraqi authorities overseeing the Zaha Hadid-designed Central Bank headquarters project.

Both men were subsequently convicted on fraud allegations and sentenced to five years in prison alongside substantial financial penalties, charges that Pether and his legal representatives consistently denied as an unlawful criminalization of a civil contract disagreement.

The high-profile detention drew significant international scrutiny, including an official review in 2022 by the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, which concluded that Pether’s imprisonment breached international law and raised serious concerns regarding judicial process, fair trial guarantees, and detention conditions.

The resolution of Pether’s travel restrictions closes a contentious legal saga that had strained consular relations between Baghdad and Western capitals for half a decade.

World.title: Iraq and Kuwait weigh joint bid to host AFC Asian Cup 2031
World.content:
Basra (IraqiNews.com) – Basra Governor Asaad Al-Eidani revealed that preliminary verbal understandings were reached with the Kuwaiti Minister of Interior to explore a joint Iraqi-Kuwaiti bid for hosting the AFC Asian Cup 2031.

The prospective initiative aims to leverage geographic proximity, advanced stadium infrastructure, and regional event hosting experience to submit a competitive candidate portfolio.

According to the initial proposal, the joint dossier would feature prominent sporting facilities across both borders, centering on Basra’s Basra International Stadium (Palm Trunk) with its 65,000-seat capacity and Al-Minaa Olympic Stadium, backed by modernized transport and hospitality infrastructure delivered during the 25th Arabian Gulf Cup.

From the Kuwaiti side, key venues would include Jaber Al-Ahmad International Stadium and Sabah Al-Salem Stadium, supported by Kuwait’s administrative track record in hosting continental sporting fixtures.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) is evaluating bids from several prospective host candidates for the 2031 tournament, with Kuwait previously confirmed among the contending associations alongside Australia, India, Indonesia, South Korea, and a joint Central Asian bid by Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

Any formalization of an official binational Iraq-Kuwait candidature will require coordination and statutory submission through the Iraqi Football Association and Kuwait Football Association within AFC bidding frameworks.

World.title: Melbourne man linked to suspected flydubai hijacker condemns ‘false accusations’
World.content:
Sydney – A Melbourne man whose Islamic community centre has been linked by prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates to the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain of a flydubai jet has hit out at “false accusations”.

The Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda’s September 11, 2001 suicide attacks, and carried out his attempt “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”, according to the Emirati prosecutor’s findings published by state media last week.

The prosecutor said the co-pilot first became radicalised while studying in Australia “through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks”.

The prosecutor alleged he was acquainted there with an organization known as “My Centre” managed by a Lebanese man called Abu Hamza.

Neither “My Centre” nor Abu Hamza are accused of any criminal wrongdoing.

In a video posted on social media, Abu Hamza — also named by local media as Samir Mohtadi — struck back at what he called “false accusations”.

“Right through the ages… those who’re righteous, they’ve always been attacked, abused, accused, killed, imprisoned — and this is the way it is,” he said.

“The best thing sometimes is not to say anything,” he added.

“They’re going to continue accusing you… making false accusations.”

He did not comment directly on the UAE prosecutor’s claims.

During the September 30 flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the suspect used an emergency axe to attack the plane’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who fought back and tried to call for help.

Another pilot assigned to the return flight who was also on board “noticed the cockpit door opening and closing repeatedly in an unusual manner”, according to the findings.

After gaining entry, he “intervened with the assistance of a cabin crew member and several passengers, and together they rescued the injured captain and restrained the suspect”.

The return flight captain and his co-pilot then landed the plane at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.

Police and intelligence services in Australia have said they are investigating the man’s links to the country.

Police in New Zealand said last week he had spent time in the country on a six-month student visa, where he completed a portion of his flight training, national broadcaster RNZ said.

World.title: Stocks rise as oil prices tumble after Trump hails ‘energy ceasefire’
World.content:
Hong Kong – Most stock markets rose Monday as oil prices tumbled after Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, which offset a fresh wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Both main crude contracts sank more than one percent following the US president’s declaration, even as it sparked astonishment in Kyiv, which also said Moscow had struck multiple power plants in the country.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump said early Sunday on Truth Social. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”

His post came after he called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to halt attacks on Russian refineries and said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” who would finally settle the war.

Zelensky appeared to express surprise at the announcement, saying he was seeking further details, but added that “Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well”.

Russia has yet to confirm its agreement.

While the announcement was welcomed by Ukraine’s allies, Trump had come under fire after declaring a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, which European leaders and Kyiv said would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The drop in oil prices reversed an initial spike that came in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia at the weekend.

At least a dozen people were killed at Riyadh’s international airport Saturday — the deadliest attack on Saudi soil for more than a decade — and another one died following a second strike on Sunday.

The assaults marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.

The Iran-backed group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the past 24 hours and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom’s transit hubs, calling them “a theatre of operations for our forces”.

“The market is no longer paying full geopolitical premium on every headline, and that is probably the most useful signal in the morning price action,” wrote SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes.

“A strike matters if it threatens real barrels, shipping lanes, refining capacity or insurance costs; otherwise, the market is getting increasingly reluctant to pay up simply because the geopolitical ticker flashes red.

“The physical market remains tight enough to keep Brent above $100, but futures are refusing to treat every new escalation as the start of another straight-line inflation shock.”

The drop in oil prices provided support to most Asian markets, with Hong Kong, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington and Manila all up.

But Seoul and Taipei were dragged by losses in chipmakers SK hynix, Samsung and TSMC. Tokyo was closed for a holiday.

US futures were sharply higher.

Investors are also gearing up for the release of key US inflation and retail sales data, which could play a big role in the Federal Reserve’s decision-making regarding interest rates. The bank is due to meet at the end of October.

Also in view is the beginning of earnings season this week, with banking giants JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs and Bank of America due to report.

Tech giants will follow later in the month and November, with traders keen to get an idea on the outlook for the AI sector in light of the vast sums of cash pumped into it in recent years.

World.title: Software, sprints, trolls: Singapore Grand Prix talking points
World.content:
Singapore – A dominant Max Verstappen won the Singapore Grand Prix for the first time on Sunday, 24 hours after taking the chequered flag in the sprint race at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

Here are three talking points to emerge from a hot and humid weekend in Singapore:

– ‘Brake, throttle, that’s it’ –

For the second weekend in a row, software glitches on the 2026 generation of cars caused problems.

In Malaysia a week earlier the issue had occurred on a formation lap in the rain where several cars ground to a halt.

In Singapore, an erroneous deployment of the “overtake” mode meant some cars in the first sprint qualifying session had more power available than others.

Verstappen is one driver clearly fed up with the difficulty of managing and driving the modern cars, which have a 50-50 split between electrical and internal combustion energy, and called for a return to a simpler life behind the wheel.

“It is very complex now. I just hope the new rule set (for 2027) is easier,” the four-time world champion told reporters.

“The problem is there’s a lot of software in the background that can make you not pull away or there is glitch on slow laps.

“You have to make sure the battery pack is charging in the right place. That’s not what racing should be about.

“You should be able to go out, have a brake pedal and a throttle pedal and that’s it.”

– Wolff on the warpath –

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff slammed the “brainless” critics hiding “behind their screens” who have suggested the team had favoured Kimi Antonelli over George Russell this season.

Championship leader Antonelli, 20, is 102 points ahead of the luckless Russell and on the brink of becoming the youngest world champion in history.

The Englishman’s retirement in Malaysia a week ago and his consequent engine penalties, plus crashing when in the lead of the Singapore sprint race, have piled on the agony for Russell.

But Wolff hit back at the conspiracy theorists.

“They’re brainless, whoever thinks that. I mean, it’s completely nonsensical. We’ve had it in the past with Lewis fans,” Wolff told reporters.

“Do they think I have a button that says, ‘George — engine failure now’?

“I guess this is maybe where social media goes today.

“People hide behind their screens and then they lash out.

“Sometimes I read what people write. I find it hilarious.

“These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they are abusing the team or myself. ‘I’m Satan’, I’ve heard. So, yeah, overall it’s funny.”

– Time to change track? –

The weekend saw the first time Singapore had hosted an F1 sprint, and drivers seemed to agree it should be the last — unless more overtaking opportunities can be introduced on the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

“I think we shouldn’t host a sprint where you can’t pass,” said double winner Verstappen after a processional weekend of racing on the tight city centre track, only enlivened by some heavy rain just before Saturday’s sprint.

“The track is great, but also the problem we have at the moment is with the overtake mode, it barely does anything here,” said Verstappen of the electrical boost available to drivers.

Sunday’s 62-lap GP was largely uneventful once the field settled after the start, with only Lewis Hamilton’s blunder on tyre choice having an effect on the order of the top six on the grid.

Hamilton was one of many drivers calling for the circuit to be modified to allow more wheel-to-wheel racing.

“I think there’s some adjustments that can be made to make this 100 percent a great circuit,” said the seven-time world champion.

“But whether they’re going to do that, I don’t know.

“I think they need to change the track to maybe a longer straight somewhere in order to allow us to overtake for it to be truly a great racing circuit.”

World.title: Top NATO commander set to issue warning to Russia over any attack
World.content:
Brussels – NATO’s top military commander is expected to deliver a warning to Russia on Monday over the alliance’s ability to counter any attack, as worries grow over the threat from Moscow.

NATO officials have said US General Alexus Grynkewich — the alliance’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe — will elaborate his “theory of victory” over any potential attack at a security conference in Warsaw.

The move from the top military commander comes as NATO seeks to send a message to Moscow to halt what Western officials say is a “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine’s backers in the war against Russia.

Fears have grown in recent months that the Kremlin is stepping up its actions after high-profile incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport.

“The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage, which is consistent with and grounded upon the alliance’s deterrence and defence plans,” Colonel Martin O’Donnell, a spokesman for the US general, said last week.

“But given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked,” O’Donnell said, noting the theory sets out a framework to do just that.

NATO — which was founded in the wake of World War II to counter the Soviet Union — traditionally closely guards its defence plans to counter any attack by Russia.

Grynkewich’s intervention looks unlikely to divulge many new details on NATO’s strategy and is intended to both send a signal to Moscow and reassure members on the alliance’s eastern flank.

NATO insists it remains a defensive alliance and has no intention of attacking Russia.

Western officials say that Moscow’s “hybrid attacks” have become more reckless as the Kremlin’s forces are stalled in Ukraine, and that they risk causing significant loss of life.

The alliance — whose primary purpose is deterring an armed Russian invasion — has struggled to work out how to cope with incidents in the grey zone beneath open conflict.

NATO civilian head Mark Rutte has urged countries to keep “calm, carry on and support Ukraine”.

“We should not be naive… about Russia, but they know we are stronger,” Rutte said last month.

But the uptick in Russian activity comes at a time of potential vulnerability for Europe. Allies are currently bracing for possible cuts to US forces in Europe as the Pentagon conducts a review of its deployments on the continent.

The results of the process are expected to be announced towards the end of the year.

European countries are already rushing to bolster their militaries as doubts have soared over the reliability of the United States under President Donald Trump.

World.title: BJP Mahila Morcha protests against Congress MP Akoijam over harassment allegations, burns Rahul Gandhi's effigy

NEW DELHI: BJP Mahila Morcha workers staged protests across the country on Monday, burning effigies of leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Congress MP Angomcha Bimol Akoijam over allegations of sexual harassment involving female students at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU).The protesters demanded action against Akoijam, who represents Inner Manipur in the Lok Sabha, and accused the Congress leadership of remaining silent over the allegations.BJP workers also marched towards the Congress office in Delhi, calling for the MP's removal and arrest.The protests followed reports that JNU had dismissed Akoijam from his position as a professor after an internal committee found allegations made by 11 female students to be true, according to the BJP. The allegations have not been independently verified in the material provided.Sharing a video on X, the BJP criticised the Congress leadership over its response to the allegations. BJP leader and MP Bansuri Swaraj questioned Rahul Gandhi's silence and challenged the party to take action against Akoijam.She said, âOn October 9, 2026, a report from JNU's internal committee emerges, in which the allegations of sexual exploitation made by 11 female students against Congress MP Angomcha Bimol Akoijam are found to be true, and he is immediately dismissed from his job.âI want to ask Rahul Gandhi ji and the Congress... why have you remained silent until now? âWhy haven't you taken action yet?âRahul Gandhi ji, is âSmash The Patriarchyâ just an electoral slogan for you? âIf not, then take action against Bimol Akoijam.âSwaraj also contrasted the BJP's position on women's political representation with her criticism of the Congress.âOn one side is PM Shri Narendra Modi, who is increasing women's political representation through 'Women's Reservation.' On the other side is Rahul Gandhi, who obstructs even its implementation, gives a place in the Lok Sabha to a Sexual Predator, and provides protection to him through his silence,â she added.In another post, BJP MP Kamaljeet Sehrawat called on Rahul Gandhi to respond to the allegations."Rahul Gandhi should answer to those daughters who had come to India's renowned university (JNU) with trust. And today, a Congress MP himself is sexually exploiting them. These daughters, who are unsafe today, hold Rahul Gandhi and his party responsible."The BJP also questioned whether the Congress was living up to its stated commitment to women's safety.âIs Rahul Gandhi forgetting âSmash the Patriarchyâ now, or are the 'echoes of complaints' from 11 female students not reaching him?â the party said in a post.In another statement, the BJP alleged that Akoijam had been suspended from his position as a professor at JNU over sexual harassment allegations and accused the Congress of taking no action against him.âDespite the seriousness of the allegations, Congress has taken NO ACTION against him. Rahul Gandhiâs silence is deafening,â the party said.Earlier, addressing a press conference at the BJP headquarters, Swaraj described the allegations as âbone-chillingâ and accused the Congress of hypocrisy over women's safety and empowerment."From media sources and media reports, the kind of allegations that have emerged are bone-chilling; they shake one's very soul. I would like to place before you the details of the kind of allegations that have surfaced. The Congress MP, who was a professor at JNU, asked sexually inappropriate questions to female students during assessments. It is alleged that he indulged in unwelcome physical contact with female students in JNU," Swaraj said.She further alleged that assessments were conducted at unusual hours at the MP's residence."Not only this, but media reports also reveal the allegation that this Congress MP used to call these female students to his home late at night to conduct academic assessments. He conducted one viva examination until 11:40 at night! And not just that-allegations of sexually explicit classroom conduct have also come to light. All of these are grave allegations," she stated.Earlier, Delhi Police registered an FIR following a complaint lodged by JNU's chief security officer, officials said.The FIR was registered on October 11 at Vasant Kunj North police station under Sections 75, 75(1)(i), 75(1)(iv) and 79 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). According to the details of the FIR, Akoijam's name has been mentioned. Police said further investigation into the matter was underway.

World.title: Jantar Mantar no longer a protest site; three new venues designated
World.content:
Jantar Mantar no longer protest site

Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground, CBD Ground named new protest sites
