World.title: Delhi braces for INDIA bloc march; major traffic curbs and metro restrictions announced
World.content: Delhi is set to witness extensive traffic restrictions, heightened security and temporary metro station closures as INDIA bloc leaders prepare to march for allegations related to the Election Commission and the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

World.title: Iran ‘deeply concerned’ over escalation between Houthis, Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Iran said on Monday (October 12, 2026), it was "deeply concerned" by escalating attacks between Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, after 14 people died in two days of strikes on Riyadh's airport.

"We are deeply concerned about the developments taking place in the Arabian Peninsula," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told a weekly press conference, adding that Tehran was ready "to help facilitate dialogue between the parties."

A Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday (October 11, 2026), killed one person and wounded 11 others, a day after 13 died in the deadliest strike on Saudi soil in more than a decade.

"We absolutely do not want hostilities and war to continue between two Islamic countries," Mr. Baqaei said, urging the parties to resolve the situation "through dialogue and engagement."

The Houthis are part of the Iran-backed "Axis of Resistance," a network of groups opposed to Israel that also includes Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iraqi Shiite armed groups.

World.title: Chennai-bound Indigo flight from Delhi diverted to Hyderabad following 'smoke' onboard, lands safely
World.content:
A Chennai-bound Indigo flight from Delhi was diverted here on Sunday (October 11, 2026) after smoke was detected from a customer's personal electronic device kept in the overhead bin and the plane landed safely, the carrier said.

"IndiGo flight 6E 6115, operating from Delhi to Chennai on October 11, 2026, was diverted to Hyderabad after smoke was detected from a customer's personal electronic device. The cabin crew responded promptly and the situation was brought under control," Indigo said in a statement.

"In line with established protocols, the pilots diverted the flight and landed safely at Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad," it added.

An alternative aircraft was arranged for the passengers to continue the journey to Chennai, it added.

World.title: Fear grips residents as carnivore that killed man remains elusive in Erode district
World.content:
Fear has gripped residents of forest-fringe habitations near Hasanur in Erode district as the animal suspected of killing a man on the night of October 3, 2026, remains elusive despite efforts by the Forest Department to capture it. The killing of two cows and a calf in separate incidents on the night of October 10 has heightened concerns over the movement of carnivores near residential areas.

The partially consumed body of V. Periyasamy of Bungalow Thotti was found along a stream near the forest fringes under the Hasanur Range of the Hasanur Forest Division of the Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve (STR) on October 4. Residents suspect a leopard was responsible, citing a series of cattle kills in nearby villages in the last six months.

The department has installed camera traps at 10 locations and deployed 50 staff for night patrols. Residents of forest-fringe villages have also been advised not to venture out after sunset.

Attacks on cattle

On the night of October 10, two cows and a calf were killed in separate incidents in Old Hasanur, Ongalwadi, and Bungalow Thotti, with one animal killed in each location. Residents suspect that multiple carnivores could have been involved in the attacks.

Following the latest incidents, residents from the three habitations, along with those from Centre Thotti, questioned Hasanur Forest Ranger N. Anandkumar about the department’s efforts to capture the animal or animals involved. They demanded that a cage be installed, citing the suspected attack on Periyasamy and the subsequent cattle kills. Residents also pointed to thick bushes near residential areas that they feared could serve as hiding places for the animals. Mr. Anandkumar explained the measures being taken to track the animals and assured the residents that a cage would be installed soon.

World.title: BJD slams State government for Hockey India’s notice to downgrade Odisha’s status
World.content:
Hockey Association of Odisha (HAO) faces the risk of losing its Permanent Member status in Hockey India (HI) after being issued a show-cause notice over the absence of elected representatives at the helm of district-level units, which are instead being managed by bureaucrats.

The Biju Janata Dal (BJD) reacted sharply, calling it a fall from Odisha’s position as a national sponsor of hockey to the brink of losing its permanent membership in the sport’s governing body.

“In Odisha, Hockey is an emotion. With the consistent efforts of former Chief Minister Naveen Patnaik, Hockey in Odisha and across India, touched new heights. Odisha became the sponsor of Indian Hockey. In the last two years of apathy towards Hockey by the present double engine government, there has been a fall in the quality of hockey in Odisha,” said former Sports Minister and BJD leader Tushar Kanti Behera in Bhubaneswar on Monday (October 12, 2026).

The party criticised the Mohan Charan Majhi government for its alleged neglect towards hockey in Odisha for which a show-cause had been issued by Hockey India to Odisha Hockey Association questioning why Odisha Hockey’s status should not be changed from Permanent Member to Associate Member.’

In its October 7, 2026 letter, HI had taken exceptions to not holding elections for district units of HAO.

“District wise statement record that in each of the 30 district units, the president is district collector and the secretary in each is additional district magistrate or equivalent ranked officers. Ganjam, Sundargarh and Rayagada have no persons in these positions,” the hockey’s apex governing body says.

“Where office attaches to government post and not to election by the members of the units, the governing body is prima facie not democratically constituted. Article 6.1 and 6.4 of the bye-laws of HI require democratic constitution of a permanent member of its affiliated units,” the show-cause notices says. The association asserted no district unit in Odisha had produced record of an election.

During regime of previous BJD government, Odisha successfully hosted the FIH (The Fédération Internationale de Hockey) Hockey Champions Trophy in 2014, the Indo-Japan Hockey Series in 2015, the Hockey World League in 2017, the Hockey Men’s World Cup in 2018, and the FIH Hockey Olympic Qualifiers in 2019, making the State powerhouse of hockey. In 2018, Odisha had gone on to become the official sponsor of both the men’s and women’s national hockey teams for five years and subsequently, it was increased by another 10 years.

World.title: 'Unacceptable': CJP on Jantar Mantar being denotified as protest site
World.content:
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convener Saurav Das on Monday (October 12, 2026) said the government's decision to denotify Jantar Mantar as a protest site is "unacceptable", and they "do not accept this arbitrary decision".

Anti-CEC protests: October 12, 2026

The remarks came as Delhi Police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated site for protests and named three new spots for holding such demonstrations, according to an official order.

"Unacceptable. Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar?" Mr. Das said in a post on X.

"The Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India. Did the Ministry of Home Affairs consult with the people of India? Were any stakeholders consulted? Were any organisations consulted?" he said.

Attacking the Prime Minister, he said that said soon the government would denotify India as a democracy.

"Take it in writing — just how they are denotifying people's Jantar Mantar, the prime minister will soon denotify democracy in India. This move is a step towards that," Mr. Das said.

"We do not accept this arbitrary decision. It is an assault on people's fundamental right to protest and peaceful assembly. Now the whole country is becoming Jantar Mantar," he said.

Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar issued the standing order on October 11, naming Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in east Delhi as the new designated sites for protests and demonstrations.

The move comes amid heightened security arrangements in the national capital following calls to gather for protests at Jantar Mantar. PTI AO SKY

World.title: Will examine whether to go ahead with ‘Sthree Suraksha’ pension scheme: Satheesan
World.content:
The State government will examine whether to go ahead with the ‘Sthree Suraksha’ pension scheme or not, Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan has said.

Responding to questions on the scheme by MLAs during Question Hour in the Assembly on Monday, the Chief Minister said it had been implemented through a government order issued on November 1, 2025, and the first instalment of pension was paid to over 10 lakh beneficiaries in February this year.

However, the government was reviewing aspects of the scheme, including the financial burden, since it had been launched by the previous Left Democratic Front (LDF) just before elections even though it had been in power for two successive terms. Only then could it be implemented.

Mr. Satheesan denied the Opposition charge that the United Democratic Front government was discontinuing welfare schemes. “This Onam, the government had given all arrears that the LDF government had not paid.”

Instead of announcing this scheme just before polls, the LDF government should have paid the arrears due to many segments, including retiring workers, he added.

The government was not claiming that all beneficiaries were ineligible. However, it had to look into complaints pertaining to beneficiary selection that had arisen at the time of elections itself. Without it, there was no way of determining the actual beneficiaries, Mr. Satheesan said.

He added that complaints had been given to the then Chief Electoral Officer about misuse of scheme beneficiary data for election campaigning. However, the UDF government had not ordered an investigation into the complaints, he said.

The government would also examine whether the scheme was effective and its implementation.

The Chief Minister said the government would announce and implement multiple schemes in a time-bound manner to bring women into the mainstream. He cited the Priyadarsini free travel scheme and the increase in honorariums and pensions for ASHAs, anganwadi workers, pre-primary teachers, and midday meal cooks that had already been implemented.

To empower women, the government wanted to bring out schemes to make the women financially independent, provide them revolving fund, provide them guidance, be it technical or marketing or management.

World.title: 'Can sacrifice development, not security': Governor Kundi, Naqvi chair KP apex committee meeting
World.content:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi co-chaired a meeting of the KP apex committee on Monday, a day after the imposition of the governor’s rule and emergency in the province.

Addressing the meeting, Governor Kundi asserted that under the new set-up, tackling terrorism would be the priority.

“We can sacrifice our development, but never security,” Kundi vowed.

He noted a “lack of synergy” in counterterrorism efforts in the province.

“Now it will show that there is (synergy),” he said, adding that the administration will “fulfil the demands of the counterterrorism department and police”. He stressed that the administration will “work 24/7” as the federal government and the “people had put faith in us”.

“We have to show the difference,” he said, adding that there was no time for holidays or weekends.

He stressed that the administration was moving towards “result-oriented” actions, rather than cosmetic measures.

Noting the scourge of terrorism in the province, Kundi said, “People have no freedom to live, travel and do other things,” in districts such as Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, and Waziristan.

He stressed working towards restoring freedom of movement for people in terrorism affected districts of KP.

“People from our province also want peace, prosperity, and development,” he said.

Kundi expressed hope that he and his administration should be remembered well. “It should be written in history that these people came and restored peace in the province.”

The governor added that he will hold apex committee meetings regularly.

Co-chairing the meeting alongside Kundi, Naqvi remarked: “Today is the first time I can proudly say that the federal and the provincial governments are on the same page.”

He recalled, “In the past 2.5 years, we have seen many ups and downs.” The minister stated that the most difficult work was that of people fighting this war with “no backend support”.

“I remember we would reach from Islamabad, but the people living here would not even attend those funerals.”

Criticising the PTI-led government, he said: “It was the [provincial] government’s job to lead this war against terrorism, but they did not do it. They kept bowing their heads only because they did not want to compromise. “But any war, no matter how many resources you have, cannot be won until the government there leads it,” he stressed.

“Not once, not twice; we requested them to work with us dozens of times,“ Naqvi emphasised.

“One thing I will ask you to note is that this is the same force, these are the same people, but the only difference you will see in them is that when the government is leading, the same people will show you the results.”

The people haven’t changed; they’re all the same. But you will see when a government leads, the results will be very good, Naqvi said. The minister said the advisors do not have to worry about the “ups and downs.”

“It’s not like things will change in a day; there will be difficult times. But all of us, including the governor, police, administration, and federal government.

“We have to face and defeat them together. Our intentions are pure; god will help us produce results.“

A day earlier, Kundi addressed the first meeting of the KP Advisory Council — formed by the federal government after the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule — where he outlined similar directions.

“We have to fast-track things. There will be zero tolerance for corruption. Things should be done in a timely manner,” he said, adding that they would have to demonstrate a clear difference from the work done by their predecessors.

Kundi also stressed that the first order of business was the law and order situation, adding that there should be no hesitation in taking inspiration from other provinces.

Sunday’s directives came after a meeting of the federal cabinet deliberated on the security situation in PTI-led KP. During the meeting, the cabinet noted the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”.

Subsequently, the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and the governor’s rule under Article 234.

Soon after, it also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in the province. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment.

Meanwhile, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre sought to explain that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there.

The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks .

The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations.

World.title: 2 Pakistan Army pilots martyred as training aircraft crashes in Quetta: ISPR
World.content:
Two Pakistan Army pilots were martyred on Monday after a training aircraft crashed in Quetta due to a technical fault, the military’s media wing affairs said.

In a statement, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said: “[At] midday, a Mushshak training aircraft of Pakistan Army Aviation crashed near Nawan Killi, Quetta due to a technical fault.”

It said both pilots, Major Husnain Shehzad Humayun, the instructor, and Captain Abdul Samad, a student, embraced martyrdom in the crash.

President Asif Ali Zardari expressed grief over at the martyrdom of the two pilots and extended his condolences to the bereaved families.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also expressed grief and sorrow over the martyrdom of the two pilots, state-run Associated Press of Pakistan reported.

More to follow

World.title: Suspended KP CM Sohail Afridi, assembly speaker in preventative custody: police
World.content:
Now-suspended Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi and some of his cabinet members were in preventative custody after the Centre imposed emergency and governor’s rule in the province, officials confirmed on Monday.

The federal government took the measures under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution on Sunday, citing the PTI-led KP government’s “deliberate” inaction on countering terrorism. Opposition parties have condemned the move, alleging it is politically motivated.

Following the imposition, the whereabouts of Afridi were unknown to even his party members, with the PTI saying a day ago he had been arrested. However, there was no official confirmation of his detention, although sources said that Afridi and MNA Junaid Akbar were under house arrest under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO).

On Monday, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry told Reuters, “Yes, I can confirm that the chief minister (Sohail Afridi) and some of his cabinet members have been taken into preventive custody.”

If any of them have any cases to be tried against them, they will be charged and tried but the others will be released, he said, adding that the detentions happened on Sunday.

A senior police official privy to the developments also confirmed to Dawn that eight people — including Afridi, Akbar and assembly speaker Babar Saleem Swati — had been taken into “preventative custody”.

On Sunday, PTI spokesperson Sheikh Waqas Akram was quoted as saying that Afridi’s “arrest” could not be viewed in isolation from the federal government’s decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule.

“The arrest of Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and Junaid Akbar has exposed the political nature of the federal government’s actions,” he contended.

“These measures are not directed at addressing security challenges; they are intended to weaken [the] PTI, undermine the elected government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and disregard the democratic will of its people,” Akram added.

In Peshawar, shipping containers blocked several roads, with heavy police deployment. Residents were also impacted by internet disruptions and mobile service suspensions a day earlier.

Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has assumed the role of running the province on behalf of the Centre, with an 11-member technocratic KP Advisory Council formed to assist him.

Chairing the council’s first meeting, Kundi reaffirmed that his top priority was “taking effective steps against terrorism”.

Besides the imposition of emergency, the federal government has also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP.

The emergency follows heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the PTI-led KP government. The Centre and opposition have been at odds over various issues, particularly the counterterrorism policy, which is one of the main reasons cited by both parties behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks .

The move also coincided with the PTI’s planned week-long march to Islamabad, which remained limited to KP. While the party has vowed to continue with its planned protest, the provincial police have been directed to thwart any such move.

World.title: DPM Dar defends emergency and governor's rule in KP, says measures not politically motivated
World.content:
A day after the government imposed governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar defended the move, saying it was not politically motivated but instead taken to curb terrorism.

DPM Dar made the comments while addressing a seminar in Islamabad, a day after the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and the governor’s rule under Article 234 in KP.

The Cabinet recommended the move, citing the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”.

Referring to “recent developments” in the country, Dar said, “It is not a political move; it is surely against the menace of terrorism which that province (KP) has been hit with in the past decade and a half.”

He asked if the Centre could “keep sleeping and looking towards one another because it may be deemed as a political move?

“No, it is not. I can guarantee you.”

Dar recalled that he negotiated with PTI in 2014 during a sit-in in Islamabad.

Defending the move further, Dar held it was the federal government’s responsibility to take such steps “once it is totally determined that there is no solution other than what we have done yesterday”.

He stressed that the ruling party PML-N bore a “heavy political cost” when the country was on the brink of default in 2022.

Dar recalled that the government had to take difficult structural measures. “Political cost was paid, unpopularity was there, and we recovered a lot because we saved the country from the brink of default.”

Dar said the government “had no choice but to take the measures we took yesterday, and we will implement it in totality”.

He hoped the progress would show in the time ahead.

“I am sure the province will be quite happy to see peace restored, their lives are safe and the radicalisation [will end].

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar also spoke at the seminar and defended the federal government’s actions.

Following the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, the federal government also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in the province.

On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment.

On Sunday, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre explained that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there.

The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks .

The previous night, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had posted on X along the same lines, saying that the decision was “neither a political decision nor an easy step”.

He added, “It was a difficult CONSTITUTIONAL course made necessary by the circumstances on the ground.

“When every avenue for cooperation has been exhausted, the Constitution and Pakistan should be the priority.”

He reiterated that the government and its allies had “exhausted every avenue of parliamentary engagement, direct dialogue and back channel diplomacy”.

“KP has borne a heavy burden of terrorism and our security forces and civilians have made immense sacrifices. In these circumstances, cooperation should have been the priority,” Naqvi said.

Pakistan’s desire for peace must not be misconstrued as weakness: Tarar

Tarar, in his address, spoke of counterterrorism, particularly the threat emanating from Afghan soil.

He said that Pakistan wanted peaceful coexistence with Afghanistan, but went on to warn that the country’s desire for peace must not be “misconstrued as weakness”.

Tarar said Pakistan had been at the forefront of the war against terrorism, paying a heavy price in terms of human lives and economic losses.

“No other nation in the world can say that it has lost more than 90,000 lives in the war against terrorism,” he said, adding that Pakistan had suffered economic losses exceeding $100 billion.

“When we represent Pakistan at conferences like this one, we stand before you as ambassadors of peace,” he said, describing Pakistan as a symbol of defiance against violent extremism and resilience against terrorism.

He said Pakistan had acted as a shield between terrorists and the rest of the world, adding that the sacrifices made by Pakistanis in the fight against terrorism contributed to global peace.

“When a Pakistani lays down his or her life fighting terrorism, it is not only to make Pakistan a safer place, but also to contribute to global peace,” he said.

Tarar said Pakistan’s recent role in mediating between the United States and Iran had demonstrated its commitment to peace. He said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, DPM Dar and Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir had made immense efforts to facilitate the mediation process, which had received international recognition.

Given its strategic location and shared border with Afghanistan, Pakistan had always sought regional stability, he said, adding that a peaceful and stable Afghanistan would promote trade with Central Asia, attract foreign investment and strengthen regional cooperation and connectivity.

He said Pakistan had participated in negotiations and engaged with the Afghan interim government to convey its desire for peace and prosperity in the region, particularly in Afghanistan. However, he added, Pakistan’s advice had “fallen on deaf ears”.

Tarar said Pakistan had hosted more than four million Afghan refugees for over four decades and had paid a high price for its generosity. He regretted that Pakistan’s hospitality had not been reciprocated.

He alleged that Afghanistan’s interim rulers believed in violence and extremism, adding that terrorist safe havens existed across the border.

Citing United Nations and independent assessments, he said more than 6,000 Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) terrorists were estimated to be present in Afghanistan, with the total number of terrorists exceeding 20,000.

Since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP has continued to exploit Afghan territory for recruitment, training, facilitation and planning attacks against Pakistan, he said.

Pakistan had responded to these attacks because it could not allow terrorists to use safe havens in Afghanistan to target the country, he added.

Tarar also criticised the restrictions imposed on Afghan women, particularly the denial of their right to education and economic empowerment and their exclusion from the workforce. He said the regime’s interpretation of Islam had led to the denial of basic rights to women and minorities and promoted violent extremism.

Referring to a recent visit to Kohat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where a terrorist attack had taken place, he said he had met injured people at the Combined Military Hospital.

Tarar also referred to the 38th report of the United Nations Monitoring Team, which he said had recorded the relocation of nearly 2,000 family members of TTP terrorists from border areas to locations deeper inside Afghanistan.

“If Afghanistan continues to provide safe havens to these terrorists, how can peace be achieved?” he asked.

He said Pakistan would achieve peace and eradicate terrorism not only within its borders but across the region.

Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

World.title: Pakistan looking to raise more than $1bn under govt push for privatisation, says finance minister
World.content:
The government is looking to push for the privatisation of five to six entities that could raise upwards of $1 billion, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb told Reuters on Monday, stating that he expected the economy to grow by more than 4 per cent this fiscal year despite elevated oil prices.

Pakistan’s economy is considered to be highly vulnerable to a prolonged Middle East conflict given its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing support from the region, even as it remains reliant on external financing to bolster foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments.

Pakistan has been able to procure adequate quantities of fuel, successfully avoiding any shortages, and critical sectors such as agriculture were holding up, Aurangzeb said.

“So I’m still quite clear that we should clock north of 4pc,” he said in an interview on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok.

“And on the inflation side, obviously, we are keeping a very close eye because it does have a knock-on impact in terms of the commodity prices.”

Following a period of severe economic turmoil exacerbated by the Covid-19 pandemic, the cash-strapped economy has recovered some of its footing, supported by a $7bn, 37-month IMF loan program known as the Extended Fund Facility signed in 2024 that includes some tough measures such as raising tax revenue on farm income.

Following the privatisation of flag carrier Pakistan International Airlines last year, Aurangzeb said the government has around another dozen entities in the pipeline, including state-owned power distribution companies and the outsourcing of airport operations.

“I expect about five or six of these to go through during this fiscal year,” he said, adding that they could raise more than $1bn.

Privatisation has been seen as a key test of Pakistan’s reform credibility with the IMF, with officials previously underlining that failure to offload loss-making state firms risked renewed pressure on public finances.

“We are quite clear that we want the private sector to lead the country,” said Aurangzeb. “So our role is to help support, assist any way we can in terms of the ecosystem.”

Exchange stabilisation facility

The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and the inflation and hardship it has caused, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the meetings that are being held outside Washington for the first time in three years.

Pakistan, which reached a staff-level agreement with the IMF last week, potentially unlocking about $1.21bn in financing under the Extended Fund Facility and a climate program, is continuing discussions with the United States for a proposed $10bn exchange stabilisation facility, Aurangzeb said.

But he declined to provide a time frame for the conclusion of negotiations.

“If it comes through, this will be a great help for us,” he said, referring to the facility, which is in addition to ongoing talks with the Export-Import Bank of the United States and the US International Development Finance Corporation.

“If it doesn’t come through, this does not, you know, create any problem for us in terms of access to market.”

World.title: LHC directs jail authorities to provide heart medication to Imran's sister Uzma
World.content:
LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Monday directed jail authorities to provide heart medication to Dr Uzma Khan, sister of PTI founder and former premier Imran Khan.

Imran’s three sisters, Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Uzma, have been in detention for nearly three weeks under the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance (MPO).

Uzma and Noreen were detained for 30 days on September 21, ahead of the party’s Sept 27 protest call, later postponed to October 4. The development came a day after Aleema ’s detention on Sept 20.

On Monday, Justice Abher Gul Khan took up a petition challenging the preventive detention of Imran’s sisters. Sakeena Niazi, daughter of Noreen, had filed the petition on Oct 6.

During the hearing, Uzma’s husband, Ahad Khan, appeared before the court and stated that his wife had a heart condition and needed three medicines daily.

He asked the court to direct the authorities to ensure that the medicines were delivered to her in jail daily.

Petitioner’s counsel Rana Mudassar Umar requested the court to allow Noreen to receive clothes, medicines and spectacles in jail, saying these were basic necessities and her fundamental right.

He also sought permission for family members and lawyers to meet the detained women.

The counsel further requested the court to summon the Lahore Capital City Police Officer and the deputy commissioner in person, arguing that their appearance would help clarify the circumstances surrounding the detention notifications.

After hearing the arguments, the judge ordered the jail authorities to provide medicines to Uzma and reserved decision on the request to summon the officials in person.

In the previous hearing, the LHC sought a report on the provision of medicines, clothes and other basic facilities to the sisters and adjourned the hearing till October 12.

On Sept 24, the LHC had turned down a request to immediately suspend the preventive detention notifications issued against Noreen and Dr Uzma.

Earlier this month, Imran’s cousin, Qasim Zaman, was also taken into custody when he went to Adiala jail to meet the ex-prime minister.

World.title: Pakistani national killed, 11 wounded as Riyadh airport hit by Houthi strike
World.content:
A fresh Houthi strike hit Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday, killing one person — a Pakistani resident — and wounding 11 others, a day after another deadly attack claimed by the Yemeni group forced authorities to suspend operations there.

Saturday’s attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.

The group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom’s transit hubs, calling them “a theatre of operations for our forces”.

Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire.

Air defences also intercepted a missile nearby, it added.

The fresh attack on the airport killed one person — a Pakistani resident — and wounded 11 others, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said on X.

Authorities have extended the closure of the airport by 24 hours until 2100 GMT (2am PKT) on Monday, the tracking site Flightradar24 said on the same platform.

AFP journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the Saudi capital on Sunday.

“The birds went into a frenzy after the sound. The whole house shook,” said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the north of the city.

The civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east — which the Houthis also said they had targeted — a day after the Saudi coalition reported a projectile landing nearby.

Shortly afterwards, the coalition reported shooting down a drone, also in the east.

It said early on Monday that it had also “intercepted and destroyed” a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base.

‘Full-fledged war crime’

The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on the Riyadh airport — where three people were also killed on Thursday — as well as on other key targets in the world’s top crude oil exporter.

And although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through.

“Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves against Houthi attacks,” said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.

The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday’s attack a “full-fledged war crime” and vowed to “respond decisively”.

Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate on Sunday.

Saturday’s attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, also denounced the “horrific terrorist attack”.

Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 wounded.

The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded the day before.

A Riyadh-based Western diplomat told AFP the official number of injured may not give a full picture, as it did not appear to include those with minor wounds.

Operations suspended

Authorities suspended operations at the airport into Sunday, a senior aviation source said, with air traffic monitor Flightradar24 saying the closure was extended until 21:00 GMT (2am PKT on Monday).

A second aviation source confirmed the halt in operations “until further notice”, adding radar and communications equipment was damaged and runways needed to be assessed.

Witnesses to Saturday’s strike described chaos in the aftermath.

“People who were in Terminal 3 started running towards us,” a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP.

“Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood.”

The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors, a medical source said.

The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport, while Australia urged its citizens on Sunday to stay indoors altogether and “shelter in place”.

The Houthis also claimed to have targeted the Dammam airport, whose official website on Sunday showed many flights — both departures and arrivals — were delayed.

‘Rewrite the rules’

Saturday’s airport strike, on the eve of Saudi Arabia’s high-profile convention and entertainment season, was the deadliest attack in the kingdom since a 2015 suicide bombing.

With the summer heat subsiding, October also usually marks the beginning of the high season for Umrah pilgrims, with millions of Muslims from across the world flocking to Makkah.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.

Ottawa University’s Juneau said the Houthis now “want to rewrite the rules of the game”.

“They want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them,” he said.

“So if their airport in Sanaa has to be closed because of the Saudi air embargo, they want to do the same thing to Saudi Arabia.”

On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counter-offensive against the Houthis around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping route, military sources said on Saturday.

The Houthis claimed to have repelled them.

Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

World.title: Unease among Punjab police personnel on reports of deployment in KP
World.content:
LAHORE: The concerns of the Punjab Police personnel, already facing issues of bad food and missing facilities during deployment in Rawalpindi division to counter the PTI march, further deepened on Sunday on the ‘rumours’ that 25,000 of the total 40,000 would be moved from Attock (Punjab) to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa after declaration of an emergency and imposition of the governor’s rule.

Disillusioned by fatigue, lack of sleep and poor living conditions, a Punjab Police officer said, the exhausted police personnel were viewing the expected movement from Attock to KP as a new challenge and a serious trouble for them amid reports of poor facilities.

During the last few weeks, there was a barrage of allegations surfacing against the Rawalpindi division police administration of supplying rotten and stale food to the deployed personnel while reports confirmed death of five policemen during the last two weeks in line of duty at Attock and Wah Cantt in connection with the PTI protest march. Two died of heart attacks, one drowned in a canal, two others died of medical complications while a constable was fighting for life after a snakebite in the jungle.

As per the emerging reports, the police personnel have been complaining about the foul-smelling food, bad catering, poor washroom facilities and risky living conditions during the deployment, particularly in district Attock.

IGP rejects reports, says no decision taken yet; 40,000 cops deployed to counter PTI march face lack of facilities, getting bad food; five lose life in line of duty

Some senior officers also came to the support of their force and held the Rawalpindi police authorities responsible for the mismanagement. A senior officer said the videos recorded by the police personnel regarding the stale food continued to appear on social media with every passing day while the local police administration dubbed them merely ‘a conspiracy by some individual employees’ instead of resolving the problems.

Some recordings showed insects or worms in food served to the force with personnel raising the issue. Most complaints were related to the foul-smelling food, poor catering and washroom facilities.

Quoting some internal reports, the officer said that the Rawalpindi police top brass exchanged arguments with some senior officers of Punjab Police who highlighted the issue. The senior officers had arrived from other regions of the province to command their respective police force in Attock and Wah Cantt.

About the deployment in KP, Punjab Inspector General of Police Abdul Kareem clarified that no final decision had been taken or any directive was issued for the relocation of the police force from Punjab to KP.

“Although no final decision has been made yet to send the force to KP, if it happens, we will make it public officially,” he told Dawn.

Regarding bad quality of food, he said steps to provide quality food to the force at Attock and Wah Cantt were being taken on a priority basis. He rejected the allegations of supply of adulterated food ‘on a large scale,’ terming the reports incorrect.

“When complaints were inquired into, one of the police employees was caught mixing water in the food deliberately,” said Mr Kareem. Even then, he added, the Punjab Food Authority (PFA) had been tasked with checking the food quality and it had fielded teams to ensure provision of hygienic food and drinking water.

The IGP confirmed the deaths of five personnel, saying, “Five police employees have lost their lives during the last two-week security deployment at Attock and Wah Cantt”. He identified them as constables Zulfiqar Ahmed, Zain Ali, Muhammad Imran, Muhammad Shahzad and Usman Idrees.

“Two of them were martyred due to heart attack while one of them – Zain Ali - accidentally drowned after slipping into Ghazi Canal. The two other police personnel died in the line of duty due to severe medical complications,” the IG says.

He rejected the reports about the death of a police employee by a snakebite, saying he was under treatment.

Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
