World.title: Crackdown exposes limits of Modi’s playbook for maintaining power
World.content:
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has long cultivated an image abroad as the popular elected leader of the world’s largest democracy, a sober voice of peace in a world of violence.

He has balanced that role at home in India with another penchant, as a strongman whose lieutenants have wielded the arms of the state at dissenters, exploiting an increasingly pliant legal system and bureaucracy. These efforts have undercut and splintered the opposition, cowed independent media and jailed activists.

On Saturday, Modi’s balancing act broke down as violent scenes across the capital city were beamed to screens around the world, exposing the rough edges of his rule and the limits of his formula for maintaining power.

World.title: War is forcing the world to reckon with geography’s power
World.content:
For decades we have lived in a world that seemed to transcend geography.

Information, money, goods, germs and weapons have come to defy distance. Whispered confidences and billion-dollar bounties are traded instantaneously. Smartphones, satsumas and sandals are delivered to your doorstep from across the globe. Ballistic missiles are able to traverse continents in minutes.

But such everyday assumptions have been challenged by the economic havoc wrought by the blockage of a single vital shipping and energy route in the Persian Gulf.

World.title: UNRWA warns Gaza is becoming an increasingly unlivable place
World.content:
Gaza is “becoming an increasingly unlivable place for humans” due to Israel’s large-scale military operations, a senior official from the U.N. Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) has said.

Akihiro Seita, head of the U.N. agency’s health department, was interviewed online, ahead of the one-year anniversary of the ceasefire deal between Israel and Hamas, which came into effect on Oct. 10.

The Israeli military’s large-scale operations began in October 2023 and have left over 74,000 people dead in Gaza. Reconstruction has been slow in the Palestinian territory mainly due to Israeli troops continuing attacks and occupying a vast area of the territory even after the ceasefire agreement.

The Israeli military is believed to have seized control of about 70% of Gaza, expanding beyond the areas agreed by the two sides in the deal. About 2 million Gaza residents have been forced to live in the remaining 30% of the territory, most of them in tents.

Gaza faces persistent shortages of medical supplies due to delivery restrictions. Hygiene conditions also remain dire even under the ceasefire, as the territory has been hit by skin and other infectious diseases. “Residents’ living environment has fallen apart,” Seita said.

Akihiro Seita, head of the U.N. Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East's health department, during an online interview on Sept. 25 | JIJI

While food rations have reached some residents since the deal, Seita said that impoverished residents continue to lack food, and that malnutrition remains an issue.

In August last year, before the ceasefire, famine became a major issue in Gaza City, the center of the Gaza Strip. A follow-up survey by UNRWA found that some infants who had been malnourished during that period showed developmental delays in talking and walking.

“Even though combat has decreased, the children’s plight continues,” Seita said.

According to Seita, the international community’s shift in focus from the Gaza situation to U.S.-Israeli military attacks against Iran, which began in late February this year, has become a major point of concern. The people of Gaza are “worried that no one is willing to help them,” he said.

Although Hamas, which maintains effective control over Gaza, has expressed its willingness to disarm, Israel is doubtful and refuses to withdraw its troops from Gaza. This has made it difficult to implement a Gaza peace plan compiled under the initiative of U.S. President Donald Trump.

The United States has suspended funding for UNRWA, and the organization is excluded from the framework of the peace plan. Nevertheless, it continues to provide aid to Gaza using its organizational strength developed over many years of on-the-ground activities.

World.title: Taiwan says it is closely monitoring a series of Chinese live-fire drills
World.content:
Taiwanese defense minister Wellington Koo said on Monday that the island is monitoring a series of Chinese live-fire drills taking place along that country’s coast this week.

Starting from Thursday, the China Maritime Safety Administration announced no-sail notices for five areas, from the South China Sea up to the northeastern province of Liaoning, though none around Taiwan itself.

The closest one to Taiwan is off China’s eastern province of Zhejiang. The drills are scheduled to last all week, according to the notices.

Speaking to reporters in parliament, Koo said the preliminary assessment is that these activities were firing drills by coastal artillery and related units.

“However, we adhere to the principle of ’anticipating the enemy as broadly as possible,’ so we will continue to closely monitor their activities, whether firing or military training,” he said.

President Lai Ching-te, in his National Day speech on Saturday, said Taiwan cherishes peace but will not give up its freedom, and there must be respect for the right of Taiwan’s people to exist.

China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, condemned his remarks, as it always does. China views Lai as a “separatist” and has rebuffed his repeated offers of talks.

While China has not linked the drills this week to Lai’s speech, on Sunday the country’s defense ministry said he was exaggerating the threat from China and trying to “seek independence through force.”

“The People’s Liberation Army’s regular training and exercises around Taiwan are meant to deter reckless ’Taiwan independence’ moves and outside interference, and to safeguard the security and well-being of the Taiwanese people. This is entirely justified,” it said.

China’s military operates around Taiwan on an almost daily basis, though it has not held full war games since late December, which were in response to an $11 billion arms sale announced by Washington, the largest ever.

Last week, the U.S. State Department said China’s maritime actions off Taiwan’s east coast are “deeply destabilizing” and only worsen tension, after Reuters reported the first known sighting of a Chinese militia boat in those waters in August.

Speaking in Beijing on Monday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said those waters belonged to China and its activities there were “beyond reproach.”

“It has never been China that stirs up trouble and undermines stability in this sea,” she told reporters, without elaborating.

Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future, and that Beijing has no right to claim the island as its territory.

World.title: IMF chief warns of threat from AI to jobs and taxes
World.content:
The head of the International Monetary Fund has warned of the disruptive threat from artificial intelligence to the labor market and taxation, urging policymakers to rethink education and act now to help society adapt.

“It is a slow-moving tsunami, but tsunami none the less,” Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Monday during her first appearance at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.

Speaking at a session on AI’s impact on employment, she said the technology is already hollowing out demand for many human workers by taking over routine, repetitive tasks. At the same time, it is increasing low-paying jobs in sectors like construction, which she said is “not a story to celebrate.”

It’s a transformation with far-reaching consequences for public finances, Georgieva said. The risk is that AI strains government revenues by tilting the economy toward capital and away from labor — traditionally the main source of tax income.

The comments are the latest warning about the potential shock from AI on jobs and the global economy. Young workers in AI-exposed fields have already seen a slowdown in hiring, leaving new entry-level applicants far more vulnerable. Concern is also growing that the technology will widen inequality, with its gains so far concentrated among a narrow set of workers and economies despite a global investment super-cycle.

“We cannot today imagine what exactly the world of work will be five years from now,” she said. “But we can be disciplined and carefully assess what is happening, and then draw lessons, but — most importantly — act on them now.”

Despite the employment headwinds, the technology can ultimately prove a positive for growth overall. The IMF estimates the spread of AI can add up to a percentage point to growth in advanced Asian economies.

Such a growth boost “is a very big deal,” Georgieva said, adding it will “more than offset” the drag from aging in rich countries across the region.

World.title: China’s $7.5 billion EU hybrid boom faces new curbs under deal with bloc
World.content:
China’s deal with the European Union to curb exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc is a fresh hit to Chinese EV makers that have ramped up hybrid shipments exempt from EU tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, as sales growth slows at home.

China’s exports of hybrids to the EU’s 27 member states tripled to $7.5 billion in the first half of this year from $2.5 billion a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. The figure was nearly nine times the $845 million exported in all of 2021.

Since the EU imposed additional tariffs on Chinese-made EVs in 2024, Chinese automakers have increasingly turned to plug-in hybrids, which are exempt from the extra duties. Weak charging infrastructure in parts of Europe has also supported demand for plug-in hybrids, which are marketed for their long range and strong fuel economy.

World.title: French defense firm Thales to build Japan base, media report says
World.content:
French defense contractor Thales will establish a maintenance and operational support base in Japan in what is seen as the first such move by a foreign firm in the country, a report said Monday.

Thales Chairman and CEO Patrice Caine told the Nikkei business daily that the base “will mark a milestone toward Thales’s long-term engagement in Japan.”

It is believed to be the first time a foreign defense company has established a dedicated base in Japan for the maintenance and operation of Japanese defense equipment, the Nikkei said.

It added that Thales may also expand its Japan-based business to civilian use in the future.

The report comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi boosts defense spending in the face of China’s rapid military expansion and an unpredictable North Korea, moving away from the traditional pacifist stance that limited the use of force to self-defense.

Thales already supplies equipment to the Self-Defense Forces, the Nikkei said.

Caine cited technologies such as radar and sonar as possible areas to share with Japan, saying that he hoped to “provide support in areas where Thales has an advantage in terms of performance.”

Thales will transfer its technology to partner Japan Steel Works and production of the 2R2M heavy mortar system will begin in Japan from next year, the Nikkei said.

World.title: Tokyo police to set up section for autonomous driving accidents
World.content:
Tokyo’s Metropolitan Police Department plans to set up next spring a section dedicated to the investigation and prevention of accidents involving autonomous driving, the force has said.

High-level knowledge and skills are necessary to investigate the causes of such accidents and the Tokyo police hope to accumulate expertise and share it with police departments in other prefectures amid the spread of autonomous driving trials held across the country.

The new section, to be created within the police department’s traffic bureau, will be in charge of handling applications for Level 4 services — under which a system handles all driving operations under specified conditions — as well as investigating accidents and advocating accident prevention.

Taxi-hailing app operator Go, U.S. self-driving technology firm Waymo and taxi operator Nihon Kotsu announced in September that they will jointly launch driverless taxi services in Tokyo in 2027, marking Japan’s first such commercial service.

The service would use Level 4 autonomous driving and the companies plan to expand the fleet to about 100 vehicles gradually.

The government aims to increase the number of buses, taxis and trucks operating with autonomous driving services to 10,000 vehicles in fiscal 2030.

Translated by The Japan Times

World.title: Ex-US FDA official to lead Hong Kong’s new medical products regulator
World.content:
A Beijing-educated former official at the US federal drug regulator has been appointed to lead Hong Kong’s new medical products body, tasked with accelerating the clinical use of medicines and medical devices as part of a regulatory overhaul.

Li Zili, who previously worked at the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), would take up the post of controller for medical products regulation under the Department of Health on a three-year term beginning October 20, the government said on Monday.

He will lead the Centre for Medical Products Regulation, to be established later this year, which aims to promote proactive “primary evaluation”, speed up the clinical application of drugs and medical devices, and give patients access to advanced products that meet quality and safety standards.

World.title: Hong Kong domestic helper arrested for alleged murder of 93-year-old employer
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested a domestic helper on suspicion of murdering her 93-year-old employer, a cancer survivor, with an investigation suggesting she was repeatedly assaulted in the hours before her death.

The elderly woman was found unresponsive in her flat in Long Yiu House at Tak Long Estate in Ngau Tau Kok on Sunday morning, police said.

The 52-year-old helper, hired to provide round-the-clock care for the woman, sought help from building security staff at about 8.20am, saying her employer was unresponsive and needed an ambulance.

Paramedics rushed the woman to hospital after performing emergency treatment at the scene but she was pronounced dead at 9.12am.

World.title: ‘A pack of lies’: Abby Choi’s mother rejects claims Kwong family repaid her debts
World.content:
The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has denied in court that she was repeatedly in debt because of gambling, calling her former son-in-law’s claim that he had financially supported her “a pack of lies”.

Cheung Yin-fa accused Alex Kwong Kong-chi on Monday of acting unscrupulously by demanding the return of HK$150,000 in shopping expenses she owed him, while failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million he had received from Choi for investment.

Testifying in the High Court for a fifth day, Cheung also rejected the defence’s suggestion that she was so addicted to mahjong that Choi had to pledge a property she received as a wedding gift to secure a HK$4 million mortgage to repay her mother’s debts.

Cheung appeared emotional as she responded to the defence’s contention that Kwong, who said he had run a restaurant in mainland China and worked as a parallel betting agent in Macau, had helped repay her debts and supported her over the years.

World.title: US can choose to deport Hongkongers under Deferred Enforced Departure scheme
World.content:
US authorities could deport Hong Kong residents granted extended stay under the Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) programme and have not ruled out the option of doing so after a dozen were reportedly detained at local airports.

“The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is not precluded from placing aliens with such temporary administrative designation into removal proceedings, nor is it currently removing them,” a department spokesman said in a reply to the South China Morning Post on Sunday evening.

“Work authorisation or a pending application do not confer legal status in the United States.”

The remarks followed a report by US media outlet Politico that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents had detained at least a dozen Hong Kong residents under the DED programme at local airports.

World.title: Minibus driver hospitalised, 18 others injured, after collision with goods truck
World.content:
A minibus driver has been hospitalised after her vehicle collided with a medium goods truck in Hong Kong, causing injuries to 18 others.

Police said the accident occurred at around 9.22am on Monday, when a green minibus and a medium goods truck collided on San Tin Highway on the Yuen Long-bound side of the road near Fairview Park.

According to police, nine men and 10 women were injured in the crash. The accident prompted authorities to close two lanes of the road, leading to severe traffic congestion.

“Two men from the truck were injured, while the remaining injured were the driver and passengers from the minibus,” a police spokeswoman said, adding that the minibus driver was briefly trapped inside the wreckage before being rescued.

World.title: Trump’s China-savvy spokeswoman, Hong Kong trail emergencies: 5 weekend reads you missed
World.content:
Trump’s China-savvy spokeswoman, Hong Kong trail emergencies: 5 weekend reads you missed

From a museum replica sparking US-China collaboration to Malaysian doctors shunning Borneo, here are five stories you may have missed over the weekend

World.title: ‘Just a little spark’: disability advocate on inclusion, belonging in Hong Kong
World.content:
Greater awareness of disability in Hong Kong has not necessarily made it easier for people with disabilities to find work, according to advocate Faride Shroff, who says tighter corporate budgets and a difficult job market have made the next stage of inclusion more challenging.

Shroff, founder of SENsational Foundation, said employers that recruited people with disabilities also needed to provide guidance, suitable workplace arrangements and roles that matched individual strengths.

“Every person has got certain skills,” she said. “It is finding those skills and matching them to the right job.”

World.title: Hong Kong’s ‘AI city brain’ could undergo testing next typhoon season: Eric Chan
World.content:
Hong Kong’s artificial intelligence management system could take shape and be tested as early as the typhoon season next year, the government’s No 2 official has said, adding that the project will give authorities a “full picture” of the city once it is in full swing.

In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post, Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki said the “ AI city brain ” system aimed to connect independent databases maintained by different government bodies.

“With the invention of AI, I think it is a good idea to connect them together, so that we can have a full picture of Hong Kong,” he said.

The data includes traffic information, flood monitoring and drainage systems, landslide warning systems, weather information and public inquiries and complaints under the 1823 hotline.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019108/China Drafts Landmark Gig Worker Labor Rights Rules
World.title: China Drafts Landmark Gig Worker Labor Rights Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019108/China Drafts Landmark Gig Worker Labor Rights Rules
World.content:
China has drafted its first departmental rules on gig workers’ labor rights, strengthening protections for platform-based flexible employees such as food delivery riders.

The draft, released by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security on Oct. 8, is open for online public feedback until Nov. 8.

The proposal comes as flexible employment grows in China, with the number of people in flexible employment — including those who rely on internet platforms to earn a living — projected to reach 320 million this year, according to the China New Employment Research Center. Gig work has also come under fire for subjecting workers to excessive hours, opaque algorithms, and gaps in social security coverage.

In 2021, China introduced its first guidelines clarifying platforms’ responsibilities toward gig workers regarding employment, remuneration, social security, and workplace safety. In 2024, the country issued related guiding cases, and this July, it expanded occupational injury insurance for gig workers.

Under the new draft, platforms and their partner businesses must sign labor contracts with workers that meet the legal criteria for employment relationships, such as full-time employees. It excludes people who use online platforms to run their own businesses independently or offer freelance services on their own terms.

For workers in more flexible arrangements, such as part-time work or work across multiple platforms, platforms must sign written employment agreements specifying pay, labor protections, and liability for breaking the agreement, among others. When platform companies and partner businesses jointly manage workers, all three parties must sign a written agreement.

The draft also clarifies dispute resolution procedures. Platforms bear primary responsibility for overseeing partner businesses’ employment practices, and workers involved in legal disputes may name both the platform and its partner as parties to a case. When workers challenge pay, working hours, performance reviews, or account bans, companies must investigate and respond within 48 hours.

Platforms must also build reasonable task-allocation systems and performance metrics into their algorithms, avoid encouraging excessive work through targets or incentives, and explain relevant algorithmic rules to workers and authorities.

Decisions with “significant consequences for workers,” including suspending work assignments or banning accounts, must also undergo human review.

The draft further states that employers will face legal responsibilities and penalties for violations under existing legislation. For instance, employers may be required to pay outstanding wages, overtime pay, or economic compensation. If wages fall below the local minimum wage, employers must pay the difference.

“The draft’s biggest breakthrough is placing workers who are under the management of platforms but do not fully fit into an employment relationship under protections, and applying past traditional labor laws to flexible platform-based work,” Wang Tianyu, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Law, wrote in a related commentary.

“At the same time, it establishes mechanisms to hold companies accountable and prevent them from evading employment obligations, such as through subcontracting or inducing workers to register as individual businesses,” he said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019032/In China’s Universities, Students Are Majoring in Second Chances
World.title: In China’s Universities, Students Are Majoring in Second Chances
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019032/In China’s Universities, Students Are Majoring in Second Chances
World.content:
Until this spring, Weng Yujia was studying management because of its supposed job prospects. At the same university in Shanghai, Lin Yuanhao studied international relations and public affairs, presented as the best option based on her college entrance exam score.

Today, both now study Chinese language and literature.

Within weeks of starting university, Weng had soured on management and its math- and science-heavy coursework. “I just plain disliked” many required classes, she said, adding that she struggled to see some of their educational value.

Lin had wanted to study Chinese language and literature from the start, but her college entrance exam score fell short of the cutoff. By the time she switched majors, a sixth of the roughly 120 students enrolled in her international relations course had moved to other fields, mostly economics, management, or law.

“Changing majors is like giving students a second chance to choose,” she told Sixth Tone.

Across China, more students are making that choice as universities give them greater freedom to reconsider majors they picked under pressure from college entrance exams, parental expectations, or worries about future employment.

For years, changing majors was difficult, with universities limiting transfers or requiring students to meet strict grade and class-rank thresholds. It wasn’t until 2005 that, for the first time at the national level, the Ministry of Education issued a new regulation allowing students to change majors if their universities agreed.

National rules were further loosened in 2017, when students with an “interest or particular strength in another field” were explicitly allowed to apply for transfers.

This June, several schools nationwide eased transfer caps and academic requirements, while Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, in the southwestern Sichuan province, has allowed 2026 entrants to earn a degree in a different major by taking its required courses. At Wuhan University, in central China’s Hubei province, more than 600 undergraduates switched majors in 2025 and over 70% of cross-college applications were approved, a record high.

As transfers become more common, more students will have to decide whether starting over is worth the trade-offs. Changing course can still mean entrance exams, lost credits, extra years of study, and difficult conversations with parents, all before they know whether the new major will prove a better fit.

Take two

On her college applications, Weng initially ranked management as her top major — a factor universities consider alongside cutoff scores when granting admission — because of its solid job prospects. In contrast, Lin listed Chinese language and literature as her top choice, but her score on China’s national college entrance exam, the gaokao, did not meet the cutoff.

At Weng and Lin’s university, transfer requirements differ by department. The Chinese department, which both transferred into, weighs GPA at a relatively high 70%, alongside an admissions interview, partially in English, with department faculty at 30%. To prepare for the transfer, Lin also self-studied traditional Chinese characters and took courses in the Chinese department.

After the two were notified of their own transfer acceptances this spring, they watched as others in their circles followed the trend. Several of Weng’s friends at other Chinese schools changed majors: one switched from French to chemistry, while another went from civil engineering to biological sciences.

Chen, a 22-year-old tourism management major at Jiaying University, in the southern Guangdong province, initially majored in English education because her parents told her to.

But by the end of her first semester, she felt the major was a bad fit. “I don’t like teaching, and I’m not interested in psychology or education either,” she said.

She decided to transfer to tourism management after a friend in the department told her about it. Chen felt the major would fit her personality: describing herself as “outgoing” and “drawn to challenges,” she said her dream is to travel the world.

She consulted others who had transferred to tourism management about the GPA requirement and the pressure to catch up on the curriculum. Some told her the major was a bad choice, while others were incredulous as to why she’d want to transfer. Chen’s parents were also initially opposed, but later came around after she explained her rationale.

To transfer majors, Chen had to take an entrance exam and undergo an interview with department faculty — both of which she passed. Now a senior in the tourism management department, she has no regrets and is preparing to take the entrance exam to pursue a master’s in the same field.

A philosophy faculty member involved in major transfers at a top Shanghai university, who asked to remain anonymous, sees the trend growing because students want to have more choices.

He said he supports universities offering major transfers, noting that gaokao score cutoffs keep students out of fields that might suit them and that they know what they like and what fits them better after taking courses in college.

However, he cautioned that transferring majors is not a decision to be taken lightly. “Students shouldn’t see it as a way to obtain better prospects or a better way out,” he said. “That leads them to (transfer majors) for utilitarian reasons rather than their own ideas.”

Long road

But switching majors can come with its own set of challenges.

Wu Wenjun, another student in Shanghai, was accepted as a transfer student from history into her dream major, law — something she hadn’t gotten into originally due to her gaokao score. The law school had a steep requirement, however: to earn her degree, Wu would have to drop down a grade and spend four years on top of the year she had already completed as a history major.

Wu was prepared to make that time sacrifice — even if it meant future employers might assume she had delayed graduation and look down on her application, a common phenomenon in China. If the transfer fell through, she was also prepared to delay graduation by a year to finish her original history degree, since she had taken only law by that point.

Now a senior in law school, Wu said she sometimes struggles with how much she has to memorize. She also said she finds law especially competitive. And when she switched majors as a sophomore, Wu felt she trailed her classmates, many of whom had already begun interning at prestigious law firms.

But being a transfer student has had upsides too. Wu said the five-year graduation requirement brought unexpected benefits, including lighter course loads each term, since she had already completed various general graduation requirements during her first year as a history student.

Wu has also found internship interviewers to be fairly understanding once they learned she had transferred rather than delayed graduation. She notes that personal advantages also matter greatly to law firms, not just how long it took to graduate. Her English proficiency, for example, gives her an edge at foreign firms. “In law, you don’t have to stand at the top of the pyramid and be number one to find a job,” Wu said.

The Shanghai philosophy instructor noted that students who transfer majors often have one more year of experience than their peers, richer résumés, and greater freedom in course arrangements.

He observed that many students who transfer into philosophy are more enthusiastic and motivated than students who have been in the program longer. He attributed this to transfer students’ “second choice” feeling like a “rebirth” in learning, and they cherish their opportunities more.

Looking back, Wu said her transfer gave her more room for error, but added that as another one-time option, it also carries risk.

She hopes the transfer process will eventually look different: students take courses in a certain major, discover they are suited to or interested in it, and then decide to transfer. “It’s best to go with what suits you and what you like,” she said.

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo; editors: Marianne Gunnarsson and Apurva.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019103/Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.title: Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019103/Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.content:
Two books translated into English from Chinese have been shortlisted for the 2026 U.S. National Translation Awards, which recognize excellence in both original and translated literary works.

The shortlist, announced Tuesday by the American Literary Translators Association, includes two originally written in Chinese: Chinese author Shuang Xuetao’s short story collection “Hunter,” translated by Jeremy Tiang, and Hong Kong writer Hon Lai Chu’s “Mending Bodies,” translated by Jacqueline Leung, among a total of 11 poetry and prose works translated from nine languages.

“The Ruins,” an anthology by Chinese poet Ye Hui and translated by Li Dong, was longlisted among 23 works across prose and poetry on Sept. 3 but did not make the shortlist. Ye is known for his spare, understated poems that draw on everyday life and nature and explore questions of time, memory, and existence.

Established in 1998, the awards rank among the world’s top professional accolades for literary translation. Winning translators in both categories — poetry and prose — each receive a $4,000 prize. Translations of Chinese works have previously been listed for the prize, including works by contemporary writers Xu Zechen and Yan Lianke, as well as Qing dynasty (1644–1911) novelist and playwright Li Yu.

Shuang Xuetao, author of “Hunter,” one of the two shortlisted Chinese works, was born in 1983 in Shenyang, capital of the northeastern Liaoning province. He is widely considered a leading figure in the “Dongbei Renaissance,” a cultural movement emerging from northeast China, or Dongbei. Known for his use of local dialect, Shuang often portrays the lives of ordinary people in the region, long dismissed as a cultural backwater and rust belt. Several of his works have been adapted into films.

“Hunter” features 11 standalone stories, some of which were originally written in Dongbei dialect: from provincial ambulance drivers searching for a hospital in the middle of the night, to a legendary knife fighter working in a factory. In a note about their selection published alongside the announcement, the competition’s judges wrote that Shuang’s stories “paint a portrait of a region marked by gritty pragmatism, dark humor, and magical realism.”

The work was translated by Shuang’s long-term collaborator Jeremy Tiang — a novelist in his own right. The judges wrote that Tiang “expertly translated Shuang’s often inventive, utterly unique description; his English texts are layered and witty.”

The second book nominated for the prize, “Mending Bodies” by Hong Kong writer Hon Lai Chu, is a work of speculative fiction and follows a young woman adjusting to life after surgically binding her body to a partner, in a future where people are encouraged to do so. Hon has previously drawn praise for her surreal, introspective fiction, which often explores the fragility of the body, memory, and human relationships.

According to the judges, Jacqueline Leung, the book’s Hong Kong-based translator, “flawlessly translates the between-the-lines subtleties of the languages.”

“The shortlisting of these works carries substantial significance for the overseas circulation of Sinophone literature and its greater visibility within global professional literary circuits, representing, in a sense, a multifaceted retelling of Chinese stories across fiction and poetry,” Shao Dong, an assistant professor of creative writing at Hong Kong Metropolitan University, told Sixth Tone.

The overall award winners will be announced on Oct. 23 as part of the American Literary Translators Association’s annual conference.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Covers of “Hunter,” “Mending Bodies,” and “The Ruins,” by Shuang Xuetao, Hon Lai Chu, and Ye Hui, respectively. Reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.title: ‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.content:
The thieves came in the dead of night in late August — seven ghostly figures illuminated only by the glow of their flashlights and burning cigarettes. When they left, tucked under their arms were 10 chickens and two geese.

The next day, watching footage of the theft recorded by a security camera, Xu Lingni’s heart sank. It was the end of a dream.

The poultry had been kept overnight in a hilltop coop at the bucolic Huxi campus of the Sichuan Fine Arts Institute (SCFAI), in the southwestern megacity of Chongqing, and belonged to the Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative, a student-led club aimed at rebuilding the bonds between humans and nature.

The group had intended to use the project to promote interest across campus and beyond in food-waste conversion, community-supported agriculture, plastics consumption, and other sustainability issues.

For Xu, the club’s leader, those plans vanished along with those 12 birds. Yet worse was to come.

After a brief investigation, the Chongqing police discovered that several workers hired by SCFAI for a summer construction project had taken the poultry and eaten them. Their crew manager agreed to pay 7,000 yuan ($1,040) to compensate for the financial loss and the students’ emotional distress.

However, the theft drew widespread attention and sparked fresh criticism over raising animals on campus. Facing mounting pressure, the school’s leadership decided to ban the practice. The cooperative was over.

Hatching a plan

The Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative was a key part of the Healing Garden Project, which inhabits a patch of land on campus once piled high with construction waste. Seven years ago, Jin Lipeng, an associate professor in SCFAI’s School of Experimental Art, led students in repurposing the debris to pave paths and build planting beds. He envisioned an area that could restore nature and nurture people.

At the time, the campus cafeteria was sending hundreds of kilograms of food scraps — often mixed with unsorted plastic waste — to an incinerator dozens of kilometers away. Jin and his students began to use these leftovers as compost, converting roughly 40 tons of food waste into fertilizer over the years.

The idea for the cooperative stemmed from a graduate student’s thesis project in spring 2025 that looked at permaculture and the role of foraging chickens in loosening soil, eating pests, clearing weeds, and providing eggs. To test a theory, the student purchased five chickens of a local breed with red combs and black skin. They were allowed to roam freely through campus and returned at night to their hilltop coop.

Xu, an undergraduate majoring in sculpture, was already involved in the garden project and began informally caring for the chickens, buying them grain and taking them to the veterinarian.

In summer last year, as temperatures soared above 40 degrees Celsius, one bird died of heatstroke, and three others disappeared. Fearing that the sole survivor would get lonely, Xu bought a new one from the market. Then one of the escapees returned.

A few days later, Xu found six new adolescent chickens in the coop. A school janitor, who had bought them to raise for their meat, agreed to sell the birds to the students. These were soon joined by a common chicken brought from a roadside stall, a Plymouth Rock chicken, a new hatchling, and a wuhei black-boned chicken. (Two birds died before the theft — one from hypothermia, the other from a wild animal attack. The wuhei chicken was the only one left behind by the thieves; its dark plumage likely made it hard to spot at night.)

As the flock grew, the birds began producing more eggs than the students could eat. Jin, whose research area includes labor issues, proposed creating the cooperative as a student club and asked Xu to lead it. Soon, the students were dividing up their responsibilities: caring for the animals, sourcing and selling merchandise, writing articles, and managing social media channels. In June this year, several attended an international conference to introduce the cooperative’s work.

Those who joined the project felt that caring for the chickens brought them “healing energy.” Xu recalls one classmate who would often hold the birds and cry. “The theft this summer hit her especially hard, and she wasn’t the only one,” Xu says, adding that the cooperative not only fostered friendships but also helped some members find meaning.

While she doesn’t exactly share Jin’s grand ideals, Xu believes that through her work she came to understand seemingly distant but deeply personal issues such as permaculture and climate change.

“Most university students have no idea where eggs come from, what happens to food waste, or why rubbish gets incinerated,” she said in a speech at a climate change forum in May. “Dorm rooms are piled with takeout plastic. Delivery workers risk heatstroke in extreme temperatures. Yet few students have enough awareness to connect these to drought, heat, and carbon emissions.

“Our work lets people feel the pressure and causes of climate change firsthand,” she added, “and shows that through campus community-supported agriculture we can mount a small resistance.”

Making a mess

The cooperative began selling eggs for about 2 yuan each to residents on and around campus this March. The chickens laid two to eight eggs a day. Xu stored them in her apartment’s refrigerator, took orders through an online group chat, and delivered them to customers on her electric bike. She calculates that this brought in just over 500 yuan in total.

Fans of the project were kept up to date through the club’s channel on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, which has more than 6,300 followers. In addition, the cooperative sold themed merchandise including fridge magnets, tote bags, and silk scarves, which brought in about 2,000 yuan.

Not everyone was supportive, though. The most common complaint was that the free-roaming chickens often defecated on the pathways and at the entrance to the student dormitories. To prevent this, this summer the birds were fenced in on the hillside.

In 2022, Chongqing introduced regulations prohibiting the raising of livestock and poultry in urban areas. However, the restrictions apply only to commercial-scale farming, while exceptions can be made for educational purposes and scientific research.

While the number of chickens at SCFAI was far below commercial scale, the activity fell outside the definition of “backyard rearing,” putting it in a gray area. As such, the school took an open-minded approach, requiring only proper fencing and separation, despite repeated objections from others in the campus community.

The cooperative used old bamboo posts and tall netting to enclose the poultry on the hilltop. But the gate was never locked. “This is a public welfare project. Anyone was welcome to come in to spend time with the chickens,” Xu explains.

For security, the group installed an infrared camera to watch the flock at night and raised two goslings to guard the coop. “Geese bite hard. Once I went up the hill in a raincoat, and they didn’t recognize me, so they bit me,” Xu adds. “We’d thought the intruders would be stray cats or weasels — never thieves.”

Ruffling feathers

The theft sparked an outpouring of grief online. “Come home, little ones” and “My babies are gone” were typical comments posted by students in the aftermath.

In the coming weeks and months, Xu and her classmates had planned to step up marketing and sales, offer egg-based food delivery services, and write a handbook on community supported agriculture that could inspire other schools and universities.

That’s now all been scrapped. This fall, the school’s leadership announced a ban on keeping poultry on campus.

In a statement, it also said that officials had learned during mediation that the maintenance workers who took the birds had endured long hours of intense labor in hot weather, with limited food and lodging. Some students strongly objected to this version of events, arguing that chicken meat is cheap and widely available — and that the workers weren’t “desperate,” they just wanted to taste free-range birds.

“Pioneering ecological practice is inherently accompanied by trial and error and waiting,” the statement read. “We will review and consolidate, continue deepening our existing work, and wait for the right conditions to restart explorations.”

The cooperative maintained that its activities “filled a gap” in the school’s labor education by giving students hands-on experience as well as teaching responsibility and empathy. But there was no overturning the decision.

The sole survivor of the theft, the wuhei chicken, was moved to a student’s home for safekeeping and has quickly adapted to her new environment. Xu says the bird is even laying eggs again.

(Due to privacy concerns, Xu Lingni is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Kong Lingyu.

A version of this article originally appeared in FoodThink. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.title: China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.content:
DeepZang, China’s first Tibetan-language large language model, is being upgraded to better adapt to Tibetan dialects, enable real-time translation between Tibetan and Mandarin Chinese, and support offline use.

At a Monday seminar in Hohhot, capital of northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, the model’s developer unveiled a series of upgrades scheduled between October and December. The seminar featured representatives from companies, research institutions, and universities.

DeepZang, developed by local technology company Choknor, was launched in March in Lhasa, capital of the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region. Its app supports AI-powered conversations, translation, and speech transcription in Tibetan, Mandarin Chinese, and English.

At the model’s launch, organizations including the Xizang branches of China Mobile and the People’s Insurance Company of China, as well as Sichuan Minzu Publishing House, signed agreements with Choknor to promote its adoption.

According to Choknor, DeepZang has attracted nearly 400,000 users across Xizang, the northwestern Qinghai and Gansu provinces, and southwestern Sichuan province, where most of China’s Tibetan speakers reside.

The company has said the model has cut the time needed for some Tibetan-Chinese translation tasks involving two or three people from 40 minutes to just over 10 minutes for one person. It also reported that the model has been used in such varied settings as helping non-Tibetan-speaking doctors communicate with local patients, generating Tibetan-language contracts for yak sales, and assisting grassroots officials in drafting Tibetan work reports.

The model has been trained on nearly 70 million pairs of standardized Tibetan and Chinese texts, along with more than 30,500 hours of Tibetan speech covering its three major dialect groups — Ü-Tsang, Kham, and Amdo. The team collected the data from libraries, medical institutions, and monasteries, among other settings.

At Monday’s seminar, Choknor unveiled plans to develop offline language packages for Tibetan, Chinese, and English, allowing the app to function with limited or no internet access. The company also plans to pilot 50 simultaneous interpretation devices among at least 300 participants in Lhasa this December.

Tenzin Norbu, Choknor’s founder, said the company aims to bring DeepZang into “pastoral tents, tourist service counters, and grassroots hospitals,” enabling Tibetan speakers to “enjoy the benefits of artificial intelligence on an equal footing.”

Choknor said on Sunday that beyond fostering exchanges and integration among ethnic groups, DeepZang could help ensure the accuracy of Tibetan-language information and contribute to social stability and long-term security.

Founded in 2016, Choknor specializes in Tibetan-Chinese bilingual speech technology, scanning and translation tools, and optical character recognition. Its products include smart computer mice, scanning and translation pens, and an AI-powered Tibetan subtitling system.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.title: The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.content:
With hundreds of concerts scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, some fans found the cheapest way to upgrade a seat was to rent a better camera phone.

For about 100 to 200 yuan ($15 to $30) a day, concertgoers can rent flagship smartphones with powerful telephoto cameras that pull distant performers into clearer view, a useful option when high demand leaves fans seated far from the stage and professional cameras and long lenses are often barred from venues.

On Chinese rental platform Renrenzu and Xianyu, a secondhand marketplace owned by Chinese tech giant Alibaba, some flagship phones are listed as “concert essentials.”

One Renrenzu ad touted a “200-megapixel telephoto, crystal clear — even the nosebleed seats feel VIP,” while the platform has also offered concert ticket reimbursements through prize draws.

The phones on offer are among the latest flagships from Chinese smartphone makers such as vivo and OPPO, with high-resolution telephoto cameras, image stabilization, and, in some cases, detachable lens kits that extend their reach.

A vivo X300 Ultra bundled with a telephoto lens, for example, rents for about 215 yuan for one day, while a two-day rental brings the average daily cost down to about 125 yuan. Other popular models include OPPO’s Find X10 Pro Max, which packs three 200-megapixel rear cameras and is advertised as supporting up to “20x lossless zoom” with its official telephoto kit.

Such high-end models typically sell for about 5,000 to 8,000 yuan, while official telephoto lens kits can add another 1,000 to 2,000 yuan, making a short rental far cheaper for fans who only want the extra reach for one concert.

Online, concertgoers are comparing phones and lens attachments, posting photos from the stands, and swapping tips on which setups work best from distant seats.

Liu Hang, who attended Taiwan singer Steve Chou’s concert at Beijing Workers’ Stadium, told Time Finance that he brought a Ruiying Z10 camera module and telephoto attachment made by Chinese tech giant Huawei into the venue. “I had a 580-yuan ticket, but with the ‘Huawei cannon,’ it felt like a 1,680-yuan seat,” he said.

Another social media user, who said he had attended nearly 100 concerts, compared several phones and camera setups for live shows. He said such phones were easy to carry, worked well for close-up shots, and had a dedicated stage mode that automatically adjusted exposure, though adding a telephoto attachment made it tiring to hold through an entire concert.

Renrenzu said orders for concert-related equipment jumped 388% year on year over the summer, far outpacing a 67% rise in short-term rentals overall. A total of 257 concerts were scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, according to Alibaba’s entertainment data platform Lighthouse.

Chen Shenyu, a manager at consulting firm China Insights Consultancy, told Time Finance that smartphone photography was becoming less about simply recording daily life and more about performing well in specific situations. Concerts are especially challenging because fans may be seated far from the stage, lighting changes constantly, and they are often shooting handheld photos and video.

That also makes concerts a natural showcase for smartphone makers, Chen said. If consumers increasingly reach for telephoto cameras at sporting events, on trips, and during family activities, demand for the same high-end imaging features could extend well beyond concerts.

(Header image: Posts show concertgoers using flagship camera phones with telephoto attachments to capture performers from the stands. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.title: China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.content:
Chinese travelers are increasingly stringing together multiple destinations during the weeklong National Day holiday, boosting mid-holiday air travel and drawing more visitors to smaller cities and counties.

More than 20% of air travelers booked flights to two or more destinations during the holiday, which runs from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, according to online travel platform Tongcheng Travel. Demand for flights in the middle of the holiday rose 35% from a year earlier.

Smaller destinations were among the biggest beneficiaries of the holiday travel boom, with data from travel platform Qunar showing that its 10 top trending scenic spots were all in county-level destinations.

In Qilian County in northwestern Qinghai province, which has a population of about 50,000, more than 100,000 tourists arrived on Oct. 3, filling local hotels and prompting authorities to house nearly 500 stranded visitors in school dormitories as temperatures fell to minus 4 degrees Celsius and snow covered nearby mountaintops.

The county’s culture and tourism department received more than 400 calls for help in seven hours, according to local authorities. Posts on Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, showed tourists searching for rooms as hotels across the county filled up.

One traveler told domestic outlet Jimu News that he spent the afternoon and evening searching major booking platforms after arriving in Qilian from Xi’an but could not find a room. After seeing a notice from local tourism authorities, he called for help and was assigned a school dormitory room shared by four people, with new bedding provided.

Wansui Mountain Martial Arts City in central Henan province also struggled with heavy crowds, repeatedly capping admissions and suspending same-day ticket sales after interest surged 22-fold from a year earlier.

Many travelers were also going farther and staying away longer. According to Tongcheng Travel, people on multi-city trips visited an average of 1.2 more cities than in 2025, with Chengdu, Suzhou, and Wuhan among the busiest transfer hubs.

More than 70% of multi-city travelers booked both natural and cultural attractions, suggesting that many were combining different types of destinations within a single itinerary.

Interest in six- to 10-day groups and customized tours to destinations including Xinjiang, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou rose more than 60% on Tongcheng from a year earlier. Couples and families accounted for more than half of those bookings.

(Header image: Tourists visit the Zhuo’er Mountain Scenic Area in Qilian County, Qinghai province, Oct. 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.title: Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.content:
Researchers have identified a new species of feathered dinosaur from northeastern China whose anatomy suggests that birds and their close dinosaur relatives developed flight-related features along separate evolutionary paths.

The fossil — a nearly complete 57-centimeter skeleton with some feathers preserved — dates to the Early Cretaceous, more than 100 million years ago. Discovered by a local farmer in Liaoning province’s Jianchang County, it was donated to Hebei Geo University’s museum in 2023.

Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and Hebei Geo University, working with colleagues from around the world, named the species Norellraptor barsboldi in a study published Sept. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The fossil adds evidence to a long-running debate over whether birds and their close dinosaur relatives inherited flight-related anatomy from a common ancestor or developed it separately.

Norellraptor belongs to the microraptorines, a group of small, feathered predators closely related to birds. Fossils of some members show long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting they were adapted to move through the air.

The researchers compared Norellraptor with other fossils and found that roughly 30% of the anatomical changes they traced through microraptorine evolution also appeared in the bird lineage. In microraptorines, finger bones shortened before wrist and hand bones fused and the breastbone lengthened. In the bird lineage, those changes appeared in the opposite order.

Growth marks in Norellraptor’s forearm bone suggest it was at least 3 years old and still growing when it died, an age estimate the researchers factored into their comparisons with other fossils.

The different sequences challenge the idea that microraptorines and birds inherited the same flight apparatus or followed a shared pattern of development, the researchers said. They argue that the similar features arose independently in the two lineages.

(Header image: Left and right: Fossilized limb bones of Norellraptor barsboldi. Center: An artist’s reconstruction of the species by Zhang Chuang. From Nature)

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. World.title: [Vantage Point] DBP’s bad loans: The failures behind the billions
World.content:
The Commission on Audit has uncovered serious deficiencies in state-owned DBP's lending practices, credit safeguards, and recovery procedures

Following Vantage Point’s exposé earlier this year on the Development Bank of the Philippines’ P36.21-billion non-performing loan portfolio, the Commission on Audit (COA) has uncovered serious deficiencies in the state-owned bank’s lending practices, credit safeguards and recovery procedures. With gross bad loans swelling to P46.50 billion and net income plunging by nearly 43%, COA’s 2025 audit reveals how weaknesses in credit administration, delayed collections and questionable loan-loss estimates have placed mounting pressure on DBP’s profitability, financial resilience and stewardship of public funds.

When Vantage Point exposed the Development Bank of the Philippines’ (DBP) P36.21-billion non-performing loan portfolio last January, the underlying concern extended far beyond the identities of delinquent borrowers.

The fundamental question was how a government-owned development institution could amass billions in troubled loans without triggering immediate alarms regarding its credit discipline, financial resilience, and internal accountability.

Now, the Commission on Audit’s (COA) newly obtained 2025 Annual Audit Report provides disturbing answers to those exact concerns. According to the government’s own auditors, the bank suffers from documented deficiencies in loan releases, inadequate collateral verification, sluggish recovery measures, and an outdated expected-credit-loss model.

The financial consequences of these operational shortcomings are unmistakable. DBP’s parent-bank gross non-performing loans escalated significantly, rising from P42.68 billion in 2024 to P46.50 billion in 2025.

To absorb this, its allowance against non-performing loans jumped from P23.03 billion to P33.49 billion. Consequently, the bank’s net income plunged by 42.9%, dropping from P7.30 billion to P4.17 billion. Put simply, while DBP technically remained profitable, its rapidly deteriorating credit quality took a heavy toll on its overall earnings.

The initial investigation scrutinized P36,208,917,505.63 in non-performing exposures across 442 businesses and individual borrowers. Among the largest exposures were Premium Megastructures Inc. with P3.4 billion, Manuel and Theresa Chua with P3.31 billion, Dennis Uy‘s Phoenix Petroleum Philippines Inc. with P2.93 billion, and Megaship Builders Inc. with P2.4 billion. Combined, these four accounts represented approximately one-third of the entire troubled portfolio examined.

While COA’s audit anonymized its sampled borrowers—meaning no direct documentary link has been formally established between these specific named accounts and the latest audit cases—the newly documented systemic failures substantially confirm our January exposé. The core issue was whether DBP’s internal systems for evaluating, monitoring, and recovering funds were robust enough to safeguard the public interest.

ICONS program

This systemic vulnerability is most vividly illustrated by COA’s examination of the Infrastructure Contractor Support (ICONS) program. Launched in 2017 to finance contractors for the government’s Build, Build, Build initiative, the program devolved into a financial liability.

Image from DBP Development Banker, April-June 2018 issue

By December 31, 2025, ICONS carried P6.67 billion in outstanding loans. Alarmingly, P4.09 billion—or approximately 61.4% of that portfolio—was already past due. For every P10 outstanding, more than P6 was overdue, representing a troubling outcome for a program supposedly anchored by secure government infrastructure contracts.

COA’s deep dive into specific loans reveals exactly how these funds were mismanaged. Auditors examined a P300-million corporate loan approved in August 2019, where funds were released against assigned receivables from government projects.

However, releases bypassed progress-based disbursement rules, and actual project accomplishments were never properly verified before the capital was deployed. The borrower ceased payments in June 2020, and several of the underlying projects were eventually terminated for delays.

More than five years after default, the P300-million principal remains unpaid, forcing DBP to provide a 100% allowance against the exposure. Similarly, a P490.46-million loan account revealed that the underlying security projects were completed between 2017 and 2021, yet the debt remained unsettled. Auditors discovered the borrower had aggressively subcontracted the work, retaining an actual economic interest of only 3.5%, raising questions about how DBP assessed the borrower’s repayment cash flows.

Recovery efforts were equally flawed. One P97.24-million loan defaulted in June 2021, yet the first recorded demand notice was not issued until July 2025 after passing through six different account officers, undermining accountability. Another P82.21-million exposure languished waiting for foreclosure proceedings simply because the lending center lacked a full-time lawyer.

Most concerning is that DBP’s board was aware of these mounting issues. Under Resolution No. 0044, dated January 19, 2022, the board instructed units to investigate the 20 largest non-performing loans. Yet, it took more than four years for the board to officially terminate the ICONS program on June 3, 2026. COA has now recommended investigating potential negligence among officers, prompting DBP’s Management Committee to direct its Legal Services Group to conduct an inquiry.

Furthermore, COA discovered that DBP’s P49.88-billion allowance for credit losses relied on an expected-credit-loss model that was not properly recalibrated to current observable data, violating Philippine Financial Reporting Standard 9.

Expected-credit-loss models dictate how much a bank must recognize today against loans that may not be recovered tomorrow, relying heavily on probabilities of default and collateral values.

When uncalibrated, the reported allowances may fail to reflect prevailing risks. Consequently, auditors stated that the faithful representation of the bank’s P491.42-billion net loans balance and P12.52-billion impairment expense could not be established.

While DBP’s gross loan portfolio remained static at roughly P536.69 billion, its allowance surged by P11.78 billion. Concurrently, the appraised value of collateral held against impaired loans plummeted by P39.62 billion, dropping from P104.17 billion in 2024 to just P64.55 billion in 2025.

Although DBP maintains financial soundness with an 11.22% capital adequacy ratio and an unmodified audit opinion, regulatory capital compliance does not eliminate the necessity to fix costly internal control weaknesses.

The fact that 25 of COA’s 38 previous audit recommendations remained unimplemented by December 2025 underscores a sluggish approach to structural reform.

These findings firmly vindicate the demand for a transparent, independent asset-quality review and a serious reconsideration of merging DBP with LandBank to consolidate risk oversight. Public confidence in a development institution must be earned through disciplined lending, transparent accounting, and decisive accountability when financial safeguards inevitably fail. – Rappler.com

Documentary basis: DBP’s 2025 COA Annual Audit Report, particularly printed pages 6, 50–57, 76–79, 91–94, 102–103 and 158–164. The named borrower exposures derive from Vantage Point’s earlier investigation, not from COA’s anonymized ICONS findings. The audit’s unmodified opinion and unresolved recommendations are recorded in its executive summary.
