World.title: Russia striking fuel reserves despite 'energy ceasefire', Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Ukrainian officials say Russia has continued to strike Ukraine's energy facilities despite US President Donald Trump's announcement that the countries had agreed on an "energy ceasefire".

On Monday a statement from the Regional Prosecutor's Office of Kharkiv said Russian forces had attacked an energy facility on the outskirts of the city.

That came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he "welcomed" Mr Trump's announcement, but Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv.

Mr Trump's brief social media post on Sunday announcing the purported agreement to mutually cease attacks on energy sites said that the ceasefire took effect immediately.

"Do not break it!" the post said.

Residents take a shelter in a basement of an apartment building during a threat of a Russian drone strike in Kharkiv. (Reuters: Vyacheslav Madiyevskyy)

Mr Trump also claimed in a social media post on September 14 that both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure, but offered no details on that proposal either. Nothing came of the purported agreement.

Australia is joining other nations in backing the "energy ceasefire" while urging Moscow to "end its unjustified and unprovoked invasion" of its neighbour.

"Australia supports an energy ceasefire which is respected by Russia and contributes towards a just and lasting peace, on Ukraine's terms," a Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) spokesperson said.

Local officials say least 12 people were wounded in several Russian attacks on Kharkiv on Monday morning.

Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said drones struck a high-rise building in what is Ukraine's second-largest city.

This damaged Kharkiv apartment building is a sign that Russia wants to "weaponise winter", Ukrainian officials say. (Reuters: Sofiia Gatilova)

Floors seven through to nine of the building were destroyed in the attack, Mr Terekhov said, adding that there was an intense fire at the scene.

Russia has used attacks on energy facilities in order to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's invasion.

Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponising winter".

Loading

Ukraine, meanwhile, has levelled strikes against Russian energy sites such as oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory.

Such actions prompted Mr Trump to blame Mr Zelenskyy for high diesel prices in the US weeks ahead of the midterm elections.

'Stop killing our people'

Mr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to comply with Mr Trump's requests to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system. He asked Mr Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.

"We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree, if they agree," Mr Zelenskyy said.

"If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure, and stop killing our people. This is only fair."

Volodymyr Zelenskiy speaks during the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland on Monday. (Reuters: Aleksandra Szmigiel)

Mr Zelenskyy made the comments in Poland on Monday at the opening of the Warsaw Security Forum, where government officials, military leaders and experts discussed security challenges, NATO policy and regional stability.

Trump's threats to Ukraine It is hard to see Donald Trump's shifting position on Ukraine as a clear strategic change, and not one driven principally by soaring fuel prices ahead of the US mid-term elections.

Mr Zelenskyy added that he was "grateful to America", but lamented that "this is Putin's answer to Trump: Russian attacks".

"It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," he said.

" This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond. "

Earlier, the European Union's top diplomat welcomed the prospect of a pause in energy strikes in Ukraine, but said she saw no sign that Russia would be willing to respect it.

"We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg.

"Personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed, not only energy."

Wires/ABC

World.title: Chess professional's alleged stalker goes on hunger strike
World.content:
A chess professional's alleged stalker has vowed to continue a hunger strike until he suffers significant health issues.

Shumsheer Singh Ghumman, 47, began his prison hunger strike on Thursday after alleging he was assaulted by two inmates while on remand in Melbourne's west.

The cafe owner denies stalking a young female chess professional for two years, including after she obtained a restraining order.

Ghumman has outlined his custody conditions to a magistrate.

The Victorian Supreme Court rejected Shumsheer Singh Ghumman's bid for bail on September 23. (ABC News)

Police allege Ghumman's actions twice coincided with the woman being detained briefly while travelling overseas.

Media reports of the man's bail application in September were followed by an alleged assault in Ravenhall Correctional Centre, his lawyer told the Melbourne Magistrates Court on Monday.

Michael Pena Rees said his client has type-2 diabetes but has refused food after the incident was "reported and nothing was done".

"He's communicated his intention to complete the hunger strike until significant medical issues occur with him," the lawyer said.

Ghumman had been put into solitary confinement and only let out for one hour a day in handcuffs, Mr Pena Rees said.

"The prison is not complying with their own policy on hunger strikes," Ghumman, appearing via video link from prison, told the court.

"I'm left in a cell. There's a policy in place that they're not adhering to."

His lawyer also complained about access to clean clothes and contact with other people, particularly his father.

Ghumman was seen writing on a piece of paper during the hearing before he entered not guilty pleas to each of his 35 charges.

They include stalking, intimidation, attempting to pervert the course of justice and possessing a pair of nunchucks.

Allegations of cross-continental stalking

Police allege Ghumman emailed officials in Qatar about the woman, leading to her detention when she arrived at Doha International Airport (pictured). (Reuters: Hamad I Mohammed)

Ghumman allegedly stalked the professional chess player, aged in her 20s, between April 2024 and May 2026.

The woman obtained an intervention order against Ghumman in March 2025 but he allegedly continued to stalk her.

Police alleged Ghumman emailed officials in Qatar about the woman, leading to her detention when she arrived at Doha International Airport.

The woman was again detained after Ghumman allegedly contacted the Icelandic Chess Federation.

The accused stalker also allegedly threatened to use artificial intelligence to surveil the woman and scrape her data from the dark web.

Ghumman was arrested at his Burnley cafe in Melbourne's east on May 1.

The Victorian Supreme Court rejected his bid for bail on September 23.

He will appear before the Victorian County Court for a mention on November 10.

AAP

World.title: Heavy rain, hail and ferocious wind speeds of 96km/h lash Alice Springs
World.content:
Thousands of homes are without power after a surprise storm brought wind speeds of almost 100km/h to Central Australia, pulling down trees and damaging properties.

According to the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM), heavy rain and hail fell on Alice Springs at 3:30pm this afternoon and wind gusts of 96km/h were recorded locally at 3:44pm.

It's the second storm to rock Alice Springs in just a few short days. (Supplied: Damien Ryan)

"A surface trough coincides with a warm and unstable air mass in southern parts of the Territory, which has resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms," the weather bureau said.

The short-lived storm cell pushed trees onto roads, powerlines and roofs.

The Alice Springs Hilton DoubleTree was among the properties to suffer significant damage.

The Alice Springs Hilton DoubleTree sustained damage to its ceiling. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

In a statement released on Monday afternoon, Power and Water Corporation said "approximately 9,000 properties" had lost power "due to damage caused by a sudden storm cell".

"Our crews are assessing the damage and will work to restore services as quickly as is safely possible," the statement said.

"The communities of Arumbera, Burt Plain, Ilparpa, Simpson, Hermannsburg, Hugh, Namatjira and Wallace Rockhole have also been affected.

" We remind people to please stay away from fallen trees and powerlines, and always assume powerlines are live. "

Territorians can check power outages via Power and Water's online tracker.

Cars parked outside the hospital in Alice Springs were damaged in the storm. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Locals urged to remain vigilant

The BOM's Robert Urbaniak said Centralians were "not out of the woods yet", warning another similar storm cell was predicted for Tuesday afternoon and evening.

"There's still the chance of severe thunderstorms again bringing damaging wind gusts, large hail and the chance of heavy rainfall," he said.

"Unfortunately another day of it, but after that should settle down somewhat."

NT Emergency Services (NTES) said it had received 47 calls for assistance since the storm hit.

Adam White from NTES said Alice Springs residents would need to remain vigilant in the coming few days and urged people to keep an eye on SecureNT for updates.

"I've got some reports of multiple trees down, some damage from the hail and the winds," he said.

" I've just seen a couple of reports of some areas that may have experienced up to 100km/h winds, so a very, very short-lived but intense storm that came through there. "

It was the second storm to hit Alice Springs in less than a week.

Two cells are moving east over parts of Central Australia and the Barkly region, according to the BOM, which are likely to persist through the early evening.

World.title: Penny Wong urges Palestinian Authority to hold elections 'without delay'
World.content:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has labelled the Palestinian Authority's (PA) decision to postpone general elections as "deeply disappointing", as the Coalition accused Labor of "prematurely" recognising Palestinian statehood.

President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in 20 years, scheduled for November, until September 2027, citing changed conditions.

"We call on the Palestinian Authority to ensure elections take place without delay," Ms Wong said.

"Credible elections are an important element of the Palestinian Authority's commitment to the international community on reform, democratic renewal and accountable governance.

"Continuing to delay elections undermines the prospects of a two-state solution."

Australia's recognition 'will make a difference', Palestinian Authority says The Palestinian Authority's foreign minister says Australia's decision will "bring others to recognise, hopefully, and it safeguards the two-state solution".

The Executive Committee of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) cited ongoing Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank, continued strikes on Gaza, and Israel's refusal to allow election materials or international observers to enter Gaza as key factors for the delay.

"These conditions prevent the establishment of an appropriate environment for elections and undermine guarantees for the safety of voters, candidates and electoral workers," the PLO said in a statement.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar on X accused the Palestinian Authority of "once again deceiving the international community".

"[Mr Abbas's] attempt to drag Israel into this, falsely claiming that Israel imposed obstacles to holding elections, is yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability," Mr Sa'ar wrote.

Israeli outlet, the Jerusalem Post, has separately reported Israel's elections, scheduled for October 27, could be postponed if Israel returned to war with Iran within the next three weeks.

Pro-Israel group demands PA accountability

Australia last year joined 156 other UN member states in recognising Palestinian statehood, with "clear requirements" set out by the international community.

At the time of the decision, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Mr Abbas gave "direct undertakings to Australia" including commitments to hold democratic elections.

Australia/Israel & Jewish Affairs Council (AIJAC) executive director Colin Rubenstein has called on the government "to hold the PA accountable for breaking yet another key commitment underpinning Australia's recognition of a Palestinian state".

"Recognition of Palestinian statehood by Australia, however premature and counterproductive it was, should not remain a blank cheque.

"The Albanese government must explain what consequences will follow for the PA's repeated refusal to abide by the very commitments upon which recognition was based."

Coalition blasts 'premature' recognition

Shadow Foreign Minister Ted O'Brien on Monday joined AIJAC in calling on the prime minister to "explain" what actions the government would take if elections were not held next year.

"The promise of democratic elections gave Labor's premature recognition of Palestine a veneer of legitimacy, and now that veneer has been stripped away," Mr O'Brien said.

"The Australian government should be pressing for that decision to be reversed."

Ted O'Brien says the government needs to continue pressing for the decision to be reversed. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

France's government has urged the Palestinian Authority to reverse its election delay, which the French foreign ministry said would "deprive the Palestinian people of their right to democratically express themselves" for the first time in two decades.

Ms Wong has not gone that far.

"We look forward to the Palestinian Authority making progress on the commitments it has made to Australia and the international community, so that next steps like diplomatic relations and the opening of embassies can proceed," she said.

World.title: Corruption watchdog abandons Bruce Lehrmann submarine secrets probe
World.content:
Bruce Lehrmann is no longer under investigation for allegedly using secrets about French submarines for his own ends.

The ex-political staffer got the reprieve on Monday after a letter from the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) informed him it had abandoned the probe.

The notification ends part of a saga that began with officials raiding the 31-year-old's home in June 2024 over allegations he swiped secret documents from the office of former defence minister Linda Reynolds five years earlier.

The sweep, conducted under an operation dubbed "Ivanhoe", included seizing a blue moleskin diary, which the government claimed contained eight pages of classified security information.

"The former commissioner decided to take no further action concerning the investigation in Operation Ivanhoe," the corruption watchdog's letter reads.

Mr Lehrmann then sued Special Minister of State Don Farrell and then-NACC commissioner Paul Brereton, saying the raids were an abuse of the watchdog's power.

Bruce Lehrmann ordered into mediation over funds for lawyers The Federal Court orders mediation for former Liberal staffer Bruce Lehrmann over funding he says he was offered to pay for his lawyers.

He also alleges he was unlawfully forced to give evidence at two secret hearings in October 2024 in Hobart, where he resides, and described the agency's investigation as driven by "frivolous, James Bond-like allegations".

His legal skirmishes with Mr Farrell and Mr Brereton are ongoing.

"The NACC has been a colossal waste of taxpayer money," Mr Lehrmann said in response to the watchdog's letter on Monday.

"Over two years the former commissioner used his powers to personally advance a conspiracy that I was a spy and traitor to the nation, selling defence secrets to foreign countries.

" The NACC needs to be abolished and replaced with nothing. "

Mr Lehrmann was accused of foraging for the classified information on the French submarines days after he allegedly raped his colleague Brittany Higgins in then-senator Reynolds's parliament house office, in March 2019.

The rape allegations were found to be proven, on the balance of probabilities, by Federal Court Justice Michael Lee in 2024.

That finding was upheld twice by the Full Federal Court and the High Court.

Mr Lehrmann has denied the sexual assault claims, which remain untested in a criminal court.

The ex-Liberal staffer remains party to a second anti-corruption investigation, Operation Greenough, into whether federal police misused information during their probe into Ms Higgins's alleged sexual assault.

AAP

World.title: WA schools to go back to basics in classroom screen time crackdown
World.content:
The amount of time primary school students spend staring at a screen will be restricted next year in a trial aimed at limiting "unnecessary" screen time in the classroom.

Slated for rollout in Term 1, 2027, the "Back to Basics" program will be piloted in 10 public schools across Western Australia, which will each receive $50,000 in funding for the purchase of materials.

Some WA primary school children will learn more from screen-free resources from 2027. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

The aim is to restore face-to face teaching and hands on learning instead of using a digital device like a laptop or iPad.

The announcement comes just one month after Australia reported its worst numeracy and reading results on record.

WA joins digital detox

WA isn't the first state to explore implementing top-down regulations on digital devices in schools.

Last month, New South Wales introduced a strict 15-minute limit on screens per day for students in Kindergarten to Year 2 and in June, the Victorian government announced a blanket requirement for planned screen-free time in public secondary schools.

State education minister Sabine Winton said she wanted WA to have its own unique policy.

WA Premier Roger Cook (left) and Education Minister Sabine Winton (middle) are in a classroom with students. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

"It's timely that we actually pause for a little while and fully contemplate the impacts and opportunities that screens play in our schools."

Kindergarten students are enjoying lunch with their human and doll friends. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

WA Premier Roger Cook said how technology was incorporated into day-to-day learning needed to be "carefully considered."

"A classroom should be a place where kids are talking to each other, challenging each other, asking questions," he said.

"Just because technology is everywhere, it doesn't mean that there should be the default mechanism in our classrooms."

Back to basics approach celebrated

The six-month program will target the state's youngest students, with screen time limits being trialled in classes from Kindergarten to Year 2.

The early years are critical for setting children up for later life, says Hayley Christian from the Kids Research Institute. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Under trial restrictions, students will still have access to digital devices to learn skills needed to meet technology curriculum standards, and to participate in NAPLAN testing, which is now routinely conducted online.

The Kids Research Institute's Professor Hayley Christian said younger students felt the biggest impacts from too much screen time.

"The early years are so critical for setting them up for later life, it's where all that development happens, where their healthy behaviours are established," she said.

The initiative will be rolled out across 10 public primary schools in the first term. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"[Screen time] replaces things like active play which is so important for a child's physical development, social emotional development and of course their learning and cognitive development."

Schools keen to cut screens

Craigie Heights Primary School principal Leon Wilson said his school would be applying to participate.

"The prevalence of screens in the home and the hours that developing brains are accessing screens hasn't supported literacy and numeracy development," he said.

"And being able to have the right things in schools to support [students] without having the screens is a good thing."

The move is aimed at limiting "unnecessary" time spent on laptops and tablet devices in classrooms. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Mr Wilson said schools were making decisions around screen-based learning without explicit guidance from the state.

"We're the one agency that's got the face-to-face five days a week, which puts us at the coalface in terms of having to make decisions that we think will help or hinder," he said.

World.title: 'I just live on noodles': Report reveals scale of NT cost-of-living crisis
World.content:
For an Alice Springs grandmother who receives a disability pension, the struggle to afford groceries between pay cheques is constant, with the cost of food "too high".

Shirley Napurrula Miller is among the nearly 50 per cent of the Northern Territory's population who experienced food insecurity because of rising prices in 2025, according to a new report.

"Sometimes I can't buy groceries, or meat, or anything," she said.

"I just live on noodles."

Shirley Napurrula Miller says she struggles to afford the basics for herself and her family. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

The report by the NT Council of Social Service (NTCOSS), released today, examines changes in the cost of living between 2016 and 2026 across key spending areas of housing, utilities, transport and food.

It shows every day, across all spending areas, many Territorians are having to make impossible money decisions and weigh up what they must prioritise to live.

Hunger relief charity Foodbank Australia estimates that 46 per cent of NT households experienced food insecurity in 2025, above the national average of 33 per cent, according to the NTCOSS report.

The report found that while incomes have increased in real terms in the past 10 years, the cost of essentials has too. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

In remote areas, the cost of food is even more prohibitive than in urban centres such as Darwin and Alice Springs, where prices have also risen substantially.

"In 2023, the average cost of a healthy food basket was 40 per cent more in remote stores than in a supermarket," the report states.

A decade of rising costs

The 10-year comparison report found that while incomes have increased in real terms, the cost of essentials has too, making it harder for everyone — especially those on low incomes — to meet basic needs.

Power costs have risen 18 per cent and those on prepaid plans, predominantly First Nations people in urban and remote public housing, are having their electricity cut off more frequently, with 2,284 more disconnections per month on average last year than in 2019-2020.

The report found there were 103,648 involuntary self-disconnections in major centres in the NT last year. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Further compounding cost pressures for those already on the poverty line, the report states the prepaid electricity price is higher than for standard postpaid billing to account for customers not paying a fixed daily charge.

According to the report, there were 103,648 involuntary self-disconnections in major centres in the NT last year.

"Affordability challenges are a key driver of such disconnections," the report states.

" Being without power for extended amounts of time can have a significant impact on people's health and wellbeing. "

Ms Miller said she had faced disconnection many times and Aboriginal families often lent on each other to share their limited incomes and keep the power on, particularly in the heat over summer.

Linda Lechleitner says her electricity bill alone is more than her Centrelink payment. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Her daughter, Linda Lechleitner, who lives between Alice Springs and a remote Aboriginal homeland near the community of Papunya, about a 3-hour drive away, said she worried about electricity costs amid a heating climate.

"It's more than the government payment that they give you, the Centrelink payment doesn't carry people through fortnightly," she said.

"Every little dollar counts … it's not carrying through to the next fortnight or the next week, they're having to borrow money from family and then pay that back.

"So they're never in front."

'We're in crisis'

The report reveals rents have skyrocketed 55 per cent over the past decade.

Meanwhile, the NT's social housing stock only increased by 4 per cent between 2017 and 2025, while social housing applications increased by 37 per cent over the same period.

The report shows transport costs have also shot up, with an 80-litre tank of diesel now costing $28 more in Darwin and an extra $88 in Alice Springs.

Linda Lechleitner says she runs out of food after helping to feed other family members who are also struggling. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"We're in crisis," Ms Lechleitner said.

"You're always catering and your food doesn't last long, because you're always feeding other family members that are struggling at the moment as well.

"And then the fuel, it's ridiculous."

Report co-author Jonathan Pilbrow said he was concerned about "poverty premiums" paid by those on income support, who could not afford to pay for things like car registration up front: copping extra fees if they paid monthly.

He said every time people paid their registration, whether monthly or yearly, they also had to pay a $16 administration fee, meaning those who paid more frequently were also paying more overall.

Jonathan Pilbrow says lifting people out of poverty will require raising income support payments. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"You end up paying $164 more, if you're poor, because you can't afford to pay it upfront," he said.

"That's one area the government can look at immediately to relieve cost-of-living pressure."

Key recommendations of the report include raising the rates of income support payments, including JobSeeker, Youth Allowance, the Parenting Payment and the Remote Area Allowance for those living in the territory's most remote places.

While the federal government's low-cost essentials subsidy scheme for remote communities was introduced for 30 staple grocery items in remote stores, NTCOSS recommends the government extend the list of items to include more fresh and frozen meat, fruit and vegetables and nutrient-dense baby food.

Call to increase welfare

NTCOSS interim chief executive Claire Pirrett said the report showed those on the lowest incomes were struggling the most.

"We need to recognise that we have unacceptable levels of poverty here and people all over the Territory are experiencing significant hardship," she said.

"All levels of government need to take meaningful steps to ease pressure on people.

"By identifying how lives have changed over the last decade for households in the NT, this report also identifies the levers decision-makers can pull to provide relief for families and individuals."

Claire Pirrett says there are "levers decision-makers can pull to provide relief for families and individuals". (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Mr Pilbrow said lifting people out of poverty would mean raising income support payments.

"People will continue in poverty, that makes it really difficult for people to raise their families, to look after the kids, put food on the table … all the things that we need to do when we're raising families," he said.

Cost-of-living pressure 'entrenching disadvantage' in the NT The NT has the second highest rent in the country, with households having to set aside more of their weekly wages to cover essential costs.

"There's a poverty premium for living in remote areas, and there's a poverty premium for many people living in regional areas.

"There are things the government can do to address this."

Ms Lechleitner, a mother and grandmother who supports a number of children, said it felt harder to afford to live now than it did 10 years ago.

"Our politicians are all over here bickering and fighting about where the money goes, but the little people on the ground … people which are in crisis, how are you reflecting what you're saying in Canberra?" she said.

"How has that been felt on the ground here?"

World.title: Man living nomadic lifestyle granted bail for historical child sex offences
World.content:
A man charged with 18 alleged historical sexual assault offences in Brisbane has been granted bail and ordered to wear an ankle monitor, despite police concerns.

Detectives allege the 46-year-old Warwick man committed offences against a teenage girl, who was known to him, in Brisbane between 2013 and 2018.

During the bail hearing in Toowoomba Magistrates Court on Monday, police prosecutor Anita Paige objected to bail because the man had no fixed address and lived in a caravan in regional Queensland.

Police arrested the man at a campsite in Taroom, on Queensland's Western Downs, on October 10.

Police arrested the man at a campsite in Taroom. (ABC News: Nathan Morris)

He is charged with 18 offences, including nine counts of indecent treatment of children under 16, seven counts of rape and one count each of grooming a child under 16 years with intent to procure engagement in a sexual act with a child under 12 years, and sexual assaults.

The man's solicitor, Kate McIntyre, said her client intended to defend all charges against him and was willing to comply with any bail conditions imposed by the court, including surrendering his passport.

Strict bail conditions

Magistrate Veena Goverdhan granted bail on the condition the man lived at a Heritage Park address, did not leave Queensland, reported twice a week to police and wore an electronic monitoring device.

He is also not allowed to have any contact with children under the age of 16 or visit any parks or schools while on bail.

The court was told the man had sold his house in Crestmead at the start of the year and purchased two caravans to travel Australia.

Ms Paige said the man's travel plans came after he heard about the investigation in February.

Police had attempted to issue an extradition warrant, fearing he would flee to New South Wales.

However, Ms McIntyre told the court allegations that her client fled were "entirely unfounded" and not what "spurred" the travel.

The matter was adjourned to Brisbane Magistrates Court for further mention on December 7.

Investigations continue

Boondall Child Protection Investigation Unit officer-in-charge Detective Senior Sergeant Derek Harris commended the bravery of the alleged victim-survivor in a police press release.

"We acknowledge the immense courage it takes to come forward and report offences of this nature," Detective Senior Sergeant Harris said.

"Whether it is an incident that has just occurred, or one from several years ago, I want to reassure victim-survivors that police take all reports seriously and will investigate it to its full extent.

"You are not alone and support services are available."

Queensland police said investigations were ongoing.

World.title: Bed bugs ground Qantas Rome-to-Perth flight
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Bed bugs ground Qantas Rome-to-Perth flight Chris Zappone October 12, 2026 — 8:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. An outbreak of bed bugs has forced the cancellation of a Qantas flight from Rome to Perth, delaying some passengers by as much as two days. The drama began when passengers aboard QF5 travelling from Perth to Rome on October 9 complained of being bitten by bugs. On medical advice, they were given antihistamines, but the plane reportedly ran out. Economy class on a Qantas Dreamliner. The return flight, QF6 from Rome to Perth on Saturday, was cancelled and the Boeing 787 Dreamliner booked for cleaning. Passengers were given accommodation and rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, Qantas said.



A spokesperson for the airline said: “We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday’s Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue was identified on a small number of economy seats.” A bed bug. The Perth-Rome route is a popular non-stop flight that attracts passengers from the east coast who are willing to pay a premium for the direct connection between Australia and Italy. Qantas extended the seasonal flight service from May 3 to October 23, adding 40 extra services and close to 10,000 seats in that time. Bed bugs are tiny (about five millimetres). The wingless parasites feed exclusively on blood, preferring human blood, and spread via clothing, furniture and belongings. “Bed bugs are not believed to transmit diseases to humans,” according to the Victorian government’s Better Health Channel website. “Their bite typically causes a large, reddened and itchy weal that fades to a red spot.”



Bed bug bites are painless, Better Health says, and “some people do not react to the bites, but for others the bites can become itchy and swell into reddened weals [or welts].” Related Article Wellbeing Paris is being plagued by bed bugs. What does that mean for Australia? Qantas said its aircraft cabins are cleaned regularly and to an extremely high standard. A deep clean of a plane to rid it of bed bugs requires fumigation, taking the plane out of service. The airline said that as a matter of course, Qantas aircraft are disinfected every 50 days as a precaution. Still cases of bed bugs on planes are not unheard of.

World.content:

When their daughter braved a cancer diagnosis to complete one final chapter on the court, Tiana Mangakahia’s family was overcome with emotion. World.title: Bed bugs ground Qantas Rome-to-Perth flight
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Bed bugs ground Qantas Rome-to-Perth flight Chris Zappone October 12, 2026 — 8:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. An outbreak of bed bugs has forced the cancellation of a Qantas flight from Rome to Perth, delaying some passengers by as much as two days. The drama began when passengers aboard QF5 travelling from Perth to Rome on October 9 complained of being bitten by bugs. On medical advice, they were given antihistamines, but the plane reportedly ran out. Economy class on a Qantas Dreamliner. The return flight, QF6 from Rome to Perth on Saturday, was cancelled and the Boeing 787 Dreamliner booked for cleaning. Passengers were given accommodation and rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, Qantas said.



A spokesperson for the airline said: “We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday’s Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue was identified on a small number of economy seats.” A bed bug. The Perth-Rome route is a popular non-stop flight that attracts passengers from the east coast who are willing to pay a premium for the direct connection between Australia and Italy. Qantas extended the seasonal flight service from May 3 to October 23, adding 40 extra services and close to 10,000 seats in that time. Bed bugs are tiny (about five millimetres). The wingless parasites feed exclusively on blood, preferring human blood, and spread via clothing, furniture and belongings. “Bed bugs are not believed to transmit diseases to humans,” according to the Victorian government’s Better Health Channel website. “Their bite typically causes a large, reddened and itchy weal that fades to a red spot.”



Bed bug bites are painless, Better Health says, and “some people do not react to the bites, but for others the bites can become itchy and swell into reddened weals [or welts].” Related Article Wellbeing Paris is being plagued by bed bugs. What does that mean for Australia? Qantas said its aircraft cabins are cleaned regularly and to an extremely high standard. A deep clean of a plane to rid it of bed bugs requires fumigation, taking the plane out of service. The airline said that as a matter of course, Qantas aircraft are disinfected every 50 days as a precaution. Still cases of bed bugs on planes are not unheard of.

World.title: Christchurch man arrested for  EV charging station cable thefts
World.content:
A Christchurch man is before the courts in connection to a string of thefts where electric vehicle charging stations have been targeted.

Police have been investigating multiple reports of EV charging cables being cut and stolen across the Canterbury region in recent weeks.

A 26-year-old man is facing multiple charges, including five counts of theft over $2000.

He is due to appear in the Christchurch District Court on Tuesday.

Police are continuing to investigate other thefts around Christchurch and are not ruling out further arrests.

Inspector Peter Cooper said the offending had caused significant impact on both businesses and members of the public.

"The offending has caused significant disruption to EV users and substantial costs to charging network providers through damage and replacement of infrastructure.

"Police have been working closely with victims and industry partners to identify and locate those responsible to hold them to account.

"While an arrest has been made, our enquiries are ongoing and we are not ruling out further arrests."

World.title: Auckland University alumni say they weren't told of sexual misconduct review
World.content:
The University of Auckland is facing criticism after it failed to inform alumni about its review into sexual misconduct complaints.

The review will address how the university handles sexual harassment concerns raised by students or staff in relation to the conduct of university staff.

It comes after the institution faced scrutiny from its own staff and chief victims advisor over how it handled an investigation into chemistry professor Jonathan Sperry.

University of Auckland alumni told RNZ they have not received any communication regarding the review or the reviewer's details.

Geoffrey Chen, alumnus of the university and a volunteer alumni coordinator for the university in Sydney, said alumni may have been affected by the incidents and he would like to see the review communicated to them.

"They didn't communicate," he said.

"Would be good if they sent an email addressing this to all the alumni. I'm concerned as if these incidents happened many years ago some of the alumni community may have been affected. So the uni should make contact for complete transparency."

Erica Chan, volunteer coordinator for the university's alumni network in New York, also said she hasn't seen any information about the review, and thinks alumni will want to read about the details "even if not directly relevant".

The review was announced to all current staff and students on 9 September and is set to investigate sexual harassment complaints handled by the university within the last five years.

The university updated its website on 30 September with reviewers' contact details, and directly emailed students and staff on 5 October with information to contact reviewers.

The deadline to contact reviewers is 31 October.

Emails seen by RNZ show the university last contacted alumni about a conference for the Social Sciences on 1 October, and about a campus pub quiz on 22 September.

A University of Auckland spokesperson said it communicated the review through multiple channels.

"The university has used several channels to advise staff and students on how to participate in the review. This has included our website and intranet, our all-staff newsletter, and emails directly to staff and students."

Improved transparency would help ease fear - academic

Carrie Leonetti, an associate professor at the university's law school, had called for the review and said given the timeline it will cover, some affected students may have graduated already.

Leonetti said while she believes participating in the review - conducted by an accredited investigator - will be confidential, many current students may still have concerns and graduates would be more likely to share candidly.

"I think there are a lot of students who are still worried about how freely they can participate, worried about retaliation. It's the graduated students who wouldn't likely have that fear anymore."

She said anything the university did to improve transparency would help ease fear in participation.

"I'm more generally worried about trust in the process. There is a lot of distrust with victims of sexual harassment around the university's responses. I just think anything that makes it look like the university isn't facilitating their participation, even if that's not what's going on, is likely to kind of increase distrust in the process."

RNZ / Ke-Xin Li

Leonetti was also concerned about the deadline.

There's 36 working days between the deadline and when the university first announced the review, and 18 from when the university directly shared reviewers' contact details.

Leonetti said many victim-survivors may be waiting on information they requested with the university under the Official Information Act (OIA) or the Privacy Act.

"I do know that the university's response to those can be quite slow. The one concern I would have is if somebody has either an OIA request in or a Privacy Act request in, and they want to use those responses in their communications to the external investigators, there's probably no time for that."

It would help if the reviewers considered extending the deadline for people who were waiting on information from the university, she said.

The Official Information Act and Privacy Act require organisations to respond to requests within 20 working days and can extend this under certain circumstances.

Carrie Leonetti Supplied

According to the university's OIA response to RNZ this year, it takes an average of 31 working days to provide the information, with some responses taking as long as 50 working days.

A University of Auckland spokesperson said the reviewers could suggest recommendations to extend the deadline, or communicate to other groups.

"The terms of reference of the review are deliberately broad. If the reviewers find significant issues that would warrant the submission period being extended, or recommend additional communications to other groups, the university will consider their recommendations."

The spokesperson said it would not make further comment while the review was underway.

World.title: In-person appointments at Horowhenua clinic 'very limited' after 12 staff resign over past year
World.content:
A dozen staff have left a clinic in Horowhenua in the past year - including four general practitioners.

The Taitoko Health clinic in Levin is run by OmniHealth, whose clinics owned through the Tararua Health Group were put on a temporary freeze by Health New Zealand over concerns about workloads and patient safety.

The last GP at Taitoko Health where 4500 patients were registered resigned last month.

Taitoko Health had 12 staff leave or give notice in the past 12 months, including nurses, administrators and four GPs.

When asked why the clinic had such high turnover, managing director Mark Wills said it was because of retirements and individual staff's circumstances.

"We're keen to have as little change in that regard as we possibly can, but we're not in charge of or in control of all people's lives and what happens and what they need to do as well."

Several health professionals with experience at the clinic told RNZ trouble at the clinic started after the retirement of a long-serving general practitioner last year.

OmniHealth said recruitment for this first planned departure had been underway but it had not kept pace with subsequent panned and unplanned departures.

It said in-person appointments were "currently very limited", with patients waiting around three weeks for distance appointments.

World.title: ACT's disability cuts 'poorly researched' - Mental Health Foundation
World.content:
Audio player for " ACT looks to cut benefits for those not working due to mental health " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1862835%2Fact-s-disability-cuts-poorly-researched-mental-health-foundation

ACT looks to cut benefits for those not working due to mental health Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

The Mental Health Foundation is rubbishing the ACT Party's pre-election proposal to cut more than half-a-billion dollars worth of disability benefits, saying the plan is "based in bigotry".

ACT said it would cut disability benefits by more than $650 million if re-elected.

The party's fiscal plan will bring the country back to 2017-per-capita spending by slashing ministries, cutting foreign aid and cracking down on benefits.

The plan lays out cuts to disability benefits of $12m in the first year, rising to $124m, $231m and $286m in the following years.

ACT leader David Seymour said the party would require independent medical certification against clear criteria for health and disability benefits.

"People who are genuinely disabled and don't have a chance to get to work, they should be looked after well - I've always believed that," he said.

"But you can't tell me that we've had a massive blowout in mental health problems and sickness over the last six that explains the increase in people who supposedly can't work.

"Now, there's one of two failings: either New Zealand has become a much sicker place in the last seven years, or we have got a lot worse at managing and helping people who could be working. And I suspect it's the latter," he said.

ACT leader David Seymour. RNZ / Nick Monro

ACT has previously revealed plans to replace local GPs with government appointed doctors.

Mental Health Foundation chief executive Shaun Robinson told Checkpoint the approach was poorly researched.

"It's pretty simple-minded and it won't work. It's also based on a lot of assumptions and bigotry," he said.

"I've been monitoring things that Mr. Seymour's been saying today and some of it's really quite flabbergasting when he says he won't believe that there's a mental health epidemic in New Zealand. Well, he isn't looking at the numbers that are coming out of the Ministry of Health and Health New Zealand."

In the past nine years, the number of people on the job seekers benefit had gone up about 80 percent.

The number of people experiencing mental distress had increased from 7 percent to 14 percent since 2019, and for young people it had more than doubled from 11 percent to 23 percent, Robinson said.

He said the statistics showed Seymour was wrong about a "hidden health crisis".

However, Robinson did agree with the ACT leader's stance on the benefits of people with mental health distress being in work.

"I absolutely agree with that. It's really important, an important part of recovery. It's an important part of socialisation, of feeling part of the community," he said.

All of those things I agree with. I think the way he's going about it will fail because it's not that there isn't a mental health crisis."

There had been a multitude of factors that were driving increases in mental distress, Robinson said.

"Covid was definitely an inflection point, but actually those numbers have been going up for about a decade before that as well. They get worse in times of economic hardship," he said.

"So again, it's a bit rich to say, you know, we've got to force people off benefits and into jobs when 14,000 jobs have been lost in the last three years."

Robinson said the plan was based on assumptions that people were "faking" their mental distress.

He said general attitudes towards people with mental illness varied from attitudes towards people with physical ailments.

"People often don't understand mental health, they're afraid of it, you can't see it, so it's an invisible health issue, so therefore it's much easier to sort of dismiss it," Robinson said.

World.title: Man dies after speaking at South Wairarapa council meeting
World.content:
A Wairarapa man who died after speaking at a council meeting has been described as a passionate and dogged advocate for his community and the environment.

Garry Dittmer, 68, had been seeking a response from the South Wairarapa District Council regarding his long-standing concerns about 1080 use in the area when he collapsed at a meeting earlier this month.

Friend and fellow community activist Claire Bleakley said Dittmer had been raising issues with council for decades, and had become frustrated about the council's responses to his questions under OIA.

"He was extremely concerned about the environment. Once he got his teeth into something he really strove to try and make it right," Bleakley said.

A spokesperson for the family said Dittmer had repeatedly lobbied the council to prevent 1080 drops in South Wairarapa with particular emphasis on his perceived risks to public drinking water catchments.

"Garry's love for our family, his love for his community and his love for our beautiful country and its people was at the heart of everything he did.

"We cannot even begin to articulate who and what we have lost at this point in time," the spokesperson said.

Video footage of the meeting showed Dittmer speaking from behind a desk at the council meeting.

Under council rules, Dittmer was allocated three minutes during the public participation session to put his initial point or question forward, with another two minutes available for councillors to ask questions on the matter.

In response to Dittmer at the meeting, Councillor Aidan Ellims replied: "Garry, the issue about 1080 is not a South Wairarapa District Council issue".

Water infrastructure and services were provided by the council, but 1080 use for predator control was undertaken by Department of Conservation, who said on their website no drinking water in New Zealand had ever been contaminated by their 1080 operations.

Dittmer pressed his point for his final minute of allocated time, but the conversation deteriorated and Mayor Fran Wilde adjourned the meeting.

Warren Woodgyer attended the meeting, and told RNZ that Dittmer appeared stressed and crossed beneath the barrier, and attempted to follow the councillors as they exited the chamber.

He said Dittmer was escorted back towards his seat by a councillor, but collapsed, falling onto the table and then to the floor.

In a statement, Wilde said Dittmer's passing was "highly distressing" for the public as well as councillors and staff.

"Emergency services were immediately informed, along with the local medical centre. We fortunately had a person on the council with a medical background who was able to administer CPR until the other services arrived.

"Our thoughts remain with Mr Dittmer's family and friends. Several people from the council who knew the family attended last week's memorial service," Wilde said.

A police spokesperson said police were notified of a medical event on Texas Street, Martinborough at about 2.20pm on 1 October.

World.title: Gang leader serving life for murder denied parole as 'further work' needed
World.content:
A former gang leader serving a life sentence for the murder of his ex-girlfriend has been declined parole, with both the Parole Board and his lawyers agreeing that "further work" is needed - including a pending psychological report.

James Henry Wilson - former president of the Filthy Few motorcycle gang - murdered Jo-Anne van Duyvenbooden at her Welcome Bay home in Tauranga in 1999.

He was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2000 for the murder, as well as a concurrent sentence of three years for obstructing the course of justice, and five years for manufacturing methamphetamine.

Wilson was acquitted by the Supreme Court in July this year over the high profile 1987 murder of Red Fox Tavern publican Chris Bush, alongside Mark Hoggart.

Wilson appeared before the Parole Board in Christchurch last month, following his acquittal of the Red Fox Tavern murder, and a decision has now been released to RNZ.

Parole Board panel convenor Neville Trendle wrote in the board's decision: "Counsel did not seek Mr Wilson's release from prison as it is common ground further work is required before the board could be satisfied that his release would not pose an undue risk to the safety of the community."

The decision noted that it had been 10 years since a full psychological assessment had been done for Wilson, and the board needed to consider that information, as well as advice on issues relating to risk and any outstanding rehabilitation steps.

Wilson is due to appear before the Parole Board in late November, once the psychological assessment report and parole assessment report become available.

The decision said there were no concerns with Wilson's conduct or compliance, and that he had been very active in the community garden.

It said he now held a minimum security classification, with two minor misconducts - the most recent having happened within the past 12 months.

Wilson completed the Special Treatment Unit Programme for Violent Offending in 2014, and the Drug Treatment Programme the following year.

The Parole Board said it had met with the members of Jo-Anne van Duyvenbooden's family ahead of the hearing, and that they remained deeply affected by his offending.

"They made it clear that on release from prison he should not be permitted to enter the Waikato and Bay of Plenty areas. Mr Wilson is aware of his victims' views."

Meanwhile, Wilson and Hoggart are both seeking costs from the Crown following their acquittal over Red Fox Tavern murder.

At an administrative hearing at Auckland's High Court last month, Wilson's lawyer Christopher Stevenson KC told Justice Mathew Downs that the Crown should have but failed to disclose material relating to the credibility of "G" who was originally set to be a prosecution witness, but did not subsequently give evidence at the trial.

Quentin Duff, the lawyer for Hoggart, told Justice Downs that Hoggart's cost seeking case relied on Wilson's arguments.

World.title: Who is cashing in as petrol prices hit record high at the pump
World.content:
Audio player for " Fuel prices hit record high as oil giants bank $90 billion " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/business/1855601%2Fwho-is-cashing-in-as-petrol-prices-hit-record-high-at-the-pump

Fuel prices hit record high as oil giants bank $90 billion Morning Report Download MP3 8m

Producers of crude oil, owners of oil refineries and the New Zealand government are among those making more money as the price of fuel hits a record high at the pump.

According to gas price comparison app Gaspy, the average price of 91 fuel is $3.60 and diesel is sitting about $3.23.

An investigation by the Guardian in August found eight of the biggest oil companies amassed profits of more than US$90 billion (NZ$159.8b) in three months as the US-Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring.

Energy expert and former Marsden Point refiner manager David Keat told Morning Report there were a few parties cashing in for different reasons.

"Anybody who's producing crude is doing very, very well in terms of windfall profit. They're getting probably the biggest share.

"The second group would be anybody who has an oil refinery, they're making extraordinary refining margins in this period."

The New Zealand government was also an "honourable mention".

"Because of course, if the price goes up, they still charge 15 percent of that price as GST, so they're doing all right."

Keat said oil refineries and producers were the ones that profited the most but it was not the well known companies like Mobil, BP or Shell that were making the highest sum.

He said these companies produce only around 12 percent of the world's crude oil.

"The big players are all the state-owned oil companies or state-affiliated, like the Russian and Chinese oil companies are state-influenced... and, of course, you've got your OPEC countries, and they all have a national oil company. So Saudi Arabia, UAE, but also Nigeria, Guyana, other countries. All those national oil companies are making a huge amount of money."

In response to a global increase to fuel prices, US President Donald Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia who is set to supply 300,000 tons of diesel now, with more later, to the US and global markets.

Keat said this was about 2 percent of one day's global demand.

"The market will just look straight through it. Even the 3 million tons that he's talked about coming at some stage is about a quarter of one day."

He said this was "smoke and mirrors" and there was no net increase in diesel supply.

"The Russians haven't suddenly got more diesel. Even if they're bringing down the reserves, that would be short term and at the expense of the Russian people themselves."

Keat said predicting where oil prices would go from the recent spike was difficult but there were some trends in the US Iran war, which appeared to be in a "stalemate".

"They've been very, very careful not to destroy any more oil infrastructure. If they do that, then really all bets are off."

"This is going to carry on, obviously, through the midterms. You can see the Iranians may well want to keep the pressure on Trump. So that could go on for another year or two until he's out of office."

Keat added that a mitigating factor was oil production outside of the Gulf was slowly growing as the world adjusted.

"The oil system will slowly come into balance."

"New Zealand, sadly, doesn't have an oil refinery anymore. So we're kind of at the mercy of the international markets."

World.title: Eden Park train delays: 'We need to make sure that it's fixed'
World.content:
Auckland Transport has done a rapid review after train delays left hundreds of fans waiting to get home from Saturday's All Blacks game at Eden Park.

The chief executive of Eden Park is calling for rail platform upgrades and a pedestrian footbridge across Sandringham Road to prevent delays for fans.

Auckland Transport said about 15,000 people used rail to get to and from the game, but a delay to a level crossing closure stopped trains on the east-west line, leaving hundreds of people waiting at Kingsland Station.

Audio player for " Fans face major train delays after Eden Park All Blacks game " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/regions/1862487%2Feden-park-train-delays-we-need-to-make-sure-that-it-s-fixed

Fans face major train delays after Eden Park All Blacks game Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Auckland deputy mayor Desley Simpson told Checkpoint it was clear there was a meeting needed between the council, Auckland Transport and Eden Park to prevent delays from happening at future events.

"There are a couple of things that I think we can do that would make life easier... one thing was people didn't know what platform to be on."

Saturday saw trains on one platform going towards Otahuhu, and the other going to the city centre, unlike the Warriors game three weeks earlier with all trains headed in the same direction, Simpson said.

The level crossing at Morningside was also supposed to be blocked off so trains could back up and be ready to keep coming, but that crossing was not shut as intended.

Simpson said it did not matter whose responsibility it was to shut the crossing, but ultimately something had to be done to make sure the same disruptions did not happen again.

"I think collectively, all parties - it's Eden Park, Auckland Transport and council - we need to make sure that it's fixed. I'm not here to sort of put blame in one direction or the other."

While the delays were "unfortunate", Simpson said the plan to get it right had been there, it was just the execution that had fallen short.

She said they had expected people to be excited about using the trains with the new addition of the CRL, but with so many people trying to hop on board things didn't go as planned.

"I don't think as many people actually used the events buses as normally happens.

"There was a bit of a risk profile around that which wasn't executed properly, and a few other things like some signage and some better directions so people knew what platform they needed to be on."

Eden Park chief executive Nick Sautner told Morning Report the connectivity between Eden Park and the rail network had not improved in a decade, despite investment in the City Rail Link.

"We've invested in a $6 billion CRL but the adjacent infrastructure, whether it be the level crossings or platform upgrade and a footbridge into Kingsland, needs urgent attention."

Sautner said the Morningside level crossing should be moved to either above or below ground to reduce future disruption.

Simpson said discussions were being had around updating the crossing, but there were pros and cons.

"I think when it comes to events [and] closing the level crossings so the trains can back up, I think that's something that definitely needs to be executed correctly."

While she said a footbridge was an option, the money had to come from somewhere, and it would not happen overnight.

"We have the Black Caps coming at the end of the month, we've got Robbie Williams here in November, we've got Guns N' Roses here in December, and we need to be prepared for those three events so people can access Eden Park safely by bus, event buses and by train.

World.title: Butters suggests changes to AFL player movement 'wouldn't be a bad thing'
World.content:
Zak Butters says he contemplated going public with his planned move home to Victoria while playing out his final season at Port Adelaide.

The Western Bulldogs unveiled their star recruit at Whitten Oval today following his blockbuster move as a free agent on a nine-year deal worth $2 million a season.

With a year left on his contract at the Power, Butters knew he was leaving Alberton following open conversations with the club at the end of last season.

He discussed going public with his plans with manager Peter Lenton.

"I definitely contemplated and thought about that," the midfielder said.

"But I think the AFL landscape isn't probably quite ready for it."

NRL players can sign deals with rival clubs once they enter the final year of their contract or earlier if given permission.

Butters unveiled by Bulldogs after 'megadeal' Zak Butters is finally unveiled as a Western Bulldogs player as Port Adelaide receives four first-round picks in a five-team mega trade ticked off by the league.

Deals are often announced during the season.

The AFL system is more restrictive, with listed players coming off contract only able to officially move in the off-season through trade, free agency, drafts and the supplemental selection period.

"The way I play football and the way I train, I feel like I'd be able to show up and front up and do it," Butters said.

"But definitely, I feel like in the future, I couldn't see why it wouldn't be a bad thing."

Butters, a three-time All Australian, was strongly courted by the Bulldogs, Geelong, Collingwood and Richmond throughout the year.

Geelong was viewed as the frontrunner for his signature, but Butters denied he or his management ever indicated to the Cats they were his first preference.

The ball magnet insisted he never completely made up his mind until returning home to his family property at Darley, west of Melbourne, after the Power's season had ended.

"I guess I probably took my time to do that," Butters said.

"It's a pretty long contract and it's probably the rest of my career so I wanted to make sure I get it right.

"I probably leaned towards different clubs at different stages but, ultimately, I got to where I wanted to get to."

Zak Butters (right) pictured with Bulldogs supporter Hunter Zerafa. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

The Bulldogs pulled heavily on Butters's heartstrings in their pitch, drawing on his boyhood fandom for the club.

A handwritten letter from 11-year-old Hunter Zerafa, accompanied by a 20-cent coin taped inside, begging Butters to pick the Bulldogs revived childhood memories.

"I thought back to when I was younger and loving Bulldogs players and looking up to them and coming down to open trainings," Butters said.

"I used to have birthday parties at Whitten Oval when I was a kid.

"I've still got the letter at home, and the 20 cents is still in there. I might have to invest it."

AAP

World.title: Izzi Batt-Doyle smashes Australian marathon record with run in Chicago
World.content:
Adelaide's Izzi Batt-Doyle is Australia's new marathon queen after breaking the national record with a stunning run at the year's penultimate major, the Chicago Marathon.

Batt-Doyle ran a time of 2:20:38 to take 46 seconds off the mark set by fellow South Australian Jess Stenson in Valencia in December.

It also lowered the 31-year-old's own personal best by two minutes and 21 seconds.

"I'm very, very happy. I feel a sense of relief, because it's something I really felt I could achieve and it's been on my mind the past couple of years," Batt-Doyle said.

"I'm really proud I could achieve it today and I'm so happy."

Assefa's Achilles rupture Tigst Assefa ran the final two kilometres of the Berlin Marathon with a badly damaged Achilles tendon, which required immediate surgery to repair. She still ran the third-fastest women's marathon in history.

Batt-Doyle was sixth overall in the women's race, which was won by defending champion Hawi Feysa of Ethiopia in 2:13:33.

"The field here is so great, but smaller on the professional side," Batt-Doyle said.

"You don't have masses of people in groups."

Batt-Doyle was paced by her fiancé Riley Cocks.

"[We were] isolated the whole race," she said.

"The gun went off and second kilometre it was just the two of us, because we were running between groups.

"I spent most of the race trusting our plan and the pacing strategy we had hoped to run the first half in, and hope that I would feel strong in the second half."

Batt-Doyle's race was a model of control, with her splits barely moving. Every 5km block landed between 16:36 and 16:47, holding her at about 3:19 to 3:21 per kilometre from the opening kilometres to the final stretch.

Eliud Kipchoge wins Melbourne Marathon Marathon legend Eliud Kipchoge has time to slow down and wave at the crowds at the MCG and still break the race record at the Melbourne Marathon.

She went through halfway in 1:10:29 and then ran the second half in about 1:10:09, giving her a 20-second negative split.

"We went through halfway in under the time needed to run 2:21, but I wasn't sure because I felt like I was slowing in the second half as it was warmer, and just the general fatigue of the marathon," Batt-Doyle said.

"It was quite warm and we knew going into this week that it was going to be a bit warmer than ideal marathon conditions, but we did what we could do to prepare for that.

"That's hydrating a lot beforehand, and every opportunity that there were water cups I was splashing three or four water cups to keep cool."

But Batt-Doyle didn't fade in the conditions, with her quickest 5km split of 16:36 coming between 35km and 40km. She covered the last 2.2km at about 3:14 per kilometre, when she started to sense the record was hers.

"There is a small hill about 400 to go, and then you turn into the last 150 metres, and I saw the clock and that's when I really started celebrating," she said.

"It was quite emotional. You can think you can do it and hope you can do it, and be on pace to do it, but there is so much that can happen in the last 5 kilometres, or last 1 kilometre or even the last 400 metres.

" People can cramp and have all sorts of things happen. I feel you can't really celebrate or have that sense of finish line relief until you actually get there. "

Batt-Doyle said she was proud to join the list of previous Australian record-holders that included Stenson, Sinead Diver and Benita Willis.

"I think it's really validating for the hard work I've put in and it feels really special to be part of history, because there have been some fantastic runners before me, and fantastic runners to come," she said.

"I really feel honoured, that sums it up. To be in that class of athletes. I'm really proud of that."

Kenya's Amos Kipruto won the men's race in 2:01:09.

World.title: Roos and Swans in Blakey standoff as Dons explore moves for veteran duo
World.content:
North Melbourne is no closer to adding Nick Blakey after conversations with Sydney stalled following a failed opening bid.

A flurry of activity on Friday raised hopes of an exciting second week of the trade period, but Monday proved to be anything but, with just one deal completed.

Gold Coast acquired Aidan Schubert and Sam Butler from Hawthorn as the two clubs exchanged future draft selections in the deal.

After Blakey nominated North as his club of choice on Friday, the Kangaroos had an opening trade offer of pick six in this year's draft and an exchange of later selections knocked back.

Aidan Schubert (pictured) was traded to Gold Coast along with Sam Butler for an exchange of future picks with Hawthorn. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

There was little movement in negotiations on Monday with North Melbourne involved in multiple trade deadlocks as Wednesday's deadline approaches.

Aside from the Blakey deal, the Kangaroos are also trying to patch together a trade for Adelaide's Nick Murray, while figuring out what to accept for Zane Duursma and Josh Goater, who are both seeking exits.

Elsewhere, Essendon has been linked with moves for experienced duo Keidean Coleman and Gryan Miers.

Miers's manager, Liam Pickering, revealed that he had been contacted by Essendon list boss Matt Rosa regarding a move for Miers on Friday, and said the ball was in Essendon's court as to whether they presented a deal to the 27-year-old.

Essendon remains an outside chance of adding Geelong forward Gryan Miers (pictured) by Wednesday's trade deadline. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

Miers has two years left to run on his deal with Geelong, but has seemingly been deemed surplus to requirements. He is keen to remain at Geelong, according to Pickering.

Essendon has also engaged with Brisbane defender Keidean Coleman on a potential move to The Hangar, with conversations expected to progress in the coming days on what a trade might look like.

The Bombers have held long-standing interest in Coleman after bidding on the Lions Academy product in the 2019 draft, a bid which was matched by the Lions.
