Tech.title: How the 2026 Super El Niño and Climate Change Are Related
Tech.content:
The tropical Pacific has seen heat build for months as a “super” El Niño takes shape.

A climate phenomenon that forms every few years, this year’s iteration of El Niño has been on a tear of daily records and is forecast to reach unprecedented strength this winter. While it’s characterized by hotter-than-normal waters in the eastern tropical Pacific, El Niño is a global problem.

It’s fair to wonder how another global problem is interacting with El Niño: climate change, driven by burning fossil fuels. While a hotter climate begetting a hotter El Niño might seem like a done deal, “I have more questions than I have reactions” to what’s happening, says Christopher Callahan, a climate researcher at Indiana University. In other words, the relationship is still an area of active research—and this year’s event could provide vital insights.

El Niño’s added ocean heat affects the atmosphere, causing weather patterns around the world to shift. Consider it kind of like a domino run, where one tile starts a chain reaction. Such a major slug of heat in the Pacific will act more like a shove then a light flick on the atmosphere, and the resulting shifts in weather are expected to be generationally intense.

The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is forecasting 100 percent odds of an extremely strong El Niño through December and above 80 percent odds it stays that way through February. Data shows this El Niño has already set multiple all-time daily heat records including a recent peak of 3.4 degrees Celsius.

NOAA issues its El Niño forecast as a three-month rolling average, and the agency predicts heat could peak at 2.7 degrees Celsius above normal for the period from October to December. (It’s not out of the question that heat could surpass 3 degrees Celsius, though.) If the forecast holds true, it would smash the previous record of 2.4 degrees Celsius, which was set during the 1982-1983 event.

How Is Climate Change Impacting El Niño?

There is a growing body of evidence that climate change is likely playing at least some role in influencing El Niño. The magnitude and frequency of the phenomenon has increased over the past 60 years, says Francisco Estrada, coordinator of the Climate Change Research Program at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, and so has the variability and how the effects are distributed around the world. He says there shouldn’t be a debate framed as a choice between a “natural El Niño” and an “El Niño caused by climate change” but rather as an interaction between the two processes.

“You can’t separate El Niño from global warming—they’re inextricably linked,” he explains.

Modeling also indicates that El Niño is likely to strengthen as the planet warms, though Callahan notes that many models struggle to accurately represent long-term temperature trends in the eastern tropical Pacific. That can give researchers some pause, but there’s also other evidence that climate change is juicing El Niño.

Tech.title: California’s Tallest and Most Iconic Trees Are Getting Heatstroke
Tech.content:
This story originally appeared on Vox and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A grove of coast redwood trees is a forest of forests. Individual trees can live for thousands of years, and as they grow, their canopies develop mats of soils and ferns, creating something like a second forest floor hundreds of feet above the ground.

These elevated ecosystems are home to creatures like the wandering salamander, which can spend its entire life cycle on top of a single tree, and the marbled murrelet, a seabird whose nesting habits were a mystery until one day in 1974, when a tree-trimmer stumbled upon a nest 150 feet above the ground. Sometimes a stray seed—a sitka spruce or oak or even another redwood—finds its way up a massive redwood and grows into another tree entirely, nestled among the branches of a giant.

For millennia, redwoods have been the anchors of this incredibly stable ecosystem; they can even survive wildfires that devastate other tree species. They’ve also been the source of plenty of human inspiration and drive millions of dollars to California’s tourist economy. But like other living things, they aren’t immune to warming temperatures, and it turns out these trees have a particular weak spot.

A new study from researchers at the University of California, Davis, using measurements taken twice a month for two years, found that coast redwood leaves essentially dial down their photosynthesis during periods of extreme heat. This means trees are slowing their “breathing” and “eating” because they can’t cool down fast enough when temperatures rise. It’s a problem that’s only going to get worse as climate change continues to drive global temperatures up, and it raises urgent questions about the future of these iconic trees and the layers of life that live on and around their shadow-dappled lengths.

Tech.title: AI Is Getting Really Good at Messing With Cybercriminals
Tech.content:
Welcome to Kernel Panic!, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Even as AI supercharges digital scamming and cybercrime, it’s also being recruited in the fight to protect potential victims. Governments around the world have consistently struggled to address the global crisis of online crime, grappling with the limitations of attempting to crack down on criminals beyond their borders. This has inspired alternative efforts, like using automation to attempt to go after scammers en masse—perhaps by spamming the spammers to squander their resources. Now, AI platforms are turning these types of experiments into real tools in the fight against cybercrime.

For the last two years, the Australian company Apate, named after the Greek goddess of deception, has been building a system that diverts phone scammers onto calls with AI bots that are trained to keep conversations going as long as possible without, of course, ever actually falling for the scam. The goal is to give scammers enough hope that they stay on the phone, while also collecting intelligence about the scams they’re running.

“What we really like to think is that we’re building the perfect victims for scammers,” Dali Kaafar, the founder and CEO of Apate, tells us. “A minute that a scammer is talking to a bot or an agent is a minute where you’re probably saving hundreds, if not thousands of possible people being reached out to by that exact same scammer,” he says, referencing the ability for scammers to use automated dialing tools.

Kaafar says Apate’s platform, which is used by banks and supported by telecom companies, has around 350,000 bots. They not only pick up calls, but also infiltrate scam chat groups online and respond to text messages with similar goals of frustrating scammers while collecting intelligence from them. He says the company has collected more than 250,000 pieces of information about fraudsters in real-time, from scam URLs to money mule accounts and bank details.

The bots have different personalities, language skills, and profiles, Kaafar says, so scammers hopefully don’t detect that they’re conversing with an AI. Like real people, “sometimes [the bots] do have WhatsApp, sometimes they don’t. Sometimes they pick up the phone, sometimes they just actually hang up on the scammer saying, ‘I'll come back to you later,’” he says.

Tech.title: Silent Hill Townfall Is Real for Me: I’ve Been to the Actual St. Amelia
Tech.content:
I’ve just finished playing Silent Hill: Townfall, and it’s a masterclass on what a modern horror game can be. At least, it is for me. From its perfectly observed setting in Scotland to an all-too-real sense of a community that’s collapsed in the face of a disaster, this game grabbed me on a deeply personal level and pulled me in as no other Silent Hill game has done before.

Set in the fictional Scottish harbor town of St Amelia in 1996, Silent Hill: Townfall follows the journey of Simon Ordell, who, after pulling himself out of the sea at the start of the game, proceeds to unravel the mystery of what’s happened in the town, what role he played and crucially how he can put things right.

Simon washes up in St Amelia with no idea what’s going on. Konami

From the shambling monsters with planks morphing out of their heads to the impenetrable fog obscuring most of your way forward, Townfall is in many ways classic Silent Hill despite being something of a smaller-scoped spinoff, much like last year’s Silent Hill f. Like its predecessors, gameplay relies on puzzle-solving, exploration and using a mixture of stealth and combat (using limited resources) to either avoid or take down enemies.

More from CNET

So, par for the course for Silent Hill then? In many ways, yes; there’s certainly enough hallmarks of the franchise to keep regulars happy and, much like I found in 2017’s Resident Evil 7, a shift from an over-the-shoulder to a first-person perspective only helps to immerse you more in the game.

Simon’s journey is largely one of discovery. With no memories of what’s going on or why he’s in this deserted village, the game instead drip-feeds you nuggets of information — often simply through emails on computers, newspaper clippings or other pieces of environmental storytelling, many of which are easy to miss. But by slowing down and taking the time to explore the game world and pick up clues, you start to feel connected with Simon as he constructs his story.

Simon has no idea what’s going on and, for most of the game, nor will you. Konami

It’s not a unique take on Silent Hill by any means, and I don’t expect Townfall to necessarily pull in a fresh audience that’s never played a title before. But it’s got more than enough meat on its bones to keep existing fans happy and to tempt back those of you who’ve written the series off in recent years.

But there’s much more than a fresh perspective that pulled me into Townfall.

The setting of St Amelia is based on a real seaside town, called St Monan’s — a town that’s only about an hour’s drive from my home in Edinburgh and somewhere I have visited many times. While the layout isn’t a direct replication, there are numerous elements I immediately recognized from the real-life town. Considering the game was developed by the Glasgow-based developer Screen Burn Games, this fidelity to a Scottish setting is unsurprising but welcome.

Not a screenshot from the game, but from a video I shot when I visited the real St Amelia at night. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The architecture, the scattered fishing nets and lobster pots along the harbor front, the bunting strewn around the streets — all present and accurate to real-life seaside Scotland. I recognize elements of nearby North Berwick too, and there’s even a reference to the “award-winning Amelia Fish Bar” which I can only assume is a direct nod to the actually award-winning Anstruther Fish Bar, which you’ll find about a 10-minute drive from St Monans.

Even the more modern details reminiscent of towns redeveloped in the 1960s are perfectly observed, down to the phones, the office equipment and the Microsoft Word Art used on community noticeboard posters — and will be immediately recognizable to anyone, like me, who grew up in Britain in the 90s. When I visited St Monans earlier in the year to photograph the town, I focused my attention on a 1980s phone box, which struck me at the time as being “very Silent Hill”. Unsurprisingly, I found that identical boxes featured heavily in the game world.

This 1980s phonebox, seen here in real-life St Monans, features heavily in the game. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The result of all this is that St. Amelia feels like a place I’ve already been to, wandered around and actively enjoyed as I ate fish and chips on the harbor wall with family and friends. I felt a deep sense of familiarity walking around in the game, which made it all the more jarring to see the beautiful, tranquil place I knew transformed into a landscape of horror and terror.

It was an amazing — albeit disturbing — sensation to feel so personally connected with an in-game setting, but it’s not one that everyone will have. I played through most of last year’s Silent Hill f and while I broadly enjoyed the game, its admittedly interesting 1960s rural Japan setting didn’t immerse me in the same way because I’ve never been, so I lack any frame of reference. Ditto for the Silent Hill 2 remake set in the US state of Maine. It’s not that I can’t enjoy any media that I don’t have a personal connection with (I’ve never been to Connecticut but it doesn’t stop me enjoying Gilmore Girls), but having a game based essentially in your own backyard is a great way to feel a much deeper sense of immersion in what’s going on.

But there’s another connection that many more of us can appreciate.

You’ll be using a portable TV — a classic bit of 90s tech — to keep out of the way of enemies. Konami

The COVID factor

The game is set in the 1990s, so COVID-19 isn’t something it references in any way. But something’s happened here. Something that has brought a town to its knees and I’m damn sure that the game’s developer, Screen Burn, kept its memories of the pandemic firmly in mind when it was building its game world.

Shops and pharmacies lay empty, shelves are stripped of all essentials. Emergency aid stations have been set up, while flyers and posters around the village describe overstretched medical staff and a lack of supplies, advising to the population to stay at home. Sound familiar?

Walking around the empty, silent town, I was struck by how similar the game world felt to my own experiences of the COVID-19 pandemic, especially in the early days. I didn’t know how widespread things were, or if we were safe at all. Silent Hill: Townfall perfectly captures that sense of foreboding and taps into our lingering memories of those difficult days.

Messages like this are common in the game and are very reminiscent of similar signs from the Covid days. Konami

I vividly remember walking down Edinburgh’s famous Royal Mile on a Saturday in March 2020. There happened to be an extremely Silent Hill-like fog draped over the city and the usually bustling street was almost empty, apart from me. It was deeply unsettling to see, and I can still remember that real sense of unease as I walked down the cobblestones, each step echoing out far louder than usual.

At the time, I even texted my brother saying that it feels like “something from Silent Hill” — and having played Townfall, I think I was spot on. Walking around Townfall’s mist-shrouded St Amelia, seeing the empty streets, the closed businesses and the solitary figures in the distance felt like reliving my own memories.

In the daytime, St Monans is an idyllic place to visit Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Sure, most people playing the game probably haven’t been to St Monans in real life, so you may not have that same sense of familiarity. Maybe you’ve not even been to Scotland, or the UK, or even left your hometown. So much of the game’s effect on me may well be lost on you. But for me, that’s always the joy of playing some games or watching certain movies — settings, storylines or characters will resonate with us differently depending on our own backgrounds and experiences.

For me, Silent Hill: Townfall hit hard, not just because of its Scottish setting but because of its ability to conjure up real memories from a dark time that we all lived through. That one-two punch meant I connected with this game on a much deeper level than I anticipated and resulted in my enjoying Townfall more than any other Silent Hill game I’ve played. It’s rare to have horror set in your own backyard — especially when it directly evokes memories of your own home being warped by haunting calamity.

Tech.title: Gas Stoves Create Indoor Air Pollution Risk in Commercial Kitchens, Study Finds
Tech.content:
Following a July study that found switching from a household gas stove to an electric one can improve asthma symptoms, a new peer-reviewed study published on Tuesday concluded that workers in restaurant kitchens using gas and propane appliances are exposed to air pollution and heat levels that exceed health guidelines.

The National Restaurant Association reports that over 15.7 million Americans work in the food service industry. According to a statement, about five million of them spend all their working hours in the kitchen.

Published in the scientific journal Environmental Research Letters and in collaboration with chef Christopher Galarza, the study was conducted by researchers from the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability, the New York University Grossman School of Medicine and PSE Healthy Energy, an independent scientific research institute specializing in bringing science to energy policy.

More from CNET

According to the statement, this is the first US study to compare air quality and heat levels in restaurant kitchens that use gas appliances with those that use all-electric appliances under real-world working conditions. The study is part of PSE Healthy Energy’s Methane and Health Initiative, which uncovers air quality and health risks associated with methane sources to protect public health and the climate.

Researchers measured air temperature and air pollutants produced by gas stoves: methane, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and benzene. Measurements were taken in five employee work areas, both during service and overnight, in 21 gas kitchens, three propane kitchens and three all-electric kitchens in California, New York and Pennsylvania.

“Everyone likely has a favorite restaurant or fast food chain, but most people probably haven’t thought about the equipment being used and how that affects what the staff is experiencing in the kitchen area,” Drew Michanowicz, principal scientist at PSE Healthy Energy, told CNET in an email.

Air pollution findings

When kitchens are not properly ventilated, pollutants can build up and cause harmful health effects, though this depends on individual sensitivity and exposure level.

During the study, it was discovered that in most of the gas and propane kitchens included, at least one health guideline for pollutant exposure was exceeded during cooking hours.

About 70% of gas kitchens in the study surpassed the US Environmental Protection Agency’s 1-hour outdoor air standard for nitrogen dioxide. The outdoor standard was used because there is no comparable indoor standard in the US.

In kitchens with gas or propane appliances, about 170 cumulative hours (about four full work weeks) were recorded in which nitrogen dioxide concentrations exceeded the World Health Organization’s hour-averaged exposure recommendation. This recommendation is roughly equal to the EPA’s outdoor standard, and both apply to the general population.

One kitchen’s 15-minute average nitrogen dioxide level exceeded the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health’s recommended short-term workplace exposure limit.

Nitrogen dioxide can cause reduced lung function, increased asthma attacks, increased airway inflammation, and worsened cough and wheezing. This gaseous air pollutant has even been tied to causing asthma in children.

The study also found that carbon monoxide and benzene concentrations exceeded California’s 1-hour exposure guidelines in three and five gas kitchens, respectively. Carbon monoxide poisoning symptoms can range from a headache and dizziness to passing out and death. Benzene, on the other hand, is a carcinogen that has been linked to a higher risk of leukemia and other blood cell cancers.

By comparison, no all-electric kitchen exceeded pollution-exposure health guidelines during cooking hours.

“This study emphasizes that the concentrations of pollutants in commercial kitchens with gas-fired appliances can reach levels even higher than what we’ve previously observed in homes with gas stoves,” Yannai Kashtan, an air quality scientist at PSE Healthy Energy, told CNET in an email.

Those actually working in the kitchen aren’t the only ones who could be affected. Rhenizara S/Getty Images

Overnight levels matter too

Even outside cooking hours, exposure remains a concern, according to new evidence from the study.

When gas appliance pilot lights remain lit, and ventilation is turned off, cleaning crews and staff arriving early risk exposure to pollutants. About 71% of the gas kitchens with overnight monitoring recorded higher levels of nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, methane and benzene overnight than during service hours.

Aside from contributing to climate change, high concentrations of methane can displace oxygen in the air, causing fatigue, rapid breathing, vomiting, collapse, convulsions, organ damage and death.

When you consider that commercial gas appliances are also used in hospitals, schools and other buildings, the health concerns extend beyond restaurant kitchens.

None of the all-electric kitchens exceeded pollutant guidelines overnight.

Temperature findings

When it came to heat health guidelines, about 68% of gas kitchens with temperature data exceeded 90 degrees Fahrenheit, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s proposed high-heat threshold.

Even when temperatures outside were below 75 degrees Fahrenheit, 10 of 13 gas kitchens exceeded 90 degrees Fahrenheit, meaning that high heat in commercial kitchens isn’t directly tied to the weather.

When a temperature monitor was attached to a chef’s shoulder during a 5-hour cooking session, the average temperature was 92 degrees Fahrenheit, with a maximum of 106 degrees Fahrenheit.

Guidelines differ between the general population and the workplace, which could put workers’ health at risk. andresr/Getty Images

A guideline gap in kitchen worker protection

The study compared its findings with both EPA and WHO guidelines for the general population, which prioritize health protection, and with NIOSH and OSHA guidelines, which are occupational. Researchers found fewer instances of kitchens exceeding workplace thresholds.

“Compared to benchmarks for the general population, occupational thresholds are higher because they serve a different purpose by also accounting for industry cost and technical feasibility,” Kashtan said. “If work environments are exceeding health-based thresholds but are compliant with the occupational limits that govern enforcement, this points to a gap in health protection for commercial kitchen workers.”

The study’s limitations

Due to the scarcity of all-electric commercial kitchens, only three were used in this study. However, the researchers stated in the study that their findings remain consistent with prior research on nitrogen dioxide concentrations from gas versus electric appliances.

As about 80% of end-use energy in US commercial cooking is gas, the small number of all-electric kitchens used in the study also reflects the current restaurant industry.

Only restaurant kitchens in three states were used, so this may not reflect the broader US. Participation was voluntary and partly facilitated through professional partnerships, so selection bias may have been introduced, especially given that kitchens willing to participate likely had better working conditions.

While sampling locations were chosen to account for different worker roles in the kitchen, pollutant measurements may differ from actual exposure due to a worker’s movement, health, posture and proximity to emission sources. These locations also weren’t monitored continuously; instead, they were sampled for 5 to 12 minutes per cycle.

Particulate matter and WBGT, which measures occupational heat stress, were not measured.

Ensure that your range hood is maintained and turned on when cooking. SBenitez/Getty Images

Restaurant recommendations

Based on this study, Michanowicz has three recommendations for worker protections in commercial kitchens that use gas appliances.

First, it’s important to ensure that ventilation systems are properly maintained, as these are usually the first line of defense against pollution and excess heat. However, even with these systems in place, restaurant workers who work directly over a cooking surface can still be exposed to pollution and heat before they reach the ventilation system.

While converting a commercial kitchen from gas to electric can be challenging and costly, focusing on electrifying gas ranges and fryers first can yield the greatest benefits for indoor air quality.

“There are also additional benefits that chefs we worked with have mentioned, such as higher worker productivity due to more comfortable kitchen temperatures, reduced cleaning times and reduced burn and explosion risks,” Michanowicz said.

Lastly, for workers in commercial kitchens during off-hours, including cleaning crews, when pilot lights are still on, ventilation systems should be turned on. This applies to workers who arrive early in the morning, as pollution will have built up overnight.

Gas stove household advice

The recommendations for those with gas stoves at home aren’t dissimilar.

“The best way to reduce gas combustion pollution is to eliminate the source – the gas flame – and to get an electric radiant or induction stove,” said Kashtan.

However, if that’s not possible due to cost or because one is a renter, cooking can still be partially electrified with air fryers, electric kettles, rice cookers and portable induction hobs.

And when you do use your gas stove, always make sure your range hood is on, and consider putting an air purifier in your kitchen.

Tech.title: The Beautiful Blue Is My Favorite Thing About Vivo’s Foldable X Fold 6
Tech.content:
Having spent a few days with Vivo’s new foldable X Fold 6, I can say there’s plenty I like about it, from its solid camera performance to its extremely good battery life. But because I’m shallow and like pretty things, I have to admit that its vibrant blue design with frosted glass back is my favorite thing about this phone.

It’s by no means the first foldable I’ve liked based on looks alone — Oppo’s Find N6 won me over with its punchy orange color and, like the Oppo, Vivo’s foldable is tough to get hold of. It’s not officially sold in either the US or the UK, and while it’s possible to import these phones from resellers in China or the few parts of Europe where it is sold, I don’t recommend doing so as you’ll be left with no customer support should anything go wrong.

I really love that lovely blue tone. It’s delightful. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The X Fold 6 is a typical book-style foldable, akin to the Oppo Find N6 or Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. I wonder how much longer we’ll see this format of foldable now that Apple has launched its iPhone Duo with its stumpy “passport” dimensions. Samsung’s Z Fold 8 has the same proportions — as does Xiaomi’s 18 Fold that I saw at IFA 2026 — and it’s clearly becoming the fashionable way to make a folding phone, thanks to its wider internal dimensions that are better for watching videos than the square-format inner screens on the X Fold 6 and others.

More from CNET

This more “traditional” format still has its merits, and Vivo’s new model is a good example. It feels sturdy, and while it’s not as skinny when closed as Samsung’s Z Fold 8 Ultra or Oppo’s Find N6, it’s still svelte enough to slide into a pocket without much issue. It runs last year’s MediaTek Dimensity 9500 processor, which produced decent scores on our benchmark tests, and gaming and multitasking were absolutely no problem here.

It’s an impressive camera setup for a foldable phone. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The rear cameras are capable of taking some great-looking shots, thanks in part to the 200 megapixel sensor with high quality Zeiss glass in front of it. I don’t love that there are Vivo watermarks on by default (which I had to crop out of these examples — I subsequently turned off watermarks in the settings). But the main, ultrawide and telephoto cameras can take good photos.

This complex harbor scene was handled extremely well by the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The highlights are a little bright here, but I love the authentic color tones. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

When viewed at full screen, this image from the telephoto zoom camera looks pretty decent, with a solid exposure and great colors. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But cropping into 100% shows that there’s a lot of software processing going on, resulting in the fine details looking very… weird. It’s fine for an Instagram post, but little else. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There’s a variety of filmic color presets to play with if you fancy getting a bit creative with your photography. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The camera heavily relies on AI-based image processing in the longer focal lengths, resulting in fine details looking more like watercolor paintings, but that’s par for the course for most phones these days. Overall, though, I think the Vivo does a solid job with its cameras, especially for a foldable phone, which typically have watered-down versions of the camera setups from regular phones. This one feels like less of a compromise.

Where it seems to really shine though is battery life. After an hour of streaming YouTube on its massive inner screen at max brightness, it had dropped from full to… well, it was still full. It hadn’t dropped a single percent and only dropped to 94% after the second hour. That’s up there with the absolute best we’ve tested this year, including the iPhone 18 Pro.

The crease isn’t invisible, but it’s not especially obvious either. A fair effort. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Needless to say, getting through at least a full day of mixed use with the X Fold 6 should be no problem at all, and you probably won’t struggle to get most of the way into the second, as long as you’re careful with what you do.

Need to get some more juice in quickly? No problem, as its 80-watt wired charging means it’ll go from empty to full in around 30 minutes, so long as you have a compatible charger.

The X Fold 6 isn’t breaking any boundaries among foldables — it’s not the slimmest or the most powerful, nor does it have the least visible crease — but it’s a great example of a phone that ticks every box you’d expect from a high-end device. What’s a real shame is that almost none of you reading this will be able to buy it. Sad face.

Tech.title: Elon Musk Eyes ‘Complete Phone Coverage in America’ as SpaceX Clears Hurdle
Tech.content:
Elon Musk’s reach spans multiple global industries, placing the billionaire (sometimes trillionaire, depending on the stock market) at the center of the electric-vehicle industry, space exploration, artificial intelligence and national politics. He’s already involved in telecommunications through his company SpaceX and its global satellite internet service, Starlink, but recent developments may soon expand his influence with satellite-to-cellular coverage.

SpaceX announced on X Thursday that it has agreed to acquire nationwide 800 MHz low-band spectrum to help build Starlink Mobile into a major US cellular carrier. By acquiring these low-band airwaves, SpaceX said it aims to improve signal propagation, allowing satellite coverage to bypass physical obstacles like building walls, dense foliage, and hilly terrain

“This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America,” Musk posted on X.

More from CNET

A SpaceX representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Under the terms of Thursday’s announcement, SpaceX will acquire investment firm Grain Management’s nationwide 800 MHz low-band spectrum portfolio for an estimated $8 billion. The deal gives the satellite operator up to 14 megahertz of paired airwaves, enabling two-way data transmission between satellites and mobile devices. The acquisition remains subject to approval by the Federal Communications Commission, which has not yet set a timeline for a decision.

Acquiring the low-band spectrum is crucial for Starlink Mobile’s cellular ambitions. Unlike the high-frequency beams used currently, these low-band airwaves possess the physical properties required to pierce concrete walls, dense foliage and urban infrastructure, effectively solving the indoor dead zone problem that has long limited satellite-to-phone connectivity.

Also this week, the FCC gave SpaceX the go-ahead to launch 15,000 satellites, which the company said can deliver more than 100 times the bandwidth of its current satellites. These satellites are direct to device, meaning that they can transmit phone calls, texts and other data straight from space to devices on the ground. SpaceX said the new satellites will bring “high-speed service directly to unmodified devices anywhere in the world.”

What does it mean for consumers?

For people looking for an alternative to the big three cellphone carriers AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon Wireless, Starlink Mobile could eventually be an option.

If and when the FCC approves the deal with Grain Management, Starlink Mobile will combine its newly acquired low-band spectrum with a massive, freshly approved fleet of 15,000 next-generation satellites. This hybrid network will use a mix of satellite beams and ground infrastructure to penetrate walls and eliminate indoor dead zones across the US while leveraging its high-bandwidth frequencies to deliver high-speed data directly to ordinary mobile devices. SpaceX plans to accelerate deployment of the new system next year.

But according to analyst Tim Farrar, an industry expert with research firm Telecom, Media and Finance Associates, simply acquiring low-spectrum bandwidth in this week’s deal won’t be enough to compete strongly against AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon Wireless, which uses thousands of cellphone towers.

“It’s still a very limited amount of spectrum, and to get reliable building penetration in urban areas, SpaceX would have to deploy towers on the ground,” Farrar told CNBC.

Last month, T-Mobile’s chief financial officer, Peter Osvaldik, dismissed the idea that Starlink’s satellite-to-cell service could adequately compete with the traditional wireless coverage offered by the major carriers. “It’s not a competitive threat,” Osvaldik said at the Global TMT Conference.

“By the time the signal has gotten to your phone, you have no signal strength left,” he added. “You can have a million satellites up there with all the spectrum in the world, you can’t break the fundamental laws of physics.”

Tech.title: File a Claim Now in the $7.85M PlayStation Antitrust Settlement Before the Deadline
Tech.content:
Sony is paying out $7.85 million to settle allegations that it illegally locked PlayStation owners out of buying digital games anywhere other than its own store. The lawsuit alleged Sony violated antitrust law by discontinuing game-specific vouchers that allowed digital game purchases through third-party retailers, effectively eliminating competition and leaving the PlayStation Store as the only viable option.

Compensation is coming as PSN wallet credit rather than cash, with distribution expected after a final approval hearing next week. US PlayStation customers who bought digital games during the eligible period can file a claim now.

The class-action lawsuit Caccuri v. Sony Interactive Entertainment alleged that Sony’s actions caused “consumers to pay more for certain digital games than they otherwise would have paid on the PlayStation Store.” It alleges that this action violates antitrust laws by forcing PlayStation customers to buy from a single storefront at an inflated price.

More from CNET

Put simply, the lawsuit claims that Sony limited the sale of digital games on other marketplaces, funneling customers into its own PlayStation Store. Some of these games include PlayStation exclusives such as The Last of Us, as well as third-party games like the Mass Effect Trilogy and Resident Evil 4.

The lawsuit was initially settled in 2024, but the settlement was rejected twice during the approval process — most recently in July 2025, when the presiding judge said the proposed plan “[did] not provide an estimated recovery or a range of potential recovery for class members.” The approval process was reinitiated in April.

Sony denied any wrongdoing or that settlement class members were damaged by its actions, and the court has not decided if the company violated any laws. Despite this, the court has preliminarily approved the $7.85 million settlement payment, subject to the court’s final approval hearing.

The settlement website is live now. The hearing is scheduled for Oct. 15, and it’s meant to confirm the settlement amount, allocate up to 25% of the funds for attorneys’ fees and create a plan to distribute the remainder to eligible class members.

If you fit all of the criteria to be part of the Sony PlayStation game-voucher settlement, you’re automatically a class member in this lawsuit and will be able to collect a portion of the settlement money — added directly to your PlayStation Network account wallet — sometime after the final approval hearing.

Gamers who have deactivated their PlayStation Network accounts can apply for the settlement payment by sending qualifying purchase information to the email address info@PSNDigitalGamesSettlement.com. Customers with deactivated accounts will receive cash payments instead of PSN account accreditation.

The option to opt out of the settlement to retain your right to sue Sony separately in regard to its game-voucher sales practices closed on July 2. A written request to the court opting out of or objecting to the settlement had to be received by then; otherwise, you will remain part of the settlement class.

Who can be part of the Sony PlayStation settlement?

Not every PlayStation owner is automatically eligible. The money is reserved for those who purchased a digital game through the PlayStation Store after Sony ceased selling game-specific vouchers for alternative online storefronts.

In order to join, you must meet the following qualifications:

Be a living individual human being in the US or its territories. Have purchased one of the eligible digital games (PDF) through the PlayStation Store between the period of April 1, 2019, and Dec. 31, 2023.

Affected individuals are automatically part of the settlement class and will receive their compensation through their PlayStation Network account wallet, subject to approval at the final hearing, the date and time of which could change. Any updates will be posted to the settlement website.

How much will the Sony PlayStation settlement pay?

It’s unclear how much each settlement class member will receive, though we know affected parties will automatically receive compensation in the form of PlayStation account funds.

Up to a quarter of the $7.85 million settlement will be used to pay attorneys’ fees, taxes and other administrative costs. The remaining settlement money will be administered equally to every settlement class member. Settlement class members will likely see a couple of dollars added to their PlayStation accounts once the funds are fully allocated.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo’s Unfolding Animation Is Giving Z Fold 8 Owners FOMO, but Not Me
Tech.content:
When I first got my hands on the iPhone Duo, I admittedly dismissed the unfolding animation that would soon become a highlight of online discourse. I was less interested in the smooth transition as content shifted from one screen to another and more focused on details such as the matte inner display and seemingly invisible crease.

But in the weeks since Apple unveiled its first foldable iPhone, which drops Oct. 23, I’ve seen countless examples on social media of people trying to recreate that buzzed-about animation on their Android foldables. While the Play Store offers plenty of launchers for customizing Android phones — including ones that mimic the iPhone’s home screen — this appears to be one iOS design element that users are particularly eager to bring to their devices.

Sometimes, you really can’t predict what people will care about most — or the lengths they’ll go to imitate a feature.

The primary phone people have used to recreate the iPhone Duo’s cascading transition effect is Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, which debuted in July with a passport-size foldable design ahead of Apple’s release. Unlike iOS, Samsung’s One UI interface, which runs on top of Android on Galaxy devices, doesn’t include a folding animation. Instead, content simply transitions from the Z Fold 8’s cover screen to its inner display once the phone is opened about halfway. I never considered this a deficiency until I saw the flood of positive reactions to the iPhone Duo’s fluid transition effect.

To bridge that gap, several creators have posted videos explaining how to use third-party apps and developer tools on GitHub to get a similar effect on the Z Fold 8, with caveats like “the smoothness and quality won’t be the same‘” and “install it [at] your own risk.” (That’s encouraging!) The steps don’t seem particularly complicated, and some options appear to have cropped up in the Play Store as well.

I’ve chosen to forgo installing these Duo-copycat apps on my precious Galaxy Z Fold 8 for two reasons. First, I’m not much of a risk-taker. Second, I’m not interested in imitating an aesthetic element of Apple’s software with a derivative version, especially when the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a standout foldable device in its own right. While the value of the Duo’s sleek animation has since grown on me, I’m not quite desperate enough to retrofit it onto a foldable phone that’s just as functional without that flourish.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 might not have a nifty opening animation by default, but I don’t see that as a deficiency. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Don’t get me wrong: I think Apple’s combination of hardware and software expertise will elevate the iPhone Duo in a way that merits the attention the phone has received, despite being relatively “late” to the foldables game. But I also think it’s more tasteful for consumers to embrace what each phone-maker does best, rather than shoehorning in a competitor’s feature for something as superficial as an animation effect.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is one of my favorite phones I’ve tested this year, earning it a CNET Editors’ Choice Award. Its versatile design is optimized for both vertical and horizontal content: I can stream YouTube videos and movies on the 7.6-inch inner display, then rotate it to seamlessly scroll through social posts. The crease is barely noticeable, and the battery easily lasts all day. The 5.5-inch cover screen never feels cramped, while its sharp corners give the phone a highly polished look. And despite lacking a telephoto lens, the Z Fold 8’s dual rear cameras pull their weight, capturing crisp, vibrant photos.

The iPhone Duo shares many attributes with the Z Fold 8, including a palm-size design, 7.6-inch inner display and dual rear cameras. Those similarities prompted Samsung to post a series of salty tweets after Apple debuted its foldable last month, including one that reads, “Let us know when you’re done reheating our leftovers.”

That said, I am curious how app developers might optimize their platforms for the iPhone Duo in ways we haven’t seen with other foldable phones. While the Android operating system spans a wide range of devices and configurations, iOS developers only have to cater to a single foldable, potentially leading to a more tailored and streamlined experience. We got a glimpse of how Netflix is building its app for the Duo, and it’ll be interesting to see how both Apple and other third-party developers take full advantage of the phone’s 1.4:1 aspect ratio in ways that could make its predecessors seem behind the curve in that regard.

“Borrowing” features from each other is what phone-makers do best. Down the road, it’s possible companies such as Samsung will implement foldable capabilities that Apple rolled out first, and vice versa. Heck, Apple’s delayed entry into this space means it had time to analyze what worked well for its competitors before jumping in with its own rendition. It’s just how the industry works.

So maybe the Galaxy Z Fold 9 — or whatever Samsung decides to call the follow-up to the Z Fold 8 — will have its own nifty opening animation. But until Samsung itself embraces the idea, I’ll stick with using the standout foldable as-is.
